Official material Problems.pdf · p. 8
Statements and solutions: Twenty problems of the official collection that need a moving reference frame. Each card gives the statement (with the PDF page) and a worked solution in the order of the course: reference frames, bases and coordinates; the change of basis and the position vector, deduced from drawings of each plane and each rotation; kinematics with the relative-motion formulas (Notes Eqs. 3.26–3.27); forces and equations of motion with the inertia forces (Notes Eqs. 4.62–4.63); and the answers to every part with unit and limit checks. Problems 7, 25, 27, 33, 34, 36, 37, 40, 41 and 47 have an official key entry, compared in each card; the other results are derived here and checked symbolically.
Problem 07

Skater Towed by a Vehicle: Rotating Frame

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 8
Rotating Frame + Inertia ForcesIn-Class Session 10

A skater $B$ is being towed by a vehicle $A$ on a perfectly smooth horizontal plane, where we define an inertial reference frame $Oxy$. The vehicle is moving along a circumference of radius $a$ and center at $O$ with constant angular velocity $\omega$. The skater is attached to the vehicle by a bar without mass and constant length $l = a$. Initially, the vehicle is located at $(a, 0)$ and the skater is at rest at $(2a, 0)$. Defining a rotating reference frame $Ox_1y_1$ with origin at $O$ and axis $Ox_1$ along $OA$, and calling $\psi$ the angle between the axis $Ox_1$ and the bar $AB$, determine:

  • (a)
    The relative acceleration of the skater with respect to $Ox_1y_1$ as a function of $\psi$ and its time derivatives.
  • (b)
    The centripetal and Coriolis acceleration terms also as a function of $\psi$ and its time derivatives.
  • (c)
    Reduce the evolution of $\psi$ to integrals of the form $\int [\ldots]\,d\psi = \int [\ldots]\,dt$ (consider that $\dot{\psi}^2 = \int 2\dot{\psi}\ddot{\psi}\,dt$).
  • (d)
    Determine the tension on the bar.
  • (e)
    If the rigid bar is substituted by a string which cannot bear compression, determine if/when the string will become loose.
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

A vehicle $A$ moves on the circumference of radius $a$ and centre $O$ with the constant angular velocity $\omega$, on a smooth horizontal plane; a skater $B$ of mass $m$ is joined to it by a massless rigid bar of length $a$. At the start the vehicle is at $(a, 0)$ and the skater at rest at $(2a, 0)$ (Problems.pdf, p. 8). The statement asks, in the rotating frame $Ox_1y_1$ that carries $OA$ on its first axis, for the relative acceleration, the centripetal and Coriolis terms, the reduction of the motion to quadratures, the tension of the bar and whether a string would go slack. The relative kinematics follows Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.1 and Sec. 3.2, and the dynamics in the non-inertial frame Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, the frame $Oxy$ of the statement, with $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$: $\mathbf i_0$ along $Ox$, $\mathbf j_0$ along $Oy$, $\mathbf k_0$ vertical, up (Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.1)
Moving frame$S_1 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_1\}$, the frame $Ox_1y_1$: $\mathbf i_1$ along $OA$, $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$, $\mathbf j_1$ the cross product of $\mathbf k_1$ and $\mathbf i_1$; it turns by the angle $\omega t$ about $\mathbf k_0$
Origin of $S_1$the fixed point $O$ (the generic origin, called $A$ in Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2, is here $O$; the letter $A$ stays for the vehicle, as in the statement)
Bar basis$\mathcal B_2 = \{\mathbf u_{AB}, \mathbf u_\perp, \mathbf k_1\}$: $\mathbf u_{AB}$ from $A$ to $B$, $\mathbf u_\perp$ normal to the bar in the plane, in the sense of growing $\psi$
Coordinate$\psi$, the angle from $\mathbf i_1$ to the bar $AB$, measured at $A$, positive about $\mathbf k_1$ (counterclockwise seen from above)
Constraints$B$ on the horizontal plane; distance $AB$ equal to $a$; in $S_1$ the vehicle is at rest at $(a, 0)$, so $B$ moves on a circle of radius $a$ about $A$, fixed in $S_1$
Degrees of freedom3 minus 2: 1, the angle $\psi(t)$; the angle $\omega t$ of $S_1$ is prescribed
Data$m$ [kg], $a$ [m], $\omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$], constant
Unknowns$\psi(t)$, the bar force $T$ [N] (positive when the bar pulls $B$ towards $A$), the normal reaction of the plane $N$ [N]
Initial state$\psi(0) = 0$ (skater at $(2a, 0)$); skater at rest in $S_0$
Applied forcesweight $-mg\,\mathbf k_1$; the force of the bar, along the bar
Constraint forcenormal reaction of the smooth plane, $N\,\mathbf k_1$
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)of the origin, Euler, centrifugal and Coriolis (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Hypothesesthe bar is massless and hinged at both ends, so the force it exerts on $B$ lies along the bar; the plane is smooth, so its reaction is vertical; $\omega$ constant; the skater is a point particle

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. View from $+\mathbf k_0$ ($\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf k_1$ out of the paper, $\odot$). $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned counter-clockwise by $\omega t$: legs $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$ and $\sin\omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$. $\mathbf j_1$ turns the same angle from $\mathbf j_0$, so its opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ points along $-\mathbf i_0$: hence $\mathbf j_1 = -\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0$.
Basis of the rotating frame: rotation by omega t about k0 Law: elementary rotation about the third axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

View from above, along $\mathbf k_0$, which points out of the paper (⊙) because it is the cross product of $\mathbf i_0$ (to the right) and $\mathbf j_0$ (up): a positive rotation about $\mathbf k_0$ is counterclockwise, the sense in which the vehicle turns. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\omega t$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$. $\mathbf j_1$ is $\mathbf j_0$ turned by the same angle: adjacent leg $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$, opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ along minus $\mathbf i_0$ (the upward vector turned counterclockwise leans to the left: the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(right triangle of $\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \mathbf j_1 &= -\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(right triangle of $\mathbf j_1$: opposite leg on $-\mathbf i_0$)} \\ \mathbf k_1 &= \mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(axis of the rotation)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= 1\cdot\left(\cos\omega t\cos\omega t - \left(-\sin\omega t\right)\sin\omega t\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\omega t + \sin^2\omega t = 1 \quad &\text{(row 1 times row 1)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{12} &= \cos\omega t\sin\omega t - \sin\omega t\cos\omega t = 0 \quad &\text{(row 1 times row 2; row 3 is the unit row of $\mathbf k_0$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\omega t & -\sin\omega t & 0 \cr \sin\omega t & \cos\omega t & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: dimensionless direction cosines: $[1]$; $[\omega t] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}][\mathrm{T}] = [1]$

Meaning: at the start ($t$ zero) the two frames coincide; afterwards $\mathbf i_1$ always points from $O$ to the vehicle.

Figure 2. Plane of $S_1$ ($\mathbf i_1$ along $OA$, $\mathbf k_1$ out of the paper). $\mathbf r_1^B = \overrightarrow{OA} + \overrightarrow{AB}$: in the shaded right triangle $AFB$ the hypotenuse is $|AB| = a$, the leg adjacent to $\psi$ is $a\cos\psi$ along $\mathbf i_1$ and the opposite leg is $a\sin\psi$ along $\mathbf j_1$. The dashed circle is the path of $B$ relative to $S_1$; $\mathbf u_{AB}, \mathbf u_\perp$ in orange.
Position vector of the skater in the rotating frame Law: position vector as a sum of segments; right triangle of the bar Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.2; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 8

In $S_1$ the vehicle is at rest on the axis $Ox_1$ at the distance $a$ from $O$. From $O$ to $B$ we pass through $A$, because the bar fixes the distance from $A$. Let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to the line $Ox_1$: in the right triangle $AFB$ the hypotenuse is the bar, of length $a$; the leg adjacent to $\psi$ is $a\cos\psi$ along $\mathbf i_1$ and the leg opposite to $\psi$ is $a\sin\psi$ along $\mathbf j_1$. $\psi$ is measured from $\mathbf i_1$ counterclockwise, so it is already the standard polar angle about $A$ and needs no shift. For a negative $\psi$ (the case of the motion, part (c)) the opposite leg points along minus $\mathbf j_1$ and the same formula holds.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_0^O &= \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(the origin of $S_1$ is the fixed point $O$)} \\ \mathbf r_0^B &= \mathbf r_0^O + \mathbf r_1^B = \mathbf r_1^B \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.16)} \\ \mathbf r_1^B &= \overrightarrow{OA} + \overrightarrow{AB} \quad &\text{(through the hinge $A$)} \\ \overrightarrow{OA} &= a\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(vehicle at rest in $S_1$)} \\ \overrightarrow{AB} &= a\cos\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + a\sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(adjacent and opposite legs of $AFB$)} \\ \mathbf r_1^B &= a\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\mathbf i_1 + a\sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(sum, grouped by unit vector)} \\ x_1 &= a\left(1 + \cos\psi\right), \quad y_1 = a\sin\psi \quad &\text{(components in $\mathcal B_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_0^B = \mathbf r_1^B = a\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\mathbf i_1 + a\sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[a] = [\mathrm{L}]$; $\psi$ dimensionless

Meaning: $\psi$ zero gives the initial point at twice $a$ on $Ox_1$; $\psi$ equal to minus $\pi$ gives the point $O$ itself.

Figure 3. Rotation by $\psi$ about $\mathbf k_1$ (out of the paper). The triangle of $\mathbf u_\perp$ has its opposite leg along $-\mathbf i_1$: the minus sign of $\mathbf u_\perp = -\sin\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\psi\,\mathbf j_1$.
Bar basis: rotation by psi about k1 Law: elementary rotation about the third axis; change of basis matrix, its checks and its inverse Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20

View from above along $\mathbf k_1$, out of the paper (⊙); $\mathbf i_1$ to the right and $\mathbf j_1$ up. $\mathbf u_{AB}$ is $\mathbf i_1$ turned by $\psi$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\psi$ along $\mathbf i_1$, opposite leg $\sin\psi$ along $\mathbf j_1$. $\mathbf u_\perp$ is $\mathbf j_1$ turned by $\psi$: adjacent leg $\cos\psi$ along $\mathbf j_1$, opposite leg $\sin\psi$ along minus $\mathbf i_1$ (the upward vector turned counterclockwise leans to the left: the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf u_{AB} &= \frac{\overrightarrow{AB}}{a} = \cos\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(right triangle of $\mathbf u_{AB}$)} \\ \mathbf u_\perp &= -\sin\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\psi\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(right triangle of $\mathbf u_\perp$: opposite leg on $-\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \det[{}_1R_2] &= 1\cdot\left(\cos^2\psi + \sin^2\psi\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row)} \\ \left([{}_1R_2][{}_1R_2]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\psi + \sin^2\psi = 1, \quad \left([{}_1R_2][{}_1R_2]^T\right)_{12} = \cos\psi\sin\psi - \sin\psi\cos\psi = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \\ \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\psi\,\mathbf u_{AB} - \sin\psi\,\mathbf u_\perp, \quad \mathbf j_1 = \sin\psi\,\mathbf u_{AB} + \cos\psi\,\mathbf u_\perp \quad &\text{(inverse: the rows of the matrix)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_1R_2] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\psi & -\sin\psi & 0 \cr \sin\psi & \cos\psi & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_1R_2] = 1, \quad [{}_1R_2][{}_1R_2]^T = I}$$

Units: dimensionless: $[1]$

Meaning: the bar force acts along $\mathbf u_{AB}$ only, so projecting on $\mathbf u_\perp$ will give an equation free of the unknown tension.

Kinematics

Motion of the rotating frame and derivatives of its unit vectors Law: angular velocity of a simple rotation; derivative of a unit vector fixed in a rotating basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{($\mathcal B_1$ turns about the fixed $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf k_1$ with the angle $\omega t$)} \\ \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} &= \dot\omega\,\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.9; $\omega$ constant, $\mathbf k_1$ fixed)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf i_1 = \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3; $\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf j_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\omega\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.4; $\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.5)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_0\right) &= -\omega\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \omega\cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(check: chain rule on the components of $\mathbf i_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\omega\,\mathbf i_1}$$

Units: $[\omega] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: seen from $S_0$ the unit vectors of $S_1$ turn with the vehicle; seen from $S_1$ they are constant.

Absolute velocity of the skater: relative and transport terms Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the position vector written in the moving basis; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.2; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.6; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^B &= \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(definition; $\mathbf r_0^B = \mathbf r_1^B$)} \\ &= \dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + x_1\left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 + y_1\left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 \quad &\text{(product rule on each term)} \\ &= \underbrace{\dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y_1\,\mathbf j_1}_{\mathbf v_1^B} + \underbrace{\omega x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \omega y_1\,\mathbf i_1}_{\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^B} \quad &\text{(derivatives of the unit vectors substituted)} \\ \dot x_1 &= \frac{d}{dt}\left[a\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\right] = -a\sin\psi\,\dot\psi \quad &\text{(chain rule: $\tfrac{d}{d\psi}\cos\psi = -\sin\psi$)} \\ \dot y_1 &= \frac{d}{dt}\left(a\sin\psi\right) = a\cos\psi\,\dot\psi \quad &\text{(chain rule: $\tfrac{d}{d\psi}\sin\psi = \cos\psi$)} \\ \mathbf v_1^B &= -a\dot\psi\sin\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + a\dot\psi\cos\psi\,\mathbf j_1 = a\dot\psi\,\mathbf u_\perp \quad &\text{(components; $\mathbf u_\perp$ of the bar basis)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^B &= -a\omega\sin\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + a\omega\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{($x_1$ and $y_1$ substituted)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_0^B = \mathbf v_1^B + \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^B = -a\left(\dot\psi + \omega\right)\sin\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + a\left[\left(\dot\psi + \omega\right)\cos\psi + \omega\right]\mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[a\dot\psi] = [a\omega] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: the relative term comes from differentiating the components, the transport term from differentiating the turning unit vectors; it is the form of Eq. 3.20 with the origin at rest.

Absolute acceleration of the skater: relative, Coriolis and centripetal terms Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the two terms of the velocity; product rule and derivatives of the unit vectors Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]
$$\begin{aligned} \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1^B}{dt}\right|_0 &= \ddot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \ddot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + \dot x_1\,\omega\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\omega\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; derivatives of $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ &= \mathbf a_1^B + \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^B \quad &\text{(first pair: the relative acceleration; second pair: a rotation term)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left(\omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf r_1^B\right) &= \dot\omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf r_1^B + \omega\left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0\times\mathbf r_1^B + \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left.\frac{d\mathbf r_1^B}{dt}\right|_0 \quad &\text{(product rule on the three factors)} \\ &= \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\mathbf v_1^B + \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^B\right) \quad &\text{($\dot\omega$ zero; $\mathbf k_1$ fixed; velocity box)} \\ \mathbf a_0^B &= \mathbf a_1^B + \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^B + \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^B + \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^B\right) \quad &\text{(sum of the two derivatives)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_0^B = \mathbf a_1^B + 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^B + \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^B\right)}$$

Units: every term $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: one Coriolis half comes from the turning of $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$ inside the relative velocity, the other from the change of the relative position inside the transport term; with the origin at rest and constant $\omega$ the origin and Euler terms of Eq. 3.27 are absent.

(a) Relative acceleration

Relative acceleration of the skater Law: second time derivative in $S_1$, where $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf j_1$ are constant; product rule and chain rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24; Problems.pdf, p. 8
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot x_1 &= \frac{d}{dt}\left(-a\dot\psi\sin\psi\right) = -a\ddot\psi\sin\psi - a\dot\psi^2\cos\psi \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule on $\sin\psi$)} \\ \ddot y_1 &= \frac{d}{dt}\left(a\dot\psi\cos\psi\right) = a\ddot\psi\cos\psi - a\dot\psi^2\sin\psi \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule on $\cos\psi$)} \\ \mathbf a_1^B &= \ddot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \ddot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.24 with constant $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$ in $S_1$)} \\ &= a\ddot\psi\left(-\sin\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\psi\,\mathbf j_1\right) - a\dot\psi^2\left(\cos\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(grouped by $\ddot\psi$ and $\dot\psi^2$)} \\ &= a\ddot\psi\,\mathbf u_\perp - a\dot\psi^2\,\mathbf u_{AB} \quad &\text{(bar basis)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_1^B = -a\left(\ddot\psi\sin\psi + \dot\psi^2\cos\psi\right)\mathbf i_1 + a\left(\ddot\psi\cos\psi - \dot\psi^2\sin\psi\right)\mathbf j_1 = a\ddot\psi\,\mathbf u_\perp - a\dot\psi^2\,\mathbf u_{AB}}$$

Units: $[a\ddot\psi] = [a\dot\psi^2] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: in $S_1$ the skater moves on a circle of radius $a$ about $A$: a tangential part along the normal of the bar and a centripetal part pointing from $B$ towards $A$.

(b) Centripetal and Coriolis terms

Centripetal and Coriolis accelerations Law: vector products with the angular velocity of $S_1$, expanded term by term Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.25; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^B &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left[a\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\mathbf i_1 + a\sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1\right] = -a\omega\sin\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + a\omega\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^B\right) &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left[-a\omega\sin\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + a\omega\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\mathbf j_1\right] \quad &\text{(previous row)} \\ &= -a\omega^2\sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1 - a\omega^2\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(same products)} \\ 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^B &= 2\omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(-a\dot\psi\sin\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + a\dot\psi\cos\psi\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(relative velocity of the velocity box)} \\ &= -2a\omega\dot\psi\sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1 - 2a\omega\dot\psi\cos\psi\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(same products)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^B\right) = -a\omega^2\left[\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\mathbf i_1 + \sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1\right], \qquad 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^B = -2a\omega\dot\psi\left(\cos\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1\right) = -2a\omega\dot\psi\,\mathbf u_{AB}}$$

Units: $[a\omega^2] = [a\omega\dot\psi] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the centripetal term is $\omega^2$ times the position vector, reversed: it points from $B$ towards the axis through $O$, because the whole of $\mathbf r_1^B$ lies in the plane normal to $\boldsymbol\omega_{10}$. The Coriolis term lies along the bar.

Forces and Equations of Motion

The free-body diagram of the skater in $S_1$ shows the weight and the normal reaction of the plane (both vertical), the bar force along the bar, and the two inertia forces that do not vanish: the centrifugal force, away from $O$, and the Coriolis force, along the bar. The inertia force of the origin and the Euler force vanish because $O$ is fixed and $\omega$ is constant.

Figure 4. Forces on $B$ in $S_1$: the bar force $-T\,\mathbf u_{AB}$, the centrifugal force $m\omega^2\mathbf r_1^B$ away from $O$ and the Coriolis force $2ma\omega\dot\psi\,\mathbf u_{AB}$, which points towards $A$ because $\dot\psi \lt 0$; weight and reaction are normal to the plane of the drawing.
Actual and inertia forces on the skater in the rotating frame Law: inertia forces of a non-inertial frame; force of a massless two-hinged bar along the bar Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf F &= -T\,\mathbf u_{AB} - mg\,\mathbf k_1 + N\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(bar, weight, plane)} \\ \mathbf F_A &= -m\,\mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf F_E = -m\,\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^B = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{($O$ fixed; $\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}$ zero)} \\ \mathbf F_C &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^B\right) = ma\omega^2\left[\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\mathbf i_1 + \sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1\right] \quad &\text{(centripetal term of part (b) times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR} &= -2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^B = 2ma\omega\dot\psi\,\mathbf u_{AB} \quad &\text{(Coriolis term of part (b) times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_C\cdot\mathbf u_{AB} &= ma\omega^2\left[\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\cos\psi + \sin^2\psi\right] = ma\omega^2\left(1 + \cos\psi\right) \quad &\text{(components of $\mathbf u_{AB}$; $\cos^2\psi + \sin^2\psi = 1$)} \\ \mathbf F_C\cdot\mathbf u_\perp &= ma\omega^2\left[-\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\sin\psi + \sin\psi\cos\psi\right] = -ma\omega^2\sin\psi \quad &\text{(components of $\mathbf u_\perp$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf F_C = ma\omega^2\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\mathbf u_{AB} - ma\omega^2\sin\psi\,\mathbf u_\perp, \qquad \mathbf F_{COR} = 2ma\omega\dot\psi\,\mathbf u_{AB}}$$

Units: $[ma\omega^2] = [ma\omega\dot\psi] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the centrifugal force pushes $B$ away from $O$; its part normal to the bar turns the bar back towards the axis $Ox_1$, like the weight of a pendulum hung from $A$.

Newton's second law in the rotating frame, projected on the bar basis Law: Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame with the inertia forces Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Sec. 7.6; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]
$$\begin{aligned} m\,\mathbf a_1^B &= \mathbf F + \mathbf F_C + \mathbf F_{COR} \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.63; $\mathbf F_A$ and $\mathbf F_E$ zero)} \\ \mathbf u_\perp:\ ma\ddot\psi &= -ma\omega^2\sin\psi \quad &\text{(bar force and Coriolis force have no $\mathbf u_\perp$ part)} \\ \mathbf u_{AB}:\ -ma\dot\psi^2 &= -T + ma\omega^2\left(1 + \cos\psi\right) + 2ma\omega\dot\psi \quad &\text{(all forces along the bar)} \\ \mathbf k_1:\ 0 &= N - mg \quad &\text{(the skater stays on the plane)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\ddot\psi + \omega^2\sin\psi = 0, \qquad T = ma\left[\dot\psi^2 + 2\omega\dot\psi + \omega^2\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\right], \qquad N = mg}$$

Units: $[\ddot\psi] = [\omega^2] = [\mathrm{T^{-2}}]$; $[T] = [ma\dot\psi^2] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: three scalar equations for the three unknowns $\psi$, $T$ and $N$. In $S_1$ the skater swings like a pendulum of length $a$ hung from $A$, with the effective field $a\omega^2$ pointing along plus $\mathbf i_1$, away from $O$; $\psi$ zero is its stable bottom. The analogy is exact for the motion (the component along $\mathbf u_\perp$) but not for the tension: along the bar the centrifugal force is $ma\omega^2(1 + \cos\psi)$, not the $ma\omega^2\cos\psi$ of a uniform field, and the Coriolis force adds to it.

Answers and Checks

(c) Reduction to quadratures

First integral of the equation of motion Law: the equation of motion multiplied by twice the rate is an exact derivative (the hint of the statement); Barrow's rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.22; Notes.pdf, Sec. 7.7; Problems.pdf, p. 8
$$\begin{aligned} 2\dot\psi\ddot\psi + 2\omega^2\sin\psi\,\dot\psi &= 0 \quad &\text{(equation of motion times $2\dot\psi$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\dot\psi^2\right) &= 2\dot\psi\ddot\psi \quad &\text{(chain rule: $\tfrac{d}{d\dot\psi}\dot\psi^2 = 2\dot\psi$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(-2\omega^2\cos\psi\right) &= 2\omega^2\sin\psi\,\dot\psi \quad &\text{(chain rule: $\tfrac{d}{d\psi}\cos\psi = -\sin\psi$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\dot\psi^2 - 2\omega^2\cos\psi\right) &= 0 \quad &\text{(the first row is this sum)} \\ \left[\dot\psi^2 - 2\omega^2\cos\psi\right]_0^t &= 0 \quad &\text{(Barrow's rule between 0 and $t$)} \\ \dot\psi^2 - \dot\psi^2(0) &= 2\omega^2\left(\cos\psi - \cos\psi(0)\right) = 2\omega^2\left(\cos\psi - 1\right) \quad &\text{($\psi(0) = 0$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\dot\psi^2 = \dot\psi^2(0) + 2\omega^2\left(\cos\psi - 1\right)}$$

Units: $[\dot\psi^2] = [\omega^2] = [\mathrm{T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the rate squared depends on the position only; the initial rate is still to be found from the condition that the skater starts at rest in $S_0$.

Initial rate from the skater at rest in the inertial frame Law: absolute velocity of the velocity box evaluated at the initial instant Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.26; Problems.pdf, p. 8
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^B &= -a\left(\dot\psi + \omega\right)\sin\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + a\left[\left(\dot\psi + \omega\right)\cos\psi + \omega\right]\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(velocity box)} \\ \mathbf v_0^B(0) &= -a\left(\dot\psi(0) + \omega\right)\cdot 0\,\mathbf i_1 + a\left[\left(\dot\psi(0) + \omega\right)\cdot 1 + \omega\right]\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{($\psi(0) = 0$: $\sin 0 = 0$, $\cos 0 = 1$)} \\ &= a\left[\dot\psi(0) + 2\omega\right]\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(skater at rest in $S_0$)} \\ \dot\psi(0) &= -2\omega \quad &\text{(solved)} \\ \dot\psi^2 &= 4\omega^2 + 2\omega^2\left(\cos\psi - 1\right) = 2\omega^2\left(1 + \cos\psi\right) \quad &\text{(first integral)} \\ &= 4\omega^2\cos^2\frac{\psi}{2} \quad &\text{($1 + \cos\psi = 2\cos^2(\psi/2)$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\dot\psi(0) = -2\omega, \qquad \dot\psi^2 = 4\omega^2\cos^2\frac{\psi}{2}}$$

Units: $[\dot\psi] = [\omega] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: seen from $S_1$, which turns counterclockwise, a skater at rest in $S_0$ moves clockwise: her relative velocity must cancel the transport velocity of the point at twice $a$ from the axis, of magnitude $2a\omega$.

Sign of the rate and quadrature Law: continuity of the rate; separation of variables Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.44; Notes.pdf, Sec. 7.7; Problems.pdf, p. 8

The rate is a continuous function of time. Between minus $\pi$ and $\pi$ the factor $\cos(\psi/2)$ is positive, so the rate cannot vanish there and keeps the sign it has at the start, negative: $\psi$ decreases from 0 and stays between minus $\pi$ and 0.

$$\begin{aligned} \dot\psi &= -2\omega\cos\frac{\psi}{2}, \quad -\pi \lt \psi \le 0 \quad &\text{(negative root, fixed by $\dot\psi(0) = -2\omega$)} \\ \frac{d\psi}{2\cos(\psi/2)} &= -\omega\,dt \quad &\text{(variables separated)} \\ \int_0^{\psi}\frac{d\psi'}{2\cos(\psi'/2)} &= -\int_0^t\omega\,dt' \quad &\text{(integrated from the initial state $\psi(0) = 0$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\int_0^{\psi}\frac{d\psi'}{2\cos(\psi'/2)} = -\int_0^t\omega\,dt', \qquad \dot\psi = -2\omega\cos\frac{\psi}{2} \ \ \left(-\pi \lt \psi \le 0\right)}$$

Units: both integrals dimensionless; $[\omega\,dt] = [1]$

Meaning: this is the form asked for in the statement; the next box evaluates it.

Evaluation of the quadrature: the angle as a function of time Law: substitution, antiderivative of the secant, Barrow's rule; half-angle identities Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.44; Problems.pdf, p. 8

With the substitution $w = \psi'/2$ the differential is $d\psi' = 2\,dw$ and the limits 0 and $\psi$ become 0 and $\psi/2$. The antiderivative of $1/\cos w$ is $\ln|\sec w + \tan w|$; its derivative is $(\sec w\tan w + \sec^2 w)/(\sec w + \tan w) = \sec w$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\psi}\frac{d\psi'}{2\cos(\psi'/2)} &= \int_0^{\psi/2}\frac{2\,dw}{2\cos w} = \int_0^{\psi/2}\frac{dw}{\cos w} \quad &\text{(substitution $\psi' = 2w$)} \\ &= \left[\ln\left|\sec w + \tan w\right|\right]_0^{\psi/2} = \ln\left(\sec\frac{\psi}{2} + \tan\frac{\psi}{2}\right) - \ln 1 \quad &\text{(Barrow's rule; the argument is positive for $|\psi/2| \lt \pi/2$)} \\ -\int_0^t\omega\,dt' &= -\omega\left[t'\right]_0^t = -\omega t \quad &\text{(antiderivative $t'$; Barrow's rule)} \\ \sec x + \tan x &= \frac{1 + \sin x}{\cos x} = \frac{\left(\cos\tfrac{x}{2} + \sin\tfrac{x}{2}\right)^2}{\cos^2\tfrac{x}{2} - \sin^2\tfrac{x}{2}} \quad &\text{(half-angle forms: $1 + \sin x = (\cos\tfrac{x}{2} + \sin\tfrac{x}{2})^2$, $\cos x = \cos^2\tfrac{x}{2} - \sin^2\tfrac{x}{2}$)} \\ &= \frac{\left(\cos\tfrac{x}{2} + \sin\tfrac{x}{2}\right)^2}{\left(\cos\tfrac{x}{2} - \sin\tfrac{x}{2}\right)\left(\cos\tfrac{x}{2} + \sin\tfrac{x}{2}\right)} = \frac{\cos\tfrac{x}{2} + \sin\tfrac{x}{2}}{\cos\tfrac{x}{2} - \sin\tfrac{x}{2}} \quad &\text{(difference of squares; common factor cancelled)} \\ &= \frac{1 + \tan\tfrac{x}{2}}{1 - \tan\tfrac{x}{2}} = \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{x}{2}\right) \quad &\text{(numerator and denominator divided by $\cos\tfrac{x}{2}$; tangent of a sum with $\tan\tfrac{\pi}{4} = 1$)} \\ \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{\psi}{4}\right) &= e^{-\omega t} \quad &\text{(exponential of both sides, $x = \psi/2$)} \\ \psi &= 4\arctan\left(e^{-\omega t}\right) - \pi \quad &\text{(solved; $\pi/4 + \psi/4$ lies between 0 and $\pi/4$)} \\ \cos\frac{\psi}{2} &= \cos\left(2\arctan e^{-\omega t} - \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \sin\left(2\arctan e^{-\omega t}\right) = \frac{2e^{-\omega t}}{1 + e^{-2\omega t}} = \frac{1}{\cosh\omega t} \quad &\text{($\sin 2\beta = 2\tan\beta/(1 + \tan^2\beta)$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\psi(t) = 4\arctan\left(e^{-\omega t}\right) - \pi, \qquad \cos\frac{\psi}{2} = \frac{1}{\cosh\omega t}, \qquad \dot\psi = -\frac{2\omega}{\cosh\omega t}}$$

Units: $[\omega t] = [1]$

Meaning: $\psi$ starts at 0 and tends to minus $\pi$ as $t$ grows, without reaching it in a finite time: with a rigid bar the skater creeps towards the centre $O$. The rate written with the hyperbolic cosine has the value $-2\omega$ at the start, as the initial-rate box requires.

(d) Tension on the bar

Tension as a function of the angle and of time Law: tangent equation of the bar basis with the first integral substituted Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Problems.pdf, p. 8

Write $c$ for $\cos(\psi/2)$, positive during the motion.

$$\begin{aligned} T &= ma\left[\dot\psi^2 + 2\omega\dot\psi + \omega^2\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\right] \quad &\text{(equation along the bar)} \\ \dot\psi^2 &= 4\omega^2c^2, \quad \dot\psi = -2\omega c, \quad 1 + \cos\psi = 2c^2 \quad &\text{(sign box and half-angle identity)} \\ T &= ma\omega^2\left(4c^2 - 4c + 2c^2\right) = ma\omega^2\left(6c^2 - 4c\right) \quad &\text{(substituted and collected)} \\ &= 2ma\omega^2\,c\left(3c - 2\right) \quad &\text{(common factor $2c$)} \\ T(t) &= \frac{2ma\omega^2}{\cosh\omega t}\left(\frac{3}{\cosh\omega t} - 2\right) \quad &\text{($c = 1/\cosh\omega t$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{T = 2ma\omega^2\cos\frac{\psi}{2}\left(3\cos\frac{\psi}{2} - 2\right)}$$

Units: $[ma\omega^2] = [\mathrm{M}][\mathrm{L}][\mathrm{T^{-2}}] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$, a force

Meaning: at the start ($c$ equal to 1) the bar pulls with $2ma\omega^2$; the pull decreases as the skater swings in and turns into a push later on.

(e) String instead of the bar

Instant at which a string goes slack Law: a string can only pull: it stays taut while the tension of the bar solution is not negative Source: Notes.pdf, Sec. 6.4; Problems.pdf, p. 8

While the string is taut it behaves as the bar, so the motion and the tension are those found above. $c$ is the reciprocal of $\cosh\omega t$, so it decreases monotonically from 1 towards 0; the factor $c$ stays positive and the factor $3c - 2$ changes sign once.

$$\begin{aligned} T &= 0 \iff 3c - 2 = 0 \iff \cos\frac{\psi}{2} = \frac23 \quad &\text{(first zero of the tension)} \\ \psi_\ell &= -2\arccos\frac23 = -1.6821\ \text{rad} = -96.38^\circ \quad &\text{(negative branch of the motion)} \\ \cosh\omega t_\ell &= \frac32 \quad &\text{($c = 1/\cosh\omega t$)} \\ e^{\omega t_\ell} &= \frac32 + \sqrt{\frac94 - 1} = \frac{3 + \sqrt5}{2} \quad &\text{(roots of $e^{2x} - 3e^x + 1 = 0$ are $(3\pm\sqrt5)/2$, both positive; $t_\ell \gt 0$ needs $e^{\omega t_\ell} \gt 1$, so the larger one; the other is the mirror time $-t_\ell$)} \\ \omega t_\ell &= \ln\frac{3 + \sqrt5}{2} = 0.9624 \quad &\text{(logarithm)} \\ \left|\mathbf r_1^B\right| &= a\sqrt{2\left(1 + \cos\psi_\ell\right)} = 2a\cos\frac{\psi_\ell}{2} = \frac43\,a \quad &\text{(distance from $O$ at that instant)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{the string goes slack at } \psi_\ell = -2\arccos\frac23 \simeq -96.38^\circ, \quad t_\ell = \frac{1}{\omega}\ln\frac{3 + \sqrt5}{2} \simeq \frac{0.9624}{\omega}}$$

Units: $[t_\ell] = [\omega^{-1}] = [\mathrm{T}]$; angles dimensionless

Meaning: yes, it goes slack, once, after the string has turned 96.38 degrees clockwise from $Ox_1$ (it lags behind the vehicle), when the skater is at four thirds of $a$ from the centre. From then on, until the string becomes taut again (not studied here), no force acts in the plane and the skater moves in a straight line in $S_0$.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Relative acceleration$\mathbf a_1^B = -a\left(\ddot\psi\sin\psi + \dot\psi^2\cos\psi\right)\mathbf i_1 + a\left(\ddot\psi\cos\psi - \dot\psi^2\sin\psi\right)\mathbf j_1 = a\ddot\psi\,\mathbf u_\perp - a\dot\psi^2\,\mathbf u_{AB}$
(b) Centripetal term$\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^B) = -a\omega^2\left[(1 + \cos\psi)\mathbf i_1 + \sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1\right]$
(b) Coriolis term$2\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^B = -2a\omega\dot\psi\left(\cos\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1\right)$
(c) Equation of motion and quadrature$\ddot\psi + \omega^2\sin\psi = 0$; $\dot\psi = -2\omega\cos(\psi/2)$ for $-\pi \lt \psi \le 0$; $\int_0^{\psi}d\psi'/(2\cos(\psi'/2)) = -\int_0^t\omega\,dt'$, giving $\psi = 4\arctan(e^{-\omega t}) - \pi$
(d) Tension$T = 2ma\omega^2\cos(\psi/2)\left(3\cos(\psi/2) - 2\right)$
(e) Stringgoes slack at $\psi = -2\arccos(2/3) \simeq -96.38^\circ$, at $t = \ln\frac{3 + \sqrt5}{2}/\omega \simeq 0.9624/\omega$
Normal reaction of the plane$N = mg$

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 72 prints the Coriolis acceleration, the "centrifugal acceleration" (the term called centripetal here, as in Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.25), the first-order equation of motion with its range, the tension and the angle at which the string goes slack. The box below sets them side by side with the results above: every one coincides, so there is no discrepancy.

Comparison with the official key Law: term-by-term comparison of the results with the key Source: Problems.pdf, p. 72; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.25
$$\begin{aligned} \text{key: } \mathbf a_{cor} &= -2a\omega\dot\psi\left(\cos\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(same as $2\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^B$, part (b))} \\ \text{key: } \mathbf a_{cf} &= -a\omega^2\left[\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)\mathbf i_1 + \sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1\right] \quad &\text{(same as the centripetal term, part (b))} \\ \text{key: } \dot\psi &= -2\omega\cos\left(\psi/2\right), \ -\pi \lt \psi \le 0 \quad &\text{(same as the sign box, part (c))} \\ \text{key: } T &= 2ma\omega^2\cos\frac{\psi}{2}\left(3\cos\frac{\psi}{2} - 2\right) \quad &\text{(same as part (d))} \\ \text{key: } \psi &= -2\arccos\left(2/3\right) \quad &\text{(same as part (e))} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{all five results of the key coincide with this solution}}$$

Units: accelerations $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$, rate $[\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$, tension $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the key calls centrifugal acceleration the term that Notes.pdf calls centripetal; it is the same vector, pointing towards the axis.

Independent check: mechanical energy in the rotating frame Law: in $S_1$ the mechanical energy is conserved when every force that does work there has a potential Source: [Lecture 5, Slide 29]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31

Two reasons make the energy in $S_1$ a constant. First, the forces that do work in $S_1$ have a potential: $\boldsymbol\omega_{10}$ is constant, so the centrifugal force derives from $-\tfrac12 m\omega^2 r_\perp^2$, where $r_\perp$ is the distance to the axis through $O$ (here the whole of $|\mathbf r_1^B|$), while the force of the origin and the Euler force vanish. Second, the other forces do no work in $S_1$: the bar force lies along $\mathbf u_{AB}$, normal to the relative velocity along $\mathbf u_\perp$; the Coriolis force is normal to the relative velocity; the weight and the normal reaction are vertical.

$$\begin{aligned} r_\perp^2 &= a^2\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)^2 + a^2\sin^2\psi = 2a^2\left(1 + \cos\psi\right) \quad &\text{(components of $\mathbf r_1^B$; Pythagorean identity)} \\ E_1^B &= \tfrac12 m\,\mathbf v_1^B\cdot\mathbf v_1^B - \tfrac12 m\omega^2 r_\perp^2 = \tfrac12 ma^2\dot\psi^2 - ma^2\omega^2\left(1 + \cos\psi\right) \quad &\text{(kinetic energy in $S_1$ plus the centrifugal potential)} \\ E_1^B(0) &= \tfrac12 ma^2\left(4\omega^2\right) - ma^2\omega^2\cdot 2 = 0 \quad &\text{($\dot\psi(0) = -2\omega$, $\psi(0) = 0$)} \\ \dot\psi^2 &= 2\omega^2\left(1 + \cos\psi\right) \quad &\text{(constant energy equal to zero)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{E_1^B = \tfrac12 ma^2\dot\psi^2 - ma^2\omega^2\left(1 + \cos\psi\right) = 0 \ \Rightarrow\ \dot\psi^2 = 2\omega^2\left(1 + \cos\psi\right)}$$

Units: $[ma^2\omega^2] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$, an energy

Meaning: the energy route, which never uses the equation of motion, gives the same first integral; the energy is exactly that of the separatrix of the effective pendulum, which is why the skater only creeps towards the top position at $\psi$ equal to minus $\pi$.

Check at the initial instant, in the inertial frame Law: composition of accelerations at the start; Newton's second law in $S_0$ along $\mathbf i_1$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.59
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot\psi(0) &= -\omega^2\sin 0 = 0, \quad \dot\psi(0) = -2\omega \quad &\text{(equation of motion; initial rate)} \\ \mathbf a_1^B(0) &= -a\left(4\omega^2\right)\mathbf i_1 = -4a\omega^2\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(part (a) with $\mathbf u_{AB}(0) = \mathbf i_1$)} \\ 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^B(0) &= -2a\omega\left(-2\omega\right)\mathbf i_1 = 4a\omega^2\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(part (b))} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^B(0)\right) &= -2a\omega^2\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(part (b) with $\psi = 0$)} \\ \mathbf a_0^B(0) &= -4a\omega^2\,\mathbf i_1 + 4a\omega^2\,\mathbf i_1 - 2a\omega^2\,\mathbf i_1 = -2a\omega^2\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(sum)} \\ -T(0)\,\mathbf i_1 &= m\,\mathbf a_0^B(0) \ \Rightarrow\ T(0) = 2ma\omega^2 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.59 along $\mathbf i_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{T(0) = 2ma\omega^2 = \left. 2ma\omega^2\,c\left(3c - 2\right)\right|_{c = 1}}$$

Units: $[a\omega^2] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: at rest in $S_0$, the skater is set in motion by the bar alone, which pulls her towards the vehicle; the inertial frame gives the same tension as the rotating one.

Limiting cases Law: the results evaluated at extreme values of the data and of time Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Problems.pdf, p. 8
$$\begin{aligned} \omega \to 0:\quad \dot\psi &= -2\omega\cos\frac{\psi}{2} \to 0, \quad T \to 0 \quad &\text{(a vehicle at rest pulls nothing)} \\ t \to \infty:\quad \psi &\to 4\arctan 0 - \pi = -\pi, \quad \mathbf r_1^B \to a\left(1 - 1\right)\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(rigid bar: $B$ approaches $O$)} \\ t \to \infty:\quad T &\to 2ma\omega^2\cdot 0\cdot\left(0 - 2\right) = 0 \quad &\text{(the bar unloads at the end)} \\ t_\ell \lt t:\quad T &\lt 0 \quad &\text{(rigid bar in compression; $3c - 2 \lt 0$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\omega \to 0:\ T \to 0; \qquad t \to \infty:\ \psi \to -\pi,\ B \to O,\ T \to 0^-}$$

Units: $[T] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: a rigid bar pushes the skater after the instant at which a string would go slack, and the push dies out as she approaches the centre.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf (PDF page 8); key on PDF page 72
Problem 08

Kinematics, Two Trains on Tracks

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 8
Relative Motion

Two trains, $A$ and $B$, are moving along parallel tracks. The separation between the tracks is $a$. The absolute velocity of each train is $v_A$ and $v_B$, respectively. What is the relative velocity of each train with respect to the other?

Solve the same problem considering that the train $B$ is now moving along a circular track of radius $R$. The minimum distance between the circular track and the straight track of $A$ is $a$.

Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

Two trains $A$ and $B$ run on parallel tracks separated by the distance $a$, with absolute velocities $v_A$ and $v_B$; the statement asks for the velocity of each train relative to the other, first for the two straight tracks and then when train $B$ runs on a circular track of radius $R$ whose minimum distance to the straight track of $A$ is $a$ (Problems.pdf, p. 8). The problem is kinematic only: both motions are given. The observer of each train is read as a reference frame attached to it; on the circular track that frame turns with train $B$ (a reading: an observer on $B$ that only translates is also considered in the answers), and the velocity seen by a moving observer follows from the derivative of a vector in a moving frame, Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.1 and Sec. 3.2.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, the ground; $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k\}$: $\mathbf i_0$ along the track of $A$, $\mathbf j_0$ towards the track of $B$ in the plane of the tracks, $\mathbf k$ the cross product of $\mathbf i_0$ and $\mathbf j_0$, normal to that plane (Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.1)
Origin $O$the position of train $A$ at the initial instant
Frame of train $A$$S_A = \{A;\ \mathcal B_0\}$: origin on the train, axes parallel to the ground axes, since a train on a straight track does not turn
Frame of train $B$, case 1$S_B = \{B;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, for the same reason
Frame of train $B$, case 2$S_B = \{B;\ \mathcal B_B\}$, $\mathcal B_B = \{\mathbf i_B, \mathbf j_B, \mathbf k\}$: $\mathbf i_B$ along the track in the sense of motion, $\mathbf j_B$ from the train towards the centre $C$ of the track; it turns with the train
Notation$\mathbf v_A^B$: velocity of train $B$ relative to $S_A$; $\mathbf v_B^A$: velocity of train $A$ relative to $S_B$ (subscript the frame, superscript the point, as in Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19)
Coordinatescase 1: abscissas of the trains along $\mathbf i_0$; case 2: abscissa of $A$ and the angle $\theta_B$ of the segment from $C$ to $B$, measured at $C$ from the downward vertical (minus $\mathbf j_0$), positive about $\mathbf k$
Degrees of freedom1 per train (each is constrained to its track), both prescribed: no unknown coordinate
Data$a$ [m], $R$ [m], $v_A$, $v_B$ [m s$^{-1}$]; angular rate of train $B$ on the circle $\omega_B = v_B/R$ [rad s$^{-1}$]
Hypothesesthe tracks lie in one plane; the speeds are constant; $v_A$ and $v_B$ are signed components (positive along $\mathbf i_0$ where the trains are side by side; a train running the other way has a negative value); at the initial instant $A$ is at $O$ and $B$ at the point of its track closest to the track of $A$; the case 2 answers hold for this initial configuration: with $A$ starting at the abscissa $x_{A0}$ the observer on $B$ reads $[v_A - v_B(R + a)/R]\,\mathbf i_0 - (v_B/R)(x_{A0} + v_A t)\,\mathbf j_0$, and another initial angle of $B$ shifts every sine and cosine of $\theta_B$
Unknownsthe relative velocities $\mathbf v_A^B$ and $\mathbf v_B^A$ in each case

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Case 1: parallel straight tracks

Figure 1. Case 1. Both observers translate with the basis $\mathcal B_0$: the relative position $\mathbf r_A^B$ keeps the component $a$ across the tracks, and only its component along $\mathbf i_0$ changes, at the rate $v_B - v_A$.
Positions of the trains on parallel tracks Law: position vectors of points moving with constant velocity along straight lines Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.2; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.5; Problems.pdf, p. 8

$x_{B0}$ is the abscissa of $B$ at the initial instant (any value; it does not enter the velocities).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_0^A &= v_A t\,\mathbf i_0 \quad &\text{($A$ starts at $O$ and runs along $\mathbf i_0$)} \\ \mathbf r_0^B &= \left(x_{B0} + v_B t\right)\mathbf i_0 + a\,\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(track of $B$ at the distance $a$)} \\ \mathbf r_A^B &= \mathbf r_0^B - \mathbf r_0^A = \left(x_{B0} + \left(v_B - v_A\right)t\right)\mathbf i_0 + a\,\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.16 with the origin $A$ of $S_A$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_0^A = v_A t\,\mathbf i_0, \qquad \mathbf r_0^B = \left(x_{B0} + v_B t\right)\mathbf i_0 + a\,\mathbf j_0, \qquad \mathbf r_A^B = \left(x_{B0} + \left(v_B - v_A\right)t\right)\mathbf i_0 + a\,\mathbf j_0}$$

Units: $[v_A t] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}][\mathrm{T}] = [\mathrm{L}]$; $[a] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: seen from $A$, train $B$ stays at the distance $a$ across and slides along the tracks.

Case 2: train B on a circular track

Figure 2. Plane of the tracks ($\mathbf k$ out of the paper). $\mathbf r_B = \overrightarrow{OC} + \overrightarrow{CB}$: in the shaded right triangle $CFB$ the hypotenuse is $|CB| = R$, the leg opposite $\theta_B$ is $R\sin\theta_B$ (along $\mathbf i_0$) and the adjacent leg is $R\cos\theta_B$ (along $-\mathbf j_0$). The tangent $\mathbf i_B$ makes the same angle $\theta_B = \omega_B t$ with the horizontal; $\mathbf j_B$ points to $C$.
Position of train B on the circular track Law: position vector as a sum of segments; right triangle at the centre of the track Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.2; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 8

The closest point of the circle to the straight track lies on the perpendicular from the centre $C$, so $C$ is at the height $R + a$ above $O$ (its lowest point is then at the height $a$). From $O$ to $B$ we pass through $C$, because the distance from $C$ is the one that stays constant. Let $F$ be the point of the vertical through $C$ at the height of $B$: in the right triangle $CFB$ the hypotenuse is $R$; the leg opposite to $\theta_B$ is $R\sin\theta_B$, horizontal, along $\mathbf i_0$; the leg adjacent to $\theta_B$ is $R\cos\theta_B$, vertical, pointing down, along minus $\mathbf j_0$. The angle $\theta_B$ is measured from the downward vertical, not from $\mathbf i_0$: the standard polar angle about $C$ is $\varphi = \theta_B - \pi/2$, and the last two rows show that the standard form gives the same vector.

$$\begin{aligned} \theta_B &= \omega_B t = \frac{v_B}{R}\,t \quad &\text{(arc $R\theta_B$ travelled at the speed $v_B$, from the closest point)} \\ \overrightarrow{OC} &= \left(R + a\right)\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(centre above the closest point)} \\ \overrightarrow{CB} &= R\sin\theta_B\,\mathbf i_0 - R\cos\theta_B\,\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(opposite leg along $\mathbf i_0$; adjacent leg along $-\mathbf j_0$)} \\ \mathbf r_0^B &= \overrightarrow{OC} + \overrightarrow{CB} = R\sin\theta_B\,\mathbf i_0 + \left(R + a - R\cos\theta_B\right)\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(sum)} \\ \cos\left(\theta_B - \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) &= \cos\theta_B\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2} + \sin\theta_B\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} = \sin\theta_B \quad &\text{(cosine of a difference)} \\ \sin\left(\theta_B - \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) &= \sin\theta_B\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2} - \cos\theta_B\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} = -\cos\theta_B \quad &\text{(sine of a difference: $R\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_0 + R\sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_0$ is $\overrightarrow{CB}$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_0^A = v_A t\,\mathbf i_0, \qquad \mathbf r_0^B = R\sin\theta_B\,\mathbf i_0 + \left(R + a - R\cos\theta_B\right)\mathbf j_0, \qquad \theta_B = \frac{v_B t}{R}}$$

Units: $[R] = [a] = [\mathrm{L}]$; $[v_B t/R] = [1]$

Meaning: at the initial instant train $B$ is at the height $a$ just above train $A$; with a positive $v_B$ it moves counterclockwise, along plus $\mathbf i_0$ at that point, like $A$.

Figure 3. View from $+\mathbf k$ ($\odot$). $\mathbf i_B$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned counter-clockwise by $\omega_B t$: legs $\cos\omega_B t$ along $\mathbf i_0$ and $\sin\omega_B t$ along $\mathbf j_0$. $\mathbf j_B$ turns the same angle from $\mathbf j_0$, so its opposite leg $\sin\omega_B t$ points along $-\mathbf i_0$ (the minus sign of $[{}_0R_B]$).
Basis of train B: rotation by theta_B about k Law: unit tangent of the track; elementary rotation about the third axis and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.9

View along $\mathbf k$, which points out of the paper (⊙) because it is the cross product of $\mathbf i_0$ (to the right) and $\mathbf j_0$ (up). The tangent is the derivative of $\overrightarrow{CB}$ with respect to the angle, divided by its length $R$. $\mathbf i_B$ is then $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\theta_B$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\theta_B$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\theta_B$ along $\mathbf j_0$. $\mathbf j_B$ is $\mathbf j_0$ turned by the same angle: adjacent leg $\cos\theta_B$ along $\mathbf j_0$, opposite leg $\sin\theta_B$ along minus $\mathbf i_0$ (the upward vector turned counterclockwise leans to the left: the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d\overrightarrow{CB}}{d\theta_B} &= R\cos\theta_B\,\mathbf i_0 + R\sin\theta_B\,\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{($\tfrac{d}{d\theta}\sin\theta = \cos\theta$, $\tfrac{d}{d\theta}(-\cos\theta) = \sin\theta$)} \\ \mathbf i_B &= \frac{1}{R}\,\frac{d\overrightarrow{CB}}{d\theta_B} = \cos\theta_B\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\theta_B\,\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(length $R\sqrt{\cos^2\theta_B + \sin^2\theta_B} = R$)} \\ \mathbf j_B &= \mathbf k\times\mathbf i_B = -\sin\theta_B\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\theta_B\,\mathbf j_0 = -\frac{\overrightarrow{CB}}{R} \quad &\text{($\mathbf k\times\mathbf i_0 = \mathbf j_0$, $\mathbf k\times\mathbf j_0 = -\mathbf i_0$): it points to $C$} \\ \det[{}_0R_B] &= 1\cdot\left(\cos^2\theta_B + \sin^2\theta_B\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row)} \\ \left([{}_0R_B][{}_0R_B]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\theta_B + \sin^2\theta_B = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_B][{}_0R_B]^T\right)_{12} = \cos\theta_B\sin\theta_B - \sin\theta_B\cos\theta_B = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_B] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta_B & -\sin\theta_B & 0 \cr \sin\theta_B & \cos\theta_B & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_B] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_B][{}_0R_B]^T = I}$$

Units: dimensionless: $[1]$

Meaning: the frame of train $B$ turns by the same angle $\theta_B$ as the radius $CB$: the train always points along the track and its second axis always points to the centre.

Figure 4. Frame of train $B$ ($\mathbf k$ out of the paper). The components $x = \mathbf r_B^A\cdot\mathbf i_B$ and $y = \mathbf r_B^A\cdot\mathbf j_B$ are the legs of the shaded right triangle whose hypotenuse is $\mathbf r_B^A$; their time derivatives are the velocity of $A$ seen by the observer on $B$.
Position of train A seen from train B Law: relative position vector and its components in the basis of the moving frame (projections) Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.1; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_B^A &= \mathbf r_0^A - \mathbf r_0^B = \left(v_A t - R\sin\theta_B\right)\mathbf i_0 + \left(R\cos\theta_B - R - a\right)\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.16 with the origin $B$ of $S_B$)} \\ x &= \mathbf r_B^A\cdot\mathbf i_B = \left(v_A t - R\sin\theta_B\right)\cos\theta_B + \left(R\cos\theta_B - R - a\right)\sin\theta_B \quad &\text{(components of $\mathbf i_B$)} \\ &= v_A t\cos\theta_B - \left(R + a\right)\sin\theta_B \quad &\text{($R\sin\theta_B\cos\theta_B$ cancels)} \\ y &= \mathbf r_B^A\cdot\mathbf j_B = -\left(v_A t - R\sin\theta_B\right)\sin\theta_B + \left(R\cos\theta_B - R - a\right)\cos\theta_B \quad &\text{(components of $\mathbf j_B$)} \\ &= R - \left(R + a\right)\cos\theta_B - v_A t\sin\theta_B \quad &\text{($R\sin^2\theta_B + R\cos^2\theta_B = R$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_B^A = x\,\mathbf i_B + y\,\mathbf j_B, \qquad x = v_A t\cos\theta_B - \left(R + a\right)\sin\theta_B, \qquad y = R - \left(R + a\right)\cos\theta_B - v_A t\sin\theta_B}$$

Units: $[x] = [y] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: at the initial instant train $A$ is at the distance $a$ from $B$ along minus $\mathbf j_B$, on the side opposite to the centre $C$.

Kinematics

Case 1

Relative velocities on parallel tracks Law: derivative of the relative position in a frame that translates without turning Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.28; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]

The frames $S_A$ and $S_B$ have the basis $\mathcal B_0$, whose unit vectors are constant: the derivative in either frame is the derivative of the components.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^A &= \frac{d}{dt}\left(v_A t\right)\mathbf i_0 = v_A\,\mathbf i_0, \quad \mathbf v_0^B = \frac{d}{dt}\left(x_{B0} + v_B t\right)\mathbf i_0 = v_B\,\mathbf i_0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 2.3; constant speeds)} \\ \mathbf v_A^B &= \left.\frac{d\mathbf r_A^B}{dt}\right|_A = \frac{d}{dt}\left(x_{B0} + \left(v_B - v_A\right)t\right)\mathbf i_0 = \left(v_B - v_A\right)\mathbf i_0 \quad &\text{(derivative of the components; $a$ constant)} \\ \mathbf v_0^B &= \mathbf v_0^A + \mathbf v_A^B \quad &\text{(check: Eq. 3.28, no rotation term)} \\ \mathbf v_B^A &= \left.\frac{d}{dt}\left(\mathbf r_0^A - \mathbf r_0^B\right)\right|_B = \left(v_A - v_B\right)\mathbf i_0 \quad &\text{(same reasoning with the roles exchanged)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_A^B = \left(v_B - v_A\right)\mathbf i_0, \qquad \mathbf v_B^A = \left(v_A - v_B\right)\mathbf i_0 = -\mathbf v_A^B}$$

Units: $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: each observer sees the other train move along the tracks with the difference of the speeds; the separation $a$ does not enter, because it is a constant part of the relative position.

Case 2

Absolute velocities and the angular velocity of train B Law: time derivatives in $S_0$; chain rule; derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^A &= v_A\,\mathbf i_0 \quad &\text{(as in case 1)} \\ \mathbf v_0^B &= R\cos\theta_B\,\dot\theta_B\,\mathbf i_0 + R\sin\theta_B\,\dot\theta_B\,\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(chain rule; $R$ and $a$ constant)} \\ &= v_B\cos\theta_B\,\mathbf i_0 + v_B\sin\theta_B\,\mathbf j_0 = v_B\,\mathbf i_B \quad &\text{($R\dot\theta_B = R\,\omega_B = v_B$)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{B0} &= \dot\theta_B\,\mathbf k = \omega_B\,\mathbf k \quad &\text{($\mathcal B_B$ turns about the fixed $\mathbf k$ with the angle $\theta_B$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_B}{dt}\right|_0 &= -\omega_B\sin\theta_B\,\mathbf i_0 + \omega_B\cos\theta_B\,\mathbf j_0 = \omega_B\,\mathbf j_B = \boldsymbol\omega_{B0}\times\mathbf i_B \quad &\text{(chain rule; Eq. 3.3)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_B}{dt}\right|_0 &= -\omega_B\cos\theta_B\,\mathbf i_0 - \omega_B\sin\theta_B\,\mathbf j_0 = -\omega_B\,\mathbf i_B = \boldsymbol\omega_{B0}\times\mathbf j_B \quad &\text{(chain rule; Eq. 3.4)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_0^A = v_A\,\mathbf i_0, \quad \mathbf v_0^B = v_B\,\mathbf i_B, \quad \boldsymbol\omega_{B0} = \frac{v_B}{R}\,\mathbf k, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_B}{dt}\right|_0 = \omega_B\,\mathbf j_B, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_B}{dt}\right|_0 = -\omega_B\,\mathbf i_B}$$

Units: $[v_B] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[\omega_B] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: train $B$ keeps its speed but turns its direction; its frame turns at the rate of the radius $CB$.

Velocity of train B relative to train A Law: derivative of the relative position in the frame of $A$, which translates without turning Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.28
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_A^B &= \mathbf r_0^B - \mathbf r_0^A = \left(R\sin\theta_B - v_A t\right)\mathbf i_0 + \left(R + a - R\cos\theta_B\right)\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.16)} \\ \mathbf v_A^B &= \left.\frac{d\mathbf r_A^B}{dt}\right|_A = \left(R\cos\theta_B\,\omega_B - v_A\right)\mathbf i_0 + R\sin\theta_B\,\omega_B\,\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(constant $\mathcal B_0$; chain rule)} \\ &= \left(v_B\cos\theta_B - v_A\right)\mathbf i_0 + v_B\sin\theta_B\,\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{($R\,\omega_B = v_B$)} \\ \left|\mathbf v_A^B\right|^2 &= v_B^2\cos^2\theta_B - 2v_Av_B\cos\theta_B + v_A^2 + v_B^2\sin^2\theta_B \quad &\text{(squares expanded)} \\ &= v_A^2 + v_B^2 - 2v_Av_B\cos\theta_B \quad &\text{($\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_A^B = \mathbf v_0^B - \mathbf v_0^A = \left(v_B\cos\frac{v_Bt}{R} - v_A\right)\mathbf i_0 + v_B\sin\frac{v_Bt}{R}\,\mathbf j_0, \qquad \left|\mathbf v_A^B\right| = \sqrt{v_A^2 + v_B^2 - 2v_Av_B\cos\frac{v_Bt}{R}}}$$

Units: $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; inside the root $[\mathrm{L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the observer on $A$ does not turn, so he sees the plain difference of the two absolute velocities, which changes only because $B$ turns.

Velocity of train A relative to train B, which turns Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the position written in the turning basis of $S_B$; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.2; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.8; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.20; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]

The relative velocity is the derivative in $S_B$, in which $\mathbf i_B$ and $\mathbf j_B$ are constant: the derivative of the components $x$ and $y$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_0^A &= \mathbf r_0^B + x\,\mathbf i_B + y\,\mathbf j_B \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.16)} \\ \mathbf v_0^A &= \mathbf v_0^B + \dot x\,\mathbf i_B + \dot y\,\mathbf j_B + x\left.\frac{d\mathbf i_B}{dt}\right|_0 + y\left.\frac{d\mathbf j_B}{dt}\right|_0 \quad &\text{(derivative in $S_0$; product rule)} \\ &= \mathbf v_0^B + \underbrace{\dot x\,\mathbf i_B + \dot y\,\mathbf j_B}_{\mathbf v_B^A} + \underbrace{\omega_B\left(x\,\mathbf j_B - y\,\mathbf i_B\right)}_{\boldsymbol\omega_{B0}\times\mathbf r_B^A} \quad &\text{(derivatives of the unit vectors)} \\ \dot x &= v_A\cos\theta_B - v_A t\,\omega_B\sin\theta_B - \left(R + a\right)\omega_B\cos\theta_B \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule, $\dot\theta_B = \omega_B$)} \\ \dot y &= \left(R + a\right)\omega_B\sin\theta_B - v_A\sin\theta_B - v_A t\,\omega_B\cos\theta_B \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule)} \\ \dot x\cos\theta_B - \dot y\sin\theta_B &= v_A\left(\cos^2\theta_B + \sin^2\theta_B\right) - \left(R + a\right)\omega_B\left(\cos^2\theta_B + \sin^2\theta_B\right) \quad &\text{($\mathbf i_0$ part of $\dot x\,\mathbf i_B + \dot y\,\mathbf j_B$; the $v_At\omega_B$ terms cancel)} \\ \dot x\sin\theta_B + \dot y\cos\theta_B &= -v_A t\,\omega_B\left(\sin^2\theta_B + \cos^2\theta_B\right) \quad &\text{($\mathbf j_0$ part; the other terms cancel in pairs)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_B^A = \dot x\,\mathbf i_B + \dot y\,\mathbf j_B = \left[v_A - v_B\,\frac{R + a}{R}\right]\mathbf i_0 - \frac{v_Av_B t}{R}\,\mathbf j_0}$$

Units: $[v_B(R + a)/R] = [v_Av_Bt/R] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: the observer on $B$ turns with the train, so to the difference of the absolute velocities he adds minus the transport term: the ground itself seems to turn about him, and the component along minus $\mathbf j_0$ grows linearly with time, with the distance travelled by $A$.

Check: composition of velocities for the observer on B Law: absolute velocity as the velocity of the origin plus the relative and transport terms Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.26
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{B0}\times\mathbf r_B^A &= \omega_B\,\mathbf k\times\left[\left(v_A t - R\sin\theta_B\right)\mathbf i_0 + \left(R\cos\theta_B - R - a\right)\mathbf j_0\right] \quad &\text{(relative position in $\mathcal B_0$)} \\ &= -\omega_B\left(R\cos\theta_B - R - a\right)\mathbf i_0 + \omega_B\left(v_A t - R\sin\theta_B\right)\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{($\mathbf k\times\mathbf i_0 = \mathbf j_0$, $\mathbf k\times\mathbf j_0 = -\mathbf i_0$)} \\ \mathbf i_0:\ v_B\cos\theta_B + v_A - \left(R + a\right)\omega_B - \omega_B\left(R\cos\theta_B - R - a\right) &= v_A + \left(v_B - \omega_B R\right)\cos\theta_B = v_A \quad &\text{(origin + relative + transport; $\omega_B R = v_B$)} \\ \mathbf j_0:\ v_B\sin\theta_B - \omega_B v_A t + \omega_B\left(v_A t - R\sin\theta_B\right) &= \left(v_B - \omega_B R\right)\sin\theta_B = 0 \quad &\text{(same sum)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_0^B + \mathbf v_B^A + \boldsymbol\omega_{B0}\times\mathbf r_B^A = v_A\,\mathbf i_0 = \mathbf v_0^A}$$

Units: $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: the three terms rebuild the absolute velocity of train $A$, as Eq. 3.20 requires: the relative velocity of the previous box is consistent.

Answers and Checks

Case 1: parallel tracks

Answer for parallel tracks Law: relative velocity for observers that translate without turning Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.28; Problems.pdf, p. 8
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_A^B &= \left(v_B - v_A\right)\mathbf i_0 \quad &\text{(train $B$ seen from $A$)} \\ \mathbf v_B^A &= \left(v_A - v_B\right)\mathbf i_0 \quad &\text{(train $A$ seen from $B$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_A^B = -\mathbf v_B^A = \left(v_B - v_A\right)\mathbf i_0}$$

Units: $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: for trains running the same way the relative speed is the difference of the speeds; for opposite senses (a negative signed value) it is their sum.

Case 2: train B on a circular track

Answer for the circular track Law: relative velocities of the kinematics boxes, with the rate of the angle written out Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.28; Problems.pdf, p. 8
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_A^B &= \left(v_B\cos\frac{v_Bt}{R} - v_A\right)\mathbf i_0 + v_B\sin\frac{v_Bt}{R}\,\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(observer on $A$, not turning)} \\ \mathbf v_B^A &= \left[v_A - v_B\,\frac{R + a}{R}\right]\mathbf i_0 - \frac{v_Av_Bt}{R}\,\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(observer on $B$, turning with the train)} \\ \left|\mathbf v_B^A\right|^2 &= \left(v_A - v_B\,\frac{R + a}{R}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{v_Av_Bt}{R}\right)^2 \quad &\text{(sum of squares)} \\ \mathbf v_{B'}^A &= \mathbf v_0^A - \mathbf v_0^B = -\mathbf v_A^B = \left(v_A - v_B\cos\theta_B\right)\mathbf i_0 - v_B\sin\theta_B\,\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(other reading: observer $S_{B'} = \{B;\ \mathcal B_0\}$ that only translates, Eq. 3.28)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_A^B = \left(v_B\cos\frac{v_Bt}{R} - v_A\right)\mathbf i_0 + v_B\sin\frac{v_Bt}{R}\,\mathbf j_0, \qquad \mathbf v_B^A = \left[v_A - v_B\,\frac{R + a}{R}\right]\mathbf i_0 - \frac{v_Av_Bt}{R}\,\mathbf j_0 \ne -\mathbf v_A^B}$$

Units: $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: with the reading of an observer that turns with $B$, the two answers are no longer opposite: the observer on $B$ turns, and the transport term adds to his reading a part proportional to the distance of $A$ from him, which here grows with time. With the other reading, an observer on $B$ that does not turn, the answer is just minus the velocity of $B$ relative to $A$.

Part of the statementAnswer
Case 1, velocity of $B$ relative to $A$$\mathbf v_A^B = (v_B - v_A)\,\mathbf i_0$
Case 1, velocity of $A$ relative to $B$$\mathbf v_B^A = (v_A - v_B)\,\mathbf i_0$
Case 2, velocity of $B$ relative to $A$$\mathbf v_A^B = (v_B\cos(v_Bt/R) - v_A)\,\mathbf i_0 + v_B\sin(v_Bt/R)\,\mathbf j_0$, modulus $\sqrt{v_A^2 + v_B^2 - 2v_Av_B\cos(v_Bt/R)}$
Case 2, velocity of $A$ relative to $B$, observer not turning (other reading)$\mathbf v_{B'}^A = -\mathbf v_A^B = (v_A - v_B\cos(v_Bt/R))\,\mathbf i_0 - v_B\sin(v_Bt/R)\,\mathbf j_0$
Case 2, velocity of $A$ relative to $B$ (frame turning with $B$)$\mathbf v_B^A = [v_A - v_B(R + a)/R]\,\mathbf i_0 - (v_Av_Bt/R)\,\mathbf j_0$; in the basis of the train, $\dot x\,\mathbf i_B + \dot y\,\mathbf j_B$ with $\dot x$ and $\dot y$ of the kinematics box
Intermediate results$\omega_B = v_B/R$; $\mathbf r_B^A = x\,\mathbf i_B + y\,\mathbf j_B$ with $x = v_At\cos\theta_B - (R + a)\sin\theta_B$, $y = R - (R + a)\cos\theta_B - v_At\sin\theta_B$

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 72 lists item 8 with no answer, so there is no key to compare with. Independent checks: the composition box rebuilds the absolute velocity of train $A$ from the three terms of Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.20, and the limiting cases below give back case 1.

Limiting cases Law: the case 2 results at the initial instant and for a straight track Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.28
$$\begin{aligned} t = 0:\quad \mathbf v_A^B &= \left(v_B - v_A\right)\mathbf i_0 \quad &\text{($\cos 0 = 1$, $\sin 0 = 0$: the velocities are parallel)} \\ t = 0:\quad \mathbf v_B^A &= \left(v_A - v_B\right)\mathbf i_0 - \frac{a}{R}\,v_B\,\mathbf i_0 \quad &\text{(transport term of a point at the distance $a$ from $B$)} \\ R \to \infty:\quad \mathbf v_A^B &\to \left(v_B - v_A\right)\mathbf i_0, \quad \mathbf v_B^A \to \left(v_A - v_B\right)\mathbf i_0 \quad &\text{($v_Bt/R \to 0$, $a/R \to 0$: case 1)} \\ v_A = 0:\quad \left|\mathbf v_A^B\right| &= v_B \quad &\text{(a train at rest sees the speed of $B$)} \\ v_A = v_B = v:\quad \left|\mathbf v_A^B\right| &= v\sqrt{2 - 2\cos\frac{vt}{R}} = 2v\left|\sin\frac{vt}{2R}\right| \quad &\text{($1 - \cos\beta = 2\sin^2(\beta/2)$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{t = 0 \text{ or } R \to \infty: \ \text{case 1 recovered, except the term } -\tfrac{a}{R}\,v_B\,\mathbf i_0 \text{ of the turning observer at } t = 0}$$

Units: $[a\,v_B/R] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: even at the start, when the two trains run side by side and parallel, the turning observer on $B$ reads a different speed for $A$, by the fraction $a/R$ of $v_B$, because $A$ is at the distance $a$ from the axis about which he turns; the difference disappears for a straight track.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf
Problem 09

Artificial Gravity in a Rotating Cylinder

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 8
Centrifugal + Coriolis Forces

In "2001: A Space Odyssey" an idea to obtain artificial gravity in a spaceship was presented. It consists of a cylinder rotating at constant angular velocity around its axis. The astronauts would live in the inner surface of the cylinder and the centrifugal force would act as artificial gravity.

  • (a)
    If the cylinder has radius $R$, determine the angular velocity $\omega$ required to obtain a given level artificial gravity $g$. Consider $R = 10$ m and $g = 9.81$ m/s$^2$ for a particular case.
  • (b)
    An astronaut runs inside the surface of the cylinder with a constant speed $u$ with respect to the cylinder. Determine the artificial gravity that she feels (neglect the height of the astronaut $h$ with respect to the radius of the cylinder $R$, $h \ll R$).
  • (c)
    What is the condition for her to feel no artificial gravity at all?
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

A cylindrical spaceship of radius $R$ spins with constant angular velocity $\omega$ about its axis, and the astronauts live on its inner surface, where the centrifugal force plays the part of gravity (Problems.pdf, p. 8). The statement asks for the spin rate that gives the artificial gravity $g$ (with $R$ of 10 m and $g$ of 9.81 m/s$^2$), for the artificial gravity felt by an astronaut running on the surface with the constant speed $u$ relative to the cylinder, and for the condition to feel none. What the astronaut feels is defined in the frame of the hull, so the solution works in that frame with the inertia forces of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9, after deriving the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $O$ on the axis of the cylinder, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$ with $\mathbf k_0$ along the axis (Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.1)
Moving frame$S_1 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_1\}$ fixed to the hull, $\mathcal B_1 = \{\mathbf i_1, \mathbf j_1, \mathbf k_1\}$, $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$; it coincides with $S_0$ at the initial instant and turns by $\omega t$
Cylindrical basis (in $S_1$)$\mathcal B_2 = \{\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\theta, \mathbf k_1\}$ at the astronaut: $\mathbf e_r$ from the axis to the floor, $\mathbf e_\theta$ along the floor in the sense of rotation, $\mathbf k_1$ along the axis
Coordinates$\varphi$, the azimuth of the astronaut in $S_1$, measured from $\mathbf i_1$ about $\mathbf k_1$; $z$, her position along the axis
Constraintshe stays on the floor: distance $R$ from the axis
Degrees of freedom3 minus 1: 2, $\varphi$ and $z$, both prescribed by her running
Running velocity$u_\theta = R\dot\varphi$ (along $\mathbf e_\theta$, positive in the sense of rotation) and $u_z = \dot z$ (along the axis), constant; $\gamma$ is the angle between the running direction and $\mathbf e_\theta$, so that $u_\theta = u\cos\gamma$ and $u_z = u\sin\gamma$
Data$R$ [m] (10 m), $g$ [m s$^{-2}$] (9.81 m s$^{-2}$), $u$ [m s$^{-1}$], $m$ [kg] the mass of the astronaut
Unknowns(a) $\omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$]; (b) and (c) the floor force $\mathbf N$ [N] and the artificial gravity it means
Applied forcesnone other than the floor: no external gravity (deep space)
Constraint forcethe total force of the floor on her feet, $\mathbf N$ (normal part and any friction)
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)of the origin, Euler, centrifugal and Coriolis (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Artificial gravitywhat she feels as weight is the force she must receive from the floor: $g_{art}$ is the magnitude of $\mathbf N$ per unit mass, felt in the direction opposite to $\mathbf N$ (the reading of a scale under her feet). Another reading, the sum of the inertia forces per unit mass, $\omega^2R + 2\omega u\cos\gamma$, would vanish at the circumferential running speed $-\omega R/2$; it is rejected because there the floor still pushes her with $m u_\theta^2/R$, so a scale would not read zero
Hypotheses$\omega$ constant; $O$ fixed in an inertial frame; her height $h$ is negligible against $R$ (statement), so she is a point particle at the distance $R$ from the axis; the running is uniform (constant components)

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. Cross-section along the axis ($\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf k_1$ out of the paper, $\odot$). The hull axes $\mathbf i_1, \mathbf j_1$ are $\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0$ turned counter-clockwise by $\omega t$. In the shaded right triangle the hypotenuse is $R$, the leg along $\mathbf i_1$ is $R\cos\varphi$ and the leg along $\mathbf j_1$ is $R\sin\varphi$; $\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\theta$ in orange.
Basis of the hull: rotation by omega t about k0 Law: elementary rotation about the third axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

Cross-section seen along the axis, $\mathbf k_0$ out of the paper (⊙) because it is the cross product of $\mathbf i_0$ (to the right) and $\mathbf j_0$ (up); a positive $\omega$ turns the hull counterclockwise. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\omega t$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$. $\mathbf j_1$ is $\mathbf j_0$ turned by the same angle: adjacent leg $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$, opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ along minus $\mathbf i_0$ (the upward vector turned counterclockwise leans to the left: the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf j_1 = -\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles; axis)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= 1\cdot\left(\cos^2\omega t + \sin^2\omega t\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\omega t + \sin^2\omega t = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{12} = \cos\omega t\sin\omega t - \sin\omega t\cos\omega t = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\omega t & -\sin\omega t & 0 \cr \sin\omega t & \cos\omega t & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: dimensionless: $[1]$

Meaning: the hull axes follow the hull; seen from them the floor is at rest.

Cylindrical basis at the astronaut and her position vector Law: elementary rotation by the azimuth about the axis; position vector as a sum of segments Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.2; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.24; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.28; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16

Same view along the axis (⊙). $\mathbf e_r$ is $\mathbf i_1$ turned by $\varphi$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\varphi$ along $\mathbf i_1$, opposite leg $\sin\varphi$ along $\mathbf j_1$. $\mathbf e_\theta$ is $\mathbf j_1$ turned by $\varphi$: adjacent leg $\cos\varphi$ along $\mathbf j_1$, opposite leg $\sin\varphi$ along minus $\mathbf i_1$ (the minus sign, for the same reason). From $O$ we go along the axis to the cross-section of the astronaut and then out along the radius to the floor.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_r &= \cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf e_\theta = -\sin\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(right triangles of the shaded figure)} \\ \det[{}_1R_2] &= \cos^2\varphi + \sin^2\varphi = 1, \quad \mathbf e_r\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = -\cos\varphi\sin\varphi + \sin\varphi\cos\varphi = 0 \quad &\text{(checks of the rotation)} \\ \mathbf r_0^O &= \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(the origin of $S_1$ is the fixed point $O$)} \\ \mathbf r_0^P &= \mathbf r_1^P = z\,\mathbf k_1 + R\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(along the axis, then radially to the floor)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_0^P = \mathbf r_1^P = R\,\mathbf e_r + z\,\mathbf k_1, \qquad \mathbf e_r = \cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1, \qquad \mathbf e_\theta = -\sin\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[R] = [z] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: the part of the position normal to the spin axis is $R\,\mathbf e_r$, the same for every cross-section: every point of the floor is at the distance $R$ from the axis.

Figure 2. Running direction on the floor ($\mathbf e_r$ out of the paper). The leg along $\mathbf e_\theta$ is $u_\theta = u\cos\gamma$ and the leg along the axis is $u_z = u\sin\gamma$; only $u_\theta$ changes the artificial gravity.
Running direction on the floor Law: components of a vector from its right triangle in the plane tangent to the floor Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.24; Problems.pdf, p. 8

The tangent plane of the floor at the astronaut contains $\mathbf e_\theta$ (around the hull) and $\mathbf k_1$ (along it); the figure shows it from outside, with $\mathbf e_r$ out of the paper (⊙), since $\mathbf e_\theta\times\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf e_r$. The running velocity is the hypotenuse $u$ of a right triangle; its leg along $\mathbf e_\theta$ is adjacent to $\gamma$ and its leg along $\mathbf k_1$ is opposite.

$$\begin{aligned} u_\theta &= R\dot\varphi = u\cos\gamma \quad &\text{(adjacent leg)} \\ u_z &= \dot z = u\sin\gamma \quad &\text{(opposite leg)} \\ u_\theta^2 + u_z^2 &= u^2\left(\cos^2\gamma + \sin^2\gamma\right) = u^2 \quad &\text{(Pythagorean identity: speed $u$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{u_\theta = u\cos\gamma, \qquad u_z = u\sin\gamma, \qquad \dot\varphi = \frac{u\cos\gamma}{R}}$$

Units: $[u] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[\dot\varphi] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: $\gamma$ zero is running around the hull in the sense of rotation, $\gamma$ equal to $\pi$ against it, and $\gamma$ equal to $\pi/2$ along the axis.

Kinematics

Derivatives of the unit vectors in each frame Law: derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis; chain rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(simple rotation about the fixed $\mathbf k_0$; $\omega$ constant)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 to 3.5)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_r}{dt}\right|_1 &= -\sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\varphi\,\dot\varphi\,\mathbf j_1 = \dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(in $S_1$, $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf j_1$ are constant; chain rule)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{dt}\right|_1 &= -\cos\varphi\,\dot\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 - \sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi\,\mathbf j_1 = -\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_r}{dt}\right|_0 &= \dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta + \cos\varphi\,\omega\,\mathbf j_1 - \sin\varphi\,\omega\,\mathbf i_1 = \left(\dot\varphi + \omega\right)\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(in $S_0$: also the derivatives of $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{dt}\right|_0 &= -\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_r - \sin\varphi\,\omega\,\mathbf j_1 - \cos\varphi\,\omega\,\mathbf i_1 = -\left(\dot\varphi + \omega\right)\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(same)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\left.\frac{d\mathbf e_r}{dt}\right|_1 = \dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_r}{dt}\right|_0 = \left(\dot\varphi + \omega\right)\mathbf e_\theta, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{dt}\right|_0 = -\left(\dot\varphi + \omega\right)\mathbf e_r}$$

Units: $[\dot\varphi] = [\omega] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: seen from the hull the cylindrical basis turns with her running only; seen from inertial space it turns with her running plus the spin, which is the extra part $\boldsymbol\omega_{10}$ applied to each unit vector.

Relative velocity and relative acceleration Law: time derivatives in $S_1$; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24
