$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_1^P &= \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_1\left(R\,\mathbf e_r + z\,\mathbf k_1\right) = R\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta + \dot z\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.19; $R$ constant, $\mathbf k_1$ fixed in $S_1$)} \\ &= u_\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta + u_z\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(running velocity)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P &= \dot u_\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta + u_\theta\left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{dt}\right|_1 + \dot u_z\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.24; product rule)} \\ &= -u_\theta\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_r = -\frac{u_\theta^2}{R}\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(constant components; $\dot\varphi = u_\theta/R$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_1^P = u_\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta + u_z\,\mathbf k_1, \qquad \mathbf a_1^P = -\frac{u_\theta^2}{R}\,\mathbf e_r}$$

Units: $[u_\theta^2/R] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: in the hull she runs on a helix of radius $R$ (a circle when she runs around, a straight line along the axis), and only the part around the hull bends her path.

Absolute velocity and acceleration: relative, transport, Coriolis and centripetal terms Law: time derivatives in $S_0$ of the position written in the turning bases; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.25; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P &= \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left(R\,\mathbf e_r + z\,\mathbf k_1\right) = R\left(\dot\varphi + \omega\right)\mathbf e_\theta + \dot z\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(derivatives in $S_0$ of the previous box)} \\ &= \underbrace{u_\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta + u_z\,\mathbf k_1}_{\mathbf v_1^P} + \underbrace{\omega R\,\mathbf e_\theta}_{\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P} \quad &\text{($\omega\,\mathbf k_1\times(R\,\mathbf e_r + z\,\mathbf k_1) = \omega R\,\mathbf e_\theta$)} \\ \mathbf a_0^P &= R\ddot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta + R\left(\dot\varphi + \omega\right)\left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{dt}\right|_0 + \ddot z\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; $\dot\omega$ zero)} \\ &= -R\left(\dot\varphi + \omega\right)^2\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(uniform running: $\ddot\varphi$ and $\ddot z$ zero)} \\ &= -R\dot\varphi^2\,\mathbf e_r - 2R\omega\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_r - R\omega^2\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(square expanded)} \\ 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P &= 2\omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(u_\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta + u_z\,\mathbf k_1\right) = -2\omega u_\theta\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf e_\theta = -\mathbf e_r$, $\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf 0$)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(\omega R\,\mathbf e_\theta\right) = -\omega^2R\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(same products)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_0^P = \mathbf v_1^P + \omega R\,\mathbf e_\theta, \qquad \mathbf a_0^P = \underbrace{-\frac{u_\theta^2}{R}\,\mathbf e_r}_{\mathbf a_1^P}\ \underbrace{- 2\omega u_\theta\,\mathbf e_r}_{2\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P}\ \underbrace{- \omega^2R\,\mathbf e_r}_{\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P)} = -\frac{\left(\omega R + u_\theta\right)^2}{R}\,\mathbf e_r}$$

Units: every term $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$: $[u_\theta^2/R] = [\omega u_\theta] = [\omega^2R]$

Meaning: the three terms of the expanded square are the relative, Coriolis and centripetal accelerations of Eq. 3.25 (the origin and Euler terms vanish); the axial running gives none of them.

Forces and Equations of Motion

The free-body diagram of the astronaut in $S_1$ shows the floor force, the centrifugal force away from the axis and the Coriolis force, which is radial too. There is no weight in deep space; the inertia force of the origin and the Euler force vanish ($O$ fixed, $\omega$ constant).

Figure 3. Forces in $S_1$ on the astronaut at $P$ ($\mathbf k_1$ out of the paper). With $u_\theta \gt 0$ (running in the sense of rotation) both $\mathbf F_C = m\omega^2R\,\mathbf e_r$ and $\mathbf F_{COR} = 2m\omega u_\theta\,\mathbf e_r$ point away from the axis; the floor force $\mathbf N$ points to the axis and balances them plus $m\mathbf a_1^P$.
Inertia forces and the floor force Law: Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame with the inertia forces Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf F_A &= -m\,\mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf F_E = -m\,\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{($O$ fixed; $\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}$ zero)} \\ \mathbf F_C &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) = m\omega^2R\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(centripetal term times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR} &= -2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P = 2m\omega u_\theta\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(Coriolis term times $-m$)} \\ m\,\mathbf a_1^P &= \mathbf N + \mathbf F_C + \mathbf F_{COR} \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.63; the floor is the only actual force)} \\ -m\frac{u_\theta^2}{R}\,\mathbf e_r &= \mathbf N + m\omega^2R\,\mathbf e_r + 2m\omega u_\theta\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(substituted)} \\ \mathbf N &= -m\left(\omega^2R + 2\omega u_\theta + \frac{u_\theta^2}{R}\right)\mathbf e_r = -\frac{m}{R}\left(\omega R + u_\theta\right)^2\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(solved; perfect square)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf N = -\frac{m}{R}\left(\omega R + u_\theta\right)^2\mathbf e_r, \qquad N_\theta = N_z = 0}$$

Units: $[m\,\omega^2R] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: three scalar equations give the three components of the floor force; it points to the axis and has no part along the floor, so uniform running needs no friction.

Answers and Checks

(a) Spin rate for the artificial gravity g

Astronaut at rest on the floor Law: static balance in $S_1$ between the floor force and the centrifugal force Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; Problems.pdf, p. 8
$$\begin{aligned} u_\theta &= u_z = 0 \ \Rightarrow\ \mathbf N = -m\omega^2R\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(floor-force box at rest; no Coriolis force)} \\ g_{art} &= \frac{|\mathbf N|}{m} = \omega^2R \quad &\text{(definition of the artificial gravity)} \\ \omega^2R &= g \ \Rightarrow\ \omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{R}} \quad &\text{(positive root)} \\ \omega &= \sqrt{\frac{9.81}{10}}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} = \sqrt{0.981}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} = 0.9905\ \text{rad/s} \quad &\text{(data)} \\ T_{rev} &= \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = 6.344\ \mathrm{s}, \quad \frac{60\,\omega}{2\pi} = 9.458\ \text{rpm}, \quad \omega R = 9.905\ \text{m/s} \quad &\text{(period, revolutions per minute, floor speed)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{R}} = 0.9905\ \text{rad/s} \quad (\text{one turn in } 6.34\ \mathrm{s})}$$

Units: $[\sqrt{g/R}] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}\,\mathrm{L^{-1}}]^{1/2} = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: the floor pushes her towards the axis with the force $m\omega^2R$, and she reads it as a weight pointing away from the axis, towards the floor; the floor itself moves at 9.90 m/s in inertial space.

(b) Artificial gravity while running

Artificial gravity felt by the running astronaut Law: floor-force box with the relative velocity of the running Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]; Problems.pdf, p. 8
$$\begin{aligned} g_{art} &= \frac{|\mathbf N|}{m} = \frac{\left(\omega R + u_\theta\right)^2}{R} \quad &\text{(floor-force box)} \\ &= \omega^2R + 2\omega u_\theta + \frac{u_\theta^2}{R} = g + 2\omega u_\theta + \frac{u_\theta^2}{R} \quad &\text{(square expanded; $\omega^2R = g$ from part (a))} \\ &= g\left(1 + \frac{u\cos\gamma}{\omega R}\right)^2 = g\left(1 + \frac{u\cos\gamma}{\sqrt{gR}}\right)^2 \quad &\text{($u_\theta = u\cos\gamma$; $\omega R = \sqrt{gR}$)} \\ \gamma = 0:\quad g_{art} &= \frac{\left(\omega R + u\right)^2}{R} \gt g \quad &\text{(around the hull, with the rotation)} \\ \gamma = \pi:\quad g_{art} &= \frac{\left(\omega R - u\right)^2}{R} \lt g \ \ (0 \lt u \lt 2\omega R) \quad &\text{(around the hull, against the rotation)} \\ \gamma = \tfrac{\pi}{2}:\quad g_{art} &= g \quad &\text{(along the axis: relative velocity parallel to $\boldsymbol\omega_{10}$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{g_{art} = \frac{\left(\omega R + u\cos\gamma\right)^2}{R} = g + 2\omega u\cos\gamma + \frac{u^2\cos^2\gamma}{R}}$$

Units: $[\omega u] = [u^2/R] = [g] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: with the data of part (a), running at 2 m/s around the hull gives 14.17 m/s$^2$ (1.44 g) with the rotation and 6.25 m/s$^2$ (0.64 g) against it; at 5 m/s, 22.21 m/s$^2$ (2.26 g) and 2.41 m/s$^2$ (0.25 g).

(c) Condition for no artificial gravity

Weightlessness while running Law: a perfect square vanishes only when its base vanishes Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Problems.pdf, p. 8
$$\begin{aligned} g_{art} &= 0 \iff \omega R + u_\theta = 0 \iff u_\theta = -\omega R \quad &\text{(part (b))} \\ u\cos\gamma &= -\omega R \ \Rightarrow\ \cos\gamma = -\frac{\omega R}{u}, \quad \text{possible only if } u \ge \omega R \quad &\text{(running direction; $|\cos\gamma| \le 1$)} \\ \mathbf v_0^P &= \mathbf v_1^P + \omega R\,\mathbf e_\theta = \left(u_\theta + \omega R\right)\mathbf e_\theta + u_z\,\mathbf k_1 = u_z\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(absolute velocity box)} \\ \mathbf a_0^P &= -\frac{\left(\omega R + u_\theta\right)^2}{R}\,\mathbf e_r = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(absolute acceleration box)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{u_\theta = u\cos\gamma = -\omega R = -\sqrt{gR}\ \ (9.90\ \text{m/s}); \quad \text{running only around the hull: } u = \omega R \text{ against the rotation}}$$

Units: $[\omega R] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: she must run against the rotation so fast that the part of her running around the hull cancels the speed of the floor; she is then at rest in inertial space (or drifts uniformly along the axis if she also runs along it), no force is needed and the floor slides under her feet. A speed below 9.90 m/s, a sprinter's speed, cannot achieve it.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Spin rate$\omega = \sqrt{g/R} = 0.9905$ rad/s for $R = 10$ m and $g = 9.81$ m/s$^2$ (one turn in 6.34 s, 9.46 rpm)
(b) Artificial gravity while running$g_{art} = (\omega R + u\cos\gamma)^2/R = g + 2\omega u\cos\gamma + u^2\cos^2\gamma/R$, felt away from the axis; the floor force is $\mathbf N = -m(\omega R + u_\theta)^2\,\mathbf e_r/R$
(c) No artificial gravity$u_\theta = -\omega R$: the part of the running velocity around the hull equal to the floor speed $\sqrt{gR}$ (9.90 m/s), against the rotation; any axial part is allowed; it needs $u \ge \omega R$
Intermediate results$\mathbf a_1^P = -u_\theta^2\,\mathbf e_r/R$; Coriolis acceleration $-2\omega u_\theta\,\mathbf e_r$; centripetal acceleration $-\omega^2R\,\mathbf e_r$; $\mathbf v_0^P = (\omega R + u_\theta)\,\mathbf e_\theta + u_z\,\mathbf k_1$

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 72 lists item 9 with no answer, so there is no key to compare with. Independent checks: the inertial reading below gives the same floor force without inertia forces, and the limiting cases close the results.

Independent check in the inertial frame Law: Newton's second law in $S_0$ with the absolute acceleration Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.59; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.25
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P &= \left(\omega R + u_\theta\right)\mathbf e_\theta + u_z\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(absolute velocity box)} \\ m\,\mathbf a_0^P &= \mathbf N \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.59: the floor is the only force)} \\ \mathbf N &= -\frac{m\left(\omega R + u_\theta\right)^2}{R}\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(absolute acceleration box)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf N = -\frac{m}{R}\left(\omega R + u_\theta\right)^2\mathbf e_r \quad \text{(same as in } S_1\text{)}}$$

Units: $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: in inertial space she moves on a circle or helix of radius $R$ with the speed around the axis $\omega R + u_\theta$, so the floor must provide the centripetal force of that speed; the rotating observer splits the same force into the centrifugal, Coriolis and relative parts.

Limiting cases Law: the artificial gravity of part (b) at extreme values of the data Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Problems.pdf, p. 8
$$\begin{aligned} u \to 0:\quad g_{art} &\to \omega^2R = g \quad &\text{(part (a) recovered)} \\ u \ll \omega R:\quad g_{art} &\simeq g\left(1 + \frac{2u\cos\gamma}{\sqrt{gR}}\right) \quad &\text{(first order in $u$: the Coriolis term alone)} \\ R \to \infty,\ g \text{ fixed}:\quad \frac{2u}{\sqrt{gR}} &\to 0 \quad &\text{(relative Coriolis correction of a larger hull)} \\ u = 2\ \text{m/s},\ R = 10\ \text{m}:\quad \frac{2u}{\sqrt{gR}} &= \frac{4}{9.905} = 0.404 \quad &\text{(first-order correction for the data)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{g_{art} \to g \ \text{for} \ u \to 0; \qquad \text{first-order change } \pm 2\omega u \ \text{around the hull}}$$

Units: $2u/\sqrt{gR}$ is dimensionless

Meaning: a runner in a small hull feels a large change of weight (about 40 percent at 2 m/s in the hull of 10 m, to first order), which is why large habitats are more comfortable.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf (PDF page 8); no official key
Problem 20

Heavy Particle on a Rotating Circumference

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 10
Energy in a Rotating Frame

A heavy particle is moving along a smooth circumference of radius $R$ and center $O$. One of the diameters of the circumference is along the local vertical, and the circumference is rotating with constant angular velocity $\omega$ about it. The position of the particle with respect to the circumference is described by the angle $\theta$ between the particle and the lowest point of the circumference.

  • (a)
    Discuss the conservation of mechanical energy in the moving reference frame and compute its value.
  • (b)
    Compute the reaction of the circumference in the direction normal to its plane, as a function of $\theta$.
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

A heavy particle moves along a smooth circumference of radius $R$ and centre $O$; one diameter is vertical and the circumference turns about it with the constant angular velocity $\omega$; $\theta$ is the angle between the particle and the lowest point (Problems.pdf, p. 10). The statement asks to discuss the conservation of the mechanical energy in the moving frame and compute its value, and for the reaction of the circumference normal to its plane as a function of $\theta$. The wire is fixed in the frame that turns with it, so the solution works in that frame, with the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2 and the inertia forces of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$, $\mathbf k_0$ vertical, up, along the axis of rotation (Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.1)
Moving frame$S_1 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_1\}$ attached to the circumference: $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$; $\mathbf i_1$ horizontal, in the plane of the circumference, on the side where $\theta$ is positive; $\mathbf j_1$ the cross product of $\mathbf k_1$ and $\mathbf i_1$, normal to the plane of the circumference; it turns by $\omega t$ about $\mathbf k_0$
Wire basis$\mathcal B_2 = \{\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\theta, -\mathbf j_1\}$: $\mathbf e_r$ from $O$ to the particle $P$, $\mathbf e_\theta$ tangent to the circumference in the sense of growing $\theta$
Coordinate$\theta$, the angle at $O$ from the downward vertical to $OP$, positive towards $\mathbf i_1$
Constraints$P$ on the circumference: distance $R$ from $O$ and plane of the circumference, both fixed in $S_1$; smooth and bilateral (a bead on the wire)
Degrees of freedom3 minus 2: 1, the angle $\theta(t)$
Data$m$ [kg], $R$ [m], $\omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$], $g$ [m s$^{-2}$]; initial values $\theta_0$ [rad] and $\dot\theta_0$ [rad s$^{-1}$] (not given in the statement, kept as symbols)
Unknowns$\theta(t)$; reaction $\mathbf N = N_r\,\mathbf e_r + N_b\,\mathbf j_1$ (normal subspace of a curve, Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.16): $N_r$ in the plane, $N_b$ normal to it
Applied forceweight $-mg\,\mathbf k_1$
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)of the origin, Euler, centrifugal and Coriolis (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial with $O$ fixed; uniform gravity; $\omega$ constant; smooth wire, so the reaction has no component along the tangent

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. View from $+\mathbf k_0$ ($\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf k_1$ out of the paper, $\odot$). The wire is seen edge-on, along $\mathbf i_1$, turned counter-clockwise by $\omega t$; $\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1$ is normal to it. The opposite leg of $\mathbf j_1$ points along $-\mathbf i_0$: hence $\mathbf j_1 = -\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0$.
Basis of the rotating circumference: rotation by omega t about k0 Law: elementary rotation about the third axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

Top view along $\mathbf k_0$, out of the paper (⊙) because it is the cross product of $\mathbf i_0$ (to the right) and $\mathbf j_0$ (up); the circumference is seen edge-on, along $\mathbf i_1$, and turns counterclockwise. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\omega t$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$. $\mathbf j_1$ is $\mathbf j_0$ turned by the same angle: adjacent leg $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$, opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ along minus $\mathbf i_0$ (the upward vector turned counterclockwise leans to the left: the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf j_1 = -\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles; axis)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= 1\cdot\left(\cos^2\omega t + \sin^2\omega t\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\omega t + \sin^2\omega t = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{12} = \cos\omega t\sin\omega t - \sin\omega t\cos\omega t = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\omega t & -\sin\omega t & 0 \cr \sin\omega t & \cos\omega t & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: dimensionless: $[1]$

Meaning: $\mathbf j_1$ is horizontal and normal to the plane of the circumference: the direction of the reaction asked for in part (b).

Figure 2. Plane of the wire, fixed in $S_1$ ($\mathbf i_1$ right, $\mathbf k_1$ up, so $\mathbf j_1$ points into the paper, $\otimes$). In the shaded right triangle $OFP$ the hypotenuse is $R$, the leg opposite $\theta$ is $R\sin\theta$ along $\mathbf i_1$ and the adjacent leg is $R\cos\theta$ along $-\mathbf k_1$. $\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\theta$ in orange.
Position vector and wire basis in the plane of the circumference Law: right triangle in the plane of the wire; relation with the standard polar angle; rotation in that plane and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.2; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 10

Plane of the circumference, fixed in $S_1$, drawn with $\mathbf i_1$ to the right and $\mathbf k_1$ up; then $\mathbf j_1$, the cross product of $\mathbf k_1$ (up) and $\mathbf i_1$ (right), points into the paper (⊗), and minus $\mathbf j_1$ out of it. Let $F$ be the point of the vertical diameter at the height of $P$: in the right triangle $OFP$ the hypotenuse is $R$; the leg opposite to $\theta$ is $R\sin\theta$, horizontal, along $\mathbf i_1$; the leg adjacent to $\theta$ is $R\cos\theta$, vertical, pointing down, along minus $\mathbf k_1$ (the minus sign: $\theta$ is measured from the downward vertical). The standard polar angle of this plane, measured from $\mathbf i_1$ towards $\mathbf k_1$, is $\theta - \pi/2$. The tangent is the derivative of $\mathbf e_r$ with respect to $\theta$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_0^O &= \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf r_0^P = \mathbf r_1^P = \overrightarrow{OP} \quad &\text{(origin of $S_1$ at the fixed centre; Eq. 3.16)} \\ \mathbf e_r &= \sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 - \cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(legs of $OFP$ divided by $R$)} \\ \cos\left(\theta - \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) &= \sin\theta, \quad \sin\left(\theta - \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\cos\theta \quad &\text{(difference formulas: the standard form gives the same $\mathbf e_r$)} \\ \mathbf e_\theta &= \frac{d\mathbf e_r}{d\theta} = \cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{($\tfrac{d}{d\theta}\sin\theta = \cos\theta$, $\tfrac{d}{d\theta}(-\cos\theta) = \sin\theta$; unit length)} \\ \mathbf e_r\times\mathbf e_\theta &= \sin^2\theta\,\mathbf i_1\times\mathbf k_1 - \cos^2\theta\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = -\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf i_1\times\mathbf k_1 = -\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf j_1$)} \\ \det[{}_1R_2] &= -(-1)\left(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the second row, entry $-1$ in place (2,3))} \\ \mathbf e_r\cdot\mathbf e_\theta &= \sin\theta\cos\theta - \cos\theta\sin\theta = 0 \quad &\text{(columns orthogonal: $[{}_1R_2][{}_1R_2]^T = I$)} \\ \mathbf r_1^P &= R\,\mathbf e_r = R\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 - R\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(position vector)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^P = R\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 - R\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1, \quad [{}_1R_2] = \begin{pmatrix} \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & -1 \cr -\cos\theta & \sin\theta & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_1R_2] = 1}$$

Units: $[R] = [\mathrm{L}]$; direction cosines dimensionless

Meaning: $\theta$ zero is the lowest point and $\theta$ equal to $\pi/2$ the end of the horizontal diameter; the distance of $P$ to the axis is the horizontal leg $R\sin\theta$.

Kinematics

Derivatives of the unit vectors Law: derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis; chain rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(simple rotation about the fixed vertical; $\omega$ constant)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 to 3.5)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_r}{dt}\right|_1 &= \frac{d\mathbf e_r}{d\theta}\,\dot\theta = \dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule; $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf k_1$ constant in $S_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{dt}\right|_1 &= \left(-\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1\right)\dot\theta = -\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_r}{dt}\right|_1 = \dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{dt}\right|_1 = -\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_r}$$

Units: $[\omega] = [\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: in $S_1$ only the wire basis turns, with the particle; in $S_0$ the whole plane turns about the vertical as well.

Relative velocity and relative acceleration Law: time derivatives in $S_1$; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_1^P &= \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_1\left(R\,\mathbf e_r\right) = R\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{($R$ constant)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P &= R\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta + R\dot\theta\left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{dt}\right|_1 = R\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta - R\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(product rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_1^P = R\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta, \qquad \mathbf a_1^P = R\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta - R\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf e_r}$$

Units: $[R\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[R\ddot\theta] = [R\dot\theta^2] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: in $S_1$ the particle moves on a fixed circle: a tangential acceleration and a centripetal one towards $O$.

Absolute velocity and acceleration: relative, transport, Coriolis and centripetal terms Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the position written in the turning basis $\mathcal B_1$; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P &= \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left(R\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 - R\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1\right) = R\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + R\sin\theta\,\omega\,\mathbf j_1 + R\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule; derivatives of $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf k_1$)} \\ &= \underbrace{R\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta}_{\mathbf v_1^P} + \underbrace{\omega R\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1}_{\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P} \quad &\text{(grouped; $\omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf r_1^P = \omega R\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1^P}{dt}\right|_0 &= \frac{d}{dt}\left(R\dot\theta\cos\theta\right)\mathbf i_1 + \frac{d}{dt}\left(R\dot\theta\sin\theta\right)\mathbf k_1 + R\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\omega\,\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf a_1^P + \omega R\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(components in $S_1$ plus the turning of $\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left(\omega R\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1\right) &= \omega R\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 - \omega^2R\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(chain rule; derivative of $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P &= 2\omega R\dot\theta\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1\right) = 2\omega R\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(the two $\mathbf j_1$ terms above)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(\omega R\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1\right) = -\omega^2R\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(the $\mathbf i_1$ term above; $\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\mathbf i_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_0^P = R\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta + \omega R\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1, \qquad \mathbf a_0^P = R\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta - R\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf e_r + 2\omega R\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 - \omega^2R\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1}$$

Units: every acceleration term $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the Coriolis acceleration is normal to the plane of the wire; it appears because the distance to the axis changes while the plane turns. The centripetal one points horizontally to the axis.

Forces and Equations of Motion

The free-body diagram of the particle in $S_1$ shows the weight, the reaction (in the plane along $\mathbf e_r$, normal to the plane along $\mathbf j_1$), the centrifugal force, horizontal and away from the axis, and the Coriolis force, normal to the plane. The inertia force of the origin and the Euler force vanish ($O$ fixed, $\omega$ constant).

Figure 3. Forces on $P$ in $S_1$. In the plane of the wire: weight, $N_r\,\mathbf e_r$ and the centrifugal force $m\omega^2R\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1$. Normal to it: the reaction $N_b\,\mathbf j_1$ and the Coriolis force $-2m\omega R\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1$, which balance each other.
Newton's second law in the rotating frame, projected on the wire basis Law: Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame with the inertia forces; reaction of a smooth curve Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.16; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf F_C &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) = m\omega^2R\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(centripetal term times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR} &= -2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P = -2m\omega R\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(Coriolis term times $-m$)} \\ m\,\mathbf a_1^P &= -mg\,\mathbf k_1 + N_r\,\mathbf e_r + N_b\,\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf F_C + \mathbf F_{COR} \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.63; $\mathbf F_A$, $\mathbf F_E$ zero)} \\ \mathbf k_1\cdot\mathbf e_\theta &= \sin\theta, \quad \mathbf i_1\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = \cos\theta, \quad \mathbf k_1\cdot\mathbf e_r = -\cos\theta, \quad \mathbf i_1\cdot\mathbf e_r = \sin\theta \quad &\text{(components of the wire basis)} \\ \mathbf e_\theta:\ mR\ddot\theta &= -mg\sin\theta + m\omega^2R\sin\theta\cos\theta \quad &\text{(tangent: no reaction)} \\ \mathbf e_r:\ -mR\dot\theta^2 &= mg\cos\theta + N_r + m\omega^2R\sin^2\theta \quad &\text{(in the plane, along the radius)} \\ \mathbf j_1:\ 0 &= N_b - 2m\omega R\dot\theta\cos\theta \quad &\text{(normal to the plane: no relative motion there)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\ddot\theta = -\frac{g}{R}\sin\theta + \omega^2\sin\theta\cos\theta, \qquad N_r = -mR\dot\theta^2 - mg\cos\theta - m\omega^2R\sin^2\theta, \qquad N_b = 2m\omega R\dot\theta\cos\theta}$$

Units: $[g/R] = [\omega^2] = [\mathrm{T^{-2}}]$; $[m\omega R\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: three scalar equations for the three unknowns $\theta$, $N_r$ and $N_b$: the tangent equation is the equation of motion, the other two give the reaction afterwards. The normal reaction balances the Coriolis force alone.

Answers and Checks

(a) Mechanical energy in the moving frame

Which forces do work in the rotating frame, and their potentials Law: power of each force on the relative velocity; potential as minus the work along the wire, with Barrow's rule Source: [Lecture 5, Slide 29]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.14; Notes.pdf, Sec. 6.4

The energy in $S_1$ is conserved if every force that does work in $S_1$ has a potential. Two reasons hold here. First, the forces that do no work in $S_1$: the reaction, because the wire is smooth and at rest in $S_1$, so the reaction is normal to the relative velocity; the Coriolis force, always normal to the relative velocity; and the force of the origin and the Euler force, which vanish. Second, the forces that do work have potentials: the weight, and the centrifugal force because $\boldsymbol\omega_{10}$ is constant. Along the wire the displacement is $R\,\mathbf e_\theta\,d\theta'$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf N\cdot\mathbf v_1^P &= R\dot\theta\left(N_r\,\mathbf e_r + N_b\,\mathbf j_1\right)\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = 0, \quad \mathbf F_{COR}\cdot\mathbf v_1^P = -2m\omega R^2\dot\theta^2\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = 0 \quad &\text{(no power in $S_1$)} \\ V_g(\theta) - V_g(0) &= -\int_0^{\theta}\left(-mg\,\mathbf k_1\right)\cdot\mathbf e_\theta\,R\,d\theta' = mgR\int_0^{\theta}\sin\theta'\,d\theta' \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.14; $\mathbf k_1\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = \sin\theta'$)} \\ &= mgR\left[-\cos\theta'\right]_0^{\theta} = mgR\left(1 - \cos\theta\right) \quad &\text{(antiderivative $-\cos\theta'$; Barrow's rule)} \\ V_C(\theta) - V_C(0) &= -\int_0^{\theta} m\omega^2R\sin\theta'\,\mathbf i_1\cdot\mathbf e_\theta\,R\,d\theta' = -m\omega^2R^2\int_0^{\theta}\sin\theta'\cos\theta'\,d\theta' \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.14; $\mathbf i_1\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = \cos\theta'$)} \\ &= -m\omega^2R^2\left[\tfrac12\sin^2\theta'\right]_0^{\theta} = -\tfrac12 m\omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta \quad &\text{(antiderivative $\tfrac12\sin^2\theta'$; Barrow's rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{V_g = -mgR\cos\theta \ \ \text{(zero at the height of $O$)}, \qquad V_C = -\tfrac12 m\omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta = -\tfrac12 m\omega^2 r_\perp^2}$$

Units: $[mgR] = [m\omega^2R^2] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$, energies

Meaning: the centrifugal potential of the wire is the potential of Slide 30 with the distance to the axis $R\sin\theta$; it is lowest where the particle is farthest from the axis.

Energy integral in the rotating frame Law: the tangent equation multiplied by the relative speed is an exact derivative (chain rule); Barrow's rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.29; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]
$$\begin{aligned} mR^2\dot\theta\ddot\theta + mgR\sin\theta\,\dot\theta - m\omega^2R^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\theta &= 0 \quad &\text{(tangent equation times $R\dot\theta$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac12 mR^2\dot\theta^2\right) &= mR^2\dot\theta\ddot\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(-mgR\cos\theta\right) &= mgR\sin\theta\,\dot\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(-\tfrac12 m\omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta\right) &= -m\omega^2R^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule on $\sin^2\theta$)} \\ \left[\tfrac12 mR^2\dot\theta^2 - mgR\cos\theta - \tfrac12 m\omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta\right]_0^t &= 0 \quad &\text{(Barrow's rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{E_1^P = \tfrac12 mR^2\dot\theta^2 - mgR\cos\theta - \tfrac12 m\omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta = \tfrac12 mR^2\dot\theta_0^2 - mgR\cos\theta_0 - \tfrac12 m\omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta_0}$$

Units: each term $[\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the mechanical energy in $S_1$ (kinetic energy of the relative motion plus the potentials of the weight and of the centrifugal force) is conserved; its value is fixed by the initial angle and rate, which the statement leaves free.

The energy in the inertial frame is not conserved Law: power of the reaction on the absolute velocity; kinetic energy in $S_0$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.11; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf N\cdot\mathbf v_0^P &= \left(N_r\,\mathbf e_r + N_b\,\mathbf j_1\right)\cdot\left(R\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta + \omega R\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1\right) = N_b\,\omega R\sin\theta \quad &\text{(absolute velocity box)} \\ &= 2m\omega^2R^2\dot\theta\sin\theta\cos\theta \quad &\text{($N_b$ of the equations of motion)} \\ E_0^P &= \tfrac12 m\left(R^2\dot\theta^2 + \omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta\right) - mgR\cos\theta = E_1^P + m\omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta \quad &\text{(kinetic energy in $S_0$ plus the weight potential)} \\ \frac{dE_0^P}{dt} &= 0 + 2m\omega^2R^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\theta \quad &\text{($E_1^P$ constant; chain rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\frac{dE_0^P}{dt} = \mathbf N\cdot\mathbf v_0^P = N_b\,\omega R\sin\theta \ne 0}$$

Units: $[N_b\,\omega R] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-3}}]$, a power

Meaning: in $S_0$ the wire moves and its reaction does work, so the energy there changes at the rate of that power (Eq. 4.11); in $S_1$ the wire is at rest and the energy is a constant.

(b) Reaction normal to the plane of the circumference

Normal reaction as a function of theta Law: equation normal to the plane with the rate eliminated through the energy integral Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.19; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]
$$\begin{aligned} N_b &= 2m\omega R\dot\theta\cos\theta \quad &\text{(equation along $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ R^2\dot\theta^2 &= \frac{2E_1^P}{m} + 2gR\cos\theta + \omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta \quad &\text{(energy integral solved for the squared rate)} \\ &= R^2\dot\theta_0^2 + 2gR\left(\cos\theta - \cos\theta_0\right) + \omega^2R^2\left(\sin^2\theta - \sin^2\theta_0\right) \quad &\text{(value of $E_1^P$)} \\ R\dot\theta &= \pm\sqrt{R^2\dot\theta_0^2 + 2gR\left(\cos\theta - \cos\theta_0\right) + \omega^2R^2\left(\sin^2\theta - \sin^2\theta_0\right)} \quad &\text{(sign of $\dot\theta$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{N_b(\theta) = \pm\,2m\omega\cos\theta\sqrt{\frac{2E_1^P}{m} + 2gR\cos\theta + \omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta} \quad (\text{sign of } \dot\theta), \qquad \text{along } \mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[2E_1^P/m] = [gR] = [\omega^2R^2] = [\mathrm{L^2\,T^{-2}}]$, so $[N_b] = [\mathrm{M}][\mathrm{T^{-1}}][\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$, a force

Meaning: the normal reaction vanishes when the particle is at rest on the wire and when it crosses the horizontal diameter; it pushes the particle forwards, in the sense of the rotation, while the particle moves away from the axis, and backwards while it comes closer (the angular momentum box below shows why).

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Energy in the moving frameconserved: the reaction and the Coriolis force do no work in $S_1$, the origin and Euler forces vanish, and the weight and the centrifugal force (constant $\omega$) have potentials; $E_1^P = \frac12 mR^2\dot\theta^2 - mgR\cos\theta - \frac12 m\omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta$, equal to its initial value $\frac12 mR^2\dot\theta_0^2 - mgR\cos\theta_0 - \frac12 m\omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta_0$
(b) Reaction normal to the plane$N_b = 2m\omega R\dot\theta\cos\theta = \pm 2m\omega\cos\theta\sqrt{2E_1^P/m + 2gR\cos\theta + \omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta}$ along $\mathbf j_1$
Intermediate resultsequation of motion $\ddot\theta = -(g/R)\sin\theta + \omega^2\sin\theta\cos\theta$; reaction in the plane $N_r = -mR\dot\theta^2 - mg\cos\theta - m\omega^2R\sin^2\theta$; energy in $S_0$ not conserved, its rate is $N_b\,\omega R\sin\theta$

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 72 lists item 20 with no answer, so there is no key to compare with. Independent checks: the normal reaction follows again from the angular momentum about the vertical axis in $S_0$ (box below), without inertia forces, and the limiting cases close the results.

Independent check: angular momentum about the vertical axis Law: angular momentum about the fixed point $O$ and its rate, equal to the moment of the forces Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.48; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.51; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.53
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf H_{O,0}\cdot\mathbf k_1 &= m\left(\mathbf r_0^P\times\mathbf v_0^P\right)\cdot\mathbf k_1 = m\left(x_1v_{y1} - y_1v_{x1}\right) \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.48; $x_1$, $y_1$ the components on $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ &= m\left(R\sin\theta\cdot\omega R\sin\theta - 0\cdot R\dot\theta\cos\theta\right) = m\omega R^2\sin^2\theta \quad &\text{(absolute velocity box)} \\ \mathbf M_O\cdot\mathbf k_1 &= \left(\mathbf r_0^P\times N_b\,\mathbf j_1\right)\cdot\mathbf k_1 = R\sin\theta\,N_b \quad &\text{(weight vertical and $N_r\,\mathbf e_r$ through $O$: no axial moment)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(m\omega R^2\sin^2\theta\right) &= 2m\omega R^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule; $\mathbf k_1$ fixed)} \\ R\sin\theta\,N_b &= 2m\omega R^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\theta \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.53, axial component)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{N_b = 2m\omega R\dot\theta\cos\theta \quad (\sin\theta \ne 0)}$$

Units: $[H] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-1}}]$; $[R\,N_b] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: to keep turning at the rate $\omega$ while its distance to the axis changes, the particle needs an axial moment, and only the normal reaction can give it: the same result as the Coriolis balance in $S_1$.

Limiting cases and relative equilibria Law: the results at extreme values of the data; rest in $S_1$ in the equation of motion Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.32; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63
$$\begin{aligned} \omega \to 0:\quad N_b &\to 0, \quad E_1^P \to \tfrac12 mR^2\dot\theta^2 - mgR\cos\theta \quad &\text{(simple pendulum of length $R$)} \\ \dot\theta = 0,\ \ddot\theta = 0:\quad \sin\theta\left(\omega^2\cos\theta - \frac{g}{R}\right) &= 0 \quad &\text{(relative equilibria)} \\ \theta_e &= 0, \quad \theta_e = \pi, \quad \cos\theta_e = \frac{g}{\omega^2R} \ \ (\omega^2R \gt g) \quad &\text{(the three families)} \\ N_b(\theta_e) &= 0 \quad &\text{(no relative velocity)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\omega \to 0: \ N_b \to 0; \qquad \text{relative equilibria } \theta = 0,\ \pi \ \text{and}\ \cos\theta = g/(\omega^2R) \ \text{if}\ \omega^2R \gt g}$$

Units: $[g/(\omega^2R)] = [1]$

Meaning: without rotation the bead is a pendulum and the wire does not push sideways; a bead at rest on the turning wire needs no normal reaction either, and above the critical rate it can rest off the bottom (these equilibria are not asked for).

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf (PDF page 10); no official key
Problem 21

Apparent Weight on a Spinning Planet

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 10
Centrifugal Force

On a spinning spherical planet of radius $R$ and gravitational acceleration $g_p$, the bodies weight [sic] twice as much on the poles as on the equator. Determine the duration of the day on that planet.

Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

On a spinning spherical planet of radius $R$ and gravitational acceleration $g_p$, bodies weigh twice as much at the poles as at the equator; the statement asks for the duration of the day (Problems.pdf, p. 10). The weight of a body is what a scale on the ground reads, a quantity defined in the frame of the planet, where the body is at rest; the solution works in that frame, with the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2 and the inertia forces of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $O$ at the centre of the planet, axes fixed with respect to the stars; $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$ with $\mathbf k_0$ along the polar axis, towards the north pole (Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.1)
Moving frame$S_1 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_1\}$ fixed to the planet: $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$; $\mathbf i_1$ in the equatorial plane and in the meridian plane of the body; $\mathbf j_1$ the cross product of $\mathbf k_1$ and $\mathbf i_1$ (towards the east); it turns by $\Omega t$ about $\mathbf k_0$
Local basis at the body$\mathcal B_2 = \{\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_n, -\mathbf j_1\}$: $\mathbf e_r$ the local vertical, from $O$ to the body $P$; $\mathbf e_n$ horizontal, towards the north pole
Coordinate$\lambda$, the latitude of $P$: the angle at $O$ from the equatorial plane to $OP$, positive towards the north
Degrees of freedomnone to find: the body is at rest on the ground, at a fixed latitude
Data$R$ [m], $g_p$ [m s$^{-2}$], $m$ [kg] the mass of the body; the ratio 2 between the weights at a pole and at the equator
Unknownsthe spin rate $\Omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$] and the day $T_{day}$ [s]; on the way, the contact force $\mathbf N$ [N]
Applied forcethe attraction of the planet, $-mg_p\,\mathbf e_r$ at the surface
Constraint forcethe contact force of the ground (or of a scale) $\mathbf N$
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)of the origin, Euler, centrifugal and Coriolis (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Weightthe magnitude $W$ of the contact force on a body at rest on the ground, what a scale reads
Hypothesesthe frame of the centre is inertial; $\Omega$ constant; rigid spherical planet with a spherical mass distribution, so the attraction at the surface has the same magnitude $g_p$ everywhere and points to $O$; the ground can push but not pull; the day is the period of one rotation with respect to the stars (the statement gives no orbit, so a solar day is not computed)

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. View from above the north pole ($\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf k_1$ out of the paper, $\odot$). $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned counter-clockwise by $\Omega t$ (legs $\cos\Omega t$, $\sin\Omega t$); $\mathbf j_1$ turns the same angle from $\mathbf j_0$, so its opposite leg points along $-\mathbf i_0$.
Basis of the planet: rotation by Omega t about k0 Law: elementary rotation about the third axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

View from above the north pole, along $\mathbf k_0$, out of the paper (⊙) because it is the cross product of $\mathbf i_0$ (to the right) and $\mathbf j_0$ (up); a positive $\Omega$ turns the planet counterclockwise. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\Omega t$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\Omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$. $\mathbf j_1$ is $\mathbf j_0$ turned by the same angle: adjacent leg $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$, opposite leg $\sin\Omega t$ along minus $\mathbf i_0$ (the upward vector turned counterclockwise leans to the left: the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf j_1 = -\sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles; axis)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= 1\cdot\left(\cos^2\Omega t + \sin^2\Omega t\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\Omega t + \sin^2\Omega t = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{12} = \cos\Omega t\sin\Omega t - \sin\Omega t\cos\Omega t = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\Omega t & -\sin\Omega t & 0 \cr \sin\Omega t & \cos\Omega t & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: dimensionless: $[1]$

Meaning: the planet axes come back to their initial position after the time in which $\Omega t$ grows by $2\pi$: that time is the day.

Figure 2. Meridian plane of the body ($\mathbf i_1$ right, $\mathbf k_1$ up, $\mathbf j_1$ into the paper, $\otimes$). In the shaded right triangle $OFP$ the hypotenuse is $R$, the leg adjacent to $\lambda$ is $R\cos\lambda$ along $\mathbf i_1$ and the opposite leg is $R\sin\lambda$ along $\mathbf k_1$. The centrifugal force $m\Omega^2\mathbf r_\perp$ is horizontal, away from the axis; the attraction $-mg_p\mathbf e_r$ points to $O$.
Position of the body in its meridian plane Law: right triangle in the meridian plane; part of the position normal to the spin axis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.2; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]

Meridian plane of the body, drawn with $\mathbf i_1$ to the right and $\mathbf k_1$ up; $\mathbf j_1$, the cross product of $\mathbf k_1$ (up) and $\mathbf i_1$ (right), points into the paper (⊗). Let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the equatorial line: in the right triangle $OFP$ the hypotenuse is $R$, the leg adjacent to $\lambda$ is $R\cos\lambda$ along $\mathbf i_1$ and the leg opposite to $\lambda$ is $R\sin\lambda$ along $\mathbf k_1$. $\lambda$ is measured from $\mathbf i_1$ towards $\mathbf k_1$, so it is already the standard polar angle of this plane.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_0^O &= \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf r_0^P = \mathbf r_1^P = \overrightarrow{OP} \quad &\text{(origin of $S_1$ at the centre; Eq. 3.16)} \\ \mathbf r_1^P &= R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf i_1 + R\sin\lambda\,\mathbf k_1 = R\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(legs of $OFP$)} \\ \mathbf r_\parallel &= \left(\mathbf r_1^P\cdot\mathbf k_1\right)\mathbf k_1 = R\sin\lambda\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(part along the spin axis)} \\ \mathbf r_\perp &= \mathbf r_1^P - \mathbf r_\parallel = R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(part normal to the spin axis, Slide 30)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^P = R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf i_1 + R\sin\lambda\,\mathbf k_1, \qquad \mathbf r_\perp = R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf i_1}$$

Units: $[R] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: at a pole the body is on the axis and its distance to it is zero; at the equator the distance is the whole radius.

Figure 3. Rotation by $\lambda$ in the meridian plane ($-\mathbf j_1$ out of the paper). The triangle of $\mathbf e_n$ has its opposite leg along $-\mathbf i_1$: the minus sign of $\mathbf e_n = -\sin\lambda\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\lambda\,\mathbf k_1$.
Local basis: rotation by the latitude in the meridian plane Law: elementary rotation in the meridian plane; change of basis matrix, its checks and its inverse Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.19

Same meridian view: $\mathbf j_1$ into the paper (⊗), so minus $\mathbf j_1$, the cross product of $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf k_1$, points out of it (⊙), and positive angles about minus $\mathbf j_1$ are counterclockwise. $\mathbf e_r$ is $\mathbf i_1$ turned by $\lambda$: adjacent leg $\cos\lambda$ along $\mathbf i_1$, opposite leg $\sin\lambda$ along $\mathbf k_1$. $\mathbf e_n$ is $\mathbf k_1$ turned by $\lambda$: adjacent leg $\cos\lambda$ along $\mathbf k_1$, opposite leg $\sin\lambda$ along minus $\mathbf i_1$ (the upward vector turned counterclockwise leans to the left: the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_r &= \cos\lambda\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\lambda\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf e_n = -\sin\lambda\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\lambda\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles)} \\ \mathbf e_r\times\mathbf e_n &= \cos^2\lambda\,\mathbf i_1\times\mathbf k_1 - \sin^2\lambda\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = -\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf i_1\times\mathbf k_1 = -\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf j_1$)} \\ \det[{}_1R_2] &= (-1)\cdot(-1)^{2+3}\left(\cos^2\lambda + \sin^2\lambda\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the second row, entry $-1$ in place (2,3), cofactor sign $(-1)^5$)} \\ \mathbf e_r\cdot\mathbf e_n &= -\cos\lambda\sin\lambda + \sin\lambda\cos\lambda = 0 \quad &\text{(checks: $[{}_1R_2][{}_1R_2]^T = I$)} \\ \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\lambda\,\mathbf e_r - \sin\lambda\,\mathbf e_n \quad &\text{(inverse: first row of the matrix)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_1R_2] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\lambda & -\sin\lambda & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & -1 \cr \sin\lambda & \cos\lambda & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_1R_2] = 1, \quad \mathbf i_1 = \cos\lambda\,\mathbf e_r - \sin\lambda\,\mathbf e_n}$$

Units: dimensionless: $[1]$

Meaning: the inverse relation splits the centrifugal force, along $\mathbf i_1$, into a part along the local vertical and a local horizontal part along minus $\mathbf e_n$, towards the equator (south in the northern hemisphere).

Kinematics

Composition of motions for a body at rest on the planet Law: derivatives of the unit vectors of a turning basis; time derivatives in $S_0$ of the position written in $\mathcal B_1$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.25; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]

In $S_1$ the latitude and the radius are constant and $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf k_1$ are fixed, so the relative velocity and the relative acceleration vanish.

$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(simple rotation about the polar axis; $\Omega$ constant)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\Omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 to 3.5)} \\ \mathbf v_1^P &= \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf a_1^P = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(constant components in $S_1$)} \\ \mathbf v_0^P &= \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left(R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf i_1 + R\sin\lambda\,\mathbf k_1\right) = R\cos\lambda\,\Omega\,\mathbf j_1 = \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P \quad &\text{(only the turning of $\mathbf i_1$: transport term)} \\ \mathbf a_0^P &= \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left(\Omega R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf j_1\right) = -\Omega^2R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(only the turning of $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) &= \Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(\Omega R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf j_1\right) = -\Omega^2R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(the same vector: centripetal term)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_1^P = \mathbf a_1^P = \mathbf 0, \qquad \mathbf v_0^P = \Omega R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf j_1, \qquad \mathbf a_0^P = \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) = -\Omega^2\,\mathbf r_\perp}$$

Units: $[\Omega R] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[\Omega^2R] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: of the terms of Eq. 3.27 only the centripetal one survives: the body describes its parallel of latitude, of radius $R\cos\lambda$, once per day; with no relative velocity there is no Coriolis term.

Forces and Equations of Motion

The free-body diagram of the body in $S_1$ shows the attraction of the planet towards $O$, the contact force of the ground and the centrifugal force, horizontal and away from the axis. The Coriolis force vanishes (the body is at rest in $S_1$), and so do the inertia force of the origin and the Euler force.

Figure 4. At the pole the body is on the spin axis: the contact force balances the attraction alone, $W_{pole} = mg_p$. At the equator the centrifugal force $m\Omega^2R$ takes away part of it, $W_{eq} = m(g_p - \Omega^2R)$; the ratio 2 of the statement means $\Omega^2R = g_p/2$.
Static balance in the planet frame Law: Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame with the inertia forces, at relative rest Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf F_C &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) = m\Omega^2R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(centripetal term times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR} &= -2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf F_A = \mathbf F_E = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(rest in $S_1$; $O$ fixed; $\Omega$ constant)} \\ m\,\mathbf a_1^P &= \mathbf 0 = -mg_p\,\mathbf e_r + \mathbf N + m\Omega^2R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.63)} \\ \mathbf N &= mg_p\,\mathbf e_r - m\Omega^2R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(solved)} \\ &= m\left(g_p - \Omega^2R\cos^2\lambda\right)\mathbf e_r + m\Omega^2R\cos\lambda\sin\lambda\,\mathbf e_n \quad &\text{($\mathbf i_1 = \cos\lambda\,\mathbf e_r - \sin\lambda\,\mathbf e_n$)} \\ W^2 &= \left|\mathbf N\right|^2 = m^2\left[\left(g_p - \Omega^2R\cos^2\lambda\right)^2 + \Omega^4R^2\cos^2\lambda\sin^2\lambda\right] \quad &\text{(components squared and added)} \\ &= m^2\left[g_p^2 - \left(2g_p\Omega^2R - \Omega^4R^2\right)\cos^2\lambda\right] \quad &\text{($\cos^4\lambda + \cos^2\lambda\sin^2\lambda = \cos^2\lambda$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf N = m\left(g_p - \Omega^2R\cos^2\lambda\right)\mathbf e_r + m\Omega^2R\cos\lambda\sin\lambda\,\mathbf e_n, \qquad W = m\sqrt{g_p^2 - \left(2g_p\Omega^2R - \Omega^4R^2\right)\cos^2\lambda}}$$

Units: $[g_p] = [\Omega^2R] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$, so $[W] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: three scalar equations give the three components of the contact force. Away from the poles and the equator it has a horizontal part towards the north (in the northern hemisphere), which a rigid spherical ground must supply by friction: the plumb line does not point to the centre.

Answers and Checks

Weights at a pole and at the equator Law: static balance of the previous box at the latitudes of a pole and of the equator; contact condition of a unilateral constraint Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Sec. 6.4; Problems.pdf, p. 10
$$\begin{aligned} \lambda = \tfrac{\pi}{2}:\quad \mathbf N_{pole} &= mg_p\,\mathbf k_1, \quad W_{pole} = mg_p \quad &\text{($\cos\lambda = 0$: on the axis, no centrifugal force)} \\ \lambda = 0:\quad \mathbf N_{eq} &= m\left(g_p - \Omega^2R\right)\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf e_r = \mathbf i_1$: centrifugal force radial and outward)} \\ g_p - \Omega^2R &\ge 0 \ \Rightarrow\ W_{eq} = m\left(g_p - \Omega^2R\right) \quad &\text{(the ground pushes, it cannot pull)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{W_{pole} = mg_p, \qquad W_{eq} = m\left(g_p - \Omega^2R\right) \ \ \left(\Omega^2R \le g_p\right)}$$

Units: $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the spin does not change the weight at a pole and lightens it at the equator; a body could not stay on the equator of a planet spinning faster than the break-up rate.

Spin rate and duration of the day Law: condition of the statement on the two weights; period of a uniform rotation Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Problems.pdf, p. 10
$$\begin{aligned} W_{eq} &= m\left|g_p - \Omega^2R\right|, \quad W_{pole} = 2W_{eq} \ \Rightarrow\ mg_p = 2m\left|g_p - \Omega^2R\right| \quad &\text{(statement; magnitude of $\mathbf N_{eq}$)} \\ g_p - \Omega^2R &= \pm\frac{g_p}{2} \ \Rightarrow\ \Omega^2R = \frac{g_p}{2} \ \ \text{or} \ \ \Omega^2R = \frac{3g_p}{2} \quad &\text{(two roots)} \\ \Omega^2R = \frac{3g_p}{2}:\quad \mathbf N_{eq} &= m\left(g_p - \frac{3g_p}{2}\right)\mathbf i_1 = -\frac{mg_p}{2}\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(the ground would pull: rejected; it gives $T = 2\pi\sqrt{2R/(3g_p)} \simeq 5.130\sqrt{R/g_p}$)} \\ \Omega^2R &= \frac{g_p}{2} \le g_p \ \Rightarrow\ \Omega = \sqrt{\frac{g_p}{2R}} \quad &\text{(kept: the contact condition holds; positive root)} \\ \Omega\,T_{day} &= 2\pi \quad &\text{(one turn of $\mathcal B_1$, first box)} \\ T_{day} &= \frac{2\pi}{\Omega} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2R}{g_p}} = 2\sqrt2\,\pi\sqrt{\frac{R}{g_p}} \simeq 8.886\sqrt{\frac{R}{g_p}} \quad &\text{(substituted)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\Omega = \sqrt{\frac{g_p}{2R}}, \qquad T_{day} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2R}{g_p}}}$$

Units: $[\sqrt{R/g_p}] = [\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{L^{-1}\,T^{2}}]^{1/2} = [\mathrm{T}]$

Meaning: the centrifugal force at the equator cancels half of the attraction there. The second root would need the ground to pull the body.

Part of the statementAnswer
Duration of the day$T_{day} = 2\pi\sqrt{2R/g_p} \simeq 8.886\sqrt{R/g_p}$ (one rotation with respect to the stars)
Intermediate results$\Omega = \sqrt{g_p/(2R)}$; $W_{pole} = mg_p$, $W_{eq} = m(g_p - \Omega^2R) = mg_p/2$; contact force $\mathbf N = m(g_p - \Omega^2R\cos^2\lambda)\,\mathbf e_r + m\Omega^2R\cos\lambda\sin\lambda\,\mathbf e_n$

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 72 lists item 21 with no answer, so there is no key to compare with. Independent checks: Newton's law in the inertial frame gives the same contact force (box below), and the limiting cases close the result.

Independent check in the inertial frame Law: Newton's second law in $S_0$ with the absolute acceleration of the kinematics box Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.59
$$\begin{aligned} m\,\mathbf a_0^P &= -mg_p\,\mathbf e_r + \mathbf N \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.59: attraction and contact are the only forces)} \\ -m\Omega^2R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf i_1 &= -mg_p\,\mathbf e_r + \mathbf N \quad &\text{(kinematics box)} \\ \mathbf N &= mg_p\,\mathbf e_r - m\Omega^2R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(solved)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf N = mg_p\,\mathbf e_r - m\Omega^2R\cos\lambda\,\mathbf i_1 \quad \text{(same as in } S_1\text{)}}$$

Units: $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: seen from the stars the body moves on its parallel of latitude and needs a centripetal force towards the axis; the attraction minus the contact force provides it.

Limiting cases and the weight at any latitude Law: the weight formula of the balance box at extreme values and with the rate found Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Problems.pdf, p. 10
$$\begin{aligned} \Omega \to 0:\quad W_{eq} &\to mg_p = W_{pole} \quad &\text{(no spin, no difference)} \\ \Omega_b &= \sqrt{\frac{g_p}{R}}:\quad W_{eq} = 0 \quad &\text{(break-up rate: weightless equator)} \\ \frac{\Omega}{\Omega_b} &= \sqrt{\frac{g_p/(2R)}{g_p/R}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2} \simeq 0.707 \quad &\text{(the planet of the statement)} \\ \Omega^2R = \frac{g_p}{2}:\quad W(\lambda) &= m\sqrt{g_p^2 - \left(g_p^2 - \tfrac14 g_p^2\right)\cos^2\lambda} = mg_p\sqrt{1 - \tfrac34\cos^2\lambda} \quad &\text{(balance box at a general latitude)} \\ \lambda = \tfrac{\pi}{4}:\quad W &= mg_p\sqrt{1 - \tfrac38} = mg_p\sqrt{\tfrac58} \simeq 0.791\,mg_p \quad &\text{($\cos^2\tfrac{\pi}{4} = \tfrac12$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{W(\lambda) = mg_p\sqrt{1 - \tfrac34\cos^2\lambda}: \ \ mg_p/2 \ \text{at the equator}, \ \ mg_p \ \text{at the poles}}$$

Units: $[mg_p] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the planet spins at 0.707 of its break-up rate; the weight grows monotonically from the equator to the poles (0.791 of the polar value at 45 degrees), so the ratio 2 of the statement is the largest ratio of weights between two places of the planet.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf (PDF page 10); no official key
Problem 22

Particle on a Curve

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 10
1D Curve Constraint

A heavy point particle $P$ of mass $m$ is constrained to move without friction along the curve:

$$ y = a\left(1 - \cos\frac{x}{a}\right) \tag{4} $$

in the range $-\pi a \le x \le \pi a$, where $a$ is a positive constant. Initially, the particle is located at $x = 0$ with velocity $v_0$ along the positive $x$ axis.

  • (a)
    Reduce the problem to integrals.
  • (b)
    If $v_0 = \sqrt{ga}$, determine the minimum and maximum value of $x$ along the motion.
  • (c)
    What should be the minimum value of $v_0$ in order to reach $x = \pi a$?

Let's assume now that the curve containing the point particle rotates around the $OY$ axis with constant angular velocity $\boldsymbol{\omega} = \Omega\mathbf{j}$.

  • (d)
    Define a convenient moving reference frame with origin in $O$, $OX_1Y_1Z_1$. Determine the inertia force that acts on the particle in this moving reference frame as a function of $m, \Omega, x_1$ and $\dot{x}_1$, where $x_1$ represents the position coordinate of $P$ along $OX_1$.
  • (e)
    Reduce the problem to quadratures and determine the value of the reaction force.
  • (f)
    Find out a trascendental [sic] equation whose solutions are the equilibrium positions of the point particle in $OX_1Y_1Z_1$.
  • (g)
    If $\Omega$ were a function of time, would it be possible to use the energy equation in the same way as before? Justify your answer.
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

A heavy particle $P$ of mass $m$ slides without friction on a plane curve of the shape given in the table, between the two crests at plus and minus $\pi a$; it starts at $O$ with the speed $v_0$ along the positive $x$ axis (Problems.pdf, p. 10). Parts (a) to (c) take the curve at rest; parts (d) to (g) let it turn about the vertical axis $OY$ with the constant rate $\Omega$. The fixed curve is solved in the inertial frame with the projections of Notes.pdf, Sec. 6.5; the turning curve in the frame attached to it, with the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2 and the inertia forces of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9.

ItemDefinition
Curve$y = a\left(1 - \cos(x/a)\right)$ for $-\pi a \le x \le \pi a$, in a vertical plane; $a \gt 0$
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$: $\mathbf i_0$ along $OX$ (horizontal), $\mathbf j_0$ along $OY$ (vertical, up; the $\mathbf j$ of the statement), $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf i_0\times\mathbf j_0$, horizontal (Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.1)
Moving frame (parts d to g)$S_1 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_1\}$, the frame $OX_1Y_1Z_1$ attached to the curve: $\mathbf i_1$ along $OX_1$ in the plane of the curve, $\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf j_0$ the axis of rotation, $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf i_1\times\mathbf j_1$ normal to the plane of the curve; it coincides with $S_0$ at $t = 0$ and turns by the angle $\Omega t$ about $\mathbf j_0$
Curve basis$\{\mathbf e_t, \mathbf n, \mathbf k\}$ at $P$: unit tangent in the sense of growing abscissa, in-plane unit normal $\mathbf n$ (the tangent turned by $+90^\circ$ in the plane), and the normal to the plane ($\mathbf k_0$ for the fixed curve, $\mathbf k_1$ for the turning one)
Coordinates$x$, abscissa of $P$ along $OX$ (fixed curve); $x_1$, abscissa of $P$ along $OX_1$ (turning curve)
Shorthand$s = \sin(x_1/a)$, $c = \cos(x_1/a)$, $D = \sqrt{1 + s^2}$ (the same letters with $x$ for the fixed curve)
Constraints$P$ in the plane of the curve and on the curve: two holonomic, smooth, bilateral constraints (rheonomic in $S_0$ when the curve turns, fixed in $S_1$)
Degrees of freedom3 minus 2: 1, the abscissa $x(t)$ or $x_1(t)$; the angle $\Omega t$ is prescribed
Data$m$ [kg], $a$ [m], $g$ [m s$^{-2}$], $v_0$ [m s$^{-1}$], $\Omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$]
Initial state$x(0) = 0$ (or $x_1(0) = 0$), absolute velocity $v_0\,\mathbf i_0$
Unknownsthe abscissa as a function of time; the reaction $\mathbf N = N_n\,\mathbf n + N_b\,\mathbf k$ (normal subspace of a curve, Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.16)
Applied forceweight $-mg\,\mathbf j_0$
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)of the origin, Euler, centrifugal and Coriolis (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial, uniform gravity, smooth curve (no tangential reaction), the rotation of the curve imposed from outside (whatever torque it needs is supplied)

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. Plane of the curve (fixed in $S_0$ for (a)–(c), fixed in $S_1$ for (d)–(g); $\mathbf k_1$ out of the paper, $\odot$). The dashed lines are the components $x_1$ and $y_1 = a(1 - \cos(x_1/a))$ of $\mathbf r_1^P$. In the shaded slope triangle the leg adjacent to the tangent angle $\alpha$ is $dx_1$, the opposite leg is $dy = \sin(x_1/a)\,dx_1$ and the hypotenuse is the arc element $d\ell$; $\mathbf e_t$ and $\mathbf n$ in orange.
Position vector and slope triangle in the plane of the curve Law: position vector as the sum of its components; chain rule; right triangle of the arc element Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.2; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.19; Problems.pdf, p. 10

The plane of the curve is drawn with the horizontal axis to the right and $\mathbf j_0$ up. For the fixed curve the horizontal axis is $OX$ with $\mathbf i_0$; for the turning curve the same drawing holds in $S_1$ with $OX_1$, $\mathbf i_1$ and $x_1$. The position of $P$ is the sum of its two dashed components: the abscissa along the horizontal axis and the height given by the equation of the curve. Moving a distance $dx_1$ along the axis, the height changes by $dy$; in the shaded right triangle the leg adjacent to the tangent angle $\alpha$ is $dx_1$, the opposite leg is $dy$ and the hypotenuse is the arc element $d\ell$ (Eq. 2.19, where it is called $ds$; here $s$ is the sine of the shorthand).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_1^P &= x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + a\left(1 - \cos\frac{x_1}{a}\right)\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(abscissa plus height on the curve)} \\ \frac{d}{dx_1}\cos\frac{x_1}{a} &= -\sin\frac{x_1}{a}\cdot\frac{d}{dx_1}\left(\frac{x_1}{a}\right) = -\frac{1}{a}\sin\frac{x_1}{a} \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \frac{dy}{dx_1} &= a\cdot\frac{1}{a}\sin\frac{x_1}{a} = s \quad &\text{(derivative of the height; shorthand $s$)} \\ d\ell^2 &= dx_1^2 + dy^2 = \left(1 + s^2\right)dx_1^2 \quad &\text{(Pythagoras in the slope triangle)} \\ d\ell &= D\,dx_1, \quad \cos\alpha = \frac{dx_1}{d\ell} = \frac{1}{D}, \quad \sin\alpha = \frac{dy}{d\ell} = \frac{s}{D} \quad &\text{(adjacent and opposite legs over the hypotenuse)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^P = x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + a\left(1 - \cos\frac{x_1}{a}\right)\mathbf j_1, \qquad \frac{d\ell}{dx_1} = D = \sqrt{1 + \sin^2\frac{x_1}{a}}, \qquad \tan\alpha = \sin\frac{x_1}{a}}$$

Units: $[x_1] = [a] = [\mathrm{L}]$; $x_1/a$ and the slope dimensionless

Meaning: $x_1$ zero gives the initial point $O$; at the crests, plus and minus $\pi a$, the height is twice $a$. The fixed curve has the same expressions with $x$, $\mathbf i_0$ and $\mathbf j_0$.

Tangent and normal of the curve: rotation by alpha in its plane Law: unit tangent along the hypotenuse of the slope triangle; elementary rotation about the normal to the plane and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.9; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20

The plane is seen with $\mathbf i_1$ to the right and $\mathbf j_1$ up, so $\mathbf k_1$, their cross product, points out of the paper (⊙) and a positive rotation about it is counterclockwise. $\mathbf e_t$ is $\mathbf i_1$ turned by $\alpha$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\alpha$ along $\mathbf i_1$, opposite leg $\sin\alpha$ along $\mathbf j_1$. $\mathbf n$ is $\mathbf j_1$ turned by the same angle: adjacent leg $\cos\alpha$ along $\mathbf j_1$, opposite leg $\sin\alpha$ along minus $\mathbf i_1$ (the upward vector turned counterclockwise leans to the left: the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_t &= \cos\alpha\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\alpha\,\mathbf j_1 = \frac{\mathbf i_1 + s\,\mathbf j_1}{D} \quad &\text{(right triangle of $\mathbf e_t$; Eq. 2.9: $d\mathbf r/d\ell$)} \\ \mathbf n &= -\sin\alpha\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\alpha\,\mathbf j_1 = \frac{-s\,\mathbf i_1 + \mathbf j_1}{D} \quad &\text{(right triangle of $\mathbf n$: opposite leg on $-\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \det[{}_1R_t] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\alpha\cos\alpha - (-\sin\alpha)\sin\alpha\right) = \frac{1 + s^2}{D^2} = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{3+3}$)} \\ \mathbf e_t\cdot\mathbf e_t &= \frac{1 + s^2}{D^2} = 1, \quad \mathbf e_t\cdot\mathbf n = \frac{-s + s}{D^2} = 0 \quad &\text{(columns orthonormal: $[{}_1R_t][{}_1R_t]^T = I$)} \\ \mathbf j_1\cdot\mathbf e_t &= \frac{s}{D}, \quad \mathbf j_1\cdot\mathbf n = \frac{1}{D}, \quad \mathbf i_1\cdot\mathbf e_t = \frac{1}{D}, \quad \mathbf i_1\cdot\mathbf n = -\frac{s}{D} \quad &\text{(projections used below)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf e_t = \frac{\mathbf i_1 + s\,\mathbf j_1}{D}, \quad \mathbf n = \frac{-s\,\mathbf i_1 + \mathbf j_1}{D}, \quad [{}_1R_t] = \begin{pmatrix} 1/D & -s/D & 0 \cr s/D & 1/D & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_1R_t] = 1}$$

Units: dimensionless: $[1]$

Meaning: the reaction of the smooth curve lies in the plane spanned by the normal $\mathbf n$ and the normal to the plane; projecting on the tangent removes it.

Figure 2. View from $+Y$, with $\mathbf j_0 = \mathbf j_1$ out of the paper ($\odot$): $\mathbf k_0$ points down the page. The plane of the curve contains $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf j_1$ and turns counter-clockwise by $\Omega t$: $\mathbf i_1$ has the components $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$ and $\sin\Omega t$ along $-\mathbf k_0$ (up the page), hence the minus sign in $\mathbf i_1 = \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 - \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0$.
Basis of the turning curve: rotation by Omega t about j0 Law: elementary rotation about the second axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.19; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

View from above, along $\mathbf j_0$, which points out of the paper (⊙). With $\mathbf i_0$ to the right, $\mathbf k_0$, the cross product of $\mathbf i_0$ and $\mathbf j_0$, points down the page (right-hand rule: fingers from $\mathbf i_0$, to the right, towards $\mathbf j_0$, towards the reader; the thumb goes down the page), so minus $\mathbf k_0$ points up the page. A positive $\Omega$ turns the curve counterclockwise in this view. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\Omega t$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\Omega t$ up the page, that is along minus $\mathbf k_0$ (the minus sign). $\mathbf k_1$ is $\mathbf k_0$ (down the page) turned by the same angle: its tip moves towards the right, adjacent leg $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf k_0$, opposite leg $\sin\Omega t$ along plus $\mathbf i_0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 - \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(right triangle of $\mathbf i_1$: opposite leg on $-\mathbf k_0$)} \\ \mathbf j_1 &= \mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(axis of the rotation)} \\ \mathbf k_1 &= \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(right triangle of $\mathbf k_1$)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\Omega t\cos\Omega t - \sin\Omega t\left(-\sin\Omega t\right)\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the second row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{2+2}$)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\Omega t + \sin^2\Omega t = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{13} = -\cos\Omega t\sin\Omega t + \sin\Omega t\cos\Omega t = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows; row 2 is the unit row of $\mathbf j_0$)} \\ \mathbf i_1\times\mathbf j_1 &= \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0\times\mathbf j_0 - \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0\times\mathbf j_0 = \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0 + \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 = \mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(right-handed; $\mathbf k_0\times\mathbf j_0 = -\mathbf i_0$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\Omega t & 0 & \sin\Omega t \cr 0 & 1 & 0 \cr -\sin\Omega t & 0 & \cos\Omega t \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: $[\Omega t] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}][\mathrm{T}] = [1]$

Meaning: it is the matrix of Eq. 1.19 with the angle $\Omega t$; at the start the two frames coincide.

Kinematics

Fixed curve: velocity and acceleration Law: time derivative of the position in $S_0$ with the constant basis $\mathcal B_0$; chain rule and product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.6; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.16
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_0^P &= x\,\mathbf i_0 + a\left(1 - \cos\frac{x}{a}\right)\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(position box with $x$, $\mathbf i_0$, $\mathbf j_0$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left[a\left(1 - \cos\frac{x}{a}\right)\right] &= a\sin\frac{x}{a}\cdot\frac{\dot x}{a} = \sin\frac{x}{a}\,\dot x \quad &\text{(chain rule through $x(t)$)} \\ \mathbf v_0^P &= \dot x\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\frac{x}{a}\,\dot x\,\mathbf j_0 = D\,\dot x\,\mathbf e_t \quad &\text{(Eq. 2.6; $\mathbf e_t$ of the tangent box)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\sin\frac{x}{a}\,\dot x\right) &= \frac{1}{a}\cos\frac{x}{a}\,\dot x\cdot\dot x + \sin\frac{x}{a}\,\ddot x \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule on the sine)} \\ \mathbf a_0^P &= \ddot x\,\mathbf i_0 + \left(s\,\ddot x + \frac{c}{a}\,\dot x^2\right)\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 2.7)} \\ \mathbf a_0^P\cdot\mathbf e_t &= \frac{\ddot x + s^2\ddot x + \frac{sc}{a}\dot x^2}{D} = \frac{\left(1 + s^2\right)\ddot x + \frac{sc}{a}\dot x^2}{D} \quad &\text{(projection on $\mathbf e_t$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_0^P = \dot x\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\frac{x}{a}\,\dot x\,\mathbf j_0, \qquad \mathbf a_0^P\cdot\mathbf e_t = \frac{1}{D}\left[\left(1 + \sin^2\frac{x}{a}\right)\ddot x + \frac{1}{a}\sin\frac{x}{a}\cos\frac{x}{a}\,\dot x^2\right]}$$

Units: $[\dot x] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[\ddot x] = [\dot x^2/a] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the speed along the curve is the factor $D$ times the horizontal rate; it is larger than the horizontal rate wherever the curve is inclined.

Motion of the turning frame and derivatives of its unit vectors Law: angular velocity of a simple rotation; derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \dot\Omega\,\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(simple rotation about the fixed $\mathbf j_0 = \mathbf j_1$; $\Omega$ constant)} \\ \mathbf r_0^O &= \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf v_0^O = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(origin of $S_1$ at the fixed point $O$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf i_1 = -\Omega\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3; $\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf i_1 = -\mathbf k_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.4)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf k_1 = \Omega\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.5; $\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf i_1$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 - \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0\right) &= -\Omega\sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 - \Omega\cos\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0 = -\Omega\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(check: chain rule on the components of $\mathbf i_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf i_1}$$

Units: $[\Omega] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: seen from above the plane of the curve turns counterclockwise; seen from $S_1$ its unit vectors are constant.

Turning curve: relative velocity and relative acceleration Law: time derivatives in $S_1$, where $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf j_1$ are constant; chain rule and product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_1^P &= \left.\frac{d\mathbf r_1^P}{dt}\right|_1 = \dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\frac{x_1}{a}\,\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(chain rule on the height, as for the fixed curve)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P &= \ddot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \left(s\,\ddot x_1 + \frac{c}{a}\,\dot x_1^2\right)\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(product rule on $\sin(x_1/a)\,\dot x_1$)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P\cdot\mathbf e_t &= \frac{\left(1 + s^2\right)\ddot x_1 + \frac{sc}{a}\dot x_1^2}{D} \quad &\text{(projection on $\mathbf e_t$)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P\cdot\mathbf n &= \frac{-s\,\ddot x_1 + s\,\ddot x_1 + \frac{c}{a}\dot x_1^2}{D} = \frac{c\,\dot x_1^2}{aD} \quad &\text{(projection on $\mathbf n$; the $\ddot x_1$ terms cancel)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_1^P = \dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\frac{x_1}{a}\,\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1, \qquad \mathbf a_1^P = \ddot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \left(\sin\frac{x_1}{a}\,\ddot x_1 + \frac{\dot x_1^2}{a}\cos\frac{x_1}{a}\right)\mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[\dot x_1] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[\ddot x_1] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: in $S_1$ the curve is at rest, so the relative motion has the kinematics of the fixed curve, with no component along $\mathbf k_1$.

Absolute velocity and acceleration: transport, Coriolis and centripetal terms Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the position written in the turning basis; product rule and derivatives of the unit vectors Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]

Write $y_1$ for the height $a(1 - \cos(x_1/a))$, so that the position is $x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P &= \dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + x_1\left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 + y_1\left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 \quad &\text{(product rule on each term)} \\ &= \underbrace{\dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y_1\,\mathbf j_1}_{\mathbf v_1^P}\ \underbrace{-\ \Omega x_1\,\mathbf k_1}_{\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P} \quad &\text{(derivatives of the unit vectors; $\Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times(x_1\mathbf i_1 + y_1\mathbf j_1) = -\Omega x_1\,\mathbf k_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1^P}{dt}\right|_0 &= \ddot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \ddot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + \dot x_1\left(-\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\right) = \mathbf a_1^P - \Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; the turning of $\mathbf i_1$ inside $\mathbf v_1^P$)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left(-\Omega x_1\,\mathbf k_1\right) &= -\Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1 - \Omega x_1\,\Omega\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; $\Omega$ constant; derivative of $\mathbf k_1$)} \\ 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P &= 2\Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) = -2\Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(the two $\mathbf k_1$ terms above)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) &= \Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\left(-\Omega x_1\,\mathbf k_1\right) = -\Omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(the $\mathbf i_1$ term above)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_0^P = \mathbf v_1^P - \Omega x_1\,\mathbf k_1, \qquad \mathbf a_0^P = \mathbf a_1^P - 2\Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1 - \Omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1}$$

Units: $[\Omega x_1] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[\Omega\dot x_1] = [\Omega^2x_1] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: one half of the Coriolis term comes from the turning of $\mathbf i_1$ inside the relative velocity, the other from the change of the distance to the axis inside the transport velocity; the centripetal term points horizontally towards the axis. With $O$ fixed and $\Omega$ constant the origin and Euler terms of Eq. 3.27 are absent.

Forces and Equations of Motion

The free-body diagram of $P$ in $S_1$ shows, in the plane of the curve, the weight, the in-plane reaction along $\mathbf n$ and the centrifugal force (horizontal, away from the axis); normal to the plane, the reaction along $\mathbf k_1$ and the Coriolis force. The inertia force of the origin and the Euler force vanish ($O$ fixed, $\Omega$ constant). For the fixed curve only the weight and the reaction act.
