Figure 3. Forces on $P$ in $S_1$. In the plane of the curve: weight, $N_n\,\mathbf n$ and the centrifugal force $m\Omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1$ (dashed, inertia). Normal to it: the reaction $N_b\,\mathbf k_1$ and the Coriolis force $2m\Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1$ (dashed, inertia), which balance each other.
Fixed curve: equation of motion along the tangent Law: Newton's second law projected on the tangent of a smooth curve Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.16; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.17
$$\begin{aligned} m\,\mathbf a_0^P &= -mg\,\mathbf j_0 + N_n\,\mathbf n + N_b\,\mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.4; smooth reaction of Eq. 6.16)} \\ m\,\mathbf a_0^P\cdot\mathbf e_t &= -mg\,\mathbf j_0\cdot\mathbf e_t = -\frac{mg\,s}{D} \quad &\text{($\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf e_t$ and $\mathbf k_0\cdot\mathbf e_t$ zero)} \\ \frac{m}{D}\left[\left(1 + s^2\right)\ddot x + \frac{sc}{a}\dot x^2\right] &= -\frac{mg\,s}{D} \quad &\text{(projection of the kinematics box)} \\ \left(1 + s^2\right)\ddot x + \frac{sc}{a}\dot x^2 + g\,s &= 0 \quad &\text{(multiplied by $D/m$; terms collected on one side)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\left(1 + \sin^2\frac{x}{a}\right)\ddot x + \frac{1}{a}\sin\frac{x}{a}\cos\frac{x}{a}\,\dot x^2 + g\sin\frac{x}{a} = 0}$$

Units: every term $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: one equation for the one unknown function $x(t)$; the other two projections would give the reaction, which parts (a) to (c) do not ask for.

(d) Inertia forces in the moving frame

Inertia forces on the particle in the turning frame Law: inertia forces of a non-inertial frame, each vector product expanded Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; Problems.pdf, p. 10
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf F_A &= -m\,\mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf F_E = -m\,\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{($O$ fixed; $\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}$ zero)} \\ \mathbf F_C &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) = -m\left(-\Omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) = m\Omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(centripetal term of the composition box times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR} &= -2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P = -m\left(-2\Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1\right) = 2m\Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Coriolis term of the composition box times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_C\cdot\mathbf e_t &= \frac{m\Omega^2x_1}{D}, \quad \mathbf F_C\cdot\mathbf n = -\frac{m\Omega^2x_1 s}{D}, \quad \mathbf F_{COR}\cdot\mathbf e_t = \mathbf F_{COR}\cdot\mathbf n = 0 \quad &\text{(projections of the tangent box)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf F_i = \mathbf F_C + \mathbf F_{COR} = m\Omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + 2m\Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1}$$

Units: $[m\Omega^2x_1] = [m\Omega\dot x_1] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the centrifugal force is horizontal and points away from the axis on both sides (it changes sign with $x_1$); the Coriolis force is normal to the plane of the curve, along plus $\mathbf k_1$ while $P$ moves towards growing $x_1$.

Newton's second law in the turning frame, projected on the curve basis Law: Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame with the inertia forces; reaction of a smooth curve Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.16; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.19; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]
$$\begin{aligned} m\,\mathbf a_1^P &= -mg\,\mathbf j_1 + N_n\,\mathbf n + N_b\,\mathbf k_1 + \mathbf F_C + \mathbf F_{COR} \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.63)} \\ \mathbf e_t:\ \frac{m}{D}\left[\left(1 + s^2\right)\ddot x_1 + \frac{sc}{a}\dot x_1^2\right] &= -\frac{mg\,s}{D} + \frac{m\Omega^2x_1}{D} \quad &\text{(no reaction and no Coriolis force along the tangent)} \\ \mathbf n:\ \frac{mc\,\dot x_1^2}{aD} &= -\frac{mg}{D} + N_n - \frac{m\Omega^2x_1 s}{D} \quad &\text{(in the plane, across the curve)} \\ \mathbf k_1:\ 0 &= N_b + 2m\Omega\dot x_1 \quad &\text{(no relative motion normal to the plane)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\left(1 + s^2\right)\ddot x_1 + \frac{sc}{a}\dot x_1^2 + g\,s - \Omega^2x_1 = 0, \qquad N_n = \frac{m}{D}\left(g + \Omega^2x_1 s + \frac{c}{a}\dot x_1^2\right), \qquad N_b = -2m\Omega\dot x_1}$$

Units: $[g] = [\Omega^2x_1] = [\dot x_1^2/a] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$; $[N_b] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: three scalar equations for the three unknowns $x_1$, $N_n$ and $N_b$. The reaction normal to the plane balances the Coriolis force alone.

Answers and Checks

(a) Reduction to integrals, fixed curve

Energy integral of the fixed curve Law: the equation of motion multiplied by the rate is an exact derivative (chain rule); Barrow's rule between 0 and $t$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; Notes.pdf, Sec. 6.5
$$\begin{aligned} m\left(1 + s^2\right)\dot x\ddot x + \frac{m}{a}sc\,\dot x^3 + mg\,s\,\dot x &= 0 \quad &\text{(equation of motion times $m\dot x$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left[\tfrac12 m\left(1 + s^2\right)\dot x^2\right] &= m\left(1 + s^2\right)\dot x\ddot x + \tfrac12 m\cdot 2s\,\frac{c}{a}\dot x\cdot\dot x^2 \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule: $\tfrac{d}{dt}s^2 = 2s\,\tfrac{c}{a}\,\dot x$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left[mga\left(1 - c\right)\right] &= mga\,\frac{s}{a}\,\dot x = mg\,s\,\dot x \quad &\text{(chain rule: $\tfrac{d}{dt}c = -\tfrac{s}{a}\,\dot x$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left[\tfrac12 m\left(1 + s^2\right)\dot x^2 + mga\left(1 - c\right)\right] &= 0 \quad &\text{(the first row is this sum)} \\ \left[\tfrac12 m\left(1 + s^2\right)\dot x^2 + mga\left(1 - c\right)\right]_0^t &= 0 \quad &\text{(Barrow's rule between 0 and $t$)} \\ \tfrac12 m\left(1 + 0\right)v_0^2 + mga\left(1 - 1\right) &= \tfrac12 mv_0^2 \quad &\text{(value at $t = 0$: $x = 0$, $\dot x(0) = v_0$, from $\mathbf v_0^P(0) = \dot x(0)\,\mathbf i_0 = v_0\,\mathbf i_0$)} \\ \left(1 + s^2\right)\dot x^2 &= v_0^2 - 2ga\left(1 - c\right) \quad &\text{(multiplied by $2/m$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\tfrac12 m\left(1 + \sin^2\frac{x}{a}\right)\dot x^2 + mga\left(1 - \cos\frac{x}{a}\right) = \tfrac12 mv_0^2}$$

Units: $[mv_0^2] = [mga] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$, energies

Meaning: the kinetic energy plus the potential energy of the weight is constant: the smooth reaction is normal to the velocity of a particle on a fixed curve and does no work.

Quadrature of the fixed curve Law: separation of variables; the sign of the rate fixed by the initial condition Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.27; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.44; Problems.pdf, p. 10

The rate starts positive ($\dot x(0) = v_0$) and keeps its sign until it first vanishes, at a turning point where the right-hand side is zero.

$$\begin{aligned} \dot x &= +\sqrt{\frac{v_0^2 - 2ga\left(1 - \cos\left(x/a\right)\right)}{1 + \sin^2\left(x/a\right)}} \quad &\text{(energy integral solved; positive root)} \\ dt &= \sqrt{\frac{1 + \sin^2\left(x/a\right)}{v_0^2 - 2ga\left(1 - \cos\left(x/a\right)\right)}}\,dx \quad &\text{(variables separated)} \\ \int_0^t dt' &= \left[t'\right]_0^t = t \quad &\text{(antiderivative $t'$; Barrow's rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{t = \int_0^{x}\sqrt{\frac{1 + \sin^2(\xi/a)}{v_0^2 - 2ga\left(1 - \cos(\xi/a)\right)}}\;d\xi \quad \text{(until the first turning point; then the sign of the root changes)}}$$

Units: the integrand is $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]^{-1}$, times $[d\xi] = [\mathrm{L}]$: a time

Meaning: the motion is reduced to one integral; the region allowed to the particle is where the radicand is not negative.

(b) Extreme abscissas of the motion

Turning points Law: the rate vanishes where the kinetic energy is zero; allowed region of the energy integral Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.27; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.28; Problems.pdf, p. 10
$$\begin{aligned} \left(1 + s^2\right)\dot x^2 &= ga - 2ga\left(1 - \cos\frac{x}{a}\right) = ga\left(2\cos\frac{x}{a} - 1\right) \quad &\text{(energy integral with $v_0^2 = ga$; terms collected)} \\ \dot x^2 \ge 0 &\iff \cos\frac{x}{a} \ge \frac12 \iff -\frac{\pi}{3} \le \frac{x}{a} \le \frac{\pi}{3} \quad &\text{(the factor $1 + s^2$ is positive; $x/a$ between $-\pi$ and $\pi$)} \\ \ddot x\left(\pm\frac{\pi a}{3}\right) &= -\frac{g\sin(\pm\pi/3)}{1 + \sin^2(\pi/3)} = \mp\frac{g\sqrt3/2}{7/4} = \mp\frac{2\sqrt3}{7}\,g \quad &\text{(equation of motion with $\dot x = 0$; $\sin^2(\pi/3) = 3/4$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{x_{\min} = -\frac{\pi a}{3}, \qquad x_{\max} = \frac{\pi a}{3}}$$

Units: $[x] = [a] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: at each end of the allowed interval the acceleration points back towards $O$, so the particle turns there: it oscillates between the two points at a height of half of $a$, symmetric about $O$, and never stays at an end.

(c) Minimum initial speed to reach the crest

Speed needed to reach x equal to pi a Law: allowed region of the energy integral; behaviour of the quadrature near a maximum of the potential Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.28; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.44; Problems.pdf, p. 10

To reach the crest the radicand must not be negative on the whole way from 0 to $\pi a$; it decreases with $x$ there, because $1 - \cos(x/a)$ grows, so the condition is its value at the crest. At the limiting speed write $\delta$ for the distance $\pi a - x$ still to go; the half-angle identity is $1 + \cos\beta = 2\cos^2(\beta/2)$.

$$\begin{aligned} v_0^2 - 2ga\left(1 - \cos\pi\right) &= v_0^2 - 4ga \ge 0 \quad &\text{(radicand at $x = \pi a$; $\cos\pi = -1$)} \\ v_0 &\ge 2\sqrt{ga} \quad &\text{(positive root, $v_0 \gt 0$)} \\ v_0^2 - 2ga\left(1 - \cos\frac{x}{a}\right) &= 2ga\left(1 + \cos\frac{x}{a}\right) = 4ga\cos^2\frac{x}{2a} \quad &\text{(case $v_0^2 = 4ga$; half-angle identity)} \\ \cos\frac{x}{2a} &= \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\delta}{2a}\right) = \sin\frac{\delta}{2a} \simeq \frac{\delta}{2a} \quad &\text{(difference formula; small $\delta$)} \\ \sqrt{\frac{1 + \sin^2(x/a)}{4ga\cos^2(x/2a)}} &\simeq \sqrt{\frac{1}{4ga}}\cdot\frac{2a}{\delta} = \sqrt{\frac{a}{g}}\,\frac{1}{\delta} \quad &\text{(integrand of the quadrature near the crest; $\sin(x/a) \simeq 0$)} \\ \int_{\delta}^{\delta_1}\sqrt{\frac{a}{g}}\,\frac{d\delta'}{\delta'} &= \sqrt{\frac{a}{g}}\left[\ln \delta'\right]_{\delta}^{\delta_1} = \sqrt{\frac{a}{g}}\,\ln\frac{\delta_1}{\delta} \to \infty \ \ (\delta \to 0) \quad &\text{(time from a point at $\delta_1$ to a point at $\delta$: antiderivative $\ln \delta'$, Barrow's rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{v_{0,\min} = 2\sqrt{ga}: \ \text{for } v_0 \gt 2\sqrt{ga} \text{ the crest is reached in a finite time; at } v_0 = 2\sqrt{ga} \text{ only as } t \to \infty}$$

Units: $[\sqrt{ga}] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[\sqrt{a/g}] = [\mathrm{T}]$

Meaning: the initial kinetic energy must pay for the rise to the crest, twice $a$ above $O$. At exactly the limiting speed the force on the particle vanishes at the crest as well as its speed, and the time to get there diverges logarithmically: $2\sqrt{ga}$ is the lower bound of the speeds that reach it.

(e) Quadratures and reaction force, turning curve

Initial relative velocity Law: composition of velocities at the initial instant Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.20; Problems.pdf, p. 10
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P(0) &= \mathbf v_1^P(0) - \Omega x_1(0)\,\mathbf k_1 = \dot x_1(0)\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin 0\cdot\dot x_1(0)\,\mathbf j_1 - 0 \quad &\text{(velocity box; $x_1(0) = 0$)} \\ &= \dot x_1(0)\,\mathbf i_0 \quad &\text{($\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf i_0$ at $t = 0$)} \\ \dot x_1(0)\,\mathbf i_0 &= v_0\,\mathbf i_0 \quad &\text{(initial condition of the statement)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{x_1(0) = 0, \qquad \dot x_1(0) = v_0}$$

Units: $[v_0] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: at the axis the transport velocity is zero, so the relative and the absolute initial velocities coincide.

Energy integral in the turning frame and quadrature Law: the tangent equation multiplied by the rate is an exact derivative (chain rule); Barrow's rule; separation of variables Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]

The energy in $S_1$ is conserved for two reasons. First, the forces that do no work in $S_1$: the reaction, because the curve is smooth and at rest in $S_1$, so the reaction is normal to the relative velocity; the Coriolis force, always normal to the relative velocity; and the force of the origin and the Euler force, which vanish. Second, the forces that do work have potentials that depend on the position only: the weight, and the centrifugal force, whose potential is minus one half of $m\Omega^2x_1^2$ only because $\Omega$ is constant.

$$\begin{aligned} m\left(1 + s^2\right)\dot x_1\ddot x_1 + \frac{m}{a}sc\,\dot x_1^3 + mg\,s\,\dot x_1 - m\Omega^2x_1\dot x_1 &= 0 \quad &\text{(tangent equation times $m\dot x_1$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(-\tfrac12 m\Omega^2x_1^2\right) &= -m\Omega^2x_1\dot x_1 \quad &\text{(chain rule; $\Omega$ constant)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left[\tfrac12 m\left(1 + s^2\right)\dot x_1^2 + mga\left(1 - c\right) - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2x_1^2\right] &= 0 \quad &\text{(the first two terms as for the fixed curve)} \\ \left[\tfrac12 m\left(1 + s^2\right)\dot x_1^2 + mga\left(1 - c\right) - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2x_1^2\right]_0^t &= 0 \quad &\text{(Barrow's rule between 0 and $t$)} \\ \tfrac12 m\left(1 + s^2\right)\dot x_1^2 + mga\left(1 - c\right) - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2x_1^2 &= \tfrac12 mv_0^2 \quad &\text{(value at $t = 0$: $x_1 = 0$, $\dot x_1 = v_0$)} \\ \dot x_1^2 &= \frac{v_0^2 - 2ga\left(1 - c\right) + \Omega^2x_1^2}{1 + s^2} \quad &\text{(multiplied by $2/m$, divided by $1 + s^2$)} \\ dt &= \sqrt{\frac{1 + s^2}{v_0^2 - 2ga\left(1 - c\right) + \Omega^2x_1^2}}\,dx_1 \quad &\text{(positive root, $\dot x_1(0) = v_0 \gt 0$; variables separated)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{t = \int_0^{x_1}\sqrt{\frac{1 + \sin^2(\xi/a)}{v_0^2 - 2ga\left(1 - \cos(\xi/a)\right) + \Omega^2\xi^2}}\;d\xi \quad \text{(until the first turning point)}}$$

Units: $[\Omega^2\xi^2] = [v_0^2] = [ga] = [\mathrm{L^2\,T^{-2}}]$; the integral is a time

Meaning: compared with the fixed curve the radicand gains the centrifugal term, which grows with the distance to the axis and helps the particle climb.

Reaction force on the turning curve Law: normal equations of the turning frame with the squared rate eliminated through the energy integral Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.16; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.19
$$\begin{aligned} N_n &= \frac{m}{D}\left(g + \Omega^2x_1 s + \frac{c}{a}\dot x_1^2\right) \quad &\text{(equation along $\mathbf n$)} \\ &= \frac{m}{D}\left[g + \Omega^2x_1 s + \frac{c\left(v_0^2 - 2ga(1 - c) + \Omega^2x_1^2\right)}{a\left(1 + s^2\right)}\right] \quad &\text{(squared rate of the energy integral)} \\ N_b &= -2m\Omega\dot x_1 = \mp 2m\Omega\sqrt{\frac{v_0^2 - 2ga(1 - c) + \Omega^2x_1^2}{1 + s^2}} \quad &\text{(equation along $\mathbf k_1$; upper sign while $x_1$ grows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf N = \frac{m}{D}\left[g + \Omega^2x_1\sin\frac{x_1}{a} + \frac{\dot x_1^2}{a}\cos\frac{x_1}{a}\right]\mathbf n - 2m\Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \dot x_1^2 = \frac{v_0^2 - 2ga\left(1 - \cos\frac{x_1}{a}\right) + \Omega^2x_1^2}{1 + \sin^2\frac{x_1}{a}}}$$

Units: $[mg] = [m\Omega^2x_1] = [m\dot x_1^2/a] = [m\Omega\dot x_1] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the in-plane part carries the weight, the centrifugal push across the curve and the centripetal need of the curved path; the part normal to the plane points along minus $\mathbf k_1$ while $x_1$ grows, against the Coriolis force.

(f) Equilibrium positions in the turning frame

Transcendental equation of the relative equilibria Law: relative rest in the tangent equation; monotony of the function sine over its argument Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.32; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63

Write $u$ for $x_1/a$ and $\lambda$ for the dimensionless number $\Omega^2a/g$. On $0 \lt u \le \pi$ the function $\sin u/u$ decreases from 1 (its limit at 0) to 0; its derivative is $h(u)/u^2$ with $h(u) = u\cos u - \sin u$, and $h$ starts at 0 with the derivative $-u\sin u$, negative there.

$$\begin{aligned} \dot x_1 = 0,\ \ddot x_1 = 0:\quad g\sin\frac{x_1}{a} - \Omega^2x_1 &= 0 \quad &\text{(tangent equation at relative rest)} \\ \sin u &= \lambda u \quad &\text{(divided by $g$; $u$ and $\lambda$ substituted)} \\ u = 0 &\ \text{always}; \quad \frac{\sin u}{u} = \lambda \ \text{for } u \ne 0 \quad &\text{(the two families)} \\ \frac{d}{du}\left(\frac{\sin u}{u}\right) &= \frac{u\cos u - \sin u}{u^2}, \quad h(u) = h(0) + \int_0^u\left(-u'\sin u'\right)du' \lt 0 \quad &\text{(quotient rule; $h' = \cos u - u\sin u - \cos u$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{g\sin\frac{x_1}{a} = \Omega^2x_1: \ \ x_1 = 0 \text{ for every } \Omega; \ \text{a symmetric pair } \pm x_1^* \ \text{with } 0 \lt x_1^* \lt \pi a \text{ exactly when } 0 \lt \Omega^2a \lt g}$$

Units: $[g] = [\Omega^2x_1] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$; $\lambda$ dimensionless

Meaning: at an off-axis equilibrium the tangential pull of the weight towards the bottom balances the tangential push of the centrifugal force; with a fast spin no off-axis balance exists inside the range of the curve.

(g) Variable spin rate

Energy in the turning frame when Omega depends on time Law: inertia forces with a variable angular velocity; power of each force on the relative velocity; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.11; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]

With $\Omega(t)$ the Euler force appears. It is normal to the plane of the curve, so it does no work in $S_1$ and drops out of the tangent equation, which keeps its form with $\Omega(t)$; it only changes the reaction along $\mathbf k_1$. The centrifugal force, however, no longer derives from a potential that depends on the position only. Write $E_1^P$ for the energy of part (e) with $\Omega(t)$ in its centrifugal term: the bracket of the last row below, the relative kinetic energy plus the potential of the weight minus one half of $m\Omega^2x_1^2$.

$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} &= \dot\Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf F_E = -m\dot\Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) = m\dot\Omega x_1\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.9 and Eq. 4.62; $\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf i_1 = -\mathbf k_1$)} \\ \mathbf F_E\cdot\mathbf v_1^P &= m\dot\Omega x_1\,\mathbf k_1\cdot\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) = 0 \quad &\text{(normal to the plane)} \\ \mathbf k_1:\ 0 &= N_b + 2m\Omega\dot x_1 + m\dot\Omega x_1 \quad &\text{(the reaction balances Coriolis and Euler forces)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left[\tfrac12 m\left(1 + s^2\right)\dot x_1^2 + mga\left(1 - c\right)\right] &= m\Omega^2x_1\dot x_1 \quad &\text{(tangent equation with $\Omega(t)$ times $m\dot x_1$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac12 m\Omega^2x_1^2\right) &= m\Omega\dot\Omega x_1^2 + m\Omega^2x_1\dot x_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule on both factors)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left[\tfrac12 m\left(1 + s^2\right)\dot x_1^2 + mga\left(1 - c\right) - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2x_1^2\right] &= -m\Omega\dot\Omega x_1^2 \quad &\text{(difference of the last two rows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\frac{dE_1^P}{dt} = -m\Omega\dot\Omega x_1^2 \ne 0: \ \text{with } \Omega(t) \text{ the energy equation is no longer a first integral}}$$

Units: $[m\Omega\dot\Omega x_1^2] = [\mathrm{M}][\mathrm{T^{-1}}][\mathrm{T^{-2}}][\mathrm{L^2}] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-3}}]$, a power

Meaning: no, it cannot be used in the same way: the balance of the last row still holds, but its right-hand side depends on the unknown position, so it does not reduce the problem to a quadrature. With constant $\Omega$ the right-hand side vanishes and part (e) is recovered.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Integrals, fixed curve$\frac12 m(1 + \sin^2\frac{x}{a})\dot x^2 + mga(1 - \cos\frac{x}{a}) = \frac12 mv_0^2$; $t = \int_0^x\sqrt{(1 + \sin^2(\xi/a))/(v_0^2 - 2ga(1 - \cos(\xi/a)))}\,d\xi$
(b) Extreme abscissas, $v_0 = \sqrt{ga}$$x_{\min} = -\pi a/3$, $x_{\max} = \pi a/3$ (oscillation between them)
(c) Minimum speed to reach $x = \pi a$$v_0 = 2\sqrt{ga}$ (lower bound: reached in a finite time for any larger speed, asymptotically at that speed)
(d) Moving frame and inertia force(answered in Forces and Equations of Motion, before (a)–(c)) $S_1$: $\mathbf i_1$ in the plane of the curve, $\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf j_0$ the axis, $\mathbf k_1$ normal to the plane; $\mathbf F_i = m\Omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + 2m\Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1$
(e) Quadrature, turning curve$t = \int_0^{x_1}\sqrt{(1 + \sin^2(\xi/a))/(v_0^2 - 2ga(1 - \cos(\xi/a)) + \Omega^2\xi^2)}\,d\xi$
(e) Reaction$\mathbf N = \frac{m}{D}\left(g + \Omega^2x_1\sin\frac{x_1}{a} + \frac{\dot x_1^2}{a}\cos\frac{x_1}{a}\right)\mathbf n - 2m\Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1$, with $\mathbf n = (-\sin\frac{x_1}{a}\,\mathbf i_1 + \mathbf j_1)/D$ and $\dot x_1^2$ from the energy integral
(f) Equilibria$g\sin(x_1/a) = \Omega^2x_1$: $x_1 = 0$ always, and a pair $\pm x_1^*$ only if $\Omega^2a \lt g$
(g) Variable $\Omega$no: $dE_1^P/dt = -m\Omega\dot\Omega x_1^2 \ne 0$; the Euler force $m\dot\Omega x_1\,\mathbf k_1$ does no work, but the centrifugal force has no time-independent potential

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 73 lists item 22 with no answer, so there is no key to compare with. Independent checks: the reaction normal to the plane follows again from the angular momentum about the vertical axis in $S_0$ (box below), and the limiting cases close the results.

Independent check: angular momentum about the vertical axis Law: angular momentum about the fixed point $O$ and its rate, equal to the moment of the forces Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.48; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.53

In $\mathcal B_1$ the position has the components $(x_1, y_1, 0)$ and the absolute velocity $(\dot x_1, \dot y_1, -\Omega x_1)$ (velocity box). The component along $\mathbf j_1$ of a vector product is the first component of the second factor times the third of the first, minus the third of the second times the first of the first.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf H_{O,0}\cdot\mathbf j_1 &= m\left(\mathbf r_0^P\times\mathbf v_0^P\right)\cdot\mathbf j_1 = m\left(0\cdot\dot x_1 - x_1\left(-\Omega x_1\right)\right) = m\Omega x_1^2 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.48)} \\ \mathbf M_O\cdot\mathbf j_1 &= \left(\mathbf r_0^P\times N_b\,\mathbf k_1\right)\cdot\mathbf j_1 = 0\cdot 0 - x_1N_b = -x_1N_b \quad &\text{(weight along $\mathbf j_1$ and $N_n\,\mathbf n$ in the plane: no axial moment)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(m\Omega x_1^2\right) &= 2m\Omega x_1\dot x_1 \quad &\text{(chain rule; $\mathbf j_1$ fixed)} \\ -x_1N_b &= 2m\Omega x_1\dot x_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.53, axial component)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{N_b = -2m\Omega\dot x_1 \quad (x_1 \ne 0)}$$

Units: $[H] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-1}}]$; $[x_1N_b] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: to keep turning at the rate $\Omega$ while its distance to the axis changes, the particle needs an axial moment that only the normal reaction can give: the same result as the Coriolis balance in $S_1$.

Limiting cases Law: the results at extreme values of the data Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63
$$\begin{aligned} \Omega \to 0:\quad t &\to \int_0^{x}\sqrt{\frac{1 + \sin^2(\xi/a)}{v_0^2 - 2ga\left(1 - \cos(\xi/a)\right)}}\,d\xi, \quad N_b \to 0 \quad &\text{(the quadrature of part (a))} \\ \Omega \to 0:\quad g\sin\frac{x_1}{a} &= 0 \Rightarrow x_1 = 0 \ \text{inside the open range} \quad &\text{(only the bottom; the crests are ends of the curve)} \\ |x_1| \ll a:\quad \left(1 + s^2\right)\ddot x_1 + \frac{sc}{a}\dot x_1^2 + g\,s - \Omega^2x_1 &\simeq \ddot x_1 + \left(\frac{g}{a} - \Omega^2\right)x_1 \quad &\text{(first order in $x_1$ and its rates; $s \simeq x_1/a$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\Omega \to 0: \text{ part (a) recovered}; \qquad |x_1| \ll a: \ \ddot x_1 + \left(\frac{g}{a} - \Omega^2\right)x_1 = 0}$$

Units: $[g/a] = [\Omega^2] = [\mathrm{T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: near the bottom the particle oscillates when the spin rate is below the square root of g over a, and drifts away from the bottom when it is above, the same threshold at which the off-axis equilibria of part (f) disappear.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf
Problem 25

Ijon Tichy's Space Walk

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 13
Orbiting Frame + Inertia Forces

A spacecraft $S$ is orbiting a celestial body $F$. The trajectory of the spacecraft with respect to an inertial reference frame $Fxy$ is given by

$$ r = \frac{p}{1 + e\cos\nu}, $$

where $p$ and $e$ are known constants and $\nu(t)$ is a known function of time. The space explorer Ijon Tichy needs to perform some extra-vehicular activities during his Seventh Voyage (footnote 1: The Star Diaries by Stanislaw Lem). He attaches himself with a massless cord of length $L$ to the spacecraft and goes for a space walk. The cord remains in tension at all times. The astronaut is very light compared to the spacecraft, so his motion does not perturb the motion of the spacecraft. Furthermore, we assume that we can consider him as a point particle of mass $m$. We define a moving reference frame $Sx_1y_1$ as depicted in the figure.

  • (a)
    Determine the acceleration of the spacecraft with respect to $Fxy$ as a function of time.
  • (b)
    Determine the tangent vector to the trajectory of $S$ as a function of time.
  • (c)
    Determine the relative velocity and relative acceleration of Ijon Tichy with respect to $Sx_1y_1$ as a function of $\theta$ and its time derivatives.
  • (d)
    Determine the fictitious forces acting on Ijon Tichy if we analyze the problem with respect to the frame $Sx_1y_1$.

The length $L$ is very small compared to the distance between $F$ and $S$. This allows us to take an approximation: in the following, assume that the gravitational acceleration on the astronaut and on the spacecraft are exactly the same vector (magnitude and direction) as a function of time. (In actual problems the small differences in gravity at the position of the astronaut and the spacecraft can give rise to small but important effects, and this approximation is usually not taken for that reason.)

  • (e)
    Write down one ordinary differential equation that once solved (with given initial conditions) would yield the angle $\theta$ as a function of time (you do not need to solve it).
  • (f)
    Assuming that you solved the previous equation, and therefore knew $\theta(t)$, determine the value of the tension on the cord as a function of time.
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

A spacecraft $S$ moves on a conic of semi-latus rectum $p$ and eccentricity $e$ about the body $F$, with the true anomaly $\nu(t)$ a known function of time; the astronaut $P$, of mass $m$, is tied to it by a massless cord of length $L$ that stays taut, and the frame $Sx_1y_1$ of the figure moves with the spacecraft (Problems.pdf, p. 13). The statement asks for the acceleration and the unit tangent of the spacecraft, the relative velocity and acceleration of the astronaut, the inertia forces in $Sx_1y_1$, and, with equal gravity on both bodies, the differential equation of the cord angle and the tension. The relative kinematics follows Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2, the inertia forces Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9, and the gravity of $F$ Notes.pdf, Eq. 8.1.

ItemDefinition
Orbit of $S$$r = p/(1 + e\cos\nu)$, with $r$ the distance $FS$ and $\nu(t)$ known; $1 + e\cos\nu \gt 0$ on the orbit, since $r$ and $p$ are positive
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{F;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, the frame $Fxy$: $\mathbf i_0$ along $Fx$, $\mathbf j_0$ along $Fy$, $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf i_0\times\mathbf j_0$ normal to the orbital plane (Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.1)
Moving frame$S_1 = \{S;\ \mathcal B_1\}$, the frame $Sx_1y_1$: $\mathbf i_1$ along $FS$, pointing away from $F$; $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$; $\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1$, in the sense of growing $\nu$ (read from the figure: $Sy_1$ is $Sx_1$ turned by a quarter turn counterclockwise)
Cord basis$\mathcal B_2 = \{\mathbf e_c, \mathbf e_\theta, \mathbf k_1\}$: $\mathbf e_c$ from $S$ to $P$, $\mathbf e_\theta$ normal to the cord in the plane, in the sense of growing $\theta$
Coordinate$\theta$, the angle from $Sx_1$ to the cord $SP$, positive counterclockwise (from $\mathbf i_1$ towards $\mathbf j_1$, read from the figure)
Constraints$P$ in the orbital plane at the distance $L$ from $S$ (taut cord)
Degrees of freedom2 minus 1: 1, the angle $\theta(t)$; the motion of $S$ is prescribed
Data$p$ [m], $e$ [1], $\nu(t)$ [rad], $L$ [m], $m$ [kg]; $\mu_F$ [m$^3$ s$^{-2}$], the gravitational parameter of $F$ (Notes.pdf, Eq. 8.1), needed for the gravity of parts (e) and (f)
Unknowns$\theta(t)$ and the tension $T(t) \ge 0$ of the cord, which pulls $P$ towards $S$
Applied forcesthe cord, $-T\,\mathbf e_c$; the gravity of $F$ on the astronaut, $m\,\mathbf g_P$
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)of the origin, Euler, centrifugal and Coriolis (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial; planar motion in the orbital plane; the astronaut does not perturb $S$; from part (e) on, $\mathbf g_P$ equal to the gravitational acceleration $\mathbf g_S$ at $S$
Readings$\dot\nu \gt 0$ (the spacecraft moves towards growing $\nu$; with $\dot\nu \lt 0$ the unit tangent of part (b) changes sign). Hypothesis: the spacecraft is in free flight about $F$, which the conic orbit of Notes.pdf, Eq. 8.14 suggests but does not imply (the statement prescribes $\nu(t)$ and gives no force on $S$); parts (e) and (f) are given both in general and under this hypothesis

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. Orbital plane seen from $+\mathbf k_0$ ($\odot$). The shaded right triangle has hypotenuse $|FS| = r$, leg $r\cos\nu$ along $\mathbf i_0$ (adjacent to $\nu$) and leg $r\sin\nu$ along $\mathbf j_0$ (opposite). $\mathbf i_1$ is the radial direction and $\mathbf j_1$ is $\mathbf i_1$ turned $+90^\circ$ (blue); $\mathbf e_t$ is the unit tangent of the orbit (orange).
Basis of the moving frame: rotation by nu about k0 Law: right triangle of the radius $FS$; elementary rotation about the third axis and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 8.2; Problems.pdf, p. 13

The orbital plane is seen from the side of $\mathbf k_0$, which points out of the paper (⊙) because it is the cross product of $\mathbf i_0$ (to the right) and $\mathbf j_0$ (up): a positive rotation about $\mathbf k_0$ is counterclockwise. $\nu$ is measured at $F$ from $Fx$ counterclockwise, so it is already the standard polar angle of $S$. In the shaded right triangle (right angle at the foot of the perpendicular from $S$ to $Fx$) the hypotenuse is $r$, the leg adjacent to $\nu$ is $r\cos\nu$ along $\mathbf i_0$ and the opposite leg is $r\sin\nu$ along $\mathbf j_0$. Dividing by $r$ gives $\mathbf i_1$. $\mathbf j_1$ is $\mathbf j_0$ turned by $\nu$: adjacent leg $\cos\nu$ along $\mathbf j_0$, opposite leg $\sin\nu$ along minus $\mathbf i_0$ (the upward vector turned counterclockwise leans to the left: the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_0^S &= \overrightarrow{FS} = r\cos\nu\,\mathbf i_0 + r\sin\nu\,\mathbf j_0 = r\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(legs of the triangle of $FS$)} \\ \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\nu\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\nu\,\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(right triangle of $\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \mathbf j_1 &= -\sin\nu\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\nu\,\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(right triangle of $\mathbf j_1$: opposite leg on $-\mathbf i_0$)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\nu\cos\nu - \left(-\sin\nu\right)\sin\nu\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{3+3}$)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\nu + \sin^2\nu = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{12} = \cos\nu\sin\nu - \sin\nu\cos\nu = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows; row 3 is the unit row of $\mathbf k_0$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_0^S = r\,\mathbf i_1, \quad r = \frac{p}{1 + e\cos\nu}, \quad [{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\nu & -\sin\nu & 0 \cr \sin\nu & \cos\nu & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1}$$

Units: $[r] = [p] = [\mathrm{L}]$; $e$ and $\nu$ dimensionless

Meaning: $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf j_1$ are the radial and transverse directions of the orbit (Eq. 8.2); the frame turns with the radius $FS$.

Figure 2. Frame $Sx_1y_1$ seen from $+\mathbf k_1$ ($\odot$), with $\mathbf i_1$ to the right. In the shaded triangle the hypotenuse is the cord $|SP| = L$, the leg adjacent to $\theta$ is $L\cos\theta$ (along $\mathbf i_1$) and the opposite leg is $L\sin\theta$ (along $\mathbf j_1$). $\mathbf e_c, \mathbf e_\theta$ in orange. The inertial axis $\mathbf i_0$ (grey) is at $-\nu$ from $\mathbf i_1$, so the cord makes $\theta + \nu$ with it.
Cord basis and position of the astronaut: rotation by theta about k1 Law: right triangle of the cord; elementary rotation about the third axis and its checks; position as a sum of segments Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.16; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 13

The frame $Sx_1y_1$ is drawn with $\mathbf i_1$ to the right, $\mathbf j_1$ up and $\mathbf k_1$ out of the paper (⊙); $F$ lies along minus $\mathbf i_1$. $\theta$ is measured from $\mathbf i_1$ counterclockwise, so it is the standard polar angle of $P$ about $S$. In the shaded right triangle the hypotenuse is the cord $L$, the leg adjacent to $\theta$ is $L\cos\theta$ along $\mathbf i_1$ and the opposite leg is $L\sin\theta$ along $\mathbf j_1$. $\mathbf e_\theta$ is $\mathbf j_1$ turned by $\theta$: adjacent leg $\cos\theta$ along $\mathbf j_1$, opposite leg $\sin\theta$ along minus $\mathbf i_1$ (the minus sign, as before). To go from $F$ to $P$ we pass through $S$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_c &= \cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf e_\theta = -\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles)} \\ \det[{}_1R_2] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta\right) = 1, \quad \mathbf e_c\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = -\cos\theta\sin\theta + \sin\theta\cos\theta = 0 \quad &\text{(third row; columns orthogonal)} \\ \mathbf r_1^P &= \overrightarrow{SP} = L\,\mathbf e_c = L\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + L\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(legs of the triangle of the cord)} \\ \mathbf r_0^P &= \mathbf r_0^S + \mathbf r_1^P = r\,\mathbf i_1 + L\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + L\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.16)} \\ \mathbf e_c &= \cos\theta\left(\cos\nu\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\nu\,\mathbf j_0\right) + \sin\theta\left(-\sin\nu\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\nu\,\mathbf j_0\right) \quad &\text{(columns of $[{}_0R_1]$ substituted)} \\ &= \cos\left(\theta + \nu\right)\mathbf i_0 + \sin\left(\theta + \nu\right)\mathbf j_0 \quad &\text{(addition formulas of cosine and sine)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^P = L\,\mathbf e_c, \quad \mathbf r_0^P = r\,\mathbf i_1 + L\,\mathbf e_c, \quad [{}_1R_2] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \cr \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf e_c = \cos(\theta + \nu)\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin(\theta + \nu)\,\mathbf j_0}$$

Units: $[L] = [\mathrm{L}]$; angles dimensionless

Meaning: the cord makes the angle $\theta + \nu$ with the inertial axis $Fx$ (product of the two rotations, Eq. 1.16); this angle is used in the independent check.

Kinematics

Motion of the moving frame and derivatives of its unit vectors Law: angular velocity and acceleration of a simple rotation; derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \dot\nu\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \left.\frac{d}{dt}\left(\dot\nu\,\mathbf k_1\right)\right|_0 = \ddot\nu\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(rotation by $\nu(t)$ about the fixed $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf k_1$; Eq. 3.9)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \dot\nu\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \dot\nu\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \dot\nu\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\dot\nu\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 and 3.4)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\cos\nu\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\nu\,\mathbf j_0\right) &= -\sin\nu\,\dot\nu\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\nu\,\dot\nu\,\mathbf j_0 = \dot\nu\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(check: chain rule on the components of $\mathbf i_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \dot\nu\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \ddot\nu\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \dot\nu\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\dot\nu\,\mathbf i_1}$$

Units: $[\dot\nu] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$; $[\ddot\nu] = [\mathrm{T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the frame turns at the rate of the true anomaly, which on a non-circular orbit is not constant: the angular acceleration does not vanish in general.

(a) Acceleration of the spacecraft

Velocity and acceleration of the spacecraft in the inertial frame Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of $r\,\mathbf i_1$; product rule and derivatives of the unit vectors Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 8.3; Problems.pdf, p. 13
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^S &= \dot r\,\mathbf i_1 + r\left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \dot r\,\mathbf i_1 + r\dot\nu\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; derivative of $\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \mathbf a_0^S &= \ddot r\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot r\dot\nu\,\mathbf j_1 + \left(\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu\right)\mathbf j_1 + r\dot\nu\left(-\dot\nu\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule on both terms; $\tfrac{d}{dt}(r\dot\nu) = \dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu$)} \\ &= \left(\ddot r - r\dot\nu^2\right)\mathbf i_1 + \left(2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu\right)\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(grouped by unit vector)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_0^S = \left(\ddot r - r\dot\nu^2\right)\mathbf i_1 + \left(2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu\right)\mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[\ddot r] = [r\dot\nu^2] = [\dot r\dot\nu] = [r\ddot\nu] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the radial part holds the centripetal term of the turning radius; the transverse part holds the change of the angular rate and the Coriolis-like term of a changing radius.

Rates of the distance as functions of time Law: chain rule through $\nu(t)$; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 8.14; Problems.pdf, p. 13

Write $D$ for $1 + e\cos\nu$, so that $r$ is $p$ times $D^{-1}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dot D &= \frac{dD}{d\nu}\,\dot\nu = -e\sin\nu\,\dot\nu \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \dot r &= -p\,D^{-2}\,\dot D = \frac{pe\,\dot\nu\sin\nu}{D^2} \quad &\text{(chain rule on $D^{-1}$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(pe\,\dot\nu\sin\nu\right) &= pe\left(\ddot\nu\sin\nu + \dot\nu^2\cos\nu\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule on the sine)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}D^{-2} &= -2D^{-3}\dot D = 2e\,\dot\nu\sin\nu\,D^{-3} \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \ddot r &= \frac{pe\left(\ddot\nu\sin\nu + \dot\nu^2\cos\nu\right)}{D^2} + pe\,\dot\nu\sin\nu\cdot\frac{2e\,\dot\nu\sin\nu}{D^3} \quad &\text{(product rule on the two factors of $\dot r$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\dot r = \frac{pe\,\dot\nu\sin\nu}{\left(1 + e\cos\nu\right)^2}, \qquad \ddot r = \frac{pe\left(\ddot\nu\sin\nu + \dot\nu^2\cos\nu\right)}{\left(1 + e\cos\nu\right)^2} + \frac{2pe^2\dot\nu^2\sin^2\nu}{\left(1 + e\cos\nu\right)^3}}$$

Units: $[\dot r] = [p][\mathrm{T^{-1}}] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[\ddot r] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: with $\nu(t)$ known, $r$, its rates, $\dot\nu$ and $\ddot\nu$ are known functions of time, and so is the acceleration of part (a).

(b) Tangent vector of the orbit

Unit tangent of the trajectory of the spacecraft Law: unit tangent as the velocity divided by the speed; right triangle of the velocity components Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.9; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.16; Problems.pdf, p. 13

The two components of the velocity are the legs of a right triangle: $e\sin\nu$ along $\mathbf i_1$ and $1 + e\cos\nu$ along $\mathbf j_1$, after the common factor is taken out; the hypotenuse gives the speed.

$$\begin{aligned} \dot r &= \frac{p}{D}\cdot\frac{e\,\dot\nu\sin\nu}{D} = r\dot\nu\,\frac{e\sin\nu}{D} \quad &\text{($p/D = r$)} \\ \mathbf v_0^S &= \frac{r\dot\nu}{D}\left[e\sin\nu\,\mathbf i_1 + D\,\mathbf j_1\right] \quad &\text{(common factor)} \\ e^2\sin^2\nu + \left(1 + e\cos\nu\right)^2 &= e^2\left(\sin^2\nu + \cos^2\nu\right) + 1 + 2e\cos\nu = 1 + 2e\cos\nu + e^2 \quad &\text{(Pythagoras for the bracket)} \\ \mathbf e_t &= \frac{\mathbf v_0^S}{|\mathbf v_0^S|} = \frac{e\sin\nu\,\mathbf i_1 + \left(1 + e\cos\nu\right)\mathbf j_1}{\sqrt{1 + 2e\cos\nu + e^2}} \quad &\text{($r$, $D$ and $\dot\nu$ positive)} \\ e\sin\nu\cos\nu - \left(1 + e\cos\nu\right)\sin\nu &= -\sin\nu, \quad e\sin^2\nu + \left(1 + e\cos\nu\right)\cos\nu = e + \cos\nu \quad &\text{(components on $\mathbf i_0$ and $\mathbf j_0$ with $[{}_0R_1]$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf e_t(t) = \frac{e\sin\nu\,\mathbf i_1 + \left(1 + e\cos\nu\right)\mathbf j_1}{\sqrt{1 + 2e\cos\nu + e^2}} = \frac{-\sin\nu\,\mathbf i_0 + \left(e + \cos\nu\right)\mathbf j_0}{\sqrt{1 + 2e\cos\nu + e^2}}, \quad \nu = \nu(t)}$$

Units: dimensionless

Meaning: on a circular orbit (zero eccentricity) the tangent is the transverse direction $\mathbf j_1$; otherwise it leans outwards while the spacecraft goes from the periapsis to the apoapsis (the factor $e\sin\nu$ positive) and inwards on the way back.

(c) Relative velocity and acceleration of the astronaut

Relative velocity and relative acceleration Law: time derivatives in $S_1$, where $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf j_1$ are constant; chain rule and product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24; Problems.pdf, p. 13
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_1^P &= \frac{d}{dt}\left(L\cos\theta\right)\mathbf i_1 + \frac{d}{dt}\left(L\sin\theta\right)\mathbf j_1 = -L\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + L\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(chain rule; $L$ constant)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P &= -L\left(\ddot\theta\sin\theta + \dot\theta^2\cos\theta\right)\mathbf i_1 + L\left(\ddot\theta\cos\theta - \dot\theta^2\sin\theta\right)\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(product rule on $\dot\theta\sin\theta$ and $\dot\theta\cos\theta$)} \\ &= L\ddot\theta\left(-\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1\right) - L\dot\theta^2\left(\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(grouped by $\ddot\theta$ and $\dot\theta^2$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_1^P = L\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta = L\dot\theta\left(-\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1\right), \qquad \mathbf a_1^P = L\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta - L\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf e_c}$$

Units: $[L\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[L\ddot\theta] = [L\dot\theta^2] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: in $S_1$ the astronaut moves on a circle of radius $L$ about the spacecraft: a tangential part and a centripetal part towards $S$.

Absolute acceleration of the astronaut: the five terms Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the position written in the turning basis; product rule and derivatives of the unit vectors Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]

Write $x_1$ and $y_1$ for the components $L\cos\theta$ and $L\sin\theta$ of $\mathbf r_1^P$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P &= \mathbf v_0^S + \dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + x_1\dot\nu\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\dot\nu\,\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf v_0^S + \mathbf v_1^P + \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P \quad &\text{(product rule; derivatives of $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1^P}{dt}\right|_0 &= \ddot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \ddot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + \dot x_1\dot\nu\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\dot\nu\,\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf a_1^P + \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P \quad &\text{(product rule; turning of $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left(\dot\nu\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) &= \ddot\nu\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf r_1^P + \dot\nu\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(\mathbf v_1^P + \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; $\mathbf k_1$ fixed; first row for $d\mathbf r_1^P/dt|_0$)} \\ \mathbf a_0^P &= \mathbf a_0^S + \mathbf a_1^P + \boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P + \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) + 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P \quad &\text{(sum of the derivatives)} \\ \boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P &= \ddot\nu\,\mathbf k_1\times L\,\mathbf e_c = L\ddot\nu\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf e_c = \mathbf e_\theta$)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) &= \dot\nu\,\mathbf k_1\times L\dot\nu\,\mathbf e_\theta = -L\dot\nu^2\,\mathbf e_c \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf e_\theta = -\mathbf e_c$)} \\ 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P &= 2\dot\nu\,\mathbf k_1\times L\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta = -2L\dot\nu\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_c \quad &\text{(same product)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_0^P = \mathbf a_0^S + L\left(\ddot\theta + \ddot\nu\right)\mathbf e_\theta - L\left(\dot\theta^2 + 2\dot\nu\dot\theta + \dot\nu^2\right)\mathbf e_c}$$

Units: every term $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the four terms beyond the acceleration of the origin add up to the acceleration of circular motion at the absolute angular rate of the cord, the sum of the two rates.

Forces and Equations of Motion

The free-body diagram of the astronaut in $S_1$ shows the pull of the cord towards $S$, the gravity of $F$, and the four inertia forces: the force of the origin (minus the mass times the acceleration of $S$), the Euler force across the cord, and the centrifugal and Coriolis forces along the cord.

Figure 3. Forces on $P$ in $S_1$: the tension $-T\,\mathbf e_c$, the gravity $m\,\mathbf g_S$ (equal at $P$ and $S$ by hypothesis) and the inertia forces $\mathbf F_A = -m\,\mathbf a_0^S$, $\mathbf F_E$ across the cord and $\mathbf F_C$, $\mathbf F_{COR}$ along it (dashed). In free flight $m\,\mathbf g_S$ and $\mathbf F_A$ cancel.

(d) Inertia forces in the moving frame

The four inertia forces on the astronaut Law: inertia forces of a non-inertial frame, each vector product expanded Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; Problems.pdf, p. 13
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf F_A &= -m\,\mathbf a_0^S = -m\left(\ddot r - r\dot\nu^2\right)\mathbf i_1 - m\left(2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu\right)\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(part (a))} \\ \mathbf F_E &= -m\,\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P = -mL\ddot\nu\,\mathbf e_\theta = mL\ddot\nu\left(\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 - \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(Euler term of the composition box times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_C &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) = mL\dot\nu^2\,\mathbf e_c \quad &\text{(centripetal term times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR} &= -2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P = 2mL\dot\nu\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_c \quad &\text{(Coriolis term times $-m$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf F_A = -m\,\mathbf a_0^S, \quad \mathbf F_E = mL\ddot\nu\left(\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 - \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1\right), \quad \mathbf F_C = mL\dot\nu^2\,\mathbf e_c, \quad \mathbf F_{COR} = 2mL\dot\nu\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_c}$$

Units: $[m\,a_0^S] = [mL\ddot\nu] = [mL\dot\nu^2] = [mL\dot\nu\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the centrifugal force pushes the astronaut away from $S$ along the cord, because the whole of $\mathbf r_1^P$ lies in the plane normal to the rotation; the Euler force is present because the true anomaly does not grow uniformly on a non-circular orbit.

Newton's second law in the moving frame, projected on the cord basis Law: Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame with the inertia forces; gravity of $F$ equal at $P$ and at $S$ (hypothesis of parts (e) and (f)) Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 8.1; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]
$$\begin{aligned} m\,\mathbf a_1^P &= -T\,\mathbf e_c + m\,\mathbf g_S + \mathbf F_A + \mathbf F_E + \mathbf F_C + \mathbf F_{COR} \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.63 with $\mathbf g_P = \mathbf g_S$)} \\ \mathbf g_S &= -\frac{\mu_F}{r^2}\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 8.1 at $S$)} \\ \mathbf i_1\cdot\mathbf e_c &= \cos\theta, \quad \mathbf j_1\cdot\mathbf e_c = \sin\theta, \quad \mathbf i_1\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = -\sin\theta, \quad \mathbf j_1\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = \cos\theta \quad &\text{(components of the cord basis)} \\ \mathbf e_\theta:\ mL\ddot\theta &= \frac{m\mu_F}{r^2}\sin\theta + m\left(\ddot r - r\dot\nu^2\right)\sin\theta - m\left(2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu\right)\cos\theta - mL\ddot\nu \quad &\text{(across the cord: no tension)} \\ \mathbf e_c:\ -mL\dot\theta^2 &= -T - \frac{m\mu_F}{r^2}\cos\theta - m\left(\ddot r - r\dot\nu^2\right)\cos\theta - m\left(2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu\right)\sin\theta + mL\dot\nu^2 + 2mL\dot\nu\dot\theta \quad &\text{(along the cord)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} mL\ddot\theta = m\left(\frac{\mu_F}{r^2} + \ddot r - r\dot\nu^2\right)\sin\theta - m\left(2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu\right)\cos\theta - mL\ddot\nu \cr T = mL\dot\theta^2 + mL\dot\nu^2 + 2mL\dot\theta\dot\nu - \frac{m\mu_F}{r^2}\cos\theta + m\left(r\dot\nu^2 - \ddot r\right)\cos\theta - m\left(2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu\right)\sin\theta \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[m\mu_F/r^2] = [\mathrm{M}][\mathrm{L^3\,T^{-2}}][\mathrm{L^{-2}}] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$, like every other term

Meaning: two scalar equations for the two unknowns $\theta$ and $T$: the projection across the cord is free of the tension and gives the motion; the projection along the cord gives the tension afterwards.

Answers and Checks

(e) Differential equation of the cord angle

Equation of motion of theta, and its form for a spacecraft in free flight Law: projection across the cord; Newton's second law of the spacecraft under the gravity of $F$ alone (radial and transverse components) Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 8.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 8.6; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Problems.pdf, p. 13

A spacecraft in free flight about $F$ (the reading stated in the table) has the acceleration $\mathbf g_S$: its radial and transverse components are Eq. 8.5 and Eq. 8.6 with $\nu$ in place of the polar angle.

$$\begin{aligned} \ddot\theta &= -\ddot\nu + \frac{1}{L}\left(\frac{\mu_F}{r^2} + \ddot r - r\dot\nu^2\right)\sin\theta - \frac{1}{L}\left(2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu\right)\cos\theta \quad &\text{(projection across the cord, divided by $mL$)} \\ \ddot r - r\dot\nu^2 &= -\frac{\mu_F}{r^2}, \quad 2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu = 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 8.5 and Eq. 8.6: free flight)} \\ \ddot\theta &= -\ddot\nu + \frac{1}{L}\left(\frac{\mu_F}{r^2} - \frac{\mu_F}{r^2}\right)\sin\theta - 0 = -\ddot\nu \quad &\text{(substituted)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\ddot\theta = -\ddot\nu + \frac{1}{L}\left(\frac{\mu_F}{r^2} + \ddot r - r\dot\nu^2\right)\sin\theta - \frac{1}{L}\left(2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu\right)\cos\theta; \qquad \text{free flight: } \ddot\theta + \ddot\nu(t) = 0}$$

Units: $[\ddot\theta] = [\ddot\nu] = [\mu_F/(Lr^2)] = [\mathrm{T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: $r$, its rates and $\nu$ are known functions of time, so the general form is one second-order equation for $\theta(t)$ alone. In free flight the weight of the astronaut and the force of the origin cancel exactly, and only the Euler force drives the angle.

(f) Tension of the cord

Tension as a function of time Law: projection along the cord; integral of the free-flight equation with Barrow's rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 8.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 8.6; Problems.pdf, p. 13
$$\begin{aligned} T(t) &= mL\dot\theta^2 + mL\dot\nu^2 + 2mL\dot\theta\dot\nu - \frac{m\mu_F}{r^2}\cos\theta + m\left(r\dot\nu^2 - \ddot r\right)\cos\theta - m\left(2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu\right)\sin\theta \quad &\text{(projection along the cord, $\theta(t)$ known)} \\ &= mL\left(\dot\theta^2 + 2\dot\theta\dot\nu + \dot\nu^2\right) - \frac{m\mu_F}{r^2}\cos\theta + \frac{m\mu_F}{r^2}\cos\theta - 0 \quad &\text{(free flight: $r\dot\nu^2 - \ddot r = \mu_F/r^2$, transverse part zero)} \\ &= mL\left(\dot\theta + \dot\nu\right)^2 \quad &\text{(square of a sum)} \\ \int_0^t\left(\ddot\theta + \ddot\nu\right)dt' &= \left[\dot\theta + \dot\nu\right]_0^t = \dot\theta + \dot\nu - \dot\theta(0) - \dot\nu(0) = 0 \quad &\text{(free-flight equation integrated; antiderivative $\dot\theta + \dot\nu$; Barrow's rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{T(t) = mL\dot\theta^2 + mL\dot\nu^2 + 2mL\dot\theta\dot\nu - \frac{m\mu_F\cos\theta}{r^2} + m\left(r\dot\nu^2 - \ddot r\right)\cos\theta - m\left(2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu\right)\sin\theta; \quad \text{free flight: } T = mL\left(\dot\theta + \dot\nu\right)^2 = mL\left(\dot\theta(0) + \dot\nu(0)\right)^2}$$

Units: $[mL\dot\theta^2] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: in free flight the cord only supplies the centripetal force of a circle of radius $L$ described at the absolute rate of the cord, which stays at its initial value: the tension is constant, and the hypothesis of a taut cord holds as long as that rate is not zero.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Acceleration of $S$$\mathbf a_0^S = (\ddot r - r\dot\nu^2)\,\mathbf i_1 + (2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu)\,\mathbf j_1$, with $r = p/(1 + e\cos\nu)$, $\dot r = pe\dot\nu\sin\nu/(1 + e\cos\nu)^2$, $\ddot r = pe(\ddot\nu\sin\nu + \dot\nu^2\cos\nu)/(1 + e\cos\nu)^2 + 2pe^2\dot\nu^2\sin^2\nu/(1 + e\cos\nu)^3$
(b) Unit tangent of $S$$\mathbf e_t = [e\sin\nu\,\mathbf i_1 + (1 + e\cos\nu)\,\mathbf j_1]/\sqrt{1 + 2e\cos\nu + e^2} = [-\sin\nu\,\mathbf i_0 + (e + \cos\nu)\,\mathbf j_0]/\sqrt{1 + 2e\cos\nu + e^2}$ for $\dot\nu \gt 0$; the opposite vector if $\dot\nu \lt 0$
(c) Relative velocity and acceleration$\mathbf v_1^P = L\dot\theta(-\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1)$; $\mathbf a_1^P = -L(\ddot\theta\sin\theta + \dot\theta^2\cos\theta)\,\mathbf i_1 + L(\ddot\theta\cos\theta - \dot\theta^2\sin\theta)\,\mathbf j_1$
(d) Inertia forces$\mathbf F_A = -m\,\mathbf a_0^S$; $\mathbf F_E = mL\ddot\nu(\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 - \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1)$; $\mathbf F_C = mL\dot\nu^2(\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1)$; $\mathbf F_{COR} = 2mL\dot\nu\dot\theta(\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1)$
(e) Equation for $\theta$general: $L\ddot\theta = -L\ddot\nu + (\mu_F/r^2 + \ddot r - r\dot\nu^2)\sin\theta - (2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu)\cos\theta$; spacecraft in free flight (reading taken): $\ddot\theta + \ddot\nu = 0$
(f) Tensiongeneral: $T = mL\dot\theta^2 + mL\dot\nu^2 + 2mL\dot\theta\dot\nu - m\mu_F\cos\theta/r^2 + m(r\dot\nu^2 - \ddot r)\cos\theta - m(2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu)\sin\theta$; free flight: $T = mL(\dot\theta + \dot\nu)^2$, constant

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 73 and p. 74 print the acceleration of the spacecraft with its rates of the distance, the Euler force and the general tension; the box below sets them side by side with the results above. Every one coincides, so there is no discrepancy. The key does not print the differential equation of part (e), nor the unit tangent of part (b).

Comparison with the official key Law: term-by-term comparison with the key; common denominator Source: Problems.pdf, p. 73; Problems.pdf, p. 74

The key writes the second rate of the distance over the denominator $(1 + e\cos\nu)^4$; dividing its numerator and denominator by $(1 + e\cos\nu)^2$ and by $(1 + e\cos\nu)$ term by term gives the form of the rates box.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{key: } \mathbf a_0^S &= \left(\ddot r - r\dot\nu^2\right)\mathbf i_1 + \left(2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu\right)\mathbf j_1, \quad \dot r = \frac{pe\dot\nu\sin\nu}{(1 + e\cos\nu)^2} \quad &\text{(same as part (a))} \\ \text{key: } \ddot r &= \frac{pe\left(\ddot\nu\sin\nu + \dot\nu^2\cos\nu\right)(1 + e\cos\nu)^2 + 2pe^2\dot\nu^2\sin^2\nu\,(1 + e\cos\nu)}{(1 + e\cos\nu)^4} \quad &\text{(as printed)} \\ &= \frac{pe\left(\ddot\nu\sin\nu + \dot\nu^2\cos\nu\right)}{(1 + e\cos\nu)^2} + \frac{2pe^2\dot\nu^2\sin^2\nu}{(1 + e\cos\nu)^3} \quad &\text{(each term simplified: same as the rates box)} \\ \text{key: } \mathbf F_{Eul} &= mL\ddot\nu\left(\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 - \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(same as part (d))} \\ \text{key: } T &= mL\dot\theta^2 - \frac{\mu_F m\cos\theta}{r^2} + mL\dot\nu^2 + 2mL\dot\theta\dot\nu + m\left(r\dot\nu^2 - \ddot r\right)\cos\theta - m\left(2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu\right)\sin\theta \quad &\text{(same as the general tension of part (f))} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{the four results of the key coincide with this solution}}$$

Units: accelerations $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$; forces $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the key keeps the gravity of $F$ and the acceleration of $S$ as separate terms, which is the general form; it does not use the free-flight reduction.

Independent check in a non-rotating frame Law: Newton's second law in $S_0$ for the astronaut and for the spacecraft in free flight; the cord at the absolute angle of the change-of-basis box Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 8.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.29

With $\mathbf e_c$ at the angle $\theta + \nu$ from $\mathbf i_0$, the vector $L\,\mathbf e_c$ is a circle of radius $L$ described with the angle $\theta + \nu$; its unit vectors turn with the rate of that angle, and the frame through $S$ with the axes of $S_0$ only translates.

$$\begin{aligned} m\,\mathbf a_0^P &= -T\,\mathbf e_c + m\,\mathbf g_S, \quad m\,\mathbf a_0^S = m\,\mathbf g_S \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.4 for $P$ with $\mathbf g_P = \mathbf g_S$; Eq. 8.4 for $S$)} \\ m\left(\mathbf a_0^P - \mathbf a_0^S\right) &= -T\,\mathbf e_c \quad &\text{(difference)} \\ \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\left(L\,\mathbf e_c\right) &= L\left(\ddot\theta + \ddot\nu\right)\mathbf e_\theta - L\left(\dot\theta + \dot\nu\right)^2\mathbf e_c \quad &\text{(chain rule on $\cos(\theta + \nu)$, $\sin(\theta + \nu)$, twice; product rule)} \\ \mathbf e_\theta:\ mL\left(\ddot\theta + \ddot\nu\right) &= 0, \quad \mathbf e_c:\ -mL\left(\dot\theta + \dot\nu\right)^2 = -T \quad &\text{(projections)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\ddot\theta + \ddot\nu = 0, \qquad T = mL\left(\dot\theta + \dot\nu\right)^2}$$

Units: $[mL\dot\theta^2] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: without any inertia force, the inertial route gives the same equation and the same tension as the free-flight forms of parts (e) and (f).

Limiting cases Law: the results at extreme values of the data Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 8.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 8.14
$$\begin{aligned} e = 0:\quad r &= p, \quad \dot r = \ddot r = 0, \quad \mathbf e_t = \mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(circular orbit)} \\ e = 0,\ \text{free flight}:\quad 2\dot r\dot\nu + r\ddot\nu &= p\,\ddot\nu = 0 \Rightarrow \ddot\nu = 0, \quad \mathbf F_E = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 8.6: uniform rotation)} \\ \dot\theta(0) + \dot\nu(0) = 0:\quad T &= 0 \quad &\text{(the astronaut keeps its direction in $S_0$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{e = 0: \ \mathbf F_E = \mathbf 0,\ \mathbf e_t = \mathbf j_1; \qquad \dot\theta(0) + \dot\nu(0) = 0: \ T = 0}$$

Units: $[T] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: on a circular orbit the frame turns uniformly and the Euler force vanishes; an astronaut that does not turn in inertial space leaves the cord without tension, and the taut-cord hypothesis of the statement then fails.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf (PDF page 13); key on PDF pages 73-74
Problem 26

Heavy Particle on a Rotating Half-Circumference (Moving-Frame Method)

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 14
Rotating Wire + Inertia Forces

A heavy point particle $P$ of mass $m$ is constrained to move without friction along the half-circumference wire of radius $a$ shown in the figure. The wire containing the point particle rotates around the $OY$ axis with constant angular velocity $\boldsymbol{\omega} = \Omega\mathbf{j}$. Initially, the particle is located at $x = 0$ with velocity $v_0$ along the positive $x$ axis.

  • (a)
    Determine the number of degrees of freedom of the problem.
  • (b)
    Define a convenient moving reference frame with origin in $O$, $OX_1Y_1Z_1$. Express the inertia force that acts on the particle in this moving reference frame.
  • (c)
    Express also the components of the weight of the particle with respect to $OX_1Y_1Z_1$.
  • (d)
    Determine if there are any equilibrium points.
  • (e)
    Reduce the problem to integrals (i.e. quadratures) and determine the value of the reaction force.
  • (f)
    Is it possible to use the energy equation? If $\Omega$ were a function of time, would it be possible to use the energy equation? Justify your answer.
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

A heavy particle $P$ of mass $m$ slides without friction on a half-circumference wire of radius $a$ whose lowest point is $O$ and whose ends are at the height $a$, at plus and minus $a$ from the axis (figure of the statement); the wire turns about the vertical axis $OY$ with the constant rate $\Omega$, and the particle starts at $O$ with the speed $v_0$ along the positive $x$ axis (Problems.pdf, p. 14). The statement asks for the degrees of freedom, a moving frame with the inertia force, the weight in that frame, the equilibrium points, the quadrature and the reaction, and the use of the energy equation. The wire is at rest in the frame that turns with it, so the solution works there, with the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2 and the inertia forces of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$: $\mathbf i_0$ along $OX$, $\mathbf j_0$ along $OY$ (vertical, up; the $\mathbf j$ of the statement), $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf i_0\times\mathbf j_0$ (Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.1)
Moving frame$S_1 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_1\}$, the frame $OX_1Y_1Z_1$ attached to the wire: $\mathbf i_1$ along $OX_1$ in the plane of the wire, $\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf j_0$ the axis of rotation, $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf i_1\times\mathbf j_1$ normal to the plane of the wire; it coincides with $S_0$ at $t = 0$ and turns by $\Omega t$ about $\mathbf j_0$
Wire basis$\mathcal B_2 = \{\mathbf e_t, \mathbf e_n, \mathbf k_1\}$: unit tangent in the sense of growing $\theta$, principal normal (from $P$ towards the centre $C$) and the normal to the plane
Coordinate$\theta$, the angle at the centre $C$ (at the height $a$ above $O$) from the downward vertical $CO$ to $CP$, positive towards $+\mathbf i_1$; $-\pi/2 \le \theta \le \pi/2$ on the wire
Constraints$P$ in the plane of the wire and at the distance $a$ from $C$: two holonomic, smooth, bilateral constraints, fixed in $S_1$ (rheonomic in $S_0$)
Data$m$ [kg], $a$ [m], $g$ [m s$^{-2}$], $v_0$ [m s$^{-1}$], $\Omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$]
Initial state$\theta(0) = 0$ (the particle at $O$), absolute velocity $v_0\,\mathbf i_0$
Unknowns$\theta(t)$; the reaction $\mathbf N = N_n\,\mathbf e_n + N_b\,\mathbf k_1$ (normal subspace of a curve, Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.16)
Applied forceweight $-mg\,\mathbf j_0$
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)of the origin, Euler, centrifugal and Coriolis (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial, uniform gravity, smooth wire (no tangential reaction), the rotation of the wire imposed from outside

(a) Degrees of freedom

Number of degrees of freedom Law: coordinates of a free particle minus independent holonomic constraints Source: Notes.pdf, Sec. 2.7; Notes.pdf, Sec. 6.5; Problems.pdf, p. 14

In $S_1$ the two constraints are the plane of the wire and the circle of centre $C$; written with the components $x_1$, $y_1$, $z_1$ of the position in $\mathcal B_1$ they are independent, because one fixes $z_1$ and the other involves $x_1$ and $y_1$ only.

$$\begin{aligned} z_1 &= 0 \quad &\text{(plane of the wire)} \\ x_1^2 + \left(y_1 - a\right)^2 - a^2 &= 0 \quad &\text{(circle of centre $C$ and radius $a$)} \\ 3 - 2 &= 1 \quad &\text{(coordinates minus constraints)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{one degree of freedom, the angle } \theta(t)}$$

Units: $[x_1^2] = [a^2] = [\mathrm{L^2}]$

Meaning: the angle $\Omega t$ of the wire is prescribed, a known function of time, so it adds no degree of freedom.

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. View from $+Y$, with $\mathbf j_0 = \mathbf j_1$ out of the paper ($\odot$): $\mathbf k_0$ points down the page. $\mathbf i_1, \mathbf k_1$ are $\mathbf i_0, \mathbf k_0$ turned counter-clockwise by $\Omega t$; the components of $\mathbf i_1$ are $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$ and $\sin\Omega t$ along $-\mathbf k_0$ (up the page), hence the minus sign.
Basis of the turning wire: rotation by Omega t about j0 Law: elementary rotation about the second axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.19; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

View from above, along $\mathbf j_0$, which points out of the paper (⊙). With $\mathbf i_0$ to the right, $\mathbf k_0$, the cross product of $\mathbf i_0$ and $\mathbf j_0$, points down the page (right-hand rule: fingers from $\mathbf i_0$, to the right, towards $\mathbf j_0$, towards the reader; the thumb goes down the page), so minus $\mathbf k_0$ points up the page. A positive $\Omega$ turns the wire counterclockwise in this view. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\Omega t$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\Omega t$ up the page, that is along minus $\mathbf k_0$ (the minus sign). $\mathbf k_1$ is $\mathbf k_0$ (down the page) turned by the same angle: adjacent leg $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf k_0$, opposite leg $\sin\Omega t$ along plus $\mathbf i_0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 - \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(right triangle of $\mathbf i_1$: opposite leg on $-\mathbf k_0$)} \\ \mathbf j_1 &= \mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(axis of the rotation; right triangle of $\mathbf k_1$)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\Omega t\cos\Omega t - \sin\Omega t\left(-\sin\Omega t\right)\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the second row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{2+2}$)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\Omega t + \sin^2\Omega t = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{13} = -\cos\Omega t\sin\Omega t + \sin\Omega t\cos\Omega t = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows; row 2 is the unit row of $\mathbf j_0$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\Omega t & 0 & \sin\Omega t \cr 0 & 1 & 0 \cr -\sin\Omega t & 0 & \cos\Omega t \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: $[\Omega t] = [1]$

Meaning: it is the matrix of Eq. 1.19 with the angle $\Omega t$; $\mathbf k_1$ stays horizontal and normal to the plane of the wire.

Figure 2. Plane of the wire, fixed in $S_1$: $\theta$ is measured at $C$ from the downward vertical $CO$. In the shaded right triangle the hypotenuse is $|CP| = a$, the leg opposite $\theta$ is $a\sin\theta$ and the adjacent leg is $a\cos\theta$; the dashed lines are the components of $\mathbf r_1^P$. $\mathbf i_1, \mathbf j_1$ in blue, $\mathbf e_t, \mathbf e_n$ in orange.
Position vector and wire basis in the plane of the wire Law: position as a sum of segments; right triangle of the radius $CP$; relation with the standard polar angle; rotation in the plane and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.9; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 14

The plane of the wire, fixed in $S_1$, is drawn with $\mathbf i_1$ to the right and $\mathbf j_1$ up, so $\mathbf k_1$ points out of the paper (⊙). From $O$ to $P$ we pass through the centre $C$, because the distance from $C$ is the one that stays constant. Let $F$ be the point of the axis at the height of $P$: in the shaded right triangle $CFP$ the hypotenuse is $a$, the leg opposite to $\theta$ is $FP$, of length $a\sin\theta$, along $\mathbf i_1$, and the leg adjacent to $\theta$ is $CF$, of length $a\cos\theta$, pointing down, along minus $\mathbf j_1$ (the minus sign: $\theta$ is measured from the downward vertical). The standard polar angle about $C$, measured from $\mathbf i_1$ counterclockwise, is $\theta - \pi/2$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_0^O &= \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf r_0^P = \mathbf r_1^P = \overrightarrow{OC} + \overrightarrow{CP} \quad &\text{(origin of $S_1$ at the fixed $O$; Eq. 3.16)} \\ \overrightarrow{OC} &= a\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \overrightarrow{CP} = a\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 - a\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(centre on the axis; legs of $CFP$)} \\ \cos\left(\theta - \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) &= \cos\theta\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2} + \sin\theta\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} = \sin\theta, \quad \sin\left(\theta - \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \sin\theta\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2} - \cos\theta\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} = -\cos\theta \quad &\text{(difference formulas: the standard form gives the same $\overrightarrow{CP}$)} \\ \mathbf r_1^P &= a\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + a\left(1 - \cos\theta\right)\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(sum, grouped by unit vector)} \\ \frac{d\mathbf r_1^P}{d\theta} &= a\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + a\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left|\frac{d\mathbf r_1^P}{d\theta}\right| = a \quad &\text{($\tfrac{d}{d\theta}\sin\theta = \cos\theta$, $\tfrac{d}{d\theta}(1 - \cos\theta) = \sin\theta$)} \\ \mathbf e_t &= \cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf e_n = \frac{d\mathbf e_t}{d\theta} = -\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 2.9; $\mathbf e_n$ is minus $\overrightarrow{CP}/a$: towards $C$)} \\ \det[{}_1R_2] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta\right) = 1, \quad \mathbf e_t\cdot\mathbf e_n = -\cos\theta\sin\theta + \sin\theta\cos\theta = 0 \quad &\text{(third row; columns orthogonal)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^P = a\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + a\left(1 - \cos\theta\right)\mathbf j_1, \quad [{}_1R_2] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \cr \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_1R_2] = 1}$$

Units: $[a] = [\mathrm{L}]$; direction cosines dimensionless

Meaning: $\theta$ zero is the lowest point $O$ and $\theta$ equal to $\pi/2$ the end of the wire at the height $a$; the distance of $P$ to the axis is the horizontal leg $a\sin\theta$.

Kinematics

Motion of the turning frame and derivatives of the unit vectors Law: angular velocity of a simple rotation; derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis; chain rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \dot\Omega\,\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(simple rotation about the fixed vertical; $\Omega$ constant; $O$ fixed)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf i_1 = -\Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf k_1 = \Omega\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 to 3.5)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 - \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0\right) &= -\Omega\sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 - \Omega\cos\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0 = -\Omega\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(check: chain rule on the components of $\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_t}{dt}\right|_1 &= \frac{d\mathbf e_t}{d\theta}\,\dot\theta = \dot\theta\,\mathbf e_n \quad &\text{(chain rule; $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$ constant in $S_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_t}{dt}\right|_1 = \dot\theta\,\mathbf e_n}$$

Units: $[\Omega] = [\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: in $S_1$ only the wire basis turns, with the particle; in $S_0$ the whole plane of the wire turns about the vertical as well.

Relative velocity and relative acceleration Law: time derivatives in $S_1$; chain rule and product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_1^P &= a\cos\theta\,\dot\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + a\sin\theta\,\dot\theta\,\mathbf j_1 = a\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_t \quad &\text{(chain rule on the components)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P &= a\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_t + a\dot\theta\left.\frac{d\mathbf e_t}{dt}\right|_1 = a\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_t + a\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf e_n \quad &\text{(product rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_1^P = a\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_t, \qquad \mathbf a_1^P = a\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_t + a\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf e_n}$$

Units: $[a\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[a\ddot\theta] = [a\dot\theta^2] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: in $S_1$ the particle moves on a fixed circle: a tangential acceleration and a centripetal one towards $C$.

Absolute velocity and acceleration: transport, Coriolis and centripetal terms Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the position written in the turning basis; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P &= \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left(a\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + a(1 - \cos\theta)\,\mathbf j_1\right) = a\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + a\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + a\sin\theta\left(-\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule; derivatives of $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ &= \underbrace{a\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_t}_{\mathbf v_1^P} + \underbrace{\left(-\Omega a\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1\right)}_{\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P} \quad &\text{(grouped; $\Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times a\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 = -\Omega a\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1^P}{dt}\right|_0 &= \frac{d}{dt}\left(a\dot\theta\cos\theta\right)\mathbf i_1 + \frac{d}{dt}\left(a\dot\theta\sin\theta\right)\mathbf j_1 + a\dot\theta\cos\theta\left(-\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\right) = \mathbf a_1^P - \Omega a\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(components in $S_1$ plus the turning of $\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left(-\Omega a\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1\right) &= -\Omega a\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 - \Omega^2a\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(chain rule; derivative of $\mathbf k_1$)} \\ 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P &= 2\Omega a\dot\theta\,\mathbf j_1\times\left(\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1\right) = -2\Omega a\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(the two $\mathbf k_1$ terms above)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) &= \Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\left(-\Omega a\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1\right) = -\Omega^2a\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(the $\mathbf i_1$ term above; $\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf i_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_0^P = a\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_t - \Omega a\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1, \qquad \mathbf a_0^P = a\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_t + a\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf e_n - 2\Omega a\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 - \Omega^2a\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1}$$

Units: every acceleration term $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the Coriolis acceleration is normal to the plane of the wire and appears because the distance to the axis changes while the plane turns; the centripetal one points horizontally to the axis.

Forces and Equations of Motion

The free-body diagram of the particle in $S_1$ shows, in the plane of the wire, the weight, the reaction along $\mathbf e_n$ and the centrifugal force (horizontal, away from the axis); normal to the plane, the reaction along $\mathbf k_1$ and the Coriolis force. The inertia force of the origin and the Euler force vanish ($O$ fixed, $\Omega$ constant).

Figure 3. Forces on $P$ in $S_1$. In the plane of the wire: weight, $N_n\,\mathbf e_n$ and the centrifugal force $m\Omega^2a\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1$ (dashed, inertia). Normal to it: the reaction $N_b\,\mathbf k_1$ and the Coriolis force $2m\Omega a\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1$ (dashed, inertia), which balance each other.

(b) Inertia force in the moving frame

Inertia forces on the particle in the turning frame Law: inertia forces of a non-inertial frame, each vector product expanded Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; Problems.pdf, p. 14
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf F_A &= -m\,\mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf F_E = -m\,\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{($O$ fixed; $\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}$ zero)} \\ \mathbf F_C &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) = m\Omega^2a\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(centripetal term of the composition box times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR} &= -2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P = 2m\Omega a\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Coriolis term times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf i_1\cdot\mathbf e_t &= \cos\theta, \quad \mathbf i_1\cdot\mathbf e_n = -\sin\theta \quad &\text{(components of the wire basis)} \\ \mathbf F_C &= m\Omega^2a\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf e_t - m\Omega^2a\sin^2\theta\,\mathbf e_n \quad &\text{(projected on the wire basis)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf F_i = \mathbf F_C + \mathbf F_{COR} = m\Omega^2a\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + 2m\Omega a\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1}$$

Units: $[m\Omega^2a] = [m\Omega a\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the centrifugal force is horizontal, away from the axis, and proportional to the distance $a\sin\theta$; the Coriolis force is normal to the plane of the wire, along plus $\mathbf k_1$ while $\theta$ grows (the factor $\cos\theta$ is positive on the whole wire).

(c) Weight in the moving frame

Components of the weight Law: the axis of rotation is the vertical, so $\mathbf j_1$ is the vertical at every instant Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.19; Problems.pdf, p. 14
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf W &= -mg\,\mathbf j_0 = -mg\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(second column of $[{}_0R_1]$: $\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf j_0$)} \\ \mathbf W\cdot\mathbf e_t &= -mg\sin\theta, \quad \mathbf W\cdot\mathbf e_n = -mg\cos\theta, \quad \mathbf W\cdot\mathbf k_1 = 0 \quad &\text{($\mathbf j_1\cdot\mathbf e_t = \sin\theta$, $\mathbf j_1\cdot\mathbf e_n = \cos\theta$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{W_{X_1} = 0, \quad W_{Y_1} = -mg, \quad W_{Z_1} = 0}$$

Units: $[mg] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the weight keeps the same components in the turning frame, because it lies along the axis of the rotation.

Newton's second law in the turning frame, projected on the wire basis Law: Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame with the inertia forces; reaction of a smooth curve Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.16; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.18; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.19; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]
$$\begin{aligned} m\,\mathbf a_1^P &= \mathbf W + N_n\,\mathbf e_n + N_b\,\mathbf k_1 + \mathbf F_C + \mathbf F_{COR} \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.63)} \\ \mathbf e_t:\ ma\ddot\theta &= -mg\sin\theta + m\Omega^2a\sin\theta\cos\theta \quad &\text{(tangent: no reaction, no Coriolis force)} \\ \mathbf e_n:\ ma\dot\theta^2 &= -mg\cos\theta + N_n - m\Omega^2a\sin^2\theta \quad &\text{(in the plane, towards $C$)} \\ \mathbf k_1:\ 0 &= N_b + 2m\Omega a\dot\theta\cos\theta \quad &\text{(normal to the plane: no relative motion there)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\ddot\theta = \sin\theta\left(\Omega^2\cos\theta - \frac{g}{a}\right), \qquad N_n = ma\dot\theta^2 + mg\cos\theta + m\Omega^2a\sin^2\theta, \qquad N_b = -2m\Omega a\dot\theta\cos\theta}$$

Units: $[g/a] = [\Omega^2] = [\mathrm{T^{-2}}]$; $[N_n] = [N_b] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: three scalar equations for the three unknowns $\theta$, $N_n$ and $N_b$: the tangent equation is the equation of motion, the other two give the reaction afterwards.

Answers and Checks

(d) Equilibrium points

Relative equilibria on the wire Law: relative rest in the tangent equation Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.32; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63
