$$\begin{aligned} \dot\theta = 0,\ \ddot\theta = 0:\quad \sin\theta\left(\Omega^2\cos\theta - \frac{g}{a}\right) &= 0 \quad &\text{(tangent equation at rest)} \\ \sin\theta = 0 &\Rightarrow \theta = 0 \quad &\text{(the only zero of the sine between $-\pi/2$ and $\pi/2$)} \\ \cos\theta_e &= \frac{g}{a\Omega^2} \quad &\text{(second factor)} \\ 0 \lt \frac{g}{a\Omega^2} \lt 1 &\iff \Omega^2 \gt \frac{g}{a} \quad &\text{(a solution with $0 \lt |\theta_e| \lt \pi/2$ exists)} \\ \theta = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}:\quad \ddot\theta &= \pm 1\cdot\left(0 - \frac{g}{a}\right) \ne 0 \quad &\text{(the ends of the wire are not equilibria)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\theta = 0 \ \text{for every } \Omega; \qquad \theta = \pm\arccos\frac{g}{a\Omega^2} \ \text{only if } \Omega^2 \gt \frac{g}{a}}$$

Units: $[g/(a\Omega^2)] = [1]$

Meaning: yes, there are equilibria: the bottom always, and two symmetric points off the axis above the critical rate, where the tangential pull of the weight towards the bottom balances the tangential push of the centrifugal force.

(e) Quadrature and reaction force

Initial relative rate Law: composition of velocities at the initial instant Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.20; Problems.pdf, p. 14
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P(0) &= a\dot\theta(0)\,\mathbf e_t(0) - \Omega a\sin 0\,\mathbf k_1 = a\dot\theta(0)\left(\cos 0\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin 0\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(velocity box; $\theta(0) = 0$)} \\ &= a\dot\theta(0)\,\mathbf i_0 = v_0\,\mathbf i_0 \quad &\text{($\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf i_0$ at $t = 0$; initial condition)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\theta(0) = 0, \qquad \dot\theta(0) = \frac{v_0}{a}}$$

Units: $[v_0/a] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: at $O$ the particle is on the axis, so the transport velocity is zero and the given velocity is the relative one.

First integral and quadrature Law: the tangent equation multiplied by the rate is an exact derivative (chain rule); Barrow's rule; separation of variables Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.44; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]
$$\begin{aligned} ma^2\dot\theta\ddot\theta + mga\sin\theta\,\dot\theta - m\Omega^2a^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\theta &= 0 \quad &\text{(tangent equation times $ma\dot\theta$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac12 ma^2\dot\theta^2\right) &= ma^2\dot\theta\ddot\theta, \quad \frac{d}{dt}\left(-mga\cos\theta\right) = mga\sin\theta\,\dot\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(-\tfrac12 m\Omega^2a^2\sin^2\theta\right) &= -m\Omega^2a^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule on $\sin^2\theta$)} \\ \left[\tfrac12 ma^2\dot\theta^2 - mga\cos\theta - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2a^2\sin^2\theta\right]_0^t &= 0 \quad &\text{(the sum is constant; Barrow's rule)} \\ \tfrac12 ma^2\dot\theta^2 - mga\cos\theta - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2a^2\sin^2\theta &= \tfrac12 mv_0^2 - mga \quad &\text{(value at $t = 0$: $\theta = 0$, $a\dot\theta = v_0$)} \\ \dot\theta^2 &= \frac{v_0^2}{a^2} - \frac{2g}{a}\left(1 - \cos\theta\right) + \Omega^2\sin^2\theta \quad &\text{(multiplied by $2/(ma^2)$)} \\ dt &= \frac{d\theta}{\sqrt{v_0^2/a^2 - (2g/a)(1 - \cos\theta) + \Omega^2\sin^2\theta}} \quad &\text{(positive root, $\dot\theta(0) \gt 0$; variables separated)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{t = \int_0^{\theta}\frac{d\theta'}{\sqrt{\dfrac{v_0^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{2g}{a}\left(1 - \cos\theta'\right) + \Omega^2\sin^2\theta'}} \quad \text{(until the first turning point or the end of the wire)}}$$

Units: every term of the radicand $[\mathrm{T^{-2}}]$; the integral is a time

Meaning: the motion is reduced to one integral; the particle turns back where the radicand vanishes, or reaches the end of the wire if it stays positive up to $\theta$ equal to $\pi/2$.

Reaction force as a function of the angle Law: normal equations of the turning frame with the squared rate eliminated through the first integral Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.18; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.19
$$\begin{aligned} N_n &= ma\dot\theta^2 + mg\cos\theta + m\Omega^2a\sin^2\theta \quad &\text{(equation along $\mathbf e_n$)} \\ &= \frac{mv_0^2}{a} - 2mg\left(1 - \cos\theta\right) + m\Omega^2a\sin^2\theta + mg\cos\theta + m\Omega^2a\sin^2\theta \quad &\text{(squared rate of the first integral times $ma$)} \\ &= \frac{mv_0^2}{a} + mg\left(3\cos\theta - 2\right) + 2m\Omega^2a\sin^2\theta \quad &\text{(terms collected)} \\ N_b &= -2m\Omega a\dot\theta\cos\theta = \mp 2m\Omega a\cos\theta\sqrt{\frac{v_0^2}{a^2} - \frac{2g}{a}\left(1 - \cos\theta\right) + \Omega^2\sin^2\theta} \quad &\text{(equation along $\mathbf k_1$; upper sign while $\theta$ grows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf N = \left[\frac{mv_0^2}{a} + mg\left(3\cos\theta - 2\right) + 2m\Omega^2a\sin^2\theta\right]\mathbf e_n - 2m\Omega a\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf e_n = -\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[mv_0^2/a] = [mg] = [m\Omega^2a] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the in-plane part carries the weight, the centrifugal push and the centripetal need of the circle; the part normal to the plane points along minus $\mathbf k_1$ while $\theta$ grows, against the Coriolis force.

(f) Energy equation

Energy in the turning frame with constant and with variable Omega Law: power of each force on the relative velocity; potentials as minus the work along the wire, with Barrow's rule; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.11; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]

With constant $\Omega$ the energy in $S_1$ is conserved for two reasons. First, the forces that do no work in $S_1$: the reaction, because the wire is smooth and at rest in $S_1$, so the reaction is normal to the relative velocity; the Coriolis force, always normal to the relative velocity; the force of the origin and the Euler force, which vanish. Second, the forces that do work have potentials that depend on the position only: the weight, and the centrifugal force because $\Omega$ is constant. Along the wire the displacement is $a\,\mathbf e_t\,d\theta'$. With $\Omega(t)$ the Euler force appears; it is normal to the plane, so it still does no work, but the centrifugal potential now depends on time.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf N\cdot\mathbf v_1^P &= a\dot\theta\left(N_n\,\mathbf e_n + N_b\,\mathbf k_1\right)\cdot\mathbf e_t = 0, \quad \mathbf F_{COR}\cdot\mathbf v_1^P = 2m\Omega a^2\dot\theta^2\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1\cdot\mathbf e_t = 0 \quad &\text{(no power in $S_1$)} \\ V_C(\theta) - V_C(0) &= -\int_0^{\theta}m\Omega^2a\sin\theta'\,\mathbf i_1\cdot\mathbf e_t\,a\,d\theta' = -m\Omega^2a^2\left[\tfrac12\sin^2\theta'\right]_0^{\theta} = -\tfrac12 m\Omega^2a^2\sin^2\theta \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.14; antiderivative $\tfrac12\sin^2\theta'$; Barrow's rule)} \\ V_g(\theta) - V_g(0) &= -\int_0^{\theta}\left(-mg\,\mathbf j_1\right)\cdot\mathbf e_t\,a\,d\theta' = mga\left[-\cos\theta'\right]_0^{\theta} = mga\left(1 - \cos\theta\right) \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.14; antiderivative $-\cos\theta'$; Barrow's rule)} \\ E_1^P &= \tfrac12 ma^2\dot\theta^2 + mga\left(1 - \cos\theta\right) - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2a^2\sin^2\theta = \tfrac12 mv_0^2 \quad &\text{(constant $\Omega$: the first integral of part (e), with its initial value)} \\ \mathbf F_E &= -m\dot\Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf r_1^P = -m\dot\Omega a\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf i_1 = m\dot\Omega a\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf F_E\cdot\mathbf v_1^P = 0 \quad &\text{(variable $\Omega$: Eq. 4.62; normal to the plane)} \\ \frac{dE_1^P}{dt} &= \dot\theta\left(ma^2\ddot\theta + mga\sin\theta - m\Omega^2a^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\right) - m\Omega\dot\Omega a^2\sin^2\theta = -m\Omega\dot\Omega a^2\sin^2\theta \quad &\text{(product and chain rules; the bracket is the tangent equation, zero)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\Omega \text{ constant: } E_1^P = \tfrac12 ma^2\dot\theta^2 + mga\left(1 - \cos\theta\right) - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2a^2\sin^2\theta = \tfrac12 mv_0^2; \qquad \Omega(t): \ \frac{dE_1^P}{dt} = -m\Omega\dot\Omega a^2\sin^2\theta \ne 0}$$

Units: $[E_1^P] = [ma^2\dot\theta^2] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$; $[m\Omega\dot\Omega a^2] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-3}}]$, a power

Meaning: yes with constant $\Omega$, in the turning frame: it is the first integral of part (e). No with $\Omega(t)$: the balance still holds but its right-hand side depends on the unknown position, so it is not a first integral.

The energy in the inertial frame is not conserved Law: power of the reaction on the absolute velocity Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.11; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31

Write $E_0^P$ for the energy in $S_0$: the kinetic energy computed with the absolute velocity plus the potential of the weight. Of the forces in $S_0$ only the weight has a potential, so the rate of $E_0^P$ is the power of the reaction (Eq. 4.11).

$$\begin{aligned} E_0^P &= \tfrac12 m\,\mathbf v_0^P\cdot\mathbf v_0^P + mga\left(1 - \cos\theta\right) = \tfrac12 m\left(a^2\dot\theta^2 + \Omega^2a^2\sin^2\theta\right) + mga\left(1 - \cos\theta\right) \quad &\text{(absolute velocity box: $\mathbf e_t$ and $\mathbf k_1$ orthogonal)} \\ \mathbf N\cdot\mathbf v_0^P &= \left(N_n\,\mathbf e_n + N_b\,\mathbf k_1\right)\cdot\left(a\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_t - \Omega a\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1\right) = -N_b\,\Omega a\sin\theta \quad &\text{(absolute velocity box)} \\ &= 2m\Omega^2a^2\dot\theta\sin\theta\cos\theta \quad &\text{($N_b$ of the equations of motion)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\frac{dE_0^P}{dt} = \mathbf N\cdot\mathbf v_0^P = 2m\Omega^2a^2\dot\theta\sin\theta\cos\theta \ne 0}$$

Units: $[m\Omega^2a^2\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-3}}]$, a power

Meaning: in $S_0$ the wire moves and its reaction does work, supplied by whatever keeps the rotation uniform; the energy equation can only be used in $S_1$.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Degrees of freedomone, the angle $\theta$ (two holonomic constraints; $\Omega t$ prescribed)
(b) Moving frame and inertia force$S_1$: $\mathbf i_1$ in the plane of the wire, $\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf j_0$ the axis, $\mathbf k_1$ normal to the plane; $\mathbf F_i = m\Omega^2a\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + 2m\Omega a\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1$
(c) Weight$\mathbf W = -mg\,\mathbf j_1$: components $(0, -mg, 0)$ in $\mathcal B_1$
(d) Equilibria$\theta = 0$ always; $\theta = \pm\arccos(g/(a\Omega^2))$ if $\Omega^2 \gt g/a$
(e) Quadrature$t = \int_0^{\theta}d\theta'/\sqrt{v_0^2/a^2 - (2g/a)(1 - \cos\theta') + \Omega^2\sin^2\theta'}$
(e) Reaction$\mathbf N = [mv_0^2/a + mg(3\cos\theta - 2) + 2m\Omega^2a\sin^2\theta]\,\mathbf e_n - 2m\Omega a\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1$
(f) Energy equationyes in $S_1$ with constant $\Omega$: $\frac12 ma^2\dot\theta^2 + mga(1 - \cos\theta) - \frac12 m\Omega^2a^2\sin^2\theta = \frac12 mv_0^2$; no with $\Omega(t)$: $dE_1^P/dt = -m\Omega\dot\Omega a^2\sin^2\theta$

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 74 lists item 26 with no answer, so there is no key to compare with. Independent checks: the reaction normal to the plane follows again from the angular momentum about the vertical axis in $S_0$ (box below), and the limiting cases close the results.

Independent check: angular momentum about the vertical axis Law: angular momentum about the fixed point $O$ and its rate, equal to the moment of the forces Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.48; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.53

In $\mathcal B_1$ the position has the components $(a\sin\theta, a(1 - \cos\theta), 0)$ and the absolute velocity $(a\dot\theta\cos\theta, a\dot\theta\sin\theta, -\Omega a\sin\theta)$. The component along $\mathbf j_1$ of a vector product is the third component of the first factor times the first of the second, minus the first of the first times the third of the second.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf H_{O,0}\cdot\mathbf j_1 &= m\left(0\cdot a\dot\theta\cos\theta - a\sin\theta\left(-\Omega a\sin\theta\right)\right) = m\Omega a^2\sin^2\theta \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.48)} \\ \mathbf M_O\cdot\mathbf j_1 &= 0\cdot 0 - a\sin\theta\,N_b = -a\sin\theta\,N_b \quad &\text{(weight along $\mathbf j_1$, $N_n\,\mathbf e_n$ in the plane: no axial moment)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(m\Omega a^2\sin^2\theta\right) &= 2m\Omega a^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule; $\mathbf j_1$ fixed)} \\ -a\sin\theta\,N_b &= 2m\Omega a^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\theta \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.53, axial component)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{N_b = -2m\Omega a\dot\theta\cos\theta \quad (\sin\theta \ne 0)}$$

Units: $[H] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-1}}]$; $[a\,N_b] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: to keep turning at the rate $\Omega$ while its distance to the axis changes, the particle needs an axial moment that only the normal reaction can give: the same result as the Coriolis balance in $S_1$.

Limiting cases Law: the results at extreme values of the data Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.38; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63
$$\begin{aligned} \Omega \to 0:\quad \ddot\theta &= -\frac{g}{a}\sin\theta, \quad N_b \to 0, \quad N_n \to \frac{mv_0^2}{a} + mg\left(3\cos\theta - 2\right) \quad &\text{(simple pendulum of length $a$, Eq. 4.38)} \\ \Omega^2 \to \infty:\quad \cos\theta_e &= \frac{g}{a\Omega^2} \to 0, \quad \theta_e \to \pm\frac{\pi}{2} \quad &\text{(the off-axis equilibria move to the ends)} \\ v_0 = 0:\quad \dot\theta^2 &= -\frac{2g}{a}\left(1 - \cos\theta\right) + \Omega^2\sin^2\theta \quad &\text{(zero at $\theta = 0$: the particle stays at the bottom)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\Omega \to 0: \text{ pendulum of length } a,\ N_b \to 0; \qquad \Omega \to \infty: \ \theta_e \to \pm\frac{\pi}{2}}$$

Units: $[g/a] = [\mathrm{T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: without rotation the wire is a pendulum and pushes nothing sideways; a very fast spin pushes the off-axis equilibria up to the ends of the wire.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf
Problem 27

Bead on a Rotating Sine-Shaped Wire with a Spring

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 15
Rotating Wire + SpringIn-Class Session 10

A heavy bead $P$ of mass $m$ slides without friction along a thin wire with shape given by the following equation:

$$ y_1(x_1) = \sin x_1. $$

Moreover, the bead is joined to a straight rail located at $y_1 = 2$ by a spring of stiffness $k$. The connection of the spring with the rail can move freely along the rail, so that the spring is always vertical. The whole setup rotates with respect to the $y_1$ axis with a constant angular velocity $\omega$. A sketch of the setup and the definition of the right-handed, rotating $Ox_1y_1z_1$ reference frame is given below.

  • (a)
    Write down the general expression for the components of the relative velocity and acceleration of $P$ in the reference frame $Ox_1y_1z_1$ as functions of the axial position of the bead, $x_1$, and its time derivatives $\dot x_1$ and $\ddot x_1$.
  • (b)
    Identify all forces acting on the bead and then write down the three components of Newton's second law in the $Ox_1y_1z_1$ reference frame. From these equations, obtain an explicit expression of the components of the reaction force on the wire as a function of $x_1$, $\dot x_1$ and the parameters of the problem only, and a second order differential equation for $x_1$ that does not depend on the reaction force.
  • (c)
    Is it possible to use the equation of conservation of mechanical energy of the relative motion of $P$? If so, write it down in terms of $x_1$, $\dot x_1$ and the parameters of the problem. What is the relation of this equation with the differential equation for $x_1$ in the previous point?
  • (d)
    For $\omega = 0$ and $x_1 \in [0, 2\pi]$, discuss the existence of equilibrium positions as a function of the parameter $\lambda = mg/k$. Are these equilibrium positions stable?
  • (e)
    Consider now that $\omega \neq 0$, and $k = 0$. We drop the bead $P$ at $x_1 = \pi$ with no initial velocity. Sketch the shape of the potential and discuss qualitatively the motion of $P$ if the parameter $\beta = \omega^2/g$ is small or large. Write down the system of equations that would allow to solve for the critical value of $\beta$ that divides between the two behaviors.
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

A heavy bead $P$ of mass $m$ slides without friction on a plane wire of sine shape; a vertical spring of stiffness $k$ joins it to a horizontal rail along which its upper end slides freely, and the whole setup turns about the vertical axis $Oy_1$ with the constant rate $\omega$ (Problems.pdf, p. 15). The statement asks for the relative velocity and acceleration, the three components of Newton's second law with the reaction and the equation of motion, the energy equation of the relative motion, the equilibria without rotation, and the motion without spring after a release at $x_1$ equal to $\pi$. The wire, rail and spring are at rest in the turning frame, so the solution works there, with the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2 and the inertia forces of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9.

ItemDefinition
Wire and railwire $y_1 = \sin x_1$, rail $y_1 = 2$, both in the plane $Ox_1y_1$, fixed in $S_1$
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$, $\mathbf j_0$ vertical, up, along the axis of rotation, $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf i_0\times\mathbf j_0$ (Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.1)
Moving frame$S_1 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_1\}$, the frame $Ox_1y_1z_1$ of the statement: $\mathbf i_1$ along $Ox_1$ in the plane of the wire, $\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf j_0$, $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf i_1\times\mathbf j_1$ normal to the plane; it coincides with $S_0$ at $t = 0$ and turns by $\omega t$ about $\mathbf j_0$
Wire directions$\mathbf t = \mathbf i_1 + \cos x_1\,\mathbf j_1$ (tangent, in the sense of growing $x_1$) and $\mathbf n = -\cos x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \mathbf j_1$ (in-plane normal), both of length $\sqrt{1 + \cos^2 x_1}$
Coordinate$x_1$, the axial position of the bead
Constraints$z_1 = 0$ and $y_1 = \sin x_1$: two holonomic, smooth, bilateral constraints, fixed in $S_1$
Degrees of freedom3 minus 2: 1, the coordinate $x_1(t)$
Data$m$ [kg], $k$ [N m$^{-1}$], $g$ [m s$^{-2}$], $\omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$]; $\lambda = mg/k$ [m] (part (d)); $\beta = \omega^2/g$ [m$^{-1}$] (part (e))
Unknowns$x_1(t)$; the reaction $\mathbf N = N_x\,\mathbf i_1 + N_y\,\mathbf j_1 + N_z\,\mathbf k_1$ with $\mathbf N\cdot\mathbf t$ zero (smooth wire)
Applied forcesweight $-mg\,\mathbf j_1$; spring, vertical, towards the rail
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)of the origin, Euler, centrifugal and Coriolis (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial; uniform gravity; smooth wire; massless spring with its upper end free on a smooth rail, so it stays vertical; $\omega$ constant
Readingsthe wire equation is numerical, with $x_1$ and $y_1$ in metres (the rail at 2 m); the natural length of the spring is taken as zero, as the energy integral of the key implies (with a natural length $\ell_0$, replace 2 by $2 - \ell_0$ in the spring terms; the bounds on $\lambda$ in part (d) then shift by $\ell_0$)

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. View from $+y_1$, with $\mathbf j_0 = \mathbf j_1$ out of the paper ($\odot$): $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf i_0\times\mathbf j_0$ points down the page. The plane of the wire turns counter-clockwise by $\omega t$: the components of $\mathbf i_1$ are $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$ and $\sin\omega t$ along $-\mathbf k_0$ (up the page), hence $\mathbf i_1 = \cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 - \sin\omega t\,\mathbf k_0$.
Basis of the turning setup: rotation by omega t about j0 Law: elementary rotation about the second axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.19; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

View from above, along $\mathbf j_0$, which points out of the paper (⊙). With $\mathbf i_0$ to the right, $\mathbf k_0$, the cross product of $\mathbf i_0$ and $\mathbf j_0$, points down the page (right-hand rule: fingers from $\mathbf i_0$, to the right, towards $\mathbf j_0$, towards the reader; the thumb goes down the page), so minus $\mathbf k_0$ points up the page. A positive $\omega$ turns the setup counterclockwise in this view. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\omega t$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ up the page, along minus $\mathbf k_0$ (the minus sign). $\mathbf k_1$ is $\mathbf k_0$ turned by the same angle: adjacent leg $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf k_0$, opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ along plus $\mathbf i_0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 - \sin\omega t\,\mathbf k_0, \quad \mathbf j_1 = \mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\omega t\,\mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles; axis)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\omega t\cos\omega t - \sin\omega t\left(-\sin\omega t\right)\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the second row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{2+2}$)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\omega t + \sin^2\omega t = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{13} = -\cos\omega t\sin\omega t + \sin\omega t\cos\omega t = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\omega t & 0 & \sin\omega t \cr 0 & 1 & 0 \cr -\sin\omega t & 0 & \cos\omega t \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: $[\omega t] = [1]$

Meaning: it is the matrix of Eq. 1.19 with the angle $\omega t$; the vertical keeps its direction, so the weight has the same components in both frames.

Figure 2. Plane of the wire, fixed in $Ox_1y_1z_1$. The dashed lines are the components $x_1$ and $\sin x_1$ of $\mathbf r_1^P$; the spring is vertical, of length $2 - \sin x_1$. In the shaded slope triangle the horizontal leg is $dx_1$ and the vertical leg is $dy_1 = \cos x_1\,dx_1$ (negative here: the wire goes down), so the tangent direction is $\mathbf t = \mathbf i_1 + \cos x_1\,\mathbf j_1$ and the in-plane normal is $\mathbf n = -\cos x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \mathbf j_1$ (orange, drawn as unit vectors).
Position vector, spring length and wire directions Law: position as the sum of its components; chain rule; slope triangle; quarter turn in the plane Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.2; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 15

The plane of the wire, fixed in $S_1$, is drawn with $\mathbf i_1$ to the right and $\mathbf j_1$ up, so $\mathbf k_1$ points out of the paper (⊙) and a quarter turn about it is counterclockwise. The bead is at the abscissa $x_1$ and at the height of the wire; the spring goes vertically from $P$ up to the rail. In the slope triangle the horizontal leg is $dx_1$ and the vertical leg $dy_1$; the hypotenuse lies along the wire, so the vector sum of the two legs divided by $dx_1$ is a tangent vector.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_0^O &= \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf r_0^P = \mathbf r_1^P = x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin x_1\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.16 with $O$ fixed; components of $P$)} \\ \ell_s &= 2 - \sin x_1 \gt 0 \quad &\text{(spring length: difference of heights; $\sin x_1 \le 1$)} \\ dy_1 &= \frac{d}{dx_1}\left(\sin x_1\right)dx_1 = \cos x_1\,dx_1 \quad &\text{(vertical leg of the slope triangle)} \\ \mathbf t &= \frac{dx_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos x_1\,dx_1\,\mathbf j_1}{dx_1} = \mathbf i_1 + \cos x_1\,\mathbf j_1, \quad |\mathbf t|^2 = 1 + \cos^2 x_1 \quad &\text{(sum of the legs; Pythagoras)} \\ \mathbf n &= \mathbf k_1\times\mathbf t = \mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 + \cos x_1\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf j_1 - \cos x_1\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n &= -\cos x_1 + \cos x_1 = 0 \quad &\text{(orthogonal)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^P = x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin x_1\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \ell_s = 2 - \sin x_1, \quad \mathbf t = \mathbf i_1 + \cos x_1\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf n = -\cos x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[x_1] = [y_1] = [\ell_s] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: the minus sign of $\mathbf n$: the tangent turned a quarter turn counterclockwise sends its horizontal part up and its vertical part to the left. The spring is never compressed below zero length, because the wire stays below the rail.

Kinematics

Motion of the turning frame and derivatives of its unit vectors Law: angular velocity of a simple rotation; derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(simple rotation about the fixed vertical; $\omega$ constant; $O$ fixed)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf i_1 = -\omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf k_1 = \omega\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 to 3.5)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 - \sin\omega t\,\mathbf k_0\right) &= -\omega\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 - \omega\cos\omega t\,\mathbf k_0 = -\omega\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(check: chain rule on the components of $\mathbf i_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \omega\,\mathbf i_1}$$

Units: $[\omega] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: seen from $S_1$ the three unit vectors are constant; seen from $S_0$ the horizontal ones turn with the setup.

(a) Relative velocity and acceleration

Relative velocity and relative acceleration Law: time derivatives in $S_1$, where $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf k_1$ are constant; chain rule and product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24; Problems.pdf, p. 15
$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dt}\sin x_1 &= \cos x_1\,\dot x_1 \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \mathbf v_1^P &= \dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos x_1\,\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 + 0\,\mathbf k_1 = \dot x_1\,\mathbf t \quad &\text{(components differentiated)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\cos x_1\,\dot x_1\right) &= -\sin x_1\,\dot x_1\cdot\dot x_1 + \cos x_1\,\ddot x_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule on the cosine)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P &= \ddot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \left(\cos x_1\,\ddot x_1 - \sin x_1\,\dot x_1^2\right)\mathbf j_1 + 0\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(components differentiated again)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_1^P = \left(\dot x_1,\ \cos x_1\,\dot x_1,\ 0\right), \qquad \mathbf a_1^P = \left(\ddot x_1,\ \cos x_1\,\ddot x_1 - \sin x_1\,\dot x_1^2,\ 0\right) \quad \text{in } \mathcal B_1}$$

Units: $[\dot x_1] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[\ddot x_1] = [\dot x_1^2] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$ (the arguments of sine and cosine in metres, numerically)

Meaning: the relative velocity is tangent to the wire; the relative acceleration has no component normal to the plane of the wire.

Absolute acceleration: transport, Coriolis and centripetal terms Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the position written in the turning basis; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P &= \dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos x_1\,\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 + x_1\left(-\omega\,\mathbf k_1\right) = \mathbf v_1^P - \omega x_1\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; derivative of $\mathbf i_1$; $\mathbf j_1$ constant)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1^P}{dt}\right|_0 &= \mathbf a_1^P + \dot x_1\left(-\omega\,\mathbf k_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; the turning of $\mathbf i_1$ inside $\mathbf v_1^P$)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left(-\omega x_1\,\mathbf k_1\right) &= -\omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1 - \omega x_1\,\omega\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; derivative of $\mathbf k_1$)} \\ 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P &= 2\omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos x_1\,\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) = -2\omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(the two $\mathbf k_1$ terms above)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) &= \omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\left(-\omega x_1\,\mathbf k_1\right) = -\omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(the $\mathbf i_1$ term above)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_0^P = \mathbf a_1^P - 2\omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1 - \omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1}$$

Units: $[\omega\dot x_1] = [\omega^2x_1] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the Coriolis term is normal to the plane of the wire and the centripetal term points horizontally to the axis; with $O$ fixed and $\omega$ constant there are no origin or Euler terms.

Forces and Equations of Motion

The free-body diagram of the bead in $S_1$ shows, in the plane of the wire, the weight, the spring force (vertical, up to the rail), the in-plane reaction along $\mathbf n$ and the centrifugal force (horizontal, away from the axis); normal to the plane, the reaction along $\mathbf k_1$ and the Coriolis force.

Figure 3. Forces on $P$ in $S_1$. In the plane of the wire: weight, spring $k(2 - \sin x_1)\,\mathbf j_1$, reaction $N_y\,\mathbf n$ and the centrifugal force $m\omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1$ (dashed, inertia). Normal to it: the reaction $N_z\,\mathbf k_1$ and the Coriolis force $2m\omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1$ (dashed, inertia), which balance each other.

(b) Forces, Newton's second law, reaction and equation of motion

Actual and inertia forces on the bead Law: linear spring along its length; smooth reaction normal to the tangent; inertia forces of a non-inertial frame Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.1; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.16; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf W &= -mg\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(weight; $\mathbf j_1$ is the vertical)} \\ \mathbf F_s &= k\,\ell_s\,\mathbf j_1 = k\left(2 - \sin x_1\right)\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(spring stretched by its whole length, pulling $P$ up to the rail)} \\ \mathbf N\cdot\mathbf t &= N_x + N_y\cos x_1 = 0 \quad &\text{(smooth wire)} \\ \mathbf F_A &= \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf F_E = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{($O$ fixed; $\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}$ zero)} \\ \mathbf F_C &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) = m\omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \mathbf F_{COR} = -2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P = 2m\omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(composition box times $-m$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf W = -mg\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf F_s = k\left(2 - \sin x_1\right)\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf N = N_x\,\mathbf i_1 + N_y\,\mathbf j_1 + N_z\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf F_C = m\omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \mathbf F_{COR} = 2m\omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1}$$

Units: $[k\,\ell_s] = [mg] = [m\omega^2x_1] = [m\omega\dot x_1] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: four actual forces (weight, spring, two reaction components in the plane tied by the smooth condition, one normal to it) and two inertia forces.

Three components of Newton's second law and their solution Law: Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame, projected on $\mathcal B_1$; elimination of the reaction Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.17; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; Problems.pdf, p. 15
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1:\ m\ddot x_1 &= N_x + m\omega^2x_1 \quad &\text{(horizontal, in the plane)} \\ \mathbf j_1:\ m\left(\cos x_1\,\ddot x_1 - \sin x_1\,\dot x_1^2\right) &= N_y - mg + k\left(2 - \sin x_1\right) \quad &\text{(vertical)} \\ \mathbf k_1:\ 0 &= N_z + 2m\omega\dot x_1 \quad &\text{(normal to the plane)} \\ m\cos x_1\,\ddot x_1 &= -N_y\cos^2 x_1 + m\omega^2x_1\cos x_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf i_1$ equation with $N_x = -N_y\cos x_1$, times $\cos x_1$)} \\ -N_y\cos^2 x_1 + m\omega^2x_1\cos x_1 - m\sin x_1\,\dot x_1^2 &= N_y - mg + k\left(2 - \sin x_1\right) \quad &\text{(substituted in the $\mathbf j_1$ equation)} \\ N_y\left(1 + \cos^2 x_1\right) &= m\left(\omega^2x_1\cos x_1 - \dot x_1^2\sin x_1\right) + mg - k\left(2 - \sin x_1\right) \quad &\text{(terms in $N_y$ collected)} \\ m\left(1 + \cos^2 x_1\right)\ddot x_1 - m\sin x_1\cos x_1\,\dot x_1^2 &= m\omega^2x_1 - mg\cos x_1 + k\cos x_1\left(2 - \sin x_1\right) \quad &\text{($\mathbf i_1$ equation plus $\cos x_1$ times the $\mathbf j_1$ equation: the reaction cancels)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} N_y = \frac{m\left(\omega^2x_1\cos x_1 - \dot x_1^2\sin x_1\right) + mg - k\left(2 - \sin x_1\right)}{1 + \cos^2 x_1}, \quad N_x = -N_y\cos x_1, \quad N_z = -2m\omega\dot x_1 \cr m\left(1 + \cos^2 x_1\right)\ddot x_1 - m\sin x_1\cos x_1\,\dot x_1^2 = m\omega^2x_1 - mg\cos x_1 + k\cos x_1\left(2 - \sin x_1\right) \end{gathered}}$$

Units: every term $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: three scalar equations plus the smooth condition for the four unknowns $x_1$, $N_x$, $N_y$, $N_z$. The in-plane reaction is $N_y$ times $\mathbf n$, normal to the wire; the reaction normal to the plane cancels the Coriolis force.

Answers and Checks

(c) Energy of the relative motion

Energy integral in the turning frame Law: power of each force on the relative velocity; potentials as minus the work along the wire, with Barrow's rule; chain rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]

Yes, it can be used, for two reasons. First, the forces that do no work in $S_1$: the reaction (smooth wire at rest in $S_1$, normal to the relative velocity), the Coriolis force (normal to the relative velocity), and the force of the origin and the Euler force, which vanish. Second, the forces that do work have potentials that depend on the position only: the weight, the spring (its upper end slides freely, so only its length matters) and the centrifugal force ($\omega$ constant). Along the wire the displacement is $\mathbf t\,dx'$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf N\cdot\mathbf v_1^P &= \dot x_1\left(N_x + N_y\cos x_1\right) = 0, \quad \mathbf F_{COR}\cdot\mathbf v_1^P = 2m\omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1\cdot\dot x_1\,\mathbf t = 0 \quad &\text{(no power in $S_1$)} \\ V_s - V_s(0) &= -\int_0^{x_1}k\left(2 - \sin x'\right)\cos x'\,dx' = \left[\tfrac12 k\left(2 - \sin x'\right)^2\right]_0^{x_1} \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.14 with $\mathbf j_1\cdot\mathbf t = \cos x'$; antiderivative by the chain rule; Barrow's rule)} \\ V_g - V_g(0) &= -\int_0^{x_1}\left(-mg\cos x'\right)dx' = mg\left[\sin x'\right]_0^{x_1} = mg\sin x_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.14; Barrow's rule)} \\ V_C - V_C(0) &= -\int_0^{x_1}m\omega^2x'\,dx' = -\tfrac12 m\omega^2\left[x'^2\right]_0^{x_1} = -\tfrac12 m\omega^2x_1^2 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.14 with $\mathbf i_1\cdot\mathbf t = 1$; Barrow's rule)} \\ T_1^P &= \tfrac12 m\,\mathbf v_1^P\cdot\mathbf v_1^P = \tfrac12 m\dot x_1^2\left(1 + \cos^2 x_1\right) \quad &\text{(kinetic energy in $S_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{E_1^P = \tfrac12 m\dot x_1^2\left(1 + \cos^2 x_1\right) + mg\sin x_1 + \tfrac12 k\left(2 - \sin x_1\right)^2 - \tfrac12 m\omega^2x_1^2 = \text{const}}$$

Units: $[m\dot x_1^2] = [mg\,x_1] = [k\,\ell_s^2] = [m\omega^2x_1^2] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the constant is fixed by the initial position and rate. The centrifugal potential is lowest far from the axis: the rotation pushes the bead outwards.

Relation of the energy equation with the equation of motion Law: time derivative of the energy along a motion; product rule and chain rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.29
$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dt}\left[\tfrac12 m\dot x_1^2\left(1 + \cos^2 x_1\right)\right] &= m\dot x_1\ddot x_1\left(1 + \cos^2 x_1\right) - m\dot x_1^3\sin x_1\cos x_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; $\tfrac{d}{dt}\cos^2 x_1 = -2\cos x_1\sin x_1\,\dot x_1$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left[mg\sin x_1 + \tfrac12 k\left(2 - \sin x_1\right)^2 - \tfrac12 m\omega^2x_1^2\right] &= \dot x_1\left[mg\cos x_1 - k\left(2 - \sin x_1\right)\cos x_1 - m\omega^2x_1\right] \quad &\text{(chain rule on each term)} \\ \frac{dE_1^P}{dt} &= \dot x_1\left[m\left(1 + \cos^2 x_1\right)\ddot x_1 - m\sin x_1\cos x_1\,\dot x_1^2 - m\omega^2x_1 + mg\cos x_1 - k\cos x_1\left(2 - \sin x_1\right)\right] \quad &\text{(sum, factor $\dot x_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\frac{dE_1^P}{dt} = \dot x_1\times\left(\text{equation of motion of part (b), all terms on the left}\right) = 0}$$

Units: $[\dot x_1][\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-3}}]$, a power

Meaning: the energy equation is a first integral of the equation of motion: it is that equation multiplied by the rate and integrated once, and differentiating it gives the equation of motion back wherever the rate is not zero.

(d) Equilibria without rotation

Equilibrium positions for omega equal to zero Law: equilibria of a conservative system are the critical points of the potential energy Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.32; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6

With $\omega$ zero the potential is the weight term plus the spring term, and the equation of motion has minus its derivative on the right-hand side.

$$\begin{aligned} V(x_1) &= mg\sin x_1 + \tfrac12 k\left(2 - \sin x_1\right)^2 \quad &\text{(potential with $\omega = 0$)} \\ V'(x_1) &= mg\cos x_1 - k\left(2 - \sin x_1\right)\cos x_1 = k\cos x_1\left(\lambda - 2 + \sin x_1\right) \quad &\text{(chain rule; $mg = k\lambda$)} \\ \cos x_1 = 0 &\Rightarrow x_1 = \frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{3\pi}{2} \quad &\text{(first factor, for every $\lambda$)} \\ \sin x_1 = 2 - \lambda, \quad -1 \le 2 - \lambda \le 1 &\iff 1 \le \lambda \le 3 \quad &\text{(second factor, only where the sine reaches the value)} \\ 1 \lt \lambda \lt 2:\quad x_1 &= \arcsin(2 - \lambda),\ \ \pi - \arcsin(2 - \lambda) \quad &\text{(two points on both sides of the crest)} \\ \lambda = 2:\quad x_1 &= 0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi \quad &\text{($\sin x_1 = 0$)} \\ 2 \lt \lambda \lt 3:\quad x_1 &= \pi + \arcsin(\lambda - 2),\ \ 2\pi - \arcsin(\lambda - 2) \quad &\text{(two points on both sides of the trough)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{x_1 = \frac{\pi}{2} \text{ and } \frac{3\pi}{2} \text{ for every } \lambda; \qquad \sin x_1 = 2 - \lambda \text{ for } 1 \le \lambda \le 3 \ \ \left(\lambda = \frac{mg}{k}\right)}$$

Units: $[\lambda] = [mg/k] = [\mathrm{L}]$, compared with the heights $2$ and $\sin x_1$ in metres

Meaning: at the crest and at the trough the wire is horizontal, so the vertical forces need no balance along the wire; at the other points the weight and the spring force balance each other exactly, which needs a spring length equal to $\lambda$.

Stability of the equilibria without rotation Law: an equilibrium is stable if and only if it is a minimum of the potential energy; second derivative, and Taylor expansion where it vanishes Source: Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6
$$\begin{aligned} V''(x_1) &= -k\sin x_1\left(\lambda - 2 + \sin x_1\right) + k\cos^2 x_1 \quad &\text{(product rule on $V'$)} \\ V''\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) &= -k\left(\lambda - 1\right) + 0 = k\left(1 - \lambda\right) \quad &\text{($\sin = 1$, $\cos = 0$)} \\ V''\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) &= k\left(\lambda - 3\right) \quad &\text{($\sin = -1$, $\cos = 0$)} \\ \sin x_1 = 2 - \lambda:\quad V'' &= 0 + k\cos^2 x_1 \gt 0 \quad &\text{(bracket zero; $\cos x_1 \ne 0$ for $1 \lt \lambda \lt 3$)} \\ \lambda = 1,\ u = x_1 - \tfrac{\pi}{2}:\quad V' &= k\left(-\sin u\right)\left(\cos u - 1\right) \simeq k\left(-u\right)\left(-\tfrac{u^2}{2}\right) = \tfrac12 ku^3 \quad &\text{($\cos x_1 = -\sin u$, $\sin x_1 = \cos u$; Taylor)} \\ \lambda = 3,\ u = x_1 - \tfrac{3\pi}{2}:\quad V' &= k\sin u\left(1 - \cos u\right) \simeq k\,u\,\tfrac{u^2}{2} = \tfrac12 ku^3 \quad &\text{($\cos x_1 = \sin u$, $\sin x_1 = -\cos u$; Taylor)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\tfrac{\pi}{2}: \text{ stable for } \lambda \le 1,\ \text{unstable for } \lambda \gt 1; \quad \tfrac{3\pi}{2}: \text{ stable for } \lambda \ge 3,\ \text{unstable for } \lambda \lt 3; \quad \sin x_1 = 2 - \lambda: \text{ stable } (1 \lt \lambda \lt 3)}$$

Units: $[V''] = [k] = [\mathrm{M\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: a stiff spring (small $\lambda$) holds the bead on the crest; a heavy bead (large $\lambda$) sits in the trough; in between the bead rests on the flank where weight and spring balance. At the two limiting values the derivative grows like the cube of the distance, a minimum of fourth order: stable, with no linear restoring force.

(e) Motion without spring after a release at pi

Scaled potential and allowed region Law: energy integral of part (c) with $k = 0$; the bead can only be where the potential does not exceed its initial value Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.27; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.28; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]
$$\begin{aligned} V(x_1) &= mg\sin x_1 - \tfrac12 m\omega^2x_1^2 \quad &\text{(potential of part (c) with $k = 0$)} \\ \tilde V(x_1) &= \frac{2V}{mg} = 2\sin x_1 - \beta x_1^2, \quad \tilde V(\pi) = -\beta\pi^2 \quad &\text{(scaled by $2/(mg)$; $\beta = \omega^2/g$)} \\ \tfrac12 m\dot x_1^2\left(1 + \cos^2 x_1\right) &= V(\pi) - V(x_1) \quad &\text{(energy integral; released at rest at $\pi$)} \\ \frac{\dot x_1^2}{g}\left(1 + \cos^2 x_1\right) &= \tilde V(\pi) - \tilde V(x_1) \quad &\text{(divided by $mg/2$)} \\ \tilde V'(\pi) &= 2\cos\pi - 2\beta\pi = -2\left(1 + \beta\pi\right) \lt 0 \quad &\text{(the generalized force minus $V'$ is positive at the start)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\tilde V(x_1) = 2\sin x_1 - \beta x_1^2, \qquad \frac{\dot x_1^2}{g}\left(1 + \cos^2 x_1\right) = \tilde V(\pi) - \tilde V(x_1)}$$

Units: $[\tilde V] = [\beta x_1^2] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: the bead starts towards larger $x_1$, down the wire into the trough near three halves of $\pi$; it moves only where the scaled potential lies below its starting value.

Figure 4. Scaled potential $\tilde V = 2\sin x_1 - \beta x_1^2$ for three values of $\beta$. The bead, released at rest at $\pi$, moves where $\tilde V$ is below its starting level (dotted): for small $\beta$ the hump near $5\pi/2$ stops it, for large $\beta$ nothing does; at $\beta_c$ the top of the hump touches the starting level at $x_c$.
Small and large beta: oscillation or escape Law: comparison of the potential beyond the start with its starting value; sign of its derivative Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.28; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6

The scaled potential is a sine of amplitude 2 riding on the downward parabola of the centrifugal term: wells near the troughs, humps near the crests, and it tends to minus infinity far from the axis. The bead is trapped if some point beyond $\pi$ has a potential at least equal to the starting value; it escapes if the potential decreases all the way.

$$\begin{aligned} \tilde V\left(\tfrac{5\pi}{2}\right) - \tilde V(\pi) &= 2 - \beta\frac{25\pi^2}{4} + \beta\pi^2 = 2 - \frac{21\pi^2}{4}\beta \quad &\text{($\sin(5\pi/2) = 1$)} \\ \beta \lt \frac{8}{21\pi^2} = 0.0386\ \mathrm{m^{-1}} &\Rightarrow \tilde V\left(\tfrac{5\pi}{2}\right) \gt \tilde V(\pi) \quad &\text{(the hump near the next crest is higher than the start: a turning point before it)} \\ \beta\pi \ge 1,\ x_1 \gt \pi:\quad \tilde V'(x_1) &= 2\left(\cos x_1 - \beta x_1\right) \lt 2\left(1 - \beta\pi\right) \le 0 \quad &\text{($\cos x_1 \le 1$, $\beta x_1 \gt \beta\pi$)} \\ \beta = 0.02\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}:\quad \tilde V(\pi) &= -0.197\ \mathrm{m}, \quad \tilde V\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = -2.444\ \mathrm{m}, \quad \tilde V\left(\tfrac{5\pi}{2}\right) = 0.766\ \mathrm{m} \quad &\text{(example of a small value)} \\ \beta = 0.1\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}:\quad \tilde V(\pi) &= -0.987\ \mathrm{m}, \quad \tilde V\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = -4.221\ \mathrm{m}, \quad \tilde V\left(\tfrac{5\pi}{2}\right) = -4.169\ \mathrm{m} \quad &\text{(example of a larger value)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\beta \text{ small: periodic oscillation between } \pi \text{ and a turning point beyond the trough}; \qquad \beta \text{ large: } x_1 \to \infty}$$

Units: $[\beta] = [\mathrm{L^{-1}}]$; $[\tilde V] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: slow rotation: gravity keeps the bead in the well of the trough, and it swings back to the release point, where it stops and starts again. Fast rotation: the centrifugal term lowers every hump below the start and throws the bead outwards along the wire. For the larger example the next hump, at 7.069 m, has the value $-3.582$ m, below the start: escape.

System for the critical value of beta Law: the separating case has a maximum of the potential exactly at the starting level Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.28; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6; Problems.pdf, p. 15

At the critical value the bead creeps towards the top $x_c$ of the first hump beyond $\pi$, where the potential is stationary and equal to its starting value.

$$\begin{aligned} \tilde V(x_c) &= 2\sin x_c - \beta_c x_c^2 = -\beta_c\pi^2 \quad &\text{(the top at the starting level)} \\ \tilde V'(x_c) &= 2\cos x_c - 2\beta_c x_c = 0 \quad &\text{(stationary)} \\ \tilde V''(x_c) &= -2\sin x_c - 2\beta_c \lt 0 \quad &\text{(a maximum: it needs $\sin x_c \gt 0$, so $x_c$ lies between $2\pi$ and $5\pi/2$, beyond the trough; a stationary point between $\pi$ and $2\pi$, where the sine is negative, is a minimum)} \\ x_c &= 7.5436\ \mathrm{m} = 2.4012\pi, \quad \beta_c = 0.040489\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}, \quad \tilde V''(x_c) = -1.985\ \mathrm{m^{-1}} \quad &\text{(numerical solution: Newton's method from the starting values 7.5 and 0.04)} \\ \beta = 0.95\beta_c:\ \max\tilde V &= -0.284\ \mathrm{m} \gt \tilde V(\pi) = -0.380\ \mathrm{m}; \quad \beta = 1.05\beta_c:\ \max\tilde V = -0.515\ \mathrm{m} \lt \tilde V(\pi) = -0.420\ \mathrm{m} \quad &\text{(top of the hump against the start, on both sides)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{cases} 2\sin x_c - \beta_c x_c^2 = -\beta_c\pi^2 \cr \cos x_c - \beta_c x_c = 0 \end{cases} \quad x_c \simeq 7.544\ \mathrm{m}, \ \ \beta_c \simeq 0.0405\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}: \ \ \beta \lt \beta_c \text{ oscillation}, \ \beta \gt \beta_c \text{ escape}}$$

Units: $[\beta_c x_c^2] = [\mathrm{L}]$; $[\beta_c x_c] = [1]$

Meaning: just below the critical value the hump still stands above the start and the bead turns back; just above it the hump is below the start and the bead passes over it.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Relative velocity and acceleration$\mathbf v_1^P = (\dot x_1,\ \cos x_1\,\dot x_1,\ 0)$, $\mathbf a_1^P = (\ddot x_1,\ \cos x_1\,\ddot x_1 - \sin x_1\,\dot x_1^2,\ 0)$ in $\mathcal B_1$
(b) Forcesweight $-mg\,\mathbf j_1$, spring $k(2 - \sin x_1)\,\mathbf j_1$, reaction $(N_x, N_y, N_z)$ with $N_x + N_y\cos x_1 = 0$, centrifugal $m\omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1$, Coriolis $2m\omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1$
(b) Newton, three components$m\ddot x_1 = N_x + m\omega^2x_1$; $m(\cos x_1\,\ddot x_1 - \sin x_1\,\dot x_1^2) = N_y - mg + k(2 - \sin x_1)$; $0 = N_z + 2m\omega\dot x_1$
(b) Reaction$N_y = [m(\omega^2x_1\cos x_1 - \dot x_1^2\sin x_1) + mg - k(2 - \sin x_1)]/(1 + \cos^2 x_1)$, $N_x = -N_y\cos x_1$, $N_z = -2m\omega\dot x_1$
(b) Equation of motion$m(1 + \cos^2 x_1)\ddot x_1 - m\sin x_1\cos x_1\,\dot x_1^2 = m\omega^2x_1 - mg\cos x_1 + k\cos x_1(2 - \sin x_1)$
(c) Energyyes: $\frac12 m\dot x_1^2(1 + \cos^2 x_1) + mg\sin x_1 + \frac12 k(2 - \sin x_1)^2 - \frac12 m\omega^2x_1^2 = $ const; it is the first integral of the equation of motion (its time derivative is the rate times that equation)
(d) Equilibria, $\omega = 0$$\pi/2$ (stable for $\lambda \le 1$), $3\pi/2$ (stable for $\lambda \ge 3$), $\sin x_1 = 2 - \lambda$ for $1 \lt \lambda \lt 3$ (stable)
(e) Motion, $k = 0$$\tilde V = 2\sin x_1 - \beta x_1^2$; small $\beta$: oscillation; large $\beta$: escape to infinity; critical value from $2\sin x_c - \beta_c x_c^2 = -\beta_c\pi^2$, $\cos x_c = \beta_c x_c$ ($x_c \simeq 7.544$ m, $\beta_c \simeq 0.0405$ m$^{-1}$)
Reading of the springnatural length zero; with a natural length $\ell_0$, replace 2 by $2 - \ell_0$ in the spring terms

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 74 prints the energy integral, the reaction, the equilibria for zero rotation and the system for the critical value. The energy integral and the reaction coincide (box below). The equilibria coincide after a change of parameter: the key writes them with a parameter $\alpha$ that the statement does not define, and its statements match these results exactly when $\alpha$ is the reciprocal of $\lambda$ (box below). The system for the critical value coincides, but the key assigns the two behaviours the other way round: see the warning.

Comparison with the official key Law: term-by-term comparison; expansion of the spring potential; change of parameter Source: Problems.pdf, p. 74
$$\begin{aligned} \tfrac12 k\left(2 - \sin x_1\right)^2 &= 2k - 2k\sin x_1 + \tfrac12 k\sin^2 x_1 \quad &\text{(square expanded)} \\ \text{key: } \tfrac12 m\dot x_1^2\left(1 + \cos^2 x_1\right) + \sin x_1\left(mg - 2k\right) + \tfrac12 k\sin^2 x_1 - \tfrac12 m\omega^2x_1^2 &= C \quad &\text{(part (c) with the constant $2k$ moved into $C$)} \\ \text{key: } \mathbf N_1 &= \frac{m\left(\omega^2x_1\cos x_1 - \dot x_1^2\sin x_1\right) - k\left(2 - \sin x_1\right) + mg}{1 + \cos^2 x_1}\left(-\cos x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \mathbf j_1\right), \quad \mathbf N_2 = -2m\omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(part (b); the key prints $\cos x$ for $\cos x_1$ in the direction)} \\ \alpha &= \frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{k}{mg} \quad &\text{(reading of the parameter of the key)} \\ \alpha \gt 1 \iff \lambda \lt 1, \quad \alpha \lt \tfrac13 &\iff \lambda \gt 3, \quad 2 - \tfrac{1}{\alpha} = 2 - \lambda, \quad \tfrac13 \lt \alpha \lt 1 \iff 1 \lt \lambda \lt 3 \quad &\text{(the three statements of the key converted)} \\ \text{key: } \alpha = 0 &\iff k = 0 \quad &\text{(the case of part (e), consistent with the same reading)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{energy integral, reaction and equilibria coincide, with } \alpha = k/(mg) = 1/\lambda}$$

Units: $[\alpha] = [\mathrm{L^{-1}}]$

Meaning: the key's stability statements are the ones of part (d) written with the reciprocal parameter; at the limiting values $\lambda$ equal to 1 and 3 this solution also finds stability (fourth-order minimum), which the key, with strict inequalities, leaves out.

Discrepancy with the official solution

The key states "$\beta \gt \beta_c$, the bead oscillates; $\beta \lt \beta_c$, the bead moves towards infinity", with the same system of equations for $x_c$ and $\beta_c$. This solution obtains the opposite assignment: the bead oscillates for $\beta \lt \beta_c$ and escapes for $\beta \gt \beta_c$. Proof, from the boxes above: for any $\beta$ with $\beta\pi \ge 1$ the scaled potential decreases for every $x_1$ beyond $\pi$, so the bead escapes; for $\beta$ below $8/(21\pi^2)$ the potential at five halves of $\pi$ is above the start, so the bead turns back. At $0.95\beta_c$ the top of the hump is $-0.284$ m, above the start, $-0.380$ m; at $1.05\beta_c$ it is $-0.515$ m, below the start, $-0.420$ m. The centrifugal term is the only one that pushes the bead outwards, so a faster spin cannot be the one that keeps it.

Independent check: angular momentum about the vertical axis Law: angular momentum about the fixed point $O$ and its rate, equal to the moment of the forces Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.48; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.53

In $\mathcal B_1$ the position has the components $(x_1, \sin x_1, 0)$ and the absolute velocity $(\dot x_1, \cos x_1\,\dot x_1, -\omega x_1)$. The component along $\mathbf j_1$ of a vector product is the third component of the first factor times the first of the second, minus the first of the first times the third of the second.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf H_{O,0}\cdot\mathbf j_1 &= m\left(0\cdot\dot x_1 - x_1\left(-\omega x_1\right)\right) = m\omega x_1^2 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.48)} \\ \mathbf M_O\cdot\mathbf j_1 &= 0\cdot N_x - x_1N_z = -x_1N_z \quad &\text{(weight and spring along $\mathbf j_1$; in-plane reaction in the plane: no axial moment)} \\ 2m\omega x_1\dot x_1 &= -x_1N_z \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.53, axial component; chain rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{N_z = -2m\omega\dot x_1 \quad (x_1 \ne 0)}$$

Units: $[x_1N_z] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the reaction normal to the plane is the one that keeps the bead turning with the wire while its distance to the axis changes: the same value as the Coriolis balance of part (b).

Limiting cases Law: the results at extreme values of the data Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6
$$\begin{aligned} \omega \to 0:\quad N_z &\to 0, \quad m\left(1 + \cos^2 x_1\right)\ddot x_1 - m\sin x_1\cos x_1\,\dot x_1^2 = -mg\cos x_1 + k\cos x_1\left(2 - \sin x_1\right) \quad &\text{(bead on a fixed wire)} \\ k \to 0\ (\lambda \to \infty):\quad \lambda - 3 &\gt 0, \quad 1 - \lambda \lt 0 \quad &\text{(stability boxes: the trough stable, the crest unstable)} \\ k \to \infty\ (\lambda \to 0):\quad 1 - \lambda &\gt 0, \quad \lambda - 3 \lt 0 \quad &\text{(the crest stable, the trough unstable)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\omega \to 0: \ N_z \to 0; \qquad k \to 0: \text{ trough stable}; \qquad k \to \infty: \text{ crest stable}}$$

Units: $[\lambda] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: without spring the bead rests in the trough like any heavy bead; with a very stiff spring it is held on the crest, nearest to the rail.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf (PDF page 15); key on PDF page 74
Problem 28

Spherical Pendulum with a Vertically Oscillating Suspension Point

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 16
Translating Frame + Inertia Force

A point particle $P$ of mass $m$ is attached with a massless cord of length $L$ to the point $A$, as shown in the figure. The point $A$ is oscillating vertically with respect to the fixed reference frame $Oxyz$ according to the law $z = a\sin\omega t$, where $a$ and $\omega$ are known constants. The position of the particle $P$ with respect to the moving reference frame $Ax'y'z'$ is completely specified by the angles $\varphi$ and $\theta$ shown in the figure.

At $t = 0$ the relative position and relative velocity of the particle are defined by the values

$$ \theta_0 = 0, \qquad \varphi_0 = 30^\circ, \qquad \dot\theta_0 = \sqrt{\frac{2g}{\sqrt{3}L}}, \qquad \dot\varphi_0 = 0, $$

where $g$ is the gravitational acceleration. We define the following unit vectors that define a spherical coordinate system

$$ \mathbf{e}_r = \sin\varphi\cos\theta\,\mathbf{i} + \sin\varphi\sin\theta\,\mathbf{j} + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf{k}, \qquad \mathbf{e}_\varphi = \cos\varphi\cos\theta\,\mathbf{i} + \cos\varphi\sin\theta\,\mathbf{j} - \sin\varphi\,\mathbf{k}, \qquad \mathbf{e}_\theta = -\sin\theta\,\mathbf{i} + \cos\theta\,\mathbf{j}. $$

The partial derivatives of these vectors with respect to $\varphi$ and $\theta$ are

$$ \frac{\partial\mathbf{e}_r}{\partial\varphi} = \mathbf{e}_\varphi, \quad \frac{\partial\mathbf{e}_\varphi}{\partial\varphi} = -\mathbf{e}_r, \quad \frac{\partial\mathbf{e}_\theta}{\partial\varphi} = \mathbf{0}, \quad \frac{\partial\mathbf{e}_r}{\partial\theta} = \sin\varphi\,\mathbf{e}_\theta, \quad \frac{\partial\mathbf{e}_\varphi}{\partial\theta} = \cos\varphi\,\mathbf{e}_\theta, \quad \frac{\partial\mathbf{e}_\theta}{\partial\theta} = -\sin\varphi\,\mathbf{e}_r - \cos\varphi\,\mathbf{e}_\varphi. $$
  • (a)
    Show that the relative acceleration of $P$ with respect to $Ax'y'z'$ can be expressed as $\mathbf{a}'_P = -L\left(\dot\varphi^2 + \dot\theta^2\sin^2\varphi\right)\mathbf{e}_r + L\left(\ddot\varphi - \dot\theta^2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\right)\mathbf{e}_\varphi + L\left(\ddot\theta\sin\varphi + 2\dot\theta\dot\varphi\cos\varphi\right)\mathbf{e}_\theta$.
  • (b)
    Write down a system of three ordinary differential equations that once solved would yield the angles $\theta$ and $\varphi$, and the tension on the cord as a function of time (you do not need to solve it).
  • (c)
    At $t = 0$, determine the relative acceleration of $P$ with respect to $Ax'y'z'$.
  • (d)
    At $t = 0$, determine the value of the tension on the cord.
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

A particle $P$ of mass $m$ hangs from a massless cord of length $L$ fixed at the point $A$, which oscillates on the vertical axis of the fixed frame with the height $a\sin\omega t$; in the frame $Ax'y'z'$ the particle is located by the angles $\varphi$ and $\theta$ of the figure, and the statement gives the spherical unit vectors, their partial derivatives and the initial values of the angles and rates (Problems.pdf, p. 16). The statement asks to show the relative acceleration, to write the equations of motion with the tension, and to evaluate the relative acceleration and the tension at the start. The frame $Ax'y'z'$ translates without turning, so the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2 reduces to Eq. 3.28 and Eq. 3.29, and the only inertia force of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9 is the force of the origin.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, the frame $Oxyz$, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k\}$ of the statement, $\mathbf k$ vertical, up (Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.1)
Moving frame$S_1 = \{A;\ \mathcal B_1\}$, the frame $Ax'y'z'$; its axes stay parallel to those of $Oxyz$ (figure of the statement), so $\mathcal B_1 = \mathcal B_0$
Spherical basis$\mathcal B_s = \{\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\varphi, \mathbf e_\theta\}$ of the statement, attached to $P$
Coordinates$\varphi$, the angle from the upward axis $Az'$ to the cord $AP$ (figure, and $\mathbf e_r\cdot\mathbf k = \cos\varphi$); $\theta$, the azimuth of the vertical plane of the cord, from $Ax'$, counterclockwise seen from above
Constraint$P$ at the distance $L$ from $A$ (taut cord)
Degrees of freedom3 minus 1: 2, the angles $\varphi(t)$ and $\theta(t)$; the motion of $A$ is prescribed
Data$m$ [kg], $L$ [m], $a$ [m], $\omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$] (the frequency of the oscillation of $A$, not a rotation of the frame), $g$ [m s$^{-2}$]
Initial state$\theta_0 = 0$, $\varphi_0 = 30^\circ$, $\dot\theta_0 = \sqrt{2g/(\sqrt3 L)}$, $\dot\varphi_0 = 0$ (relative values)
Unknowns$\varphi(t)$, $\theta(t)$ and the tension $T(t)$, positive when the cord pulls $P$ towards $A$
Applied forcesweight $-mg\,\mathbf k$; cord $-T\,\mathbf e_r$
Inertia force (in $S_1$)of the origin only (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62 with zero angular velocity)
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial; uniform gravity; massless cord, taut as long as $T \ge 0$; no friction or drag
Readingthe statement as written ($\varphi$ from the upward vertical, $P$ above the horizontal plane of $A$ at the start). The other reading, $\varphi$ from the downward vertical (a conical pendulum hanging below $A$, for which the given $\dot\theta_0$ is the steady rate), is worked out in the Answers section and listed in the table

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. Vertical plane that contains $Az'$ and the cord. $A$ moves on the fixed axis $Oz$ ($z \equiv z'$), at height $a\sin\omega t$; the axes of $Ax'y'z'$ stay parallel to those of $Oxyz$. In the shaded right triangle the hypotenuse is the cord $|AP| = L$, the leg adjacent to $\varphi$ is vertical, $L\cos\varphi$ along $\mathbf k$, and the opposite leg is horizontal, $L\sin\varphi$ along $\mathbf u = \cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j$. $\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\varphi$ in orange.
Translation of the moving frame Law: a frame whose axes stay parallel to the fixed ones: identity change of basis, zero angular velocity; position, velocity and acceleration of its origin Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.28; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.29; Problems.pdf, p. 16
$$\begin{aligned} [{}_0R_1] &= I, \quad \det I = 1, \quad I\,I^T = I, \quad \boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \mathbf 0, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{($\mathcal B_1 = \mathcal B_0$)} \\ \mathbf r_0^A &= \overrightarrow{OA} = a\sin\omega t\,\mathbf k \quad &\text{($A$ on the fixed vertical axis)} \\ \mathbf v_0^A &= a\omega\cos\omega t\,\mathbf k \quad &\text{(chain rule: $\tfrac{d}{dt}\sin\omega t = \omega\cos\omega t$)} \\ \mathbf a_0^A &= -a\omega^2\sin\omega t\,\mathbf k \quad &\text{(chain rule: $\tfrac{d}{dt}\cos\omega t = -\omega\sin\omega t$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = I, \quad \boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf r_0^A = a\sin\omega t\,\mathbf k, \quad \mathbf a_0^A = -a\omega^2\sin\omega t\,\mathbf k}$$

Units: $[a\omega^2] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$; $[\omega t] = [1]$

Meaning: the frame of $A$ only translates up and down; at the start $A$ passes through $O$ with zero acceleration.

Position of the particle: meridian triangle and azimuth Law: right triangle of the cord in its vertical plane; right triangle of the horizontal projection; relation with the standard polar angle; position as a sum of segments Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.2; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 16

First figure: the vertical plane through $Az'$ and the cord, with $\mathbf u$ its horizontal unit vector from the axis towards $P$. In the shaded right triangle the hypotenuse is the cord $L$; the angle $\varphi$ is at $A$, measured from the upward vertical, so the adjacent leg is vertical, $L\cos\varphi$ along $\mathbf k$, and the opposite leg is horizontal, $L\sin\varphi$ along $\mathbf u$. The standard polar angle of $P$ in that plane, measured from $\mathbf u$, is $\pi/2 - \varphi$: the latitude, which is the angle called $\varphi$ in the spherical coordinates of Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.31, while the $\varphi$ of the statement is the colatitude, measured from the vertical. Second figure (below): the view from above, $\mathbf k$ out of the paper (⊙), $Ax'$ to the right and $Ay'$ up; the horizontal projection, of length $L\sin\varphi$, makes the azimuth $\theta$ with $Ax'$: adjacent leg along $\mathbf i$, opposite leg along $\mathbf j$.

$$\begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{AP} &= L\sin\varphi\,\mathbf u + L\cos\varphi\,\mathbf k \quad &\text{(legs of the meridian triangle)} \\ \cos\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2} - \varphi\right) &= \cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\varphi + \sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}\sin\varphi = \sin\varphi, \quad \sin\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2} - \varphi\right) = \sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\varphi - \cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}\sin\varphi = \cos\varphi \quad &\text{(difference formulas: the polar form gives the same legs)} \\ \mathbf u &= \cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j \quad &\text{(legs of the projection divided by $L\sin\varphi$)} \\ \mathbf r_1^P &= L\left(\sin\varphi\cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\varphi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf k\right) = L\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{($\mathbf u$ substituted; the $\mathbf e_r$ of the statement)} \\ \mathbf r_0^P &= \mathbf r_0^A + \mathbf r_1^P = a\sin\omega t\,\mathbf k + L\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.16)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^P = L\,\mathbf e_r = L\left(\sin\varphi\cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\varphi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf k\right), \qquad \mathbf r_0^P = a\sin\omega t\,\mathbf k + L\,\mathbf e_r}$$

Units: $[L] = [a] = [\mathrm{L}]$; angles dimensionless

Meaning: with $\varphi$ below a right angle the vertical component $\cos\varphi$ is positive: at the start, with $\varphi$ equal to 30 degrees, the particle is above the horizontal plane through $A$, as drawn in the figure of the statement.

Figure 2. View from $+z$, with $\mathbf k$ out of the paper ($\odot$). The horizontal projection of $\overrightarrow{AP}$ has length $L\sin\varphi$ (the horizontal leg of the meridian triangle) and makes the azimuth $\theta$ with $Ax'$; its components are $L\sin\varphi\cos\theta$ (adjacent) and $L\sin\varphi\sin\theta$ (opposite). $\mathbf u$ is the unit vector of that direction and $\mathbf e_\theta$ is $\mathbf u$ turned $+90^\circ$ about $\mathbf k$.
Spherical basis: rotation by theta about k, then by phi; matrix and partial derivatives Law: unit vectors as normalised partial derivatives of the position; change of basis matrix, its determinant by cofactors, orthonormality; partial derivatives of each component Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.32; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.34; Problems.pdf, p. 16

$\mathbf e_\varphi$ is the direction in which $P$ moves when $\varphi$ grows: in the meridian plane, perpendicular to the cord, pointing down and away from the axis (the minus sign of its $\mathbf k$ component: $\varphi$ is measured from the upward vertical, so a growing $\varphi$ lowers the particle). Because the Notes measure the latitude, the unit vector of their Eq. 2.32 to Eq. 2.34 for that angle is minus the $\mathbf e_\varphi$ of the statement; $\mathbf e_r$ and $\mathbf e_\theta$ are the same. $\mathbf e_\theta$ is $\mathbf u$ turned by a quarter turn counterclockwise about $\mathbf k$ in the view from above (⊙): the horizontal part $\cos\theta\,\mathbf i$ turns into $\cos\theta\,\mathbf j$, and $\sin\theta\,\mathbf j$ turns into minus $\sin\theta\,\mathbf i$ (the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_\varphi &= \frac{\partial\mathbf e_r}{\partial\varphi} = \cos\varphi\cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \cos\varphi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j - \sin\varphi\,\mathbf k \quad &\text{($\tfrac{\partial}{\partial\varphi}\sin\varphi = \cos\varphi$, $\tfrac{\partial}{\partial\varphi}\cos\varphi = -\sin\varphi$; length 1)} \\ \frac{\partial\mathbf e_r}{\partial\theta} &= \sin\varphi\left(-\sin\theta\,\mathbf i + \cos\theta\,\mathbf j\right) = \sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(length $\sin\varphi$; $\mathbf e_\theta$ its direction)} \\ \det[{}_1R_s] &= \cos\varphi\cdot(+1)\left(\cos\varphi\cos^2\theta + \cos\varphi\sin^2\theta\right) + \left(-\sin\varphi\right)\cdot(-1)\left(\sin\varphi\cos^2\theta + \sin\varphi\sin^2\theta\right) + 0 = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row, cofactor signs $+$, $-$, $+$)} \\ \mathbf e_r\cdot\mathbf e_\varphi &= \sin\varphi\cos\varphi\left(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta\right) - \cos\varphi\sin\varphi = 0, \quad \mathbf e_r\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = \sin\varphi\left(-\cos\theta\sin\theta + \sin\theta\cos\theta\right) = 0 \quad &\text{(columns orthogonal; $\mathbf e_\varphi\cdot\mathbf e_\theta$ likewise)} \\ \frac{\partial\mathbf e_\varphi}{\partial\varphi} &= -\sin\varphi\cos\theta\,\mathbf i - \sin\varphi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j - \cos\varphi\,\mathbf k = -\mathbf e_r, \quad \frac{\partial\mathbf e_\varphi}{\partial\theta} = \cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(component by component)} \\ \frac{\partial\mathbf e_\theta}{\partial\theta} &= -\cos\theta\,\mathbf i - \sin\theta\,\mathbf j = -\left(\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_r + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi\right), \quad \frac{\partial\mathbf e_\theta}{\partial\varphi} = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{($\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_r + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi = \mathbf u$)} \\ \mathbf k &= \cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_r - \sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi \quad &\text{(third row of the matrix: the vertical in the spherical basis)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_1R_s] = \begin{pmatrix} \sin\varphi\cos\theta & \cos\varphi\cos\theta & -\sin\theta \cr \sin\varphi\sin\theta & \cos\varphi\sin\theta & \cos\theta \cr \cos\varphi & -\sin\varphi & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_1R_s] = 1, \quad \mathbf k = \cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_r - \sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi}$$

Units: dimensionless: $[1]$

Meaning: these are the vectors and the six partial derivatives given in the statement; the last row writes the vertical along the cord and across it, the two legs of the meridian triangle.

Kinematics

(a) Relative acceleration

Relative velocity and relative acceleration in the translating frame Law: time derivatives in $S_1$; multivariable chain rule through $\varphi(t)$ and $\theta(t)$; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.33; Problems.pdf, p. 16

Eq. 2.33 is written with the latitude of the Notes; with the colatitude of the statement its angle is replaced by $\pi/2 - \varphi$ and its polar unit vector by minus $\mathbf e_\varphi$, which is what the rows below do directly from the partial derivatives.

The vectors $\mathbf i$, $\mathbf j$, $\mathbf k$ are constant in $S_1$; each spherical vector depends on time through the two angles, so its rate is the partial derivative with respect to $\varphi$ times the rate of $\varphi$ plus the one with respect to $\theta$ times the rate of $\theta$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dot{\mathbf e}_r &= \frac{\partial\mathbf e_r}{\partial\varphi}\dot\varphi + \frac{\partial\mathbf e_r}{\partial\theta}\dot\theta = \dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi + \dot\theta\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \dot{\mathbf e}_\varphi &= -\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_r + \dot\theta\cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta, \quad \dot{\mathbf e}_\theta = -\dot\theta\left(\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_r + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi\right) \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \mathbf v_1^P &= L\,\dot{\mathbf e}_r = L\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi + L\dot\theta\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{($L$ constant)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(L\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi\right) &= L\ddot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi - L\dot\varphi^2\,\mathbf e_r + L\dot\varphi\dot\theta\cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(product rule)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(L\dot\theta\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta\right) &= L\ddot\theta\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta + L\dot\theta\cos\varphi\,\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta - L\dot\theta^2\sin\varphi\left(\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_r + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi\right) \quad &\text{(product rule on three factors; $\tfrac{d}{dt}\sin\varphi = \cos\varphi\,\dot\varphi$)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P &= -L\left(\dot\varphi^2 + \dot\theta^2\sin^2\varphi\right)\mathbf e_r + L\left(\ddot\varphi - \dot\theta^2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\right)\mathbf e_\varphi + L\left(\ddot\theta\sin\varphi + 2\dot\theta\dot\varphi\cos\varphi\right)\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(sum, collected by unit vector)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a'_P \equiv \mathbf a_1^P = -L\left(\dot\varphi^2 + \dot\theta^2\sin^2\varphi\right)\mathbf e_r + L\left(\ddot\varphi - \dot\theta^2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\right)\mathbf e_\varphi + L\left(\ddot\theta\sin\varphi + 2\dot\theta\dot\varphi\cos\varphi\right)\mathbf e_\theta}$$

Units: every term $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: this is the expression of the statement: along the cord the centripetal part of the motion on the sphere; across it, the angular accelerations with the centrifugal and the Coriolis-like terms of the spherical coordinates.

Absolute acceleration in a translating frame Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the position; the basis of $S_1$ is constant in $S_0$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.28; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.29; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P &= \frac{d}{dt}\left(a\sin\omega t\,\mathbf k\right) + \frac{d}{dt}\left(L\,\mathbf e_r\right) = \mathbf v_0^A + \mathbf v_1^P \quad &\text{(the derivative of $L\,\mathbf e_r$ is the same in $S_0$ and $S_1$: $\mathcal B_1 = \mathcal B_0$)} \\ \mathbf a_0^P &= \mathbf a_0^A + \mathbf a_1^P \quad &\text{(once more; Eq. 3.27 with zero $\boldsymbol\omega_{10}$ and $\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_0^P = -a\omega^2\sin\omega t\,\mathbf k + \mathbf a_1^P}$$

Units: $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: no Euler, centrifugal or Coriolis terms: the frame does not turn.

Forces and Equations of Motion

The free-body diagram of $P$ in $S_1$ shows the pull of the cord towards $A$, the weight and the inertia force of the origin, both vertical. Weight and inertia force add up to an effective weight with a gravity that changes in time.

Figure 3. Forces on $P$ in the translating frame $Ax'y'z'$: the tension $-T\,\mathbf e_r$, the weight $-mg\,\mathbf k$ and the inertia force of the origin $ma\omega^2\sin\omega t\,\mathbf k$ (dashed). The last two add up to an effective weight $-mg_e\,\mathbf k$ with $g_e = g - a\omega^2\sin\omega t$.
Forces in the translating frame and effective gravity Law: inertia force of the origin of a translating frame Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf F_A &= -m\,\mathbf a_0^A = ma\omega^2\sin\omega t\,\mathbf k, \quad \mathbf F_E = \mathbf F_C = \mathbf F_{COR} = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.62 with zero $\boldsymbol\omega_{10}$)} \\ -mg\,\mathbf k + ma\omega^2\sin\omega t\,\mathbf k &= -m\left(g - a\omega^2\sin\omega t\right)\mathbf k = -mg_e\,\mathbf k \quad &\text{(weight plus inertia force)} \\ -mg_e\,\mathbf k &= -mg_e\cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_r + mg_e\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi \quad &\text{($\mathbf k$ in the spherical basis)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf F_A = ma\omega^2\sin\omega t\,\mathbf k, \qquad g_e(t) = g - a\omega^2\sin\omega t}$$

Units: $[a\omega^2] = [g] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: in the frame of $A$ the oscillation of the support only changes the strength of gravity: weaker while $A$ is above $O$, stronger while it is below, and reversed whenever the product $a\omega^2\sin\omega t$ exceeds $g$.

(b) Equations of motion and tension

Newton's second law in the translating frame, projected on the spherical basis Law: Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame with the inertia force of the origin Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; Problems.pdf, p. 16
$$\begin{aligned} m\,\mathbf a_1^P &= -T\,\mathbf e_r - mg\,\mathbf k + \mathbf F_A = -T\,\mathbf e_r - mg_e\,\mathbf k \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.63)} \\ \mathbf e_r:\ -mL\left(\dot\varphi^2 + \dot\theta^2\sin^2\varphi\right) &= -T - mg_e\cos\varphi \quad &\text{(along the cord)} \\ \mathbf e_\varphi:\ mL\left(\ddot\varphi - \dot\theta^2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\right) &= mg_e\sin\varphi \quad &\text{(in the meridian plane, across the cord)} \\ \mathbf e_\theta:\ mL\left(\ddot\theta\sin\varphi + 2\dot\theta\dot\varphi\cos\varphi\right) &= 0 \quad &\text{(horizontal, normal to the meridian plane)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{cases} \ddot\varphi = \dot\theta^2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi + \dfrac{g - a\omega^2\sin\omega t}{L}\sin\varphi \cr \ddot\theta\sin\varphi + 2\dot\theta\dot\varphi\cos\varphi = 0 \cr T = mL\left(\dot\varphi^2 + \dot\theta^2\sin^2\varphi\right) - m\left(g - a\omega^2\sin\omega t\right)\cos\varphi \end{cases}}$$

Units: $[\dot\theta^2] = [g/L] = [\mathrm{T^{-2}}]$; $[mL\dot\theta^2] = [mg] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: three equations for the three unknowns: the first two, with the initial values, give the two angles; the third then gives the tension.

First integral of the azimuth equation Law: the azimuth equation times $\sin\varphi$ is an exact derivative (product rule); Barrow's rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.48
$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dt}\left(\dot\theta\sin^2\varphi\right) &= \ddot\theta\sin^2\varphi + \dot\theta\cdot 2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\,\dot\varphi \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule on $\sin^2\varphi$)} \\ &= \sin\varphi\left(\ddot\theta\sin\varphi + 2\dot\theta\dot\varphi\cos\varphi\right) = 0 \quad &\text{(second equation of the system)} \\ \left[\dot\theta\sin^2\varphi\right]_0^t &= 0 \Rightarrow \dot\theta\sin^2\varphi = \dot\theta_0\sin^2\varphi_0 \quad &\text{(Barrow's rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{mL^2\dot\theta\sin^2\varphi = mL^2\dot\theta_0\sin^2\varphi_0}$$

Units: $[mL^2\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-1}}]$, an angular momentum

Meaning: the quantity is the vertical component of the angular momentum about $A$ computed with the relative velocity (Eq. 4.48). Its conservation comes from the $\mathbf e_\theta$ equation of $S_1$, which contains no force: the tension lies along $\mathbf e_r$, and the weight plus the inertia force of the moving support form a vertical effective weight with no $\mathbf e_\theta$ component. It is not taken from the theorem of a fixed point, because $A$ accelerates.

Answers and Checks

(c) Relative acceleration at the start

Angular accelerations and relative acceleration at t equal to zero Law: the system of part (b) and the expression of part (a) evaluated at the initial instant Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Problems.pdf, p. 16
$$\begin{aligned} g_e(0) &= g - a\omega^2\sin 0 = g, \quad \sin\varphi_0 = \tfrac12, \quad \cos\varphi_0 = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, \quad \dot\theta_0^2 = \frac{2g}{\sqrt3 L} \quad &\text{(data)} \\ \ddot\varphi_0 &= \frac{2g}{\sqrt3 L}\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{g}{L}\cdot\frac12 = \frac{g}{2L} + \frac{g}{2L} = \frac{g}{L} \quad &\text{(first equation)} \\ \ddot\theta_0\cdot\tfrac12 &= -2\dot\theta_0\cdot 0\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = 0 \Rightarrow \ddot\theta_0 = 0 \quad &\text{(second equation; $\dot\varphi_0 = 0$)} \\ \dot\theta_0^2\sin^2\varphi_0 &= \frac{2g}{\sqrt3 L}\cdot\frac14 = \frac{g}{2\sqrt3 L}, \quad \dot\theta_0^2\sin\varphi_0\cos\varphi_0 = \frac{2g}{\sqrt3 L}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{4} = \frac{g}{2L} \quad &\text{(products of the data)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P(0) &= -\frac{g}{2\sqrt3}\,\mathbf e_r + L\left(\frac{g}{L} - \frac{g}{2L}\right)\mathbf e_\varphi + 0\,\mathbf e_\theta = -\frac{g}{2\sqrt3}\,\mathbf e_r + \frac{g}{2}\,\mathbf e_\varphi \quad &\text{(part (a))} \\ \mathbf e_r(0) &= \tfrac12\,\mathbf i + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,\mathbf k, \quad \mathbf e_\varphi(0) = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,\mathbf i - \tfrac12\,\mathbf k \quad &\text{($\theta = 0$, $\varphi = 30^\circ$)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P(0) &= \left(-\frac{g}{4\sqrt3} + \frac{\sqrt3 g}{4}\right)\mathbf i + \left(-\frac{g}{4} - \frac{g}{4}\right)\mathbf k = \frac{g}{2\sqrt3}\,\mathbf i - \frac{g}{2}\,\mathbf k \quad &\text{($\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4} - \tfrac{1}{4\sqrt3} = \tfrac{3 - 1}{4\sqrt3}$)} \\ \left|\mathbf a_1^P(0)\right| &= g\sqrt{\frac{1}{12} + \frac14} = g\sqrt{\frac{4}{12}} = \frac{g}{\sqrt3} \quad &\text{(modulus)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_1^P(0) = -\frac{g}{2\sqrt3}\,\mathbf e_r + \frac{g}{2}\,\mathbf e_\varphi = \frac{g}{2\sqrt3}\,\mathbf i - \frac{g}{2}\,\mathbf k \quad \text{(taut-cord model)}}$$

Units: $[g] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: this is the value the equations of the taut cord give; part (d) shows that the cord cannot actually be taut at that instant, and the box after it gives the acceleration of the real, slack start.

(d) Tension at the start

Tension at t equal to zero, and what a negative value means Law: projection along the cord; a cord can only pull; Newton's second law of the free particle in the translating frame Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Sec. 6.4; Problems.pdf, p. 16
$$\begin{aligned} T(0) &= mL\left(0 + \frac{g}{2\sqrt3 L}\right) - mg\,\frac{\sqrt3}{2} \quad &\text{(third equation of the system with the data)} \\ &= mg\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt3} - \frac{3}{2\sqrt3}\right) = -\frac{mg}{\sqrt3} \quad &\text{($\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = \tfrac{3}{2\sqrt3}$)} \\ m\,\mathbf a_1^P(0) &= -mg\,\mathbf k + ma\omega^2\sin 0\,\mathbf k = -mg\,\mathbf k \quad &\text{(cord slack: Eq. 4.63 without the cord)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{T(0) = -\frac{mg}{\sqrt3} \lt 0: \ \text{the cord cannot hold; a slack start has } \mathbf a_1^P(0) = -g\,\mathbf k}$$

Units: $[mg] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the given rate is too small to keep a particle above the plane of $A$ on a taut cord: the cord would have to push with the force $mg/\sqrt3$, which only a massless rigid rod could do. With a cord, the particle starts in free fall in the frame of $A$ and the taut-cord equations do not apply at the start.

Other reading: the angle measured from the downward vertical Law: the same method with the polar axis pointing down Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Problems.pdf, p. 16

If $\varphi$ is measured from the downward vertical (the particle below $A$, as in a hanging pendulum), the radial vector has the vertical component minus $\cos\varphi$, the derivative relations of the basis are the same, so the relative acceleration keeps the form of part (a), and the vertical in the new basis is minus $\cos\varphi$ times the radial vector plus $\sin\varphi$ times the new $\mathbf e_\varphi$.
