$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_r' &= \sin\varphi\cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\varphi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j - \cos\varphi\,\mathbf k, \quad \mathbf e_\varphi' = \frac{\partial\mathbf e_r'}{\partial\varphi} = \cos\varphi\cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \cos\varphi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j + \sin\varphi\,\mathbf k \quad &\text{(polar axis along $-\mathbf k$)} \\ \mathbf k &= -\cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_r' + \sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi' \quad &\text{(vertical components $-\cos\varphi$ and $\sin\varphi$)} \\ \mathbf e_r':\ -mL\left(\dot\varphi^2 + \dot\theta^2\sin^2\varphi\right) &= -T + mg_e\cos\varphi, \quad \mathbf e_\varphi':\ mL\left(\ddot\varphi - \dot\theta^2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\right) = -mg_e\sin\varphi \quad &\text{(projections)} \\ \ddot\varphi_0 &= \frac{g}{2L} - \frac{g}{2L} = 0, \quad T(0) = \frac{mg}{2\sqrt3} + \frac{\sqrt3 mg}{2} = \frac{2mg}{\sqrt3} \quad &\text{(data at $t = 0$)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P(0) &= -\frac{g}{2\sqrt3}\,\mathbf e_r' - \frac{g}{2}\,\mathbf e_\varphi' = \left(-\frac{g}{4\sqrt3} - \frac{\sqrt3 g}{4}\right)\mathbf i + \left(\frac{g}{4} - \frac{g}{4}\right)\mathbf k = -\frac{g}{\sqrt3}\,\mathbf i \quad &\text{($\mathbf e_r'(0) = \tfrac12\mathbf i - \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\mathbf k$, $\mathbf e_\varphi'(0) = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\mathbf i + \tfrac12\mathbf k$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{hanging reading: } \ddot\varphi_0 = 0, \quad \mathbf a_1^P(0) = -\frac{g}{\sqrt3}\,\mathbf i, \quad T(0) = \frac{2mg}{\sqrt3}}$$

Units: $[g] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$; $[mg] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: in this reading the given rate is exactly the one of a steady conical pendulum at 30 degrees from the downward vertical: the angle has no acceleration at the start, the relative acceleration points horizontally to the axis, and the cord pulls with twice the weight divided by the square root of 3.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Relative acceleration$\mathbf a'_P = -L(\dot\varphi^2 + \dot\theta^2\sin^2\varphi)\,\mathbf e_r + L(\ddot\varphi - \dot\theta^2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi)\,\mathbf e_\varphi + L(\ddot\theta\sin\varphi + 2\dot\theta\dot\varphi\cos\varphi)\,\mathbf e_\theta$, derived
(b) System of equations$\ddot\varphi = \dot\theta^2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi + (g - a\omega^2\sin\omega t)\sin\varphi/L$; $\ddot\theta\sin\varphi + 2\dot\theta\dot\varphi\cos\varphi = 0$; $T = mL(\dot\varphi^2 + \dot\theta^2\sin^2\varphi) - m(g - a\omega^2\sin\omega t)\cos\varphi$
(c) Relative acceleration at $t = 0$taut-cord model: $\mathbf a_1^P(0) = -\frac{g}{2\sqrt3}\,\mathbf e_r + \frac{g}{2}\,\mathbf e_\varphi = \frac{g}{2\sqrt3}\,\mathbf i - \frac{g}{2}\,\mathbf k$, modulus $g/\sqrt3$; actual cord (slack at the start): $-g\,\mathbf k$
(d) Tension at $t = 0$$T(0) = -mg/\sqrt3$: impossible for a cord, which goes slack at the start (a rod would push with $mg/\sqrt3$)
Other reading ($\varphi$ from the downward vertical)$\ddot\varphi_0 = 0$, $\mathbf a_1^P(0) = -\frac{g}{\sqrt3}\,\mathbf i$, $T(0) = 2mg/\sqrt3$

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 74 lists item 28 with no answer, so there is no key to compare with. Independent checks: the relative acceleration of part (a) is also the second derivative of the Cartesian components of $L\,\mathbf e_r$ (box below), and the limiting cases close the results.

Data inconsistency in the statement

With $\varphi$ measured from the upward axis $Az'$ (figure and the given $\mathbf e_r$), the given initial azimuthal rate cannot keep the cord taut: the tension at the start is minus $mg/\sqrt3$ (part (d)). The given value is exactly the rate of a steady conical pendulum hanging below $A$ at 30 degrees, which suggests that the statement intends the hanging reading; that reading contradicts the figure and the given unit vectors, so the answers follow the statement as written and the hanging reading is given beside them.

Independent check: Cartesian components of the relative acceleration at the start Law: second time derivative of each component of $L\,\mathbf e_r$; chain rule and product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.7; Problems.pdf, p. 16
$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\left(L\sin\varphi\cos\theta\right) &= L\left(\ddot\varphi\cos\varphi - \dot\varphi^2\sin\varphi\right)\cos\theta - 2L\dot\varphi\dot\theta\cos\varphi\sin\theta - L\sin\varphi\left(\ddot\theta\sin\theta + \dot\theta^2\cos\theta\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule on each factor)} \\ &= L\left(\frac{g}{L}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} - 0\right)\cdot 1 - 0 - L\cdot\frac12\left(0 + \frac{2g}{\sqrt3 L}\right) = \frac{\sqrt3 g}{2} - \frac{g}{\sqrt3} = \frac{g}{2\sqrt3} \quad &\text{(data at $t = 0$, $\ddot\varphi_0 = g/L$)} \\ \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\left(L\cos\varphi\right) &= -L\left(\ddot\varphi\sin\varphi + \dot\varphi^2\cos\varphi\right) = -L\cdot\frac{g}{L}\cdot\frac12 = -\frac{g}{2} \quad &\text{(chain rule twice)} \\ \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\left(L\sin\varphi\sin\theta\right) &= L\left(\ddot\varphi\cos\varphi - \dot\varphi^2\sin\varphi\right)\cdot 0 + 2L\dot\varphi\dot\theta\cos\varphi\cdot 1 + L\sin\varphi\left(\ddot\theta\cos\theta - \dot\theta^2\sin\theta\right) = 0 \quad &\text{($\sin 0 = 0$, $\dot\varphi_0 = 0$, $\ddot\theta_0 = 0$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_1^P(0) = \frac{g}{2\sqrt3}\,\mathbf i + 0\,\mathbf j - \frac{g}{2}\,\mathbf k}$$

Units: $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the Cartesian route, which never uses the spherical basis, gives the same vector as part (c).

Limiting cases Law: the results at extreme values of the data Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.38; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63
$$\begin{aligned} a \to 0 \ \text{or}\ \omega \to 0:\quad g_e &\to g \quad &\text{(spherical pendulum with a fixed support)} \\ \dot\theta \equiv 0:\quad \ddot\varphi &= \frac{g_e}{L}\sin\varphi \quad &\text{(planar pendulum written from the upward vertical: Eq. 4.38 with $\varphi = \pi - $ the hanging angle)} \\ \varphi = \pi,\ \dot\varphi = \dot\theta = 0:\quad T &= -mg_e\cos\pi = mg_e \quad &\text{(particle hanging at rest below $A$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{a\omega^2 \to 0: \ g_e \to g; \qquad \text{hanging at rest: } T = m\left(g - a\omega^2\sin\omega t\right)}$$

Units: $[mg_e] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: with a still support the problem is the ordinary spherical pendulum; a particle hanging at rest below the oscillating support feels the weight changed by the inertia force of the support, and the cord stays taut only while $g$ exceeds the product $a\omega^2\sin\omega t$.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf
Problem 30

Particle on a Rotating Quarter Circumference with a Spring

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 18
Rotating Frame + Path Variables

A point particle $P$ of mass $m$ is constrained to move on a smooth quarter of circumference as shown in the figure below. We define a moving reference frame $OX_1Y_1Z_1$ that rotates with respect to an inertial reference frame $OXYZ$. The rotation of the moving reference frame is performed along a vertical axis defined as $x_1 = -R$ and $y_1 = 0$; the angular velocity is $\boldsymbol{\omega} = \omega\mathbf{k} = \omega\mathbf{k}_1$. The particle is attached to a linear spring with the other end attached to the point $B$ of the reference frame $OX_1Y_1Z_1$ with coordinates $(-2R, 0, 0)$. The constant of the spring is $K = \alpha m\omega^2$. The angle between $\overline{OP}$ and the negative side of the $z_1$ axis, $\phi$, is used to define the position of the particle. Neglect the action of gravity on the particle.

Initially the particle is located at $\phi = 0$ and it is set to motion with a relative velocity $-\beta\omega R\,\mathbf{i}_1$. Both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are positive nondimensional parameters.

  • (a)
    Compute the relative velocity and the relative acceleration of the particle in the path variable reference frame $\{\mathbf{e}_t, \mathbf{e}_n, \mathbf{e}_b\}$ as functions of the coordinate $\phi$ and their derivatives.
  • (b)
    Write down the three components of Newton's second law expressed in the path variables reference frame $\{\mathbf{e}_t, \mathbf{e}_n, \mathbf{e}_b\}$.
  • (c)
    Express the energy conservation equation in the relative reference frame. Discuss if this equation is equivalent to one of the above ones.

Let us now consider a different problem. Depending on the values of the parameters, we may find the equilibrium of the forces at different positions.

  • (d)
    Obtain the value of $\alpha$ to have an equilibrium position when the particle is positioned at $\phi$ equal to $\pi/6$.

For this value of $\alpha$, the particle is again located at $\phi = 0$ and is set to motion with the relative velocity defined before.

  • (e)
    Describe the possible types of motion for the different values of $\beta$. In particular, obtain the critical value of $\beta$ that makes the particle reach the position $\phi = \pi/2$ and the reaction force of the curve to the particle at that instant.
  • (f)
    For a value of $\beta$ higher than the critical one, the particle leaves the arc of circumference and its motion is not anymore constrained. Under these conditions compute the maximum height reached by the particle, $z_{max}$, as a function of $\beta$. Note that the particle is still under the action of the spring.
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

A particle $P$ of mass $m$ slides on a smooth quarter circumference of radius $R$ and centre $O$, drawn in the plane $X_1Z_1$ of a frame that turns with the constant rate $\omega$ about the vertical axis through the point $(-R, 0, 0)$ of that frame; a spring of constant $K$ joins $P$ to the point $B$ of that frame, and gravity is neglected (Problems.pdf, p. 18). The statement asks for the relative velocity and acceleration in the path basis, the three components of Newton's second law, the energy equation of the relative motion, the value of $\alpha$ that gives an equilibrium at $\pi/6$, the types of motion with that value, and the maximum height after the particle leaves the arc. The arc and the point $B$ are at rest in the turning frame, so the solution works there, with the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2 and the inertia forces of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{Q;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$, origin $Q$ on the rotation axis at the height of $O$, $\mathbf k_0$ vertical, up; it plays the role of the inertial frame $OXYZ$ of the statement (see Readings)
Moving frame$S_1 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_1\}$, the frame $OX_1Y_1Z_1$ of the statement, attached to the arc: $\mathbf i_1$ horizontal, from the axis through $O$; $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$; $\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1$; $\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf i_0$ at $t = 0$
Points fixed in $S_1$$O$ (centre of the arc), at distance $R$ from the axis; $Q$, at $-R\,\mathbf i_1$ from $O$ (upper end of the arc); $B$, at $-2R\,\mathbf i_1$ from $O$
Path basis$\{\mathbf e_t, \mathbf e_n, \mathbf e_b\}$ at $P$: tangent in the sense of growing $\phi$, principal normal towards the centre of curvature $O$, binormal (deduced below)
Coordinate$\phi$, angle at $O$ between $\overline{OP}$ and the negative $z_1$ axis, $0 \le \phi \le \pi/2$
Constraints$y_1 = 0$ and $x_1^2 + z_1^2 = R^2$ (quarter with $x_1 \le 0$, $z_1 \le 0$): two holonomic, smooth, bilateral constraints, fixed in $S_1$
Degrees of freedom3 minus 2: 1, the coordinate $\phi(t)$, while $P$ is on the arc; 3 after it leaves the arc (part (f))
Data$m$ [kg], $R$ [m], $\omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$], $K = \alpha m\omega^2$ [N m$^{-1}$]; $\alpha$, $\beta$ positive numbers [1]
Initial conditions$\phi(0) = 0$; relative velocity $-\beta\omega R\,\mathbf i_1$
Unknowns$\phi(t)$; the reaction $\mathbf N = N_n\,\mathbf e_n + N_b\,\mathbf e_b$ (no tangential component: smooth arc)
Applied forcesspring only (no gravity)
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)of the origin, Euler, centrifugal and Coriolis (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial; $\omega$ constant; smooth arc acting as a bead on a wire; massless linear spring
Readings(1) The origin $O$ of the statement's inertial frame cannot be the centre of the arc, which moves on a circle; the fixed origin is taken at $Q$, on the axis. Any fixed origin gives the same velocities and accelerations. (2) No natural length is given: the spring is taken with zero natural length, force $-K$ times the vector from $B$ to $P$. With a natural length $\ell_0$ the spring potential becomes $\frac12 K\left(R\sqrt{5 - 4\sin\phi} - \ell_0\right)^2$ and every spring term below changes. (3) The arc ends at $\phi = 0$ (on the $-z_1$ axis) and at $\phi = \pi/2$ (on the rotation axis), as drawn

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. View from $+z$, with $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf k_1$ out of the paper ($\odot$) at the point $Q$ of the axis: then $\mathbf j_0 = \mathbf k_0\times\mathbf i_0$ points up the page. $\mathbf i_1, \mathbf j_1$ are $\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0$ turned counter-clockwise by $\omega t$; the dashed legs of $\mathbf i_1$ are $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$ and $\sin\omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$. The origin $O$ of $S_1$ runs on the dashed circle of radius $R$ with $\mathbf v_0^O = \omega R\,\mathbf j_1$ and $\mathbf a_0^O = -\omega^2R\,\mathbf i_1$.
Basis of the turning frame: rotation by omega t about k0 Law: elementary rotation about the third axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

View from above, along $\mathbf k_0$, which points out of the paper (⊙), with the axis at $Q$. With $\mathbf i_0$ to the right, $\mathbf j_0$, the cross product of $\mathbf k_0$ and $\mathbf i_0$, points up the page (right-hand rule: thumb towards the reader, the fingers turn $\mathbf i_0$ counterclockwise by a quarter turn). A positive $\omega$ turns the frame counterclockwise. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\omega t$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ up the page, along plus $\mathbf j_0$ (no minus sign). $\mathbf j_1$ is $\mathbf j_0$ turned by the same angle: adjacent leg $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$, and the counterclockwise turn carries its tip to the left, so the opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ lies along minus $\mathbf i_0$ (the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf j_1 = -\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles; axis)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\omega t\cos\omega t - \left(-\sin\omega t\right)\sin\omega t\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{3+3}$)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\omega t + \sin^2\omega t = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{12} = -\cos\omega t\sin\omega t + \sin\omega t\cos\omega t = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\omega t & -\sin\omega t & 0 \cr \sin\omega t & \cos\omega t & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: $[\omega t] = [1]$

Meaning: it is the matrix of Eq. 1.20 with the angle $\omega t$; the vertical keeps its direction, so heights are the same in both frames.

Figure 2. Plane $X_1Z_1$, fixed in $S_1$ ($\mathbf j_1$ points into the paper, $\otimes$). $\phi$ is measured at $O$ from the downward axis $-z_1$. In the shaded right triangle the hypotenuse is $|OP| = R$, the leg adjacent to $\phi$ is $R\cos\phi$ (downwards) and the opposite leg is $R\sin\phi$ (to the left); the distance from $P$ to the rotation axis is $R(1 - \sin\phi)$. $\mathbf i_1, \mathbf k_1$ in blue, $\mathbf e_t, \mathbf e_n$ in orange.
Position vector of P in the plane of the arc Law: position as the sum of its legs; right triangle; relation with the standard polar angle Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 18

The plane $X_1Z_1$, fixed in $S_1$, is drawn with $\mathbf i_1$ to the right and $\mathbf k_1$ up; the direction out of the paper is the cross product of $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf k_1$, which is minus $\mathbf j_1$, so $\mathbf j_1$ points into the paper (⊗). Let $F$ be the point of the $z_1$ axis at the height of $P$. In the shaded right triangle $OFP$ (right angle at $F$) the hypotenuse is $OP$, of length $R$, and the angle at $O$ is $\phi$: the adjacent leg $OF$ has length $R\cos\phi$ and points down, the opposite leg $FP$ has length $R\sin\phi$ and points to the left, towards $B$. The standard polar angle $\vartheta$ of the plane, measured from $\mathbf i_1$ towards $\mathbf k_1$, is minus the sum of a quarter turn and $\phi$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_1^P &= \overrightarrow{OF} + \overrightarrow{FP} = -R\cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1 - R\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(the two legs, with their directions)} \\ \cos\vartheta &= \cos\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2} + \phi\right) = \cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\phi - \sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}\sin\phi = -\sin\phi \quad &\text{($\vartheta = -\pi/2 - \phi$; cosine even; sum formula)} \\ \sin\vartheta &= -\sin\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2} + \phi\right) = -\left(\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\phi + \cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}\sin\phi\right) = -\cos\phi \quad &\text{(sine odd; sum formula)} \\ R\cos\vartheta\,\mathbf i_1 + R\sin\vartheta\,\mathbf k_1 &= -R\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 - R\cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(polar form gives the same vector)} \\ \mathbf r_1^Q &= -R\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \rho = x_1^P - x_1^Q = -R\sin\phi + R = R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right) \quad &\text{(horizontal distance from $P$ to the rotation axis)} \\ \mathbf r_0^O &= \overrightarrow{QO} = R\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \mathbf r_0^P = \mathbf r_0^O + \mathbf r_1^P = R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\mathbf i_1 - R\cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.16)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^P = -R\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 - R\cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1, \qquad \mathbf r_0^P = R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\mathbf i_1 - R\cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1, \qquad \rho = R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)}$$

Units: $[R\sin\phi] = [R\cos\phi] = [\rho] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: at the start the particle is at the lowest point of the arc, a distance $R$ from the axis; at a quarter turn it is at the upper end, on the axis. The angle grows clockwise in the drawing, from the downward axis towards $B$.

Path basis of the arc Law: unit tangent as the derivative of the position with respect to the arc length; principal normal; binormal as a vector product Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.9; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.11; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.15

The arc length from the lowest point is $s$, equal to $R$ times $\phi$, so the derivative with respect to $s$ is the derivative with respect to $\phi$ divided by $R$ (chain rule). The binormal is the determinant expanded along its first row, with the cofactor signs plus, minus, plus.

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d\mathbf r_1^P}{d\phi} &= -R\cos\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + R\sin\phi\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{($\tfrac{d}{d\phi}\sin\phi = \cos\phi$, $\tfrac{d}{d\phi}\cos\phi = -\sin\phi$)} \\ \mathbf e_t &= \frac{d\mathbf r_1^P}{ds} = \frac{1}{R}\frac{d\mathbf r_1^P}{d\phi} = -\cos\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\phi\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 2.9; chain rule with $ds = R\,d\phi$)} \\ \frac{d\mathbf e_t}{ds} &= \frac{1}{R}\left(\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1\right), \quad \left|\frac{d\mathbf e_t}{ds}\right| = \frac{1}{R} \quad &\text{(curvature of the circle)} \\ \mathbf e_n &= \sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1 = -\frac{\mathbf r_1^P}{R} \quad &\text{(Eq. 2.11: towards $O$)} \\ \mathbf e_b &= \mathbf e_t\times\mathbf e_n = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf i_1 & \mathbf j_1 & \mathbf k_1 \cr -\cos\phi & 0 & \sin\phi \cr \sin\phi & 0 & \cos\phi \end{vmatrix} = (+1)(0 - 0)\,\mathbf i_1 + (-1)\left(-\cos^2\phi - \sin^2\phi\right)\mathbf j_1 + (+1)(0 - 0)\,\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(first row; cofactor signs)} \\ \det[{}_1R_F] &= -\cos\phi\left(0\cdot 0 - 1\cdot\cos\phi\right) - \sin\phi\left(0\cdot 0 - 1\cdot\sin\phi\right) + 0 = \cos^2\phi + \sin^2\phi = 1 \quad &\text{(columns $\mathbf e_t, \mathbf e_n, \mathbf e_b$; first row; signs $+, -, +$)} \\ \mathbf e_t\cdot\mathbf e_n &= -\cos\phi\sin\phi + \sin\phi\cos\phi = 0 \quad &\text{(orthogonal)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf e_t = -\cos\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\phi\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf e_n = \sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf e_b = \mathbf j_1, \quad [{}_1R_F] = \begin{pmatrix} -\cos\phi & \sin\phi & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \cr \sin\phi & \cos\phi & 0 \end{pmatrix}}$$

Units: the three vectors are dimensionless; $[d\mathbf e_t/ds] = [\mathrm{L^{-1}}]$

Meaning: the tangent starts as minus $\mathbf i_1$ at the lowest point and ends as $\mathbf k_1$ at the upper end; the normal points along the radius to the centre; the binormal is the normal to the plane of the arc, into the paper.

Kinematics

Motion of the turning frame and derivatives of its unit vectors Law: angular velocity of a simple rotation; derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(simple rotation about the fixed vertical; $\omega$ constant)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 to 3.5)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_0\right) &= -\omega\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \omega\cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(check: chain rule on the components of $\mathbf i_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0}$$

Units: $[\omega] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: seen from $S_1$ the three unit vectors are constant; seen from $S_0$ the horizontal ones turn with the frame.

(a) Relative velocity and acceleration in the path basis

Relative velocity and relative acceleration Law: time derivatives in $S_1$, where $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf k_1$ are constant; chain rule and product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.16; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24; Problems.pdf, p. 18
$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dt}\sin\phi &= \cos\phi\,\dot\phi, \quad \frac{d}{dt}\cos\phi = -\sin\phi\,\dot\phi \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \mathbf v_1^P &= \left.\frac{d\mathbf r_1^P}{dt}\right|_1 = -R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + R\sin\phi\,\dot\phi\,\mathbf k_1 = R\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_t \quad &\text{(components differentiated; Eq. 3.19)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_t}{dt}\right|_1 &= \frac{d\mathbf e_t}{d\phi}\,\dot\phi = \left(\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1\right)\dot\phi = \dot\phi\,\mathbf e_n \quad &\text{(chain rule on $\mathbf e_t(\phi(t))$)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P &= \left.\frac{d}{dt}\left(R\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_t\right)\right|_1 = R\ddot\phi\,\mathbf e_t + R\dot\phi\,\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_n \quad &\text{(product rule; Eq. 3.24)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_1^P = R\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_t, \qquad \mathbf a_1^P = R\ddot\phi\,\mathbf e_t + R\dot\phi^2\,\mathbf e_n}$$

Units: $[R\dot\phi] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[R\ddot\phi] = [R\dot\phi^2] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the relative velocity is tangent to the arc; the relative acceleration has the tangential part of the change of speed and the normal part towards the centre of the circle; nothing along the binormal.

Absolute velocity and acceleration: origin, centripetal and Coriolis terms Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the position written in the turning basis; product rule; derivatives of the unit vectors Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]

The absolute position is differentiated as it stands, term by term; the terms are named afterwards.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P &= \frac{d}{dt}\left[R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\right]\mathbf i_1 + R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\omega\,\mathbf j_1 + R\sin\phi\,\dot\phi\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; derivative of $\mathbf i_1$; $\mathbf k_1$ constant)} \\ &= -R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + R\sin\phi\,\dot\phi\,\mathbf k_1 + \omega R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf v_1^P + \omega\rho\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(chain rule; relative velocity recognised)} \\ \mathbf v_0^O + \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P &= \omega R\,\mathbf j_1 + \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(-R\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 - R\cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1\right) = \omega R\,\mathbf j_1 - \omega R\sin\phi\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(the transport part is Eq. 3.26)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1^P}{dt}\right|_0 &= \mathbf a_1^P + \left(-R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\right)\omega\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; the turning of $\mathbf i_1$ inside $\mathbf v_1^P$)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left[\omega R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\mathbf j_1\right] &= -\omega R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\,\mathbf j_1 + \omega R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\left(-\omega\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule; derivative of $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ \mathbf a_0^P &= \mathbf a_1^P - 2\omega R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\,\mathbf j_1 - \omega^2R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(sum of the two lines above)} \\ 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P &= 2\omega R\dot\phi\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(-\cos\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\phi\,\mathbf k_1\right) = -2\omega R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(the $\mathbf j_1$ term: Coriolis)} \\ \mathbf a_0^O &= R\,\omega\left(-\omega\,\mathbf i_1\right) = -\omega^2R\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(second derivative of $R\,\mathbf i_1$: origin term)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(-\omega R\sin\phi\,\mathbf j_1\right) = \omega^2R\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\mathbf i_1$: centripetal term)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_0^P = \underbrace{-\omega^2R\,\mathbf i_1}_{\mathbf a_0^O} + \mathbf a_1^P + \underbrace{\omega^2R\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1}_{\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P)} + \underbrace{\left(-2\omega R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\,\mathbf j_1\right)}_{2\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P}}$$

Units: $[\omega^2R] = [\omega R\dot\phi] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the origin term and the centripetal term add up to minus the square of the rate times the distance to the true axis, along $\mathbf i_1$: the point is pulled towards the axis, not towards $O$. The Coriolis term is normal to the plane of the arc. There is no Euler term, the rate being constant.

Forces and Equations of Motion

Figure 3. Forces on $P$ in $S_1$. In the plane of the arc: the spring towards $B$, the reaction $N_n\,\mathbf e_n$ and the sum of the origin and centrifugal forces, $m\omega^2\rho\,\mathbf i_1$ (dashed, inertia), away from the rotation axis. Seen from above: the Coriolis force along $\mathbf j_1$ (dashed, inertia) and the binormal reaction, which balance each other.

(b) Newton's second law in the path basis

Actual and inertia forces on the particle Law: linear spring of zero natural length; smooth reaction normal to the tangent; inertia forces of a non-inertial frame Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.1; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.16; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]
$$\begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{BP} &= \mathbf r_1^P - \mathbf r_1^B = \left(-R\sin\phi + 2R\right)\mathbf i_1 - R\cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf r_1^B = -2R\,\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \mathbf F_K &= -K\,\overrightarrow{BP} = -\alpha m\omega^2R\left[\left(2 - \sin\phi\right)\mathbf i_1 - \cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1\right] \quad &\text{(Eq. 5.1 in vector form; $K = \alpha m\omega^2$)} \\ \mathbf N &= N_n\,\mathbf e_n + N_b\,\mathbf e_b \quad &\text{(smooth arc: no component along $\mathbf e_t$)} \\ \mathbf F_A &= -m\,\mathbf a_0^O = m\omega^2R\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \mathbf F_E = -m\,\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.62, first two terms)} \\ \mathbf F_C &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) = -m\omega^2R\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(centrifugal: composition box times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR} &= -2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P = 2m\omega R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(Coriolis: composition box times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_A + \mathbf F_C &= m\omega^2R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\mathbf i_1 = m\omega^2\rho\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(sum; Slide 30 about the true axis)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf F_K = -\alpha m\omega^2R\left[\left(2 - \sin\phi\right)\mathbf i_1 - \cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1\right], \quad \mathbf F_A + \mathbf F_C = m\omega^2R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\mathbf i_1, \quad \mathbf F_E = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf F_{COR} = 2m\omega R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\,\mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[K\,R] = [\alpha m\omega^2R] = [m\omega R\dot\phi] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: one actual applied force (the spring, towards $B$), the reaction with two unknown components, and the inertia forces: the origin and centrifugal terms together push the particle horizontally away from the true axis, and the Coriolis force is normal to the plane of the arc.

Projections of the forces on the path basis Law: scalar products with the columns of $[{}_1R_F]$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.13

From the columns of $[{}_1R_F]$: the projections of $\mathbf i_1$ on $\mathbf e_t$ and $\mathbf e_n$ are minus the cosine and the sine; those of $\mathbf k_1$ are the sine and the cosine; $\mathbf j_1$ is $\mathbf e_b$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf F_K\cdot\mathbf e_t &= -\alpha m\omega^2R\left[\left(2 - \sin\phi\right)\left(-\cos\phi\right) - \cos\phi\sin\phi\right] = -\alpha m\omega^2R\left(-2\cos\phi\right) = 2\alpha m\omega^2R\cos\phi \quad &\text{(the two sine-cosine products cancel)} \\ \mathbf F_K\cdot\mathbf e_n &= -\alpha m\omega^2R\left[\left(2 - \sin\phi\right)\sin\phi - \cos^2\phi\right] = -\alpha m\omega^2R\left(2\sin\phi - 1\right) \quad &\text{($\sin^2\phi + \cos^2\phi = 1$)} \\ \left(\mathbf F_A + \mathbf F_C\right)\cdot\mathbf e_t &= -m\omega^2R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\cos\phi, \quad \left(\mathbf F_A + \mathbf F_C\right)\cdot\mathbf e_n = m\omega^2R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\sin\phi \quad &\text{(along $\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \mathbf F_K\cdot\mathbf e_b &= 0, \quad \left(\mathbf F_A + \mathbf F_C\right)\cdot\mathbf e_b = 0, \quad \mathbf F_{COR}\cdot\mathbf e_b = 2m\omega R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi \quad &\text{(only the Coriolis force leaves the plane)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf F_K = 2\alpha m\omega^2R\cos\phi\,\mathbf e_t + \alpha m\omega^2R\left(1 - 2\sin\phi\right)\mathbf e_n, \quad \mathbf F_A + \mathbf F_C = m\omega^2R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\left(-\cos\phi\,\mathbf e_t + \sin\phi\,\mathbf e_n\right)}$$

Units: every component $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: along the arc the spring always pulls towards larger angles, up towards $B$, and the inertia forces of the rotation pull towards smaller angles, away from the axis.

Three components of Newton's second law in the path basis Law: Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame, projected on $\{\mathbf e_t, \mathbf e_n, \mathbf e_b\}$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.18; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.19; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; Problems.pdf, p. 18

Three scalar equations for three unknowns: the coordinate and the two components of the reaction.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_t:\ mR\ddot\phi &= 2\alpha m\omega^2R\cos\phi - m\omega^2R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\cos\phi \quad &\text{(Eq. 6.17: no reaction along the tangent)} \\ \mathbf e_n:\ mR\dot\phi^2 &= N_n + \alpha m\omega^2R\left(1 - 2\sin\phi\right) + m\omega^2R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\sin\phi \quad &\text{(Eq. 6.18, normal)} \\ \mathbf e_b:\ 0 &= N_b + 2m\omega R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi \quad &\text{(Eq. 6.19, binormal)} \\ \ddot\phi &= \omega^2\cos\phi\left(2\alpha - 1 + \sin\phi\right) \quad &\text{(tangential equation divided by $mR$; $\cos\phi$ factored)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\ddot\phi = \omega^2\cos\phi\left(2\alpha - 1 + \sin\phi\right), \quad N_n = mR\dot\phi^2 - \alpha m\omega^2R\left(1 - 2\sin\phi\right) - m\omega^2R\sin\phi\left(1 - \sin\phi\right), \quad N_b = -2m\omega R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi}$$

Units: $[\ddot\phi] = [\omega^2] = [\mathrm{T^{-2}}]$; $[N_n] = [N_b] = [m\omega^2R] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the tangential component is the equation of motion; the normal and binormal components give the reaction once the motion is known. The binormal reaction balances the Coriolis force: the arc pushes the particle sideways so that it keeps turning with the plane while its distance to the axis changes.

Answers and Checks

(c) Energy conservation in the relative frame

Why the energy of the relative motion is conserved Law: power of each force on the relative velocity; potentials of the forces that work Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]

Two reasons. First, the forces that do no work in $S_1$: the reaction (the arc is at rest in $S_1$ and the reaction is normal to the tangent), the Coriolis force (normal to the relative velocity) and the Euler force (zero). Second, the forces that do work have potentials that depend on the position in $S_1$ only: the spring (its end $B$ is fixed in $S_1$), and the sum of the origin and centrifugal forces, a function of the position alone because the rate $\omega$ is constant and the acceleration of the origin is a constant vector of $S_1$. With a variable rate the centrifugal force would change in time at a fixed point and the Euler force would appear: no potential.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf N\cdot\mathbf v_1^P &= \left(N_n\,\mathbf e_n + N_b\,\mathbf e_b\right)\cdot R\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_t = 0 \quad &\text{(reaction: no power in $S_1$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR}\cdot\mathbf v_1^P &= 2m\omega R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_b\cdot R\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_t = 0 \quad &\text{(Coriolis: no power)} \\ \mathbf F_E\cdot\mathbf v_1^P &= 0 \quad &\text{($\mathbf F_E = \mathbf 0$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{only } \mathbf F_K \text{ and } \mathbf F_A + \mathbf F_C \text{ work in } S_1, \text{ and both have potentials}}$$

Units: $[\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v_1^P] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-3}}]$, a power

Meaning: the conditions of Slide 29 are met, so the mechanical energy of the relative motion is a constant of the motion.

Potentials along the arc and energy integral Law: potential as minus the work along the path, with Barrow's rule; change of variable in the integral Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.24; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]

Along the arc the displacement is $\mathbf e_t$ times $R\,d\phi'$, so each potential is minus the integral of the tangential component times $R$. In the second integral the substitution $u$ equal to $\sin\phi'$ has the differential $\cos\phi'\,d\phi'$ and the limits 0 and $\sin\phi$. Potentials are taken zero at the lowest point.

$$\begin{aligned} V_K(\phi) &= -\int_0^{\phi}2\alpha m\omega^2R\cos\phi'\,R\,d\phi' = -2\alpha m\omega^2R^2\left[\sin\phi'\right]_0^{\phi} = -2\alpha m\omega^2R^2\left(\sin\phi - 0\right) \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.14; antiderivative of the cosine; Barrow's rule)} \\ V_{AC}(\phi) &= -\int_0^{\phi}\left(-m\omega^2R\left(1 - \sin\phi'\right)\cos\phi'\right)R\,d\phi' = m\omega^2R^2\int_0^{\sin\phi}\left(1 - u\right)du \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.14; $u = \sin\phi'$, $du = \cos\phi'\,d\phi'$)} \\ &= m\omega^2R^2\left[u - \tfrac12 u^2\right]_0^{\sin\phi} = m\omega^2R^2\left(\sin\phi - \tfrac12\sin^2\phi\right) \quad &\text{(antiderivative; Barrow's rule)} \\ T_1^P &= \tfrac12 m\,\mathbf v_1^P\cdot\mathbf v_1^P = \tfrac12 mR^2\dot\phi^2 \quad &\text{(kinetic energy in $S_1$)} \\ E_1^P &= T_1^P + V_K + V_{AC} \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.31 in $S_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{E_1^P = \tfrac12 mR^2\dot\phi^2 - 2\alpha m\omega^2R^2\sin\phi + m\omega^2R^2\left(\sin\phi - \tfrac12\sin^2\phi\right) = \text{const}}$$

Units: $[mR^2\dot\phi^2] = [m\omega^2R^2] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the spring potential falls as the particle climbs towards $B$; the rotation potential rises as the particle approaches the axis. Up to additive constants they are one half of the spring constant times the squared length of the spring and minus one half of the mass times the squared rate times the squared distance to the axis (Slide 30).

Constant of the motion and relation with the tangential equation Law: initial conditions; time derivative of the energy along the motion; chain rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.29; Problems.pdf, p. 18

The initial relative velocity is the velocity of part (a) at the start, where the tangent is minus $\mathbf i_1$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_1^P(0) &= R\dot\phi(0)\,\mathbf e_t(0) = R\dot\phi(0)\left(-\cos 0\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin 0\,\mathbf k_1\right) = -R\dot\phi(0)\,\mathbf i_1 = -\beta\omega R\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(part (a) at $t = 0$; statement)} \\ \dot\phi(0) &= \beta\omega, \quad E_1^P(0) = \tfrac12 mR^2\beta^2\omega^2 + 0 + 0 \quad &\text{(at $\phi = 0$ both potentials vanish)} \\ \dot\phi^2 &= \beta^2\omega^2 + 4\alpha\omega^2\sin\phi - 2\omega^2\sin\phi + \omega^2\sin^2\phi \quad &\text{(energy equation divided by $\tfrac12 mR^2$)} \\ \frac{dE_1^P}{dt} &= mR^2\dot\phi\ddot\phi - 2\alpha m\omega^2R^2\cos\phi\,\dot\phi + m\omega^2R^2\left(\cos\phi - \sin\phi\cos\phi\right)\dot\phi \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule $\tfrac{d}{dt}\sin^2\phi = 2\sin\phi\cos\phi\,\dot\phi$)} \\ &= mR^2\dot\phi\left[\ddot\phi - \omega^2\cos\phi\left(2\alpha - 1 + \sin\phi\right)\right] \quad &\text{(factor $mR^2\dot\phi$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\dot\phi^2 = \omega^2\left[\beta^2 + \left(4\alpha - 2\right)\sin\phi + \sin^2\phi\right], \qquad \frac{dE_1^P}{dt} = mR^2\dot\phi\times\left(\text{tangential equation of part (b)}\right)}$$

Units: $[\dot\phi^2] = [\omega^2] = [\mathrm{T^{-2}}]$; $[dE_1^P/dt] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-3}}]$

Meaning: the energy equation is not new information: it is the first integral of the tangential component (that equation times the relative speed, integrated once), and its derivative gives it back wherever the rate is not zero. The normal and binormal components are independent of it and give the reaction.

(d) Value of alpha for an equilibrium at pi/6

Equilibrium positions and the value of alpha Law: relative equilibrium: rate and angular acceleration zero for all time, so the tangential force vanishes Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.32; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6; Problems.pdf, p. 18
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \omega^2\cos\phi_e\left(2\alpha - 1 + \sin\phi_e\right) \quad &\text{(tangential equation with $\dot\phi = \ddot\phi = 0$)} \\ \cos\phi_e = 0 &\Rightarrow \phi_e = \tfrac{\pi}{2} \quad &\text{(first factor: the upper end, on the axis, for every $\alpha$)} \\ \sin\phi_e &= 1 - 2\alpha \quad &\text{(second factor: interior points, only for $0 \le 1 - 2\alpha \le 1$)} \\ \sin\tfrac{\pi}{6} &= \tfrac12 = 1 - 2\alpha \;\Rightarrow\; 2\alpha = \tfrac12 \quad &\text{(the required position)} \\ N_n &= 0 - \tfrac14 m\omega^2R\left(1 - 1\right) - m\omega^2R\cdot\tfrac12\left(1 - \tfrac12\right) = -\tfrac14 m\omega^2R, \quad N_b = 0 \quad &\text{(part (b) at rest at $\pi/6$ with $\alpha = 1/4$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\alpha = \tfrac14 \qquad \left(\text{reaction at that equilibrium } \mathbf N = -\tfrac14 m\omega^2R\,\mathbf e_n\right)}$$

Units: $[\alpha] = [1]$; $[N_n] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: a soft spring, a quarter of the reference stiffness, balances along the arc the outward pull of the rotation at thirty degrees. At rest there the reaction points away from $O$: the arc holds the particle against the net pull towards the centre.

(e) Types of motion for alpha equal to 1/4, critical beta and reaction at pi/2

Barrier function and quadrature Law: energy integral of part (c); the motion is possible only where the kinetic energy is not negative Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.27; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.28; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6

With $\alpha$ equal to one quarter, the factor $4\alpha - 2$ is minus one. The function $U(\phi)$ below plays the role of a potential: the motion is allowed where $U$ does not exceed $\beta^2$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dot\phi^2 &= \omega^2\left[\beta^2 - \sin\phi + \sin^2\phi\right] = \omega^2\left[\beta^2 - U(\phi)\right], \quad U(\phi) = \sin\phi\left(1 - \sin\phi\right) \quad &\text{(part (c) with $\alpha = 1/4$)} \\ U(0) &= 0, \quad U\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 1\cdot 0 = 0 \quad &\text{(ends of the arc)} \\ U'(\phi) &= \cos\phi\left(1 - \sin\phi\right) + \sin\phi\left(-\cos\phi\right) = \cos\phi\left(1 - 2\sin\phi\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule)} \\ U'(\phi) = 0,\ 0 \lt \phi \lt \tfrac{\pi}{2} &\Rightarrow \sin\phi = \tfrac12,\ \phi = \tfrac{\pi}{6}, \quad U\left(\tfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac14 \quad &\text{(single interior stationary point)} \\ U''(\phi) &= -\sin\phi\left(1 - 2\sin\phi\right) - 2\cos^2\phi, \quad U''\left(\tfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 0 - 2\cdot\tfrac34 = -\tfrac32 \lt 0 \quad &\text{(a maximum: a barrier)} \\ t &= \int_0^{\phi}\frac{d\phi'}{\omega\sqrt{\beta^2 - U(\phi')}} \quad &\text{(quadrature while $\dot\phi \gt 0$; separation of variables)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\dot\phi^2 = \omega^2\left[\beta^2 - U(\phi)\right], \qquad U(\phi) = \sin\phi\left(1 - \sin\phi\right), \qquad \max_{[0,\pi/2]}U = U\left(\tfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \tfrac14}$$

Units: $[U] = [\beta^2] = [1]$

Meaning: the barrier has its top at the equilibrium of part (d), which is therefore unstable (a maximum of the potential); the particle crosses it only if the square of $\beta$ exceeds one quarter.

Figure 4. The energy integral reads $\dot\phi^2 = \omega^2[\beta^2 - U(\phi)]$: the particle moves only where $U$ lies below $\beta^2$. Below one quarter it turns back at $\phi^*$; at one quarter it creeps towards the top at $\pi/6$; above it it crosses the barrier and reaches $\pi/2$.
Three types of motion Law: turning points where the kinetic energy vanishes; sign of the tangential force there; linearisation about the unstable equilibrium by Taylor expansion Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.27; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.28; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6

For small $\beta$ the rate vanishes where $U$ reaches the square of $\beta$; the quadratic in the sine has two roots, and the particle, starting at the lowest point, meets the smaller one first. For $\beta$ equal to one half, write $\eta$ for the angle minus its equilibrium value.

$$\begin{aligned} \sin^2\phi^* - \sin\phi^* + \beta^2 &= 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \sin\phi^* = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1 - 4\beta^2}}{2} \quad &\text{(turning points, $\beta \le 1/2$; both roots)} \\ \sin\phi^*_- &= \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - 4\beta^2}}{2} \le \tfrac12, \quad \sin\phi^*_+ = \frac{1 + \sqrt{1 - 4\beta^2}}{2} \ge \tfrac12 \quad &\text{(the root $+$ lies beyond the barrier: not reached from $\phi = 0$)} \\ \ddot\phi\left(\phi^*_-\right) &= \omega^2\cos\phi^*_-\left(\sin\phi^*_- - \tfrac12\right) \lt 0 \quad &\text{(tangential equation, $\beta \lt 1/2$: it turns back)} \\ \beta = \tfrac12:\quad \dot\phi^2 &= \omega^2\left(\tfrac14 - \sin\phi + \sin^2\phi\right) = \omega^2\left(\tfrac12 - \sin\phi\right)^2 \quad &\text{(perfect square)} \\ \dot\phi &= \omega\left(\tfrac12 - \sin\phi\right) \quad &\text{(positive root: the rate starts at $\omega/2$)} \\ \sin\left(\tfrac{\pi}{6} + \eta\right) &\simeq \tfrac12 + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\eta \;\Rightarrow\; \dot\eta \simeq -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\omega\,\eta \quad &\text{(Taylor expansion to first order; $\cos\tfrac{\pi}{6} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$)} \\ \int_{\eta_1}^{\eta}\frac{d\eta'}{\eta'} &= \left[\ln\left|\eta'\right|\right]_{\eta_1}^{\eta} = \ln\frac{\eta}{\eta_1} = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\omega\left(t - t_1\right) \quad &\text{(separation of variables from a time $t_1$ near the top; Barrow's rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \beta \lt \tfrac12: \text{ turns back at } \sin\phi^* = \tfrac12\left(1 - \sqrt{1 - 4\beta^2}\right) \text{ and leaves the arc at its lower end}; \cr \beta = \tfrac12: \ \eta = \eta_1 e^{-\sqrt3\,\omega(t - t_1)/2} \text{ (creeps towards } \pi/6 \text{ without reaching it)}; \quad \beta \gt \tfrac12: \text{ reaches } \tfrac{\pi}{2} \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[\beta] = [1]$; $[\omega\,t] = [1]$; $[\eta] = [1]$

Meaning: below the critical value the particle climbs part of the way, stops, comes back to the lowest point with its initial speed (energy conservation) and leaves the arc there, which ends at that point. At the critical value the distance to the top of the barrier decays exponentially and is never zero. Above it the rate never vanishes and the particle runs to the upper end.

Critical beta and reaction at pi/2 Law: energy integral at the end of the arc; normal and binormal components of part (b) Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.27; Problems.pdf, p. 18

At the upper end the sine is 1 and the cosine 0, the normal is the column of $[{}_1R_F]$ with these values, and the rate follows from the energy integral.

$$\begin{aligned} \dot\phi^2\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) &= \omega^2\left[\beta^2 - U\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right] = \beta^2\omega^2, \quad \dot\phi\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \beta\omega \quad &\text{(barrier crossed: the rate stayed positive)} \\ \mathbf e_n\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) &= \sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}\,\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(towards $O$)} \\ N_b &= -2m\omega R\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}\,\beta\omega = 0 \quad &\text{(binormal component)} \\ N_n &= mR\beta^2\omega^2 - \tfrac14 m\omega^2R\left(1 - 2\right) - m\omega^2R\cdot 1\cdot\left(1 - 1\right) = m\omega^2R\left(\beta^2 + \tfrac14\right) \quad &\text{(normal component, $\alpha = 1/4$)} \\ \lim_{\beta\to 1/2^+}N_n &= m\omega^2R\left(\tfrac14 + \tfrac14\right) = \tfrac12 m\omega^2R \quad &\text{(at the critical value)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\beta_c = \tfrac12, \qquad \mathbf N\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = m\omega^2R\left(\beta^2 + \tfrac14\right)\mathbf i_1 \ \xrightarrow{\ \beta\to\beta_c^+\ }\ \tfrac12 m\omega^2R\,\mathbf i_1}$$

Units: $[m\omega^2R] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: at the upper end the particle is on the axis and moves along it, so the origin and centrifugal forces together, and the Coriolis force, vanish there; the reaction points to $O$ and supplies the centripetal force of the circular path plus the balance of the spring, which there pulls towards $B$ with a quarter of the mass times the squared rate times $R$.

(f) Maximum height after leaving the arc

Vertical motion of the free particle Law: Newton's second law in $S_1$, vertical component; harmonic oscillator; initial conditions Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.6; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.8; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.9

Once free, the particle has three coordinates in $S_1$; time $\tau$ is counted from the separation. Every inertia force is normal to $\mathbf k_1$: the origin and centrifugal forces lie along the horizontal from the axis, and the Coriolis force is the cross product of $\mathbf k_1$ with a vector. Only the spring has a vertical component.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_1^P(0) &= -R\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \mathbf v_1^P(0) = R\beta\omega\,\mathbf e_t\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \beta\omega R\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(state at the separation: on the axis, moving up)} \\ \mathbf k_1\cdot\mathbf F_K &= -K\,\mathbf k_1\cdot\left[\left(x_1 + 2R\right)\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + z_1\,\mathbf k_1\right] = -\alpha m\omega^2z_1 \quad &\text{(spring, free position)} \\ \mathbf k_1\cdot\left(\mathbf F_A + \mathbf F_C + \mathbf F_{COR}\right) &= 0 \quad &\text{(all three normal to $\mathbf k_1$)} \\ m\ddot z_1 &= -\alpha m\omega^2z_1 \;\Rightarrow\; \ddot z_1 + \omega_z^2z_1 = 0, \quad \omega_z = \sqrt{\alpha}\,\omega \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.63, vertical; Eq. 5.6)} \\ z_1(\tau) &= C_1\cos\omega_z\tau + C_2\sin\omega_z\tau \quad &\text{(Eq. 5.7)} \\ \dot z_1(\tau) &= -\omega_zC_1\sin\omega_z\tau + \omega_zC_2\cos\omega_z\tau \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ z_1(0) &= C_1 = 0, \quad \dot z_1(0) = \omega_zC_2 = \beta\omega R \;\Rightarrow\; C_2 = \frac{\beta\omega R}{\sqrt{\alpha}\,\omega} = \frac{\beta R}{\sqrt{\alpha}} \quad &\text{(Eq. 5.8 and 5.9)} \\ z_{max} &= C_2 = \frac{\beta R}{\sqrt{1/4}} = 2\beta R, \quad \omega_z\tau_{max} = \tfrac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow \tau_{max} = \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{\alpha}\,\omega} = \frac{\pi}{\omega} \quad &\text{(maximum of the sine; $\alpha = 1/4$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{z_{max} = \frac{\beta R}{\sqrt{\alpha}} = 2\beta R \quad \left(\alpha = \tfrac14,\ \beta \gt \tfrac12\right), \text{ reached a time } \pi/\omega \text{ after leaving the arc}}$$

Units: $[\beta R] = [\mathrm{L}]$; $[\tau_{max}] = [\mathrm{T}]$

Meaning: the vertical motion is a harmonic oscillation driven only by the vertical pull of the spring; the horizontal motion, coupled by the rotation, does not affect it. The height is measured from the horizontal plane through $O$ and $B$, the same in $S_0$ because the frames share the vertical. The result assumes the particle does not touch the arc again, which lies below that plane while the height stays positive.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Relative velocity and acceleration$\mathbf v_1^P = R\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_t$, $\mathbf a_1^P = R\ddot\phi\,\mathbf e_t + R\dot\phi^2\,\mathbf e_n$, with $\mathbf e_t = -\cos\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\phi\,\mathbf k_1$, $\mathbf e_n = \sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1$, $\mathbf e_b = \mathbf j_1$
(b) Newton, $\mathbf e_t$$mR\ddot\phi = 2\alpha m\omega^2R\cos\phi - m\omega^2R(1 - \sin\phi)\cos\phi$, i.e. $\ddot\phi = \omega^2\cos\phi\,(2\alpha - 1 + \sin\phi)$
(b) Newton, $\mathbf e_n$$mR\dot\phi^2 = N_n + \alpha m\omega^2R(1 - 2\sin\phi) + m\omega^2R(1 - \sin\phi)\sin\phi$
(b) Newton, $\mathbf e_b$$0 = N_b + 2m\omega R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi$
(c) Energy$\frac12 mR^2\dot\phi^2 - 2\alpha m\omega^2R^2\sin\phi + m\omega^2R^2(\sin\phi - \frac12\sin^2\phi) = \frac12 m\beta^2\omega^2R^2$; equivalently $\dot\phi^2 = \omega^2[\beta^2 + (4\alpha - 2)\sin\phi + \sin^2\phi]$; it is the first integral of the $\mathbf e_t$ equation
(d) Equilibrium at $\pi/6$$\alpha = 1/4$ (and $\pi/2$ is an equilibrium for every $\alpha$); reaction there $-\frac14 m\omega^2R\,\mathbf e_n$
(e) Types of motion$\beta \lt 1/2$: turns back at $\sin\phi^* = \frac12(1 - \sqrt{1 - 4\beta^2})$, returns to $\phi = 0$ and leaves the arc; $\beta = 1/2$: approaches the unstable equilibrium $\pi/6$ asymptotically; $\beta \gt 1/2$: reaches $\pi/2$ with $\dot\phi = \beta\omega$
(e) Critical value and reaction$\beta_c = 1/2$; $\mathbf N(\pi/2) = m\omega^2R(\beta^2 + \frac14)\,\mathbf i_1$, tending to $\frac12 m\omega^2R\,\mathbf i_1$ as $\beta \to \beta_c$
(f) Maximum height$z_{max} = \beta R/\sqrt\alpha = 2\beta R$, at $\pi/\omega$ after leaving the arc
Reading of the springzero natural length; with a natural length $\ell_0$ the spring potential is $\frac12 K(R\sqrt{5 - 4\sin\phi} - \ell_0)^2$ and parts (b) to (f) change
Reading of the end of the arcthe arc ends at $\phi = 0$; if it continued below, the particle with $\beta \lt 1/2$ would keep moving to negative $\phi$ instead of leaving it there

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 74 lists the number 30 with nothing after it: the key prints no answer. The results are checked independently below, with the axial angular momentum about the fixed rotation axis and with limiting cases.

Independent check: angular momentum about the rotation axis Law: angular momentum about a fixed point of the axis and its rate, equal to the moment of the actual forces Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.48; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.53

In $\mathcal B_1$, with $Q$ as the fixed point, the position has the components $(\rho, 0, -R\cos\phi)$ and the absolute velocity $(-R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi,\ \omega\rho,\ R\sin\phi\,\dot\phi)$. The component along $\mathbf k_1$ of a vector product is the first component of the first factor times the second of the second, minus the second of the first times the first of the second. The spring force and the normal reaction lie in the plane of the arc, which contains the axis: no axial moment.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf H_{Q,0}\cdot\mathbf k_1 &= m\left(\rho\cdot\omega\rho - 0\right) = m\omega\rho^2 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.48)} \\ \mathbf M_Q\cdot\mathbf k_1 &= \rho\,N_b - 0 = \rho\,N_b \quad &\text{(only the binormal reaction, $N_b\,\mathbf j_1$, at the lever arm $\rho$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(m\omega\rho^2\right) &= 2m\omega\rho\dot\rho, \quad \dot\rho = \frac{d}{dt}\left[R\left(1 - \sin\phi\right)\right] = -R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ 2m\omega\rho\left(-R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\right) &= \rho\,N_b \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.53, axial component)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{N_b = -2m\omega R\cos\phi\,\dot\phi \quad (\rho \ne 0)}$$

Units: $[\rho N_b] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the same value as the binormal component of part (b), obtained without inertia forces: the sideways push of the arc is what changes the angular momentum about the axis as the particle moves towards it.

Limiting cases Law: the results at extreme values of the data Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6
$$\begin{aligned} \alpha \to 0:\quad \ddot\phi &= -\omega^2\cos\phi\left(1 - \sin\phi\right) \le 0 \quad &\text{(no spring: pushed to the lowest point, farthest from the axis)} \\ \alpha \gt \tfrac12:\quad 2\alpha - 1 + \sin\phi &\gt 0 \text{ on } \left[0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \quad &\text{(no interior equilibrium: the spring wins everywhere)} \\ \phi = \tfrac{\pi}{2}:\quad \mathbf F_A + \mathbf F_C &= \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf F_{COR} = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(on the axis, moving along it)} \\ \beta \to \tfrac12^+:\quad t\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) &\to \infty \quad &\text{(the quadrature diverges like the logarithm at the top of the barrier)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\alpha \to 0: \text{ particle driven to } \phi = 0; \quad \alpha \gt \tfrac12: \text{ no interior equilibrium}; \quad \beta \to \beta_c^+: \text{ infinite time to reach } \tfrac{\pi}{2}}$$

Units: $[\alpha] = [\beta] = [1]$

Meaning: both forces scale with the square of the rate, because the stiffness is a multiple of the mass times the squared rate; the rate only sets the time scale, and the type of motion depends on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ alone.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf
Problem 33

Two Repelling Particles on a Rotating Parabola

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 21
Rotating Wire + Two Particles

Two heavy point particles, $P_1$ and $P_2$, of mass $m$ each, slide without friction along a rigid wire parabola given by the equation $z = x^2/(2L)$, where $L$ is a known length. The wire rotates about its axis with a fixed, known angular velocity $\omega$. The two particles repel each other electrically with a force of magnitude $F_E = k/d^2$, where $k$ is a known constant and $d$ is the distance between the particles. We define the rotating reference frame $Oxyz$ attached to the parabola as shown in the figure below.

  • (a)
    Write down the position, velocity, and acceleration vectors of each particle relative to $Oxyz$ in a generic instant of time, as a function of $x_1$, $x_2$ (the position of $P_1$ and $P_2$ along the $Ox$ axis) and their derivatives.
  • (b)
    Write down Newton's second law for each particle in the $Oxyz$ reference frame.
  • (c)
    If the rotation of the wire is maintained by a motor, how much torque must it produce in the $Oz$ direction to keep $\omega$ constant as a function of the variables of the problem and their derivatives?
  • (d)
    Find out the equilibrium configurations of the system in the reference frame $Oxyz$ as a function of the parameters $\gamma = g/(\omega^2L)$ and $\kappa = k/(m\omega^2L^3)$.

Consider now that $P_1$ and $P_2$ are constrained to move symmetrically on each branch of the parabola, and that $\gamma = \kappa = 2$. Initially, $x_1(0) = L$ and $v_1(0) = L\omega$ (with $\dot x_1(0) \gt 0$).

  • (e)
    Write down the equation that gives the minimum and maximum values of $x_1$ occurring in this case. Hint: this equation is a third-order polynomial in $x_1$.
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

Two heavy particles $P_1$ and $P_2$ of mass $m$ slide without friction on a parabolic wire in the vertical plane $Oxz$, which turns about its axis $Oz$ with the constant rate $\omega$; they repel each other with a force of magnitude $k$ over the square of their distance (Problems.pdf, p. 21). The statement asks for the relative position, velocity and acceleration of each particle, Newton's second law in the turning frame, the motor torque that keeps the rate constant, the equilibria in terms of $\gamma$ and $\kappa$, and the equation of the extreme values of $x_1$ in a symmetric motion. The wire is at rest in $Oxyz$, so the solution works there, with the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2 and the inertia forces of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$, origin at the vertex $O$ (on the axis, fixed), $\mathbf k_0$ vertical, up
Moving frame$S_1 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_1\}$, the frame $Oxyz$ of the statement, attached to the wire: $\mathbf i_1$ along $Ox$ in the plane of the wire, $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$ along the axis, $\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1$ normal to the plane; $\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf i_0$ at $t = 0$
Wire$z = x^2/(2L)$, $y = 0$, fixed in $S_1$
Local basis of the wire at $P_i$unit tangent $\mathbf t_i$ (sense of growing $x$), in-plane unit normal $\mathbf n_i$ (towards the concave side), and $\mathbf j_1$
Coordinates$x_1$, $x_2$: abscissas of $P_1$ and $P_2$ along $Ox$
Constraintsfor each particle $y_i = 0$ and $z_i = x_i^2/(2L)$: four holonomic, smooth, bilateral constraints, fixed in $S_1$; in part (e) also $x_2 = -x_1$
Degrees of freedom6 minus 4: 2, the coordinates $x_1(t)$, $x_2(t)$; 1 in part (e)
Data$m$ [kg], $L$ [m], $\omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$], $g$ [m s$^{-2}$], $k$ [N m$^2$]; $\gamma = g/(\omega^2L)$ and $\kappa = k/(m\omega^2L^3)$ [1]
Auxiliary symbols$u_i = x_i/L$; $\sigma_i = \sqrt{1 + x_i^2/L^2}$ [1]; $\Delta x = x_1 - x_2$; $d$ distance between the particles; $D = d/L$
Unknowns$x_1(t)$, $x_2(t)$; reactions $\mathbf N_i = N_{in}\,\mathbf n_i + N_{iy}\,\mathbf j_1$ (no tangential component: smooth wire); in part (c) the motor torque $M_m$
Applied forcesweights $-mg\,\mathbf k_1$; electric repulsion, equal and opposite, along the line $P_1P_2$
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)centrifugal and Coriolis; no origin or Euler terms (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial; uniform gravity; smooth wire acting as a bead guide; $\omega$ constant (held by the motor); the wire is massless (see part (c))
Readings(1) In part (e) "$v_1(0) = L\omega$" is read as the speed of $P_1$ relative to $Oxyz$; the other reading, the rate of the abscissa equal to $L\omega$, is worked in the Answers table. (2) The initial abscissa of $P_2$ in part (e) is $-L$, by the symmetry stated

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. View from $+z$, with $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf k_1$ out of the paper ($\odot$) at the vertex $O$: then $\mathbf j_0 = \mathbf k_0\times\mathbf i_0$ points up the page. $\mathbf i_1, \mathbf j_1$ are $\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0$ turned counter-clockwise by $\omega t$; the dashed legs give $\mathbf i_1 = \cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_0$ and $\mathbf j_1 = -\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0$. The plane of the wire is seen edge-on, along $\mathbf i_1$; $P_1$ ($x_1 \lt 0$) and $P_2$ ($x_2 \gt 0$) project on it.
Basis of the wire frame: rotation by omega t about k0 Law: elementary rotation about the third axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

View from above, along $\mathbf k_0$, which points out of the paper (⊙) at the vertex. With $\mathbf i_0$ to the right, $\mathbf j_0$, the cross product of $\mathbf k_0$ and $\mathbf i_0$, points up the page (thumb towards the reader, the fingers turn $\mathbf i_0$ counterclockwise by a quarter turn). A positive $\omega$ turns the wire counterclockwise. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\omega t$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ along plus $\mathbf j_0$. $\mathbf j_1$ is $\mathbf j_0$ turned by the same angle: adjacent leg $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$; the counterclockwise turn carries its tip to the left, so the opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ lies along minus $\mathbf i_0$ (the minus sign). The plane of the wire is seen edge-on along $\mathbf i_1$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf j_1 = -\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles; axis)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\omega t\cos\omega t - \left(-\sin\omega t\right)\sin\omega t\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{3+3}$)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\omega t + \sin^2\omega t = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{12} = -\cos\omega t\sin\omega t + \sin\omega t\cos\omega t = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\omega t & -\sin\omega t & 0 \cr \sin\omega t & \cos\omega t & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: $[\omega t] = [1]$

Meaning: the matrix of Eq. 1.20 with the angle $\omega t$; heights and the weight have the same components in both frames.

Figure 2. Plane $Oxz$, fixed in $S_1$ ($\mathbf j_1$ points into the paper, $\otimes$). The position of $P_2$ has the dashed components $x_2$ and $z_2 = x_2^2/(2L)$. The shaded slope triangle at $P_2$ has a horizontal leg proportional to $1$, a vertical leg proportional to $dz/dx = x_2/L$ and the hypotenuse $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{1 + x_2^2/L^2}$ along the tangent; dividing by $\sigma_2$ gives $\mathbf t_2$, and turning it $90^\circ$ towards the concave side gives $\mathbf n_2$ (orange).
Position vectors and local basis of the wire Law: position as the sum of its components; slope triangle; quarter turn in the plane; vector product Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.9; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 21

The plane $Oxz$, fixed in $S_1$, is drawn with $\mathbf i_1$ to the right and $\mathbf k_1$ up; out of the paper is the cross product of $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf k_1$, which is minus $\mathbf j_1$, so $\mathbf j_1$ points into the paper (⊗). A particle at the abscissa $x_i$ is reached from $O$ by $x_i$ along $\mathbf i_1$ and the height of the wire along $\mathbf k_1$. In the slope triangle the horizontal leg is $dx$ and the vertical leg $dz$; the hypotenuse lies along the wire, with length $\sigma_i\,dx$. The normal is the tangent turned a quarter turn counterclockwise in the drawing (components $(a, b)$ become $(-b, a)$), towards the concave side.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_0^O &= \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf r_0^{P_i} = \mathbf r_1^{P_i} = x_i\,\mathbf i_1 + \frac{x_i^2}{2L}\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.16 with $O$ fixed and shared)} \\ dz &= \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{x^2}{2L}\right)dx = \frac{2x}{2L}\,dx = \frac{x}{L}\,dx \quad &\text{(vertical leg of the slope triangle)} \\ \mathbf t_i &= \frac{dx\,\mathbf i_1 + \frac{x_i}{L}dx\,\mathbf k_1}{\sigma_i\,dx} = \frac{1}{\sigma_i}\left(\mathbf i_1 + \frac{x_i}{L}\,\mathbf k_1\right), \quad \sigma_i^2 = 1 + \frac{x_i^2}{L^2} \quad &\text{(sum of the legs over the hypotenuse; Pythagoras)} \\ \mathbf n_i &= \frac{1}{\sigma_i}\left(-\frac{x_i}{L}\,\mathbf i_1 + \mathbf k_1\right), \quad \mathbf t_i\cdot\mathbf n_i = \frac{1}{\sigma_i^2}\left(-\frac{x_i}{L} + \frac{x_i}{L}\right) = 0 \quad &\text{(quarter turn; orthogonal)} \\ \mathbf t_i\times\mathbf n_i &= \frac{1}{\sigma_i^2}\left(\mathbf i_1\times\mathbf k_1 - \frac{x_i^2}{L^2}\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1\right) = \frac{1}{\sigma_i^2}\left(-\mathbf j_1 - \frac{x_i^2}{L^2}\,\mathbf j_1\right) = -\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf i_1\times\mathbf k_1 = -\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf j_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^{P_i} = x_i\,\mathbf i_1 + \frac{x_i^2}{2L}\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf t_i = \frac{\mathbf i_1 + (x_i/L)\,\mathbf k_1}{\sigma_i}, \quad \mathbf n_i = \frac{-(x_i/L)\,\mathbf i_1 + \mathbf k_1}{\sigma_i}, \quad \mathbf t_i\times\mathbf n_i = -\mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[x_i^2/L] = [\mathrm{L}]$; $[x_i/L] = [\sigma_i] = [1]$

Meaning: $\{\mathbf t_i, \mathbf n_i, -\mathbf j_1\}$ is a right-handed orthonormal triad at each particle; the reaction of the smooth wire lies in the plane of $\mathbf n_i$ and $\mathbf j_1$.

Figure 3. Chord $P_1P_2$: in the shaded right triangle the horizontal leg is $x_2 - x_1$, the vertical leg is $z_2 - z_1 = (x_2^2 - x_1^2)/(2L) = (x_2 - x_1)(x_1 + x_2)/(2L)$ and the hypotenuse is the distance $d$; the slope of the chord is $(x_1 + x_2)/(2L)$. The repulsions $\mathbf F_{E1}$ and $\mathbf F_{E2} = -\mathbf F_{E1}$ (pink) act along the chord, pushing the beads apart.
Chord between the particles Law: difference of position vectors; right triangle of the chord; difference of squares Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.5; Problems.pdf, p. 21

In the shaded right triangle of the chord the horizontal leg is $\Delta x$, the vertical leg is the difference of heights and the hypotenuse is the distance $d$.

$$\begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{P_2P_1} &= \mathbf r_1^{P_1} - \mathbf r_1^{P_2} = \left(x_1 - x_2\right)\mathbf i_1 + \frac{x_1^2 - x_2^2}{2L}\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(difference of positions)} \\ \frac{x_1^2 - x_2^2}{2L} &= \left(x_1 - x_2\right)\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2L} \quad &\text{(difference of squares)} \\ d^2 &= \Delta x^2 + \Delta x^2\frac{\left(x_1 + x_2\right)^2}{4L^2} = \Delta x^2\left[1 + \frac{\left(x_1 + x_2\right)^2}{4L^2}\right] \quad &\text{(Pythagoras)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\overrightarrow{P_2P_1} = \Delta x\left[\mathbf i_1 + \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2L}\,\mathbf k_1\right], \qquad d = \left|\Delta x\right|\sqrt{1 + \frac{\left(x_1 + x_2\right)^2}{4L^2}}}$$

Units: $[d] = [\Delta x] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: the slope of the chord is the mean of the slopes of the wire at its two ends.

Kinematics

Motion of the wire frame and derivatives of its unit vectors Law: angular velocity of a simple rotation; derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf v_0^O = \mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(rotation about the fixed axis; $\omega$ constant; $O$ fixed)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 to 3.5)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_0\right) &= -\omega\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \omega\cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(check: chain rule on the components of $\mathbf i_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0}$$

Units: $[\omega] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: seen from $S_1$ the unit vectors are constant; seen from $S_0$ the horizontal ones turn with the wire.

(a) Relative position, velocity and acceleration

Relative velocity and relative acceleration of each particle Law: time derivatives in $S_1$, where $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf k_1$ are constant; chain rule and product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24; Problems.pdf, p. 21
$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{x_i^2}{2L}\right) &= \frac{2x_i}{2L}\,\dot x_i = \frac{x_i\dot x_i}{L} \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \mathbf v_1^{P_i} &= \dot x_i\,\mathbf i_1 + \frac{x_i\dot x_i}{L}\,\mathbf k_1 = \sigma_i\dot x_i\,\mathbf t_i \quad &\text{(components differentiated; Eq. 3.19)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(x_i\dot x_i\right) &= \dot x_i\dot x_i + x_i\ddot x_i \quad &\text{(product rule)} \\ \mathbf a_1^{P_i} &= \ddot x_i\,\mathbf i_1 + \frac{\dot x_i^2 + x_i\ddot x_i}{L}\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(components differentiated again; Eq. 3.24)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^{P_i} = x_i\,\mathbf i_1 + \frac{x_i^2}{2L}\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf v_1^{P_i} = \dot x_i\,\mathbf i_1 + \frac{x_i\dot x_i}{L}\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf a_1^{P_i} = \ddot x_i\,\mathbf i_1 + \frac{\dot x_i^2 + x_i\ddot x_i}{L}\,\mathbf k_1 \quad (i = 1, 2)}$$

Units: $[\dot x_i] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[\ddot x_i] = [\dot x_i^2/L] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the relative velocity is tangent to the wire and the relative acceleration lies in the plane of the wire.

Absolute acceleration: centripetal and Coriolis terms Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the position written in the turning basis; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^{P_i} &= \dot x_i\,\mathbf i_1 + x_i\,\omega\,\mathbf j_1 + \frac{x_i\dot x_i}{L}\,\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf v_1^{P_i} + \omega x_i\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; derivative of $\mathbf i_1$; $\mathbf k_1$ constant)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1^{P_i}}{dt}\right|_0 &= \mathbf a_1^{P_i} + \dot x_i\,\omega\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; the turning of $\mathbf i_1$ inside $\mathbf v_1^{P_i}$)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left(\omega x_i\,\mathbf j_1\right) &= \omega\dot x_i\,\mathbf j_1 + \omega x_i\left(-\omega\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; derivative of $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^{P_i} &= 2\omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(\dot x_i\,\mathbf i_1 + \frac{x_i\dot x_i}{L}\,\mathbf k_1\right) = 2\omega\dot x_i\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(the two $\mathbf j_1$ terms above)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^{P_i}\right) &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(\omega x_i\,\mathbf j_1\right) = -\omega^2x_i\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(the $\mathbf i_1$ term above)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_0^{P_i} = \mathbf a_1^{P_i} - \omega^2x_i\,\mathbf i_1 + 2\omega\dot x_i\,\mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[\omega^2x_i] = [\omega\dot x_i] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the centripetal term points horizontally to the axis and the Coriolis term is normal to the plane of the wire; with $O$ fixed and the rate constant there are no origin or Euler terms.

Forces and Equations of Motion

Figure 4. Forces in $Oxyz$. In the plane of the wire: weight, repulsion along the chord, reaction $N_{in}\,\mathbf n_i$ and the centrifugal force $m\omega^2x_i\,\mathbf i_1$ (dashed). Seen from above: the Coriolis forces $-2m\omega\dot x_i\,\mathbf j_1$ (dashed) and the reactions $N_{iy}\,\mathbf j_1$ that cancel them.

(b) Newton's second law for each particle in Oxyz

Actual and inertia forces on each particle Law: weight; repulsion along the line of the particles; smooth reaction; inertia forces of a non-inertial frame Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.16; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; Problems.pdf, p. 21

The force on $P_1$ has the magnitude $k$ over the square of $d$ and the direction from $P_2$ to $P_1$ (repulsion); the force on $P_2$ is opposite.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf W_i &= -mg\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf N_i = N_{in}\,\mathbf n_i + N_{iy}\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(weight; smooth wire)} \\ \mathbf F_{E1} &= \frac{k}{d^2}\,\frac{\overrightarrow{P_2P_1}}{d} = \frac{k\,\Delta x}{d^3}\left[\mathbf i_1 + \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2L}\,\mathbf k_1\right], \quad \mathbf F_{E2} = -\mathbf F_{E1} \quad &\text{(chord box; action and reaction)} \\ \mathbf F_{A,i} &= \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf F_{E\!u,i} = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{($O$ fixed; $\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}$ zero)} \\ \mathbf F_{C,i} &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^{P_i}\right) = m\omega^2x_i\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(centrifugal: composition box times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR,i} &= -2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^{P_i} = -2m\omega\dot x_i\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(Coriolis: composition box times $-m$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{m\,\mathbf a_1^{P_i} = -mg\,\mathbf k_1 + N_{in}\,\mathbf n_i + N_{iy}\,\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf F_{Ei} + m\omega^2x_i\,\mathbf i_1 - 2m\omega\dot x_i\,\mathbf j_1, \qquad i = 1, 2}$$

Units: $[k/d^2] = [mg] = [m\omega^2x_i] = [m\omega\dot x_i] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: this is Newton's second law of each particle in $Oxyz$ (Eq. 4.63): six scalar equations for the six unknowns, two coordinates and four reaction components. The centrifugal force pushes each particle away from the axis.

Projections: equations of motion and reactions Law: projection of Newton's second law on $\sigma_i\mathbf t_i$, $\mathbf j_1$ and $\sigma_i\mathbf n_i$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.17; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]

The projection on the tangent removes the reaction. The electric force on $P_2$ is the one on $P_1$ with the indices exchanged, because both the sign of $\Delta x$ and the direction of the force reverse.

$$\begin{aligned} m\,\mathbf a_1^{P_1}\cdot\left(\mathbf i_1 + \tfrac{x_1}{L}\mathbf k_1\right) &= m\left[\ddot x_1 + \frac{x_1}{L}\cdot\frac{\dot x_1^2 + x_1\ddot x_1}{L}\right] = m\left[\left(1 + \frac{x_1^2}{L^2}\right)\ddot x_1 + \frac{x_1\dot x_1^2}{L^2}\right] \quad &\text{(left side, tangent)} \\ \left(-mg\,\mathbf k_1 + m\omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1\right)\cdot\left(\mathbf i_1 + \tfrac{x_1}{L}\mathbf k_1\right) &= m\omega^2x_1 - mg\frac{x_1}{L} = m\left(\omega^2 - \frac{g}{L}\right)x_1 \quad &\text{(weight and centrifugal; Coriolis and reaction give 0)} \\ \mathbf F_{E1}\cdot\left(\mathbf i_1 + \tfrac{x_1}{L}\mathbf k_1\right) &= \frac{k\,\Delta x}{d^3}\left[1 + \frac{x_1\left(x_1 + x_2\right)}{2L^2}\right] \quad &\text{(electric, tangent)} \\ \mathbf j_1:\ 0 &= N_{iy} - 2m\omega\dot x_i \quad &\text{(binormal direction)} \\ m\,\mathbf a_1^{P_i}\cdot\left(-\tfrac{x_i}{L}\mathbf i_1 + \mathbf k_1\right) &= m\left[-\frac{x_i\ddot x_i}{L} + \frac{\dot x_i^2 + x_i\ddot x_i}{L}\right] = \frac{m\dot x_i^2}{L} \quad &\text{(left side, normal)} \\ \mathbf F_{E1}\cdot\left(-\tfrac{x_1}{L}\mathbf i_1 + \mathbf k_1\right) &= \frac{k\,\Delta x}{d^3}\left[-\frac{x_1}{L} + \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2L}\right] = -\frac{k\,\Delta x^2}{2Ld^3} \quad &\text{(electric, normal; the same value for $P_2$)} \\ \frac{m\dot x_i^2}{L} &= \sigma_iN_{in} - mg - \frac{m\omega^2x_i^2}{L} - \frac{k\,\Delta x^2}{2Ld^3} \quad &\text{(normal component: $\mathbf n_i\cdot\sigma_i\mathbf n_i = \sigma_i$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} m\left[\left(1 + \frac{x_1^2}{L^2}\right)\ddot x_1 + \frac{x_1\dot x_1^2}{L^2}\right] = m\left(\omega^2 - \frac{g}{L}\right)x_1 + \frac{k\left(x_1 - x_2\right)}{d^3}\left[1 + \frac{x_1\left(x_1 + x_2\right)}{2L^2}\right] \cr m\left[\left(1 + \frac{x_2^2}{L^2}\right)\ddot x_2 + \frac{x_2\dot x_2^2}{L^2}\right] = m\left(\omega^2 - \frac{g}{L}\right)x_2 + \frac{k\left(x_2 - x_1\right)}{d^3}\left[1 + \frac{x_2\left(x_1 + x_2\right)}{2L^2}\right] \cr N_{iy} = 2m\omega\dot x_i, \qquad N_{in} = \frac{m}{\sigma_i}\left[\frac{\dot x_i^2}{L} + g + \frac{\omega^2x_i^2}{L}\right] + \frac{k\left(x_1 - x_2\right)^2}{2L\sigma_id^3} \end{gathered}}$$

Units: every term of the equations of motion $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$; $[k\,\Delta x^2/(L d^3)] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: weight and centrifugal force combine along the wire into one linear term in the abscissa: restoring towards the vertex if gravity wins ($\gamma$ above 1), repelling if the rotation wins. The reaction normal to the plane cancels the Coriolis force.

Answers and Checks

(c) Motor torque that keeps omega constant

Balance of moments on the wire about Oz Law: action and reaction between wire and particles; moment of a force about an axis; massless guide Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.48; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.53; Problems.pdf, p. 21

The particles push on the wire with minus the reactions. The wire is taken massless, so the moments about $Oz$ of all the actions on it add up to zero (a wire with mass, turning at a constant rate about its axis of symmetry, keeps its own angular momentum about the axis constant: rigid body result, extension; the torque is the same). The bearings act on the axis and have no moment about it. The component along $\mathbf k_1$ of the cross product of $x_i\,\mathbf i_1 + z_i\,\mathbf k_1$ with $N_{ix}\,\mathbf i_1 + N_{iy}\,\mathbf j_1 + N_{iz}\,\mathbf k_1$ is the first component of the first factor times the second of the second minus the second of the first times the first of the second.

$$\begin{aligned} \left[\mathbf r_1^{P_i}\times\left(-\mathbf N_i\right)\right]\cdot\mathbf k_1 &= -\left(x_iN_{iy} - 0\cdot N_{ix}\right) = -x_iN_{iy} \quad &\text{(moment of the push of $P_i$)} \\ M_m - x_1N_{1y} - x_2N_{2y} &= 0 \quad &\text{(massless wire)} \\ M_m &= x_1\cdot 2m\omega\dot x_1 + x_2\cdot 2m\omega\dot x_2 \quad &\text{(part (b): $N_{iy} = 2m\omega\dot x_i$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{M_m = 2m\omega\left(x_1\dot x_1 + x_2\dot x_2\right)}$$

Units: $[m\omega x\dot x] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$, a torque

Meaning: when the particles move away from the axis the motor must supply angular momentum (positive torque); when they move towards it, it must brake.

Check: angular momentum of the particles about Oz Law: angular momentum about the fixed point $O$ and its rate, equal to the moment of the external forces on the particles Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.26; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.48; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.53

In $\mathcal B_1$ the position of $P_i$ has the components $(x_i, 0, z_i)$ and its absolute velocity $(\dot x_i, \omega x_i, \dot z_i)$ (composition box). The weights are parallel to the axis and the electric pair acts along the line of the particles, so its total moment is zero; only the reactions have an axial moment, the moment $M_m$ transmitted through the wire.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf H_{O,0}\cdot\mathbf k_1 &= \sum_i m\left(x_i\cdot\omega x_i - 0\cdot\dot x_i\right) = m\omega\left(x_1^2 + x_2^2\right) \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.48, axial component)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left[m\omega\left(x_1^2 + x_2^2\right)\right] &= m\omega\left(2x_1\dot x_1 + 2x_2\dot x_2\right) \quad &\text{(chain rule; $\omega$ constant)} \\ \sum_i\left(\mathbf r_1^{P_i}\times\mathbf N_i\right)\cdot\mathbf k_1 &= x_1N_{1y} + x_2N_{2y} \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.53)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{x_1N_{1y} + x_2N_{2y} = 2m\omega\left(x_1\dot x_1 + x_2\dot x_2\right) = M_m}$$

Units: $[\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the same torque by a second route, without inertia forces.

(d) Equilibrium configurations in Oxyz
