Equilibrium equations in nondimensional form and their sum Law: relative equilibrium: the rates and accelerations vanish; scaling by $m\omega^2L$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.32; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6; Problems.pdf, p. 21

With the rates and accelerations zero, the equations of motion become algebraic. Divide by $m\omega^2L$ and write $\Sigma$ for the sum of the $u_i$.

$$\begin{aligned} f_1 &\equiv \left(1 - \gamma\right)u_1 + \frac{\kappa}{D^3}\left(u_1 - u_2\right)\left[1 + \frac{u_1\Sigma}{2}\right] = 0 \quad &\text{(equation of $P_1$)} \\ f_2 &\equiv \left(1 - \gamma\right)u_2 + \frac{\kappa}{D^3}\left(u_2 - u_1\right)\left[1 + \frac{u_2\Sigma}{2}\right] = 0 \quad &\text{(equation of $P_2$)} \\ D &= \left|u_1 - u_2\right|\sqrt{1 + \frac{\Sigma^2}{4}} \quad &\text{(chord box divided by $L$)} \\ f_1 + f_2 &= \left(1 - \gamma\right)\Sigma + \frac{\kappa}{D^3}\left(u_1 - u_2\right)\frac{\left(u_1 - u_2\right)\Sigma}{2} = \Sigma\left[\left(1 - \gamma\right) + \frac{\kappa\left(u_1 - u_2\right)^2}{2D^3}\right] = 0 \quad &\text{(the constant 1 cancels in the brackets)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\Sigma = 0 \ \text{(symmetric)} \qquad \text{or} \qquad \gamma - 1 = \frac{\kappa\left(u_1 - u_2\right)^2}{2D^3} \ \text{(only if } \gamma \gt 1\text{)}}$$

Units: $[\gamma] = [\kappa] = [u_i] = [1]$

Meaning: only the two nondimensional numbers matter: weight against centrifugal force, and repulsion against centrifugal force.

Cases gamma below 1 and gamma equal to 1 Law: sign of the terms of the equilibrium equations Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.32; Problems.pdf, p. 21

Two particles cannot occupy the same point, so the difference of the $u_i$ is not zero and the symmetric case has the first abscissa not zero.

$$\begin{aligned} \Sigma = 0:\quad u_2 &= -u_1, \quad D = 2\left|u_1\right|, \quad f_1 = u_1\left[\left(1 - \gamma\right) + \frac{2\kappa}{8\left|u_1\right|^3}\right] \quad &\text{(symmetric case)} \\ \gamma \lt 1:\quad \left(1 - \gamma\right) + \frac{\kappa}{4\left|u_1\right|^3} &\gt 0 \ \text{ and } \ \left(1 - \gamma\right) + \frac{\kappa\left(u_1 - u_2\right)^2}{2D^3} \gt 0 \quad &\text{(neither alternative can vanish)} \\ \gamma = 1:\quad \frac{\kappa}{4\left|u_1\right|^3} &= 0 \ \text{ and } \ \frac{\kappa\left(u_1 - u_2\right)^2}{2D^3} = 0 \iff \kappa = 0 \quad &\text{(both alternatives need $\kappa = 0$)} \\ \gamma = 1,\ \kappa = 0:\quad f_1 &= 0\cdot u_1 + 0 = 0, \quad f_2 = 0 \quad &\text{(every configuration)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\gamma \lt 1: \text{ no equilibrium}; \qquad \gamma = 1: \text{ equilibrium only if } \kappa = 0, \text{ and then every position is one}}$$

Units: dimensionless

Meaning: when the rotation beats gravity everywhere along the wire, nothing holds the particles, and the repulsion only pushes them further out; when they balance exactly, any repulsion breaks the balance.

Case gamma above 1: symmetric and asymmetric equilibria Law: solution of the algebraic equilibrium equations Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.32; Problems.pdf, p. 21

In the asymmetric case the second alternative of the sum gives $\kappa$ over the cube of $D$, which is substituted in the equation of $P_1$; then $c$ denotes the fourth root of $4\kappa$ over $\gamma - 1$.

$$\begin{aligned} \Sigma = 0:\quad \left(1 - \gamma\right) + \frac{\kappa}{4\left|u_1\right|^3} &= 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \left|u_1\right|^3 = \frac{\kappa}{4\left(\gamma - 1\right)} \;\Rightarrow\; x_1^2 = \left[\frac{\kappa L^3}{4\left(\gamma - 1\right)}\right]^{2/3} \quad &\text{(symmetric; $x_1 = Lu_1$)} \\ \Sigma \ne 0:\quad \frac{\kappa}{D^3} &= \frac{2\left(\gamma - 1\right)}{\left(u_1 - u_2\right)^2} \quad &\text{(second alternative)} \\ \left(1 - \gamma\right)u_1 + \frac{2\left(\gamma - 1\right)}{u_1 - u_2}\left[1 + \frac{u_1\left(u_1 + u_2\right)}{2}\right] &= 0 \;\Rightarrow\; u_1\left(u_1 - u_2\right) = 2 + u_1\left(u_1 + u_2\right) \quad &\text{(in $f_1$; divided by $\gamma - 1$, times $u_1 - u_2$)} \\ -u_1u_2 &= 2 + u_1u_2 \;\Rightarrow\; u_1u_2 = -1, \ \ x_1x_2 = -L^2 \quad &\text{(opposite branches)} \\ u_1 - u_2 &= u_1 + \frac{1}{u_1}, \quad 1 + \frac{\Sigma^2}{4} = \frac{\left(u_1 + 1/u_1\right)^2}{4}, \quad D^3 = \frac{\left|u_1 + 1/u_1\right|^6}{8} \quad &\text{($u_2 = -1/u_1$; $\left(u_1 - 1/u_1\right)^2 + 4 = \left(u_1 + 1/u_1\right)^2$)} \\ \gamma - 1 &= \frac{\kappa\left(u_1 + 1/u_1\right)^2\cdot 8}{2\left(u_1 + 1/u_1\right)^6} = \frac{4\kappa}{\left(u_1 + 1/u_1\right)^4} \;\Rightarrow\; \left|u_1 + \frac{1}{u_1}\right| = c \quad &\text{(back in the sum condition)} \\ u_1^2 - c\,u_1 + 1 &= 0 \;\Rightarrow\; u_1 = \frac{c \pm \sqrt{c^2 - 4}}{2}, \quad u_2 = -\frac{1}{u_1} \quad &\text{($u_1 \gt 0$; both roots, real only if $c \ge 2$)} \\ \gamma = 2,\ \kappa = 8:\quad c &= 32^{1/4} = 2.3784, \quad u_1 = 1.8328, \quad u_2 = -0.5456, \quad \Sigma = 1.2872, \quad D = 2\sqrt2, \quad \frac{\kappa}{D^3} = 0.35355 \quad &\text{(example)} \\ f_1 &= -1.8328 + 0.35355\cdot 2.3784\cdot\left(1 + \tfrac12\cdot 1.8328\cdot 1.2872\right) = -1.8328 + 0.35355\cdot 2.3784\cdot 2.1796 = -1.8328 + 1.8328 \simeq 0 \quad &\text{(first equation)} \\ f_2 &= 0.5456 + 0.35355\cdot\left(-2.3784\right)\cdot\left(1 - \tfrac12\cdot 0.5456\cdot 1.2872\right) = 0.5456 - 0.35355\cdot 2.3784\cdot 0.6488 = 0.5456 - 0.5456 \simeq 0 \quad &\text{(second equation)} \\ \left|u_1\right|^3 &= \frac{8}{4\cdot 1} = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; u_1 = 1.2599, \quad f_1 = -1.2599 + \frac{8}{4\cdot 2}\cdot 1.2599 = 0 \quad &\text{(symmetric root, same example)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \text{symmetric: } x_1 = -x_2,\quad x_1^2 = \left[\frac{\kappa L^3}{4\left(\gamma - 1\right)}\right]^{2/3}; \cr \text{asymmetric: } x_1x_2 = -L^2,\quad \frac{x_1}{L} = \frac{c \pm \sqrt{c^2 - 4}}{2},\quad c = \left(\frac{4\kappa}{\gamma - 1}\right)^{1/4}, \ \text{ real and distinct only for } \kappa \gt 4\left(\gamma - 1\right) \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[x_1^2] = [L^2] = [\mathrm{L^2}]$

Meaning: gravity, stronger than the rotation, acts along the wire as a spring towards the vertex that balances the repulsion. The two roots of the asymmetric case are a mirror pair (one root is the reciprocal of the other), with the chord through the point at height one half of $L$ on the axis; at the limiting value of $\kappa$ they merge into the symmetric equilibrium at the abscissa $L$. In the example of the last three rows ($\gamma$ equal to 2, $\kappa$ equal to 8) the asymmetric pair 1.833 and $-0.546$ and the symmetric value 1.260 satisfy the equilibrium equations to round-off. No equilibrium has both particles on the same branch, because both alternatives give abscissas of opposite sign.

(e) Symmetric motion with gamma and kappa equal to 2: extreme values of x1

Why the energy of the pair in Oxyz is conserved, and its potentials Law: power of each force on the relative velocities; potentials as minus the work, with Barrow's rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.24; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]

A symmetric start stays symmetric: the equations of part (b) are unchanged when the abscissas change sign and the labels are exchanged, so the symmetry needs no extra force. Two reasons for the conservation. First, the forces that do no work in $S_1$: the reactions (wire at rest in $S_1$, smooth), the Coriolis forces (normal to the relative velocities), and the origin and Euler forces, which vanish. Second, the forces that work have potentials of the positions in $S_1$ only: the weights, the repulsion (central pair, a function of the distance) and the centrifugal forces (rate constant, axis fixed). Along the wire the displacement is $\mathbf i_1$ plus $x/L$ times $\mathbf k_1$, times $dx$.

$$\begin{aligned} V_g(x_i) &= -\int_0^{x_i}\left(-mg\,\mathbf k_1\right)\cdot\left(\mathbf i_1 + \frac{x'}{L}\mathbf k_1\right)dx' = \frac{mg}{L}\left[\frac{x'^2}{2}\right]_0^{x_i} = \frac{mgx_i^2}{2L} \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.14; Barrow's rule)} \\ V_C(x_i) &= -\int_0^{x_i}m\omega^2x'\,dx' = -m\omega^2\left[\frac{x'^2}{2}\right]_0^{x_i} = -\tfrac12 m\omega^2x_i^2 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.14; Barrow's rule)} \\ V_E(d) &= -\int_{\infty}^{d}\frac{k}{d'^2}\,dd' = -\left[-\frac{k}{d'}\right]_{\infty}^{d} = \frac{k}{d} \quad &\text{(repulsion along growing $d$; zero at infinity; Barrow's rule)} \\ T_1 &= \sum_i\tfrac12 m\,\mathbf v_1^{P_i}\cdot\mathbf v_1^{P_i} = \sum_i\tfrac12 m\dot x_i^2\left(1 + \frac{x_i^2}{L^2}\right) \quad &\text{(kinetic energy of the pair in $S_1$)} \\ x_1 = x \gt 0,\ x_2 = -x:\quad d &= 2x, \quad T_1 = m\dot x^2\left(1 + \frac{x^2}{L^2}\right) \quad &\text{(symmetric motion)} \\ E_1 &= m\dot x^2\left(1 + \frac{x^2}{L^2}\right) + \frac{mgx^2}{L} - m\omega^2x^2 + \frac{k}{2x} \quad &\text{(two weights, two centrifugal terms, one pair)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{E_1 = m\dot x^2\left(1 + \frac{x^2}{L^2}\right) + m\left(\frac{g}{L} - \omega^2\right)x^2 + \frac{k}{2x} = \text{const}}$$

Units: $[m\dot x^2] = [mgx^2/L] = [m\omega^2x^2] = [k/x] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the abscissa stays positive: the repulsion potential grows without bound as the particles approach the vertex together.

Initial energy and the cubic of the turning points Law: initial conditions in the energy integral; turning points where the kinetic energy vanishes; all three roots of the cubic Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.27; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.28; Problems.pdf, p. 21

At the start the relative velocity of part (a) is evaluated at the abscissa $L$ and its length is set to $L\omega$ (Reading 1). Then everything is divided by $m\omega^2L^2$ with $u$ equal to $x/L$. The roots of the cubic follow from the triple-angle identity with $u$ written as twice a cosine.

$$\begin{aligned} \left|\mathbf v_1^{P_1}(0)\right|^2 &= \dot x(0)^2\left(1 + \frac{L^2}{L^2}\right) = 2\dot x(0)^2 = L^2\omega^2 \;\Rightarrow\; \dot x(0) = \frac{L\omega}{\sqrt2} \quad &\text{(part (a) at $t = 0$; $\dot x(0) \gt 0$)} \\ \frac{E_1}{m\omega^2L^2} &= \frac{\dot x^2}{\omega^2L^2}\left(1 + u^2\right) + \left(\gamma - 1\right)u^2 + \frac{\kappa}{2u} \quad &\text{(scaled energy; $k/(2x) = m\omega^2L^2\,\kappa/(2u)$)} \\ \frac{E_1(0)}{m\omega^2L^2} &= \frac12\cdot 2 + \left(2 - 1\right)\cdot 1 + \frac{2}{2} = 3 \quad &\text{($u = 1$, $\gamma = \kappa = 2$)} \\ u^2 + \frac{1}{u} &= 3 \;\Rightarrow\; u^3 - 3u + 1 = 0 \quad &\text{(rate zero; times $u \gt 0$)} \\ u = 2\cos\theta:\quad 8\cos^3\theta - 6\cos\theta + 1 &= 2\left(4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta\right) + 1 = 2\cos 3\theta + 1 = 0 \quad &\text{(triple-angle identity)} \\ \cos 3\theta = -\tfrac12 &\Rightarrow\; \theta = \tfrac{2\pi}{9},\ \tfrac{4\pi}{9},\ \tfrac{8\pi}{9} \;\Rightarrow\; u = 1.532,\ 0.347,\ -1.879 \quad &\text{(the three roots)} \\ 3 - u^2 - \frac1u \ge 0 &\iff u^3 - 3u + 1 \le 0 \ \ (u \gt 0); \quad 1 - 3 + 1 = -1 \le 0 \text{ at } u = 1 \quad &\text{(allowed region contains the start)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\frac{x_1^3}{L^3} - 3\frac{x_1}{L} + 1 = 0: \qquad x_{1,max} = 2L\cos\frac{2\pi}{9} \simeq 1.532\,L, \qquad x_{1,min} = 2L\cos\frac{4\pi}{9} \simeq 0.347\,L}$$

Units: $[u] = [1]$; $[x_1] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: the negative root, $-1.879$, is rejected: the abscissa of $P_1$ stays positive. The start lies between the two positive roots, so $P_1$ first moves out to 1.532 times $L$ and then oscillates between the two extreme values, with $P_2$ as its mirror image.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Position, velocity, acceleration$\mathbf r_1^{P_i} = x_i\,\mathbf i_1 + \frac{x_i^2}{2L}\mathbf k_1$, $\mathbf v_1^{P_i} = \dot x_i\,\mathbf i_1 + \frac{x_i\dot x_i}{L}\mathbf k_1$, $\mathbf a_1^{P_i} = \ddot x_i\,\mathbf i_1 + \frac{\dot x_i^2 + x_i\ddot x_i}{L}\mathbf k_1$ ($i = 1, 2$)
(b) Newton's second law$m\,\mathbf a_1^{P_i} = -mg\,\mathbf k_1 + N_{in}\mathbf n_i + N_{iy}\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf F_{Ei} + m\omega^2x_i\,\mathbf i_1 - 2m\omega\dot x_i\,\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf F_{E1} = -\mathbf F_{E2} = \frac{k\Delta x}{d^3}[\mathbf i_1 + \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2L}\mathbf k_1]$; tangential projections give the two equations of motion, $N_{iy} = 2m\omega\dot x_i$ and $N_{in}$ (box of part (b))
(c) Motor torque$M_m = 2m\omega(x_1\dot x_1 + x_2\dot x_2)$ along $\mathbf k$
(d) Equilibria$\gamma \lt 1$: none; $\gamma = 1$: only if $\kappa = 0$ (then every position); $\gamma \gt 1$: symmetric $x_1 = -x_2$, $x_1^2 = [\kappa L^3/(4(\gamma - 1))]^{2/3}$; asymmetric $x_1x_2 = -L^2$ with $x_1/L = (c \pm \sqrt{c^2 - 4})/2$, $c = (4\kappa/(\gamma - 1))^{1/4}$, for $\kappa \gt 4(\gamma - 1)$
(e) Extreme values of $x_1$$x_1^3/L^3 - 3x_1/L + 1 = 0$: $x_{1,min} = 2L\cos(4\pi/9) \simeq 0.347L$, $x_{1,max} = 2L\cos(2\pi/9) \simeq 1.532L$
(e) Other reading of the initial velocityif $\dot x_1(0) = L\omega$ instead of the speed: scaled energy 4, $x_1^3/L^3 - 4x_1/L + 1 = 0$, extreme values $0.254L$ and $1.861L$

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 75 prints the torque, the equilibria and the cubics of the extreme values for positive and negative $x_1$. The torque, the cases of $\gamma$ below and equal to 1, the symmetric equilibrium and the cubics coincide with parts (c), (d) and (e) (box below); the statement on the asymmetric equilibria differs (warning below). The cubic for negative $x_1$ is the mirror case of a start on the other branch, which does not apply to a start at $L$. The key's cubic confirms Reading 1 of the initial velocity (the speed); the other reading gives a different cubic.

Comparison with the official key Law: term-by-term comparison Source: Problems.pdf, p. 75
$$\begin{aligned} \text{key: } M &= 2m\omega\left(\dot x_1x_1 + \dot x_2x_2\right) = M_m \quad &\text{(part (c))} \\ \text{key: } \gamma \lt 1 &: \text{none}; \quad \gamma = 1: \text{ only } \kappa = 0, \text{ all positions} \quad &\text{(part (d), first box of cases)} \\ \text{key: } \gamma \gt 1 &: \ x_1 = -x_2,\ x_1^2 = \left[\frac{\kappa L^3}{4\left(\gamma - 1\right)}\right]^{2/3}, \text{ and "asymmetric ones also exist"} \quad &\text{(part (d); the key adds $x_1x_2 \lt 0$ for the symmetric one)} \\ \text{key: } \frac{x_1^3}{L^3} - 3\frac{x_1}{L} &+ 1 = 0 \ (x_1 \gt 0), \quad \frac{x_1^3}{L^3} - 3\frac{x_1}{L} - 1 = 0 \ (x_1 \lt 0) \quad &\text{(part (e); the second is the first with $x_1 \to -x_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{torque, symmetric equilibrium, cases } \gamma \le 1 \text{ and the cubic of the extreme values coincide with the key}}$$

Units: $[M_m] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: every result printed by the key is recovered, except the statement on the asymmetric equilibria (warning below).

Discrepancy with the official solution

The key says, for $\gamma$ above 1, that asymmetric equilibrium configurations also exist, with no condition. This solution finds that an asymmetric equilibrium must have $x_1x_2$ equal to $-L^2$ and $|x_1/L + L/x_1|$ equal to $c$, the fourth root of $4\kappa/(\gamma - 1)$; since $|u + 1/u|$ is never below 2, such configurations exist (distinct from the symmetric one) only for $\kappa$ above $4(\gamma - 1)$, the case in which the symmetric equilibrium lies beyond the abscissa $L$. For $\kappa$ at most $4(\gamma - 1)$ the only equilibrium is the symmetric one. Check: with $\gamma$ equal to 2 and $\kappa$ equal to 2, $c$ is the fourth root of 8, 1.68, below 2, so the quadratic for $u_1$ has no real root.

Limiting cases Law: the results at extreme values of the data Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6
$$\begin{aligned} \kappa \to 0:\quad x_1^2 &= \left[\frac{\kappa L^3}{4\left(\gamma - 1\right)}\right]^{2/3} \to 0 \quad &\text{(no repulsion: both particles at the vertex)} \\ \gamma \to 1^+:\quad x_1^2 &\to \infty \quad &\text{(the restoring term vanishes: nothing balances the repulsion)} \\ \omega \to 0:\quad N_{iy} &\to 0, \quad M_m \to 0 \quad &\text{(no Coriolis force and no torque without rotation)} \\ x_i = 0:\quad \mathbf t_i &= \mathbf i_1, \quad \mathbf n_i = \mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(at the vertex the wire is horizontal)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\kappa \to 0: \text{ equilibrium at the vertex}; \quad \gamma \to 1^+: \text{ equilibrium at infinity}; \quad \omega \to 0: \text{ no torque}}$$

Units: dimensionless

Meaning: each limit matches the physical picture: gravity pulls both particles to the vertex, the repulsion separates them and the rotation pushes them out.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf (PDF page 21); key on PDF page 75
Problem 34

Particle on a Circular Wire in an Oscillating Vertical Plane

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 22
Oscillating Plane + Euler ForceIn-Class Session 12Oscillations - Lecture 6 (part f)

A heavy point particle $P$ of mass $m$ slides without friction on a circular wire of center $C$ and radius $R$. The wire is located on a vertical plane $Oxy$ that rotates about the vertical axis $Oy$ with a prescribed angular frequency $\boldsymbol{\Omega}(t) = A\omega\sin(\omega t)\,\mathbf{j}$, where $A$ and $\omega$ are known positive constants, as shown in the figure. The angle that the vector $\overrightarrow{CP}$ makes with the $Ox$ axis is denoted $\varphi$.

Answer the following questions in a reasoned way:

  • (a)
    Write down the position, velocity and acceleration vectors of $P$ relative to the reference frame $Oxyz$, as a function of $\varphi$ and its derivatives.
  • (b)
    Identify the forces that act on $P$, and write down their mathematical expression for a generic instant of time $t$.
  • (c)
    Is the mechanical energy of $P$ conserved as seen from the $Oxy$ reference frame? Why?
  • (d)
    Write down a single second order differential equation to calculate $\varphi$ as a function of time. Note that you do not need to solve this equation.
  • (e)
    Compute the reaction of the wire on the particle $P$ as a function of $\varphi$, $\dot\varphi$ and $t$.
  • (f)
    Assume now that $A^2 \ll g/(R\omega^2)$ and that the motion of $P$ is such that $\varphi = \delta - \pi/2$ with $\delta \ll 1$. Around what value of $\delta$ does the particle oscillate? Are there any values of $\omega$ for which the approximation $\delta \ll 1$ will not hold?
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

A heavy particle $P$ of mass $m$ slides without friction on a circular wire of centre $C$ and radius $R$, in a vertical plane $Oxy$ that swings about the vertical axis $Oy$ with the prescribed angular velocity $A\omega\sin(\omega t)$ along $\mathbf j$ (Problems.pdf, p. 22). The statement asks for the relative position, velocity and acceleration, the forces, whether the mechanical energy seen from $Oxy$ is conserved, the equation of motion, the reaction, and the small oscillations about the lowest point. The wire is at rest in $Oxyz$, so the solution works there, with the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2 and the inertia forces of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$, $O$ on the rotation axis (fixed), $\mathbf j_0$ vertical, up, $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf i_0\times\mathbf j_0$
Moving frame$S_1 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_1\}$, the frame $Oxyz$ of the statement, attached to the plane of the wire: $\mathbf i_1$ along $Ox$, $\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf j_0$ along the axis, $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf i_1\times\mathbf j_1$ normal to the plane; it coincides with $S_0$ at $t = 0$
Wirecircle of centre $C$ on $Ox$ at distance $R$ from $O$ and radius $R$: it passes through $O$ (read from the figure)
Polar basis at $P$$\{\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\varphi, \mathbf k_1\}$: $\mathbf e_r$ from $C$ to $P$, $\mathbf e_\varphi$ tangent in the sense of growing $\varphi$
Coordinate$\varphi$, angle at $C$ from $Ox$ to $\overrightarrow{CP}$, counterclockwise towards $\mathbf j_1$
Angle of the plane$\psi(t)$, rotation of $S_1$ about $\mathbf j_0$, with rate $\Omega(t) = A\omega\sin\omega t$ and $\psi(0) = 0$
Constraints$z_1 = 0$ and the circle: two holonomic, smooth, bilateral constraints, fixed in $S_1$
Degrees of freedom3 minus 2: 1, the coordinate $\varphi(t)$ (the motion of the plane is prescribed)
Data$m$ [kg], $R$ [m], $g$ [m s$^{-2}$], $A$ [1], $\omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$]
Unknowns$\varphi(t)$; the reaction $\mathbf N = N_1\,\mathbf e_r + N_2\,\mathbf k_1$ (no tangential component: smooth wire)
Applied forcesweight $-mg\,\mathbf j_1$
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)Euler, centrifugal and Coriolis; no origin term ($O$ fixed) (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial; uniform gravity; smooth wire acting as a bead guide; the swing of the plane is imposed whatever the particle does

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Angle turned by the plane Law: angle as the time integral of the angular rate; substitution in the integral; Barrow's rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Problems.pdf, p. 22

The substitution $u$ equal to $\omega\tau$ has the differential $\omega\,d\tau$, and the limits 0 and $t$ become 0 and $\omega t$.

$$\begin{aligned} \psi(t) &= \psi(0) + \int_0^t A\omega\sin\left(\omega\tau\right)d\tau = 0 + A\int_0^{\omega t}\sin u\,du \quad &\text{(rate integrated; $u = \omega\tau$, $du = \omega\,d\tau$)} \\ &= A\left[-\cos u\right]_0^{\omega t} = A\left(-\cos\omega t + \cos 0\right) = A\left(1 - \cos\omega t\right) \quad &\text{(antiderivative; Barrow's rule)} \\ \dot\psi &= A\omega\sin\omega t = \Omega(t) \quad &\text{(check: chain rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\psi(t) = A\left(1 - \cos\omega t\right), \qquad 0 \le \psi \le 2A}$$

Units: $[A] = [\psi] = [1]$; $[A\omega] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: the plane swings back and forth between the angles 0 and $2A$; it does not spin.

Figure 1. View from $+y$, with $\mathbf j_0 = \mathbf j_1$ out of the paper ($\odot$): then $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf i_0\times\mathbf j_0$ points down the page. $\mathbf i_1, \mathbf k_1$ are $\mathbf i_0, \mathbf k_0$ turned counter-clockwise by $\psi(t) = A(1 - \cos\omega t)$; the legs of $\mathbf i_1$ are $\cos\psi$ along $\mathbf i_0$ and $\sin\psi$ along $-\mathbf k_0$ (up the page), hence $\mathbf i_1 = \cos\psi\,\mathbf i_0 - \sin\psi\,\mathbf k_0$. The plane swings between $\psi = 0$ and $\psi = 2A$ (dotted).
Basis of the swinging plane: rotation by psi about j0 Law: elementary rotation about the second axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.19; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

View from above, along $\mathbf j_0$, which points out of the paper (⊙). With $\mathbf i_0$ to the right, $\mathbf k_0$, the cross product of $\mathbf i_0$ and $\mathbf j_0$, points down the page (fingers from $\mathbf i_0$, to the right, towards $\mathbf j_0$, towards the reader; the thumb goes down the page), so minus $\mathbf k_0$ points up the page. A positive $\psi$ is counterclockwise in this view. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\psi$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\psi$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\psi$ up the page, along minus $\mathbf k_0$ (the minus sign). $\mathbf k_1$ is $\mathbf k_0$ turned by the same angle: adjacent leg $\cos\psi$ along $\mathbf k_0$, opposite leg $\sin\psi$ along plus $\mathbf i_0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\psi\,\mathbf i_0 - \sin\psi\,\mathbf k_0, \quad \mathbf j_1 = \mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \sin\psi\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\psi\,\mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles; axis)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\psi\cos\psi - \sin\psi\left(-\sin\psi\right)\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the second row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{2+2}$)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\psi + \sin^2\psi = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{13} = -\cos\psi\sin\psi + \sin\psi\cos\psi = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\psi & 0 & \sin\psi \cr 0 & 1 & 0 \cr -\sin\psi & 0 & \cos\psi \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: $[\psi] = [1]$

Meaning: the matrix of Eq. 1.19 with the angle $\psi$; the vertical, and with it the weight, is the same in both frames.

Figure 2. Plane $Oxy$, fixed in $S_1$ ($\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf i_1\times\mathbf j_1$ points out of the paper, $\odot$). $\overrightarrow{OC} = R\,\mathbf i_1$; in the shaded right triangle $CFP$ the hypotenuse is $|CP| = R$, the leg adjacent to $\varphi$ is $R\cos\varphi$ (along $\mathbf i_1$) and the opposite leg is $R\sin\varphi$ (along $\mathbf j_1$). The distance from $P$ to the rotation axis $Oy$ is $R(1 + \cos\varphi)$. $\mathbf i_1, \mathbf j_1$ in blue, $\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\varphi$ in orange.
Position vector and polar basis in the plane of the wire Law: position through the centre of the circle; right triangle; polar basis and its derivatives Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.24; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.25; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.26; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 22

The plane $Oxy$, fixed in $S_1$, is drawn with $\mathbf i_1$ to the right and $\mathbf j_1$ up, so $\mathbf k_1$ points out of the paper (⊙). From $O$ to $P$ the path goes through $C$, because the distance from $C$ is the constant one. Let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the $x$ axis: in the shaded right triangle $CFP$ (right angle at $F$) the hypotenuse is $CP$, of length $R$, the leg adjacent to $\varphi$ is $CF$, of length $R\cos\varphi$, along $\mathbf i_1$, and the opposite leg $FP$, of length $R\sin\varphi$, is along $\mathbf j_1$. The angle is measured from $\mathbf i_1$ counterclockwise towards $\mathbf j_1$: it is already the standard polar angle about $C$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_1^P &= \overrightarrow{OC} + \overrightarrow{CP} = R\,\mathbf i_1 + R\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + R\sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1 = R\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\mathbf i_1 + R\sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(the two legs)} \\ \mathbf e_r &= \frac{\overrightarrow{CP}}{R} = \cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf e_\varphi = \frac{d\mathbf e_r}{d\varphi} = -\sin\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 2.24)} \\ \frac{d\mathbf e_\varphi}{d\varphi} &= -\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 - \sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1 = -\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(derivative of each component)} \\ \mathbf e_r\times\mathbf e_\varphi &= \cos^2\varphi\,\mathbf i_1\times\mathbf j_1 - \sin^2\varphi\,\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \left(\cos^2\varphi + \sin^2\varphi\right)\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf i_1\times\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf k_1$, $\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf i_1 = -\mathbf k_1$)} \\ x_1^P &= R\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right) \ge 0 \quad &\text{(distance from $P$ to the axis $Oy$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^P = R\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\mathbf i_1 + R\sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf e_r = \cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf e_\varphi = -\sin\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[R(1 + \cos\varphi)] = [R\sin\varphi] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: at an angle of $\pi$ the particle is at $O$, on the axis; at minus a quarter turn it is at the lowest point of the wire. The abscissa is the lever arm of the centrifugal and Euler forces.

Kinematics

Motion of the swinging frame and derivatives of its unit vectors Law: angular velocity of a simple rotation; angular acceleration; derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \dot\psi\,\mathbf j_1 = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1 = A\omega\sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf v_0^O = \mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(simple rotation about the fixed vertical; $O$ on the axis)} \\ \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} &= \left.\frac{d\boldsymbol\omega_{10}}{dt}\right|_0 = \dot\Omega\,\mathbf j_1 = A\omega^2\cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.9; $\mathbf j_1$ fixed; chain rule)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf i_1 = -\Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf k_1 = \Omega\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 to 3.5)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\cos\psi\,\mathbf i_0 - \sin\psi\,\mathbf k_0\right) &= -\dot\psi\sin\psi\,\mathbf i_0 - \dot\psi\cos\psi\,\mathbf k_0 = -\Omega\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(check: chain rule on the components of $\mathbf i_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10} = A\omega\sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = A\omega^2\cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf i_1}$$

Units: $[A\omega] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$; $[A\omega^2] = [\mathrm{T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the rate of the plane changes in time, so an Euler term appears; the angular acceleration is parallel to the angular velocity, both along the fixed axis.

(a) Relative position, velocity and acceleration

Relative velocity and relative acceleration Law: time derivatives in $S_1$, where $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$ are constant; chain rule and product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.25; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.26; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24; Problems.pdf, p. 22
$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dt}\cos\varphi &= -\sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi, \quad \frac{d}{dt}\sin\varphi = \cos\varphi\,\dot\varphi \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \mathbf v_1^P &= -R\sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + R\cos\varphi\,\dot\varphi\,\mathbf j_1 = R\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi \quad &\text{(components differentiated; Eq. 3.19)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\varphi}{dt}\right|_1 &= \frac{d\mathbf e_\varphi}{d\varphi}\,\dot\varphi = -\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P &= \left.\frac{d}{dt}\left(R\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi\right)\right|_1 = R\ddot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi + R\dot\varphi\left(-\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_r\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; Eq. 3.24)} \\ &= -R\left(\ddot\varphi\sin\varphi + \dot\varphi^2\cos\varphi\right)\mathbf i_1 + R\left(\ddot\varphi\cos\varphi - \dot\varphi^2\sin\varphi\right)\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(in $\mathcal B_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^P = R\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\mathbf i_1 + R\sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf v_1^P = R\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi, \quad \mathbf a_1^P = R\ddot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi - R\dot\varphi^2\,\mathbf e_r}$$

Units: $[R\dot\varphi] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[R\ddot\varphi] = [R\dot\varphi^2] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: circular motion about $C$ seen in the plane: tangential acceleration and centripetal acceleration towards $C$.

Absolute acceleration: Euler, centripetal and Coriolis terms Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the position written in the swinging basis; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]

Write the position as $x\,\mathbf i_1 + y\,\mathbf j_1$, with $x$ and $y$ the two components of the boxed position; the time derivatives of $x$ and $y$ are the components of the relative velocity.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P &= \dot x\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y\,\mathbf j_1 + x\left(-\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\right) = \mathbf v_1^P - \Omega x\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; derivative of $\mathbf i_1$; $\mathbf j_1$ constant)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1^P}{dt}\right|_0 &= \mathbf a_1^P + \dot x\left(-\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; the turning of $\mathbf i_1$ inside $\mathbf v_1^P$)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left(-\Omega x\,\mathbf k_1\right) &= -\dot\Omega x\,\mathbf k_1 - \Omega\dot x\,\mathbf k_1 - \Omega x\,\Omega\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(product rule on three factors; derivative of $\mathbf k_1$)} \\ \boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P &= \dot\Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\left(x\,\mathbf i_1 + y\,\mathbf j_1\right) = -\dot\Omega x\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(the $\dot\Omega$ term: Euler)} \\ 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P &= 2\Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\left(\dot x\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y\,\mathbf j_1\right) = -2\Omega\dot x\,\mathbf k_1 = 2\Omega R\sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(the two $\Omega\dot x$ terms: Coriolis; $\dot x = -R\sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi$)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) &= \Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\left(-\Omega x\,\mathbf k_1\right) = -\Omega^2x\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(the $\mathbf i_1$ term: centripetal)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_0^P = \mathbf a_1^P - \dot\Omega R\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\mathbf k_1 - \Omega^2R\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\mathbf i_1 + 2\Omega R\sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi\,\mathbf k_1}$$

Units: $[\dot\Omega R] = [\Omega^2R] = [\Omega R\dot\varphi] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the Euler and Coriolis terms are normal to the plane of the wire; the centripetal term points horizontally to the axis.

Forces and Equations of Motion

Figure 3. Forces on $P$ in $Oxyz$. In the plane of the wire: the weight, the reaction $N_1\,\mathbf e_r$ and the centrifugal force along $\mathbf i_1$ (dashed). Seen from above: the Euler and Coriolis forces (dashed), both along $\mathbf k_1$, balanced by the normal reaction $N_2\,\mathbf k_1$.

(b) Forces acting on P

Actual and inertia forces on the particle Law: weight; smooth reaction normal to the tangent; inertia forces of a non-inertial frame Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.16; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; Problems.pdf, p. 22
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf W &= -mg\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(weight; $\mathbf j_1$ is the vertical)} \\ \mathbf N &= N_1\,\mathbf e_r + N_2\,\mathbf k_1 = N_1\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + N_1\sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1 + N_2\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(smooth wire: no component along $\mathbf e_\varphi$)} \\ \mathbf F_A &= -m\,\mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{($O$ fixed)} \\ \mathbf F_E &= -m\,\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P = mA\omega^2R\cos\omega t\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Euler: composition box times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_C &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) = mA^2\omega^2R\sin^2\omega t\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(centrifugal; $\Omega^2 = A^2\omega^2\sin^2\omega t$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR} &= -2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P = -2mA\omega R\sin\omega t\sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Coriolis: composition box times $-m$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf W = -mg\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf N = N_1\,\mathbf e_r + N_2\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf F_C = mA^2\omega^2R\sin^2\omega t\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\mathbf i_1, \cr \mathbf F_E = mA\omega^2R\cos\omega t\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf F_{COR} = -2mA\omega R\sin\omega t\sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi\,\mathbf k_1 \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[mg] = [mA^2\omega^2R] = [mA\omega^2R] = [mA\omega R\dot\varphi] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: two actual forces (weight and reaction) and three inertia forces: the centrifugal force lies in the plane and pushes away from the axis; the Euler and Coriolis forces are normal to the plane.

Projections of Newton's second law on the polar basis Law: Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame, projected on $\{\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\varphi, \mathbf k_1\}$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.17; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]

The projections of $\mathbf i_1$ on $\mathbf e_r$ and $\mathbf e_\varphi$ are the cosine and minus the sine; those of $\mathbf j_1$ are the sine and the cosine.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_\varphi:\ mR\ddot\varphi &= -mg\cos\varphi - mA^2\omega^2R\sin^2\omega t\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\sin\varphi \quad &\text{(weight and centrifugal; the reaction and the $\mathbf k_1$ forces drop out)} \\ \mathbf e_r:\ -mR\dot\varphi^2 &= N_1 - mg\sin\varphi + mA^2\omega^2R\sin^2\omega t\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\cos\varphi \quad &\text{(radial)} \\ \mathbf k_1:\ 0 &= N_2 + mA\omega^2R\cos\omega t\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right) - 2mA\omega R\sin\omega t\sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi \quad &\text{(normal to the plane)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{three scalar equations for the three unknowns } \varphi,\ N_1,\ N_2}$$

Units: every term $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: only the tangential equation is free of the reaction; it is the equation of motion of part (d). The other two give the reaction of part (e).

(d) Equation of motion

Single second-order equation for phi Law: tangential component of Newton's second law in $S_1$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Problems.pdf, p. 22
$$\begin{aligned} mR\ddot\varphi + mg\cos\varphi + mA^2\omega^2R\sin^2\omega t\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\sin\varphi &= 0 \quad &\text{(tangential equation, all terms on the left)} \\ \ddot\varphi + \frac{g}{R}\cos\varphi + A^2\omega^2\sin^2\omega t\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\sin\varphi &= 0 \quad &\text{(divided by $mR$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\ddot\varphi + \frac{g}{R}\cos\varphi + A^2\omega^2\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\sin^2\left(\omega t\right)\sin\varphi = 0}$$

Units: $[\ddot\varphi] = [g/R] = [A^2\omega^2] = [\mathrm{T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: a nonlinear pendulum about the lowest point whose coefficient changes periodically in time: the swing of the plane enters only through the centrifugal force.

(e) Reaction of the wire

Components of the reaction Law: radial and normal components of Newton's second law in $S_1$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.18; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.19; Problems.pdf, p. 22
$$\begin{aligned} N_1 &= mg\sin\varphi - mA^2\omega^2R\sin^2\omega t\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\cos\varphi - mR\dot\varphi^2 \quad &\text{(radial equation solved for $N_1$; Eq. 6.18)} \\ N_2 &= 2mA\omega R\sin\omega t\sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi - mA\omega^2R\cos\omega t\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right) \quad &\text{(normal equation solved for $N_2$; Eq. 6.19)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf N = N_1\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + N_1\sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1 + N_2\,\mathbf k_1, \cr N_1 = mg\sin\varphi - mA^2R\omega^2\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\sin^2\left(\omega t\right)\cos\varphi - mR\dot\varphi^2, \cr N_2 = 2mAR\omega\,\dot\varphi\sin\varphi\sin\left(\omega t\right) - mAR\omega^2\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\cos\left(\omega t\right) \end{gathered}}$$

Units: every term $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the normal component is the push the wire must give to carry the particle with the swinging plane: it balances the Euler and Coriolis forces. It depends on time even at rest in the plane, through the Euler term.

Answers and Checks

(c) Is the mechanical energy conserved in Oxy?

Power of each force in the swinging frame Law: power of each force on the relative velocity; potential of the centrifugal force; time derivative of the energy along the motion Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.29; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]

The reaction, the Euler force and the Coriolis force do no work in $S_1$ (the wire is at rest there; the last two are normal to the plane that holds the relative velocity). The weight has the potential $mgR\sin\varphi$. The centrifugal force has, at each instant, the potential minus one half of $m\Omega^2$ times the squared distance to the axis, but this potential depends explicitly on time because $\Omega$ does. Write $E_1^P$ for the kinetic energy in $S_1$ plus these two potentials.

$$\begin{aligned} \left(\mathbf N + \mathbf F_E + \mathbf F_{COR}\right)\cdot\mathbf v_1^P &= \left(N_1\,\mathbf e_r + \left(N_2 + F_{E} + F_{COR}\right)\mathbf k_1\right)\cdot R\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi = 0 \quad &\text{(no power)} \\ E_1^P &= \tfrac12 mR^2\dot\varphi^2 + mgR\sin\varphi - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2R^2\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)^2 \quad &\text{(kinetic plus the two potentials)} \\ \frac{dE_1^P}{dt} &= mR^2\dot\varphi\ddot\varphi + mgR\cos\varphi\,\dot\varphi + m\Omega^2R^2\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi - m\Omega\dot\Omega R^2\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)^2 \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule on each factor)} \\ &= mR^2\dot\varphi\left[\ddot\varphi + \frac{g}{R}\cos\varphi + \Omega^2\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\sin\varphi\right] - m\Omega\dot\Omega R^2\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)^2 \quad &\text{(first three terms grouped)} \\ &= -m\Omega\dot\Omega R^2\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)^2 = -mA^2\omega^3R^2\sin\omega t\cos\omega t\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)^2 \quad &\text{(bracket zero by part (d); $\Omega\dot\Omega$ substituted)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\frac{dE_1^P}{dt} = -mA^2\omega^3R^2\sin\left(\omega t\right)\cos\left(\omega t\right)\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)^2 \ne 0: \ \text{not conserved}}$$

Units: $[mA^2\omega^3R^2] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-3}}]$, a power

Meaning: no. The rate of the plane is not constant, so the centrifugal force has no potential independent of time, and the energy changes at the rate of the explicit time derivative of that potential. With a constant rate the energy would be conserved: the Euler force would vanish and the Coriolis force does no work. The energy in $S_0$ is not conserved either: there the wire moves and its normal reaction works.

(f) Small oscillations about the lowest point

Linearised equation about the lowest point Law: Taylor expansion to first order about the equilibrium; neglect of the small parametric term Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.46; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.32; Problems.pdf, p. 22

With $\varphi$ equal to $\delta$ minus a quarter turn, the difference formulas give the cosine and the sine of $\varphi$; then the first-order Taylor expansions in $\delta$ are kept. The hypothesis on $A$ makes the product of $A^2\omega^2$ and $\delta$ small against $g/R$ times $\delta$.

$$\begin{aligned} \cos\varphi &= \cos\delta\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2} + \sin\delta\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} = \sin\delta \simeq \delta \quad &\text{(difference formula; Taylor)} \\ \sin\varphi &= \sin\delta\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2} - \cos\delta\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} = -\cos\delta \simeq -1 \quad &\text{(difference formula; Taylor, error of order $\delta^2$)} \\ \ddot\varphi &= \ddot\delta \quad &\text{(the quarter turn is constant)} \\ \ddot\delta + \frac{g}{R}\delta - A^2\omega^2\sin^2\omega t\left(1 + \delta\right) &= 0 \quad &\text{(part (d), first order in $\delta$)} \\ A^2\omega^2\sin^2\omega t\,\delta &\ll \frac{g}{R}\delta \quad &\text{(hypothesis $A^2 \ll g/(R\omega^2)$: term dropped)} \\ \sin^2\omega t &= \tfrac12\left(1 - \cos 2\omega t\right) \quad &\text{(double-angle identity)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\ddot\delta + \frac{g}{R}\delta = \frac{A^2\omega^2}{2}\left[1 - \cos\left(2\omega t\right)\right]}$$

Units: $[g\delta/R] = [A^2\omega^2] = [\mathrm{T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: a harmonic oscillator of natural frequency the square root of $g/R$, driven by a constant push and a push at twice the frequency of the swing; both come from the mean and the oscillating part of the centrifugal force.

Solution: mean position and the frequency of breakdown Law: general solution of the forced undamped oscillator as homogeneous plus particular solution; resonance Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.6; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.32; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.41; Notes.pdf, Sec. 5.4

Write $\omega_n$ for the square root of $g/R$. A particular solution is a constant $\delta_0$ plus a term $D_1\cos 2\omega t$; the second derivative of that term is written before it is substituted.

$$\begin{aligned} \omega_n^2\delta_0 &= \frac{A^2\omega^2}{2} \;\Rightarrow\; \delta_0 = \frac{A^2\omega^2}{2\omega_n^2} = \frac{A^2R\omega^2}{2g} \quad &\text{(constant part)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(D_1\cos 2\omega t\right) &= -2\omega D_1\sin 2\omega t, \quad \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\left(D_1\cos 2\omega t\right) = -4\omega^2D_1\cos 2\omega t \quad &\text{(chain rule, twice)} \\ \left(\omega_n^2 - 4\omega^2\right)D_1 &= -\frac{A^2\omega^2}{2} \;\Rightarrow\; D_1 = -\frac{A^2\omega^2}{2\left(\omega_n^2 - 4\omega^2\right)} \quad &\text{(oscillating part, $2\omega \ne \omega_n$)} \\ \delta(t) &= \delta_0 + D_1\cos 2\omega t + a\cos\omega_nt + b\sin\omega_nt \quad &\text{(Eq. 5.7 for the homogeneous part; $a$, $b$ from the initial conditions)} \\ 2\omega = \omega_n:\quad \delta_p &= K\,t\sin\omega_nt, \quad \ddot\delta_p = 2K\omega_n\cos\omega_nt - K\omega_n^2t\sin\omega_nt \quad &\text{(trial at exact resonance; product rule)} \\ \ddot\delta_p + \omega_n^2\delta_p &= 2K\omega_n\cos\omega_nt = -\frac{A^2\omega^2}{2}\cos\omega_nt \;\Rightarrow\; K = -\frac{A^2\omega^2}{4\omega_n} \quad &\text{(amplitude growing linearly in time)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\delta \text{ oscillates about } \delta_0 = \frac{A^2R\omega^2}{2g} \text{ with } \omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{g}{R}}; \qquad \delta \ll 1 \text{ fails near } 2\omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{R}}}$$

Units: $[\delta_0] = [A^2R\omega^2/g] = [1]$; $[\omega_n] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: the mean position is shifted outward, away from the axis, by the mean centrifugal force, and the shift is small precisely because of the hypothesis on $A$. When twice the swing frequency approaches the natural frequency the forced amplitude grows without bound (no damping), so the small-angle hypothesis breaks down.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Position, velocity, acceleration$\mathbf r_1^P = R(1 + \cos\varphi)\,\mathbf i_1 + R\sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf v_1^P = R\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi$, $\mathbf a_1^P = R\ddot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi - R\dot\varphi^2\,\mathbf e_r$, with $\mathbf e_r = \cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf e_\varphi = -\sin\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf j_1$
(b) Forcesweight $-mg\,\mathbf j_1$; reaction $N_1\mathbf e_r + N_2\mathbf k_1$; $\mathbf F_A = \mathbf 0$; Euler $mA\omega^2R\cos\omega t(1 + \cos\varphi)\,\mathbf k_1$; centrifugal $mA^2\omega^2R\sin^2\omega t(1 + \cos\varphi)\,\mathbf i_1$; Coriolis $-2mA\omega R\sin\omega t\sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi\,\mathbf k_1$
(c) Energy in $Oxy$not conserved: the centrifugal potential depends explicitly on time; $dE_1^P/dt = -mA^2\omega^3R^2\sin\omega t\cos\omega t(1 + \cos\varphi)^2$
(d) Equation of motion$\ddot\varphi + (g/R)\cos\varphi + A^2\omega^2(1 + \cos\varphi)\sin^2(\omega t)\sin\varphi = 0$
(e) Reaction$\mathbf N = N_1\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + N_1\sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1 + N_2\mathbf k_1$, $N_1 = mg\sin\varphi - mA^2R\omega^2(1 + \cos\varphi)\sin^2(\omega t)\cos\varphi - mR\dot\varphi^2$, $N_2 = 2mAR\omega\dot\varphi\sin\varphi\sin(\omega t) - mAR\omega^2(1 + \cos\varphi)\cos(\omega t)$
(f) Oscillation$\ddot\delta + (g/R)\delta = \frac{A^2\omega^2}{2}[1 - \cos 2\omega t]$; oscillation about $\delta_0 = A^2R\omega^2/(2g)$ with $\omega_n = \sqrt{g/R}$; the approximation fails near $\omega = \frac12\sqrt{g/R}$ (resonance)

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 75 prints the equation of motion, the reaction with the components $N_1$ and $N_2$, the linearised equation, the centre of oscillation, the natural frequency and the resonance condition. All coincide with parts (d), (e) and (f), term by term (box below).

Comparison with the official key Law: term-by-term comparison Source: Problems.pdf, p. 75
$$\begin{aligned} \text{key: } \ddot\varphi + \frac{g\cos\varphi}{R} + A^2\omega^2\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\sin^2\left(\omega t\right)\sin\varphi &= 0 \quad &\text{(part (d))} \\ \text{key: } \mathbf N = N_1\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i + N_1\sin\varphi\,\mathbf j + N_2\,\mathbf k&, \text{ with the same } N_1,\ N_2 \quad &\text{(part (e); the key's $\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k$ are $\mathcal B_1$)} \\ \text{key: } \ddot\delta + \frac{g}{R}\delta = \frac{A^2\omega^2}{2}\left[1 - \cos\left(2\omega t\right)\right]&, \quad \delta_0 = \frac{A^2R\omega^2}{2g}, \quad \omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{g}{R}}, \quad 2\omega \simeq \omega_n \quad &\text{(part (f))} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{equation of motion, reaction and small oscillations coincide with the key}}$$

Units: as in parts (d) to (f)

Meaning: no discrepancy.

Independent check: angular momentum about the vertical axis Law: angular momentum about the fixed point $O$ and its rate, equal to the moment of the actual forces Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.48; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.53

In $\mathcal B_1$ the position has the components $(x, y, 0)$ and the absolute velocity $(\dot x, \dot y, -\Omega x)$ (composition box). The component along $\mathbf j_1$ of a vector product is the third component of the first factor times the first of the second minus the first of the first times the third of the second. The weight and the in-plane reaction lie in the plane, which contains the axis: no axial moment.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf H_{O,0}\cdot\mathbf j_1 &= m\left(0\cdot\dot x - x\left(-\Omega x\right)\right) = m\Omega x^2 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.48)} \\ \mathbf M_O\cdot\mathbf j_1 &= 0\cdot N_x - x\,N_2 = -xN_2 \quad &\text{(only $N_2\,\mathbf k_1$ at the lever arm $x$)} \\ m\dot\Omega x^2 + 2m\Omega x\dot x &= -xN_2 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.53; product rule and chain rule)} \\ N_2 &= -m\dot\Omega x - 2m\Omega\dot x = -mA\omega^2\cos\omega t\,R\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right) + 2mA\omega\sin\omega t\,R\sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi \quad &\text{(divided by $-x$; $\dot x = -R\sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{N_2 = 2mAR\omega\,\dot\varphi\sin\varphi\sin\omega t - mAR\omega^2\left(1 + \cos\varphi\right)\cos\omega t \quad (x \ne 0)}$$

Units: $[xN_2] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the same normal reaction as part (e), found without inertia forces.

Limiting cases Law: the results at extreme values of the data Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.38; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63
$$\begin{aligned} A \to 0:\quad \ddot\varphi + \frac{g}{R}\cos\varphi &= 0, \quad N_2 = 0 \quad &\text{(pendulum in a fixed plane, about the lowest point)} \\ A \to 0:\quad \delta_0 &\to 0 \quad &\text{(no outward shift without swing)} \\ \omega \to 0,\ A \text{ fixed}:\quad \Omega &\to 0, \quad \dot\Omega \to 0 \quad &\text{(the same pendulum)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{A \to 0 \text{ or } \omega \to 0: \text{ simple pendulum in a fixed vertical plane, } N_2 \to 0}$$

Units: dimensionless

Meaning: without the swing of the plane the inertia forces vanish and the particle is a pendulum on a fixed circle.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf (PDF page 22); key on PDF page 75
Problem 36

Pendulum String Dragged by a Rotating Bar

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 24
Rotating Frame + String Constraint

A heavy point particle $P$ with mass $m$ hanging from a fixed point $A$ on the ceiling with a massless string of constant length $L$. The particle is initially at rest. A bar $b$ rotates about its center $O$ in a horizontal plane at a distance $h$ from the ceiling, with a known, constant angular velocity $\omega$. The horizontal distance between $O$ and $A$ is $R$. At time $t = 0$, the bar collides with the string and drags it along its motion. The string slides over the bar without friction. We call $C$ the instantaneous point of contact of the string with the bar. We define a reference frame $S_1$ that rotates with the bar as shown in the figure. We call $\xi$ the distance between $O$ and $C$; $\ell$ the length of the string segment between $C$ and $P$; $\theta$ the angle between the vertical plane $Ox_1z_1$ and the plane defined by the bar and $P$; and $\varphi$ the angle formed between the string segment $CP$ and the bar. You are asked to study only the part of the motion in which the string remains tense and in contact with the bar.

  • (a)
    Write down the position and velocity of point $A$ in $S_1$ as a function of time.
  • (b)
    Obtain a general expression for the position, velocity, and acceleration of $P$ in $S_1$ as a function of $\xi$, $\ell$, $\theta$, $\varphi$, their derivatives, and time.
  • (c)
    Express $AC$, $\ell$, and $\varphi$ as a function of $\xi$ and time.
  • (d)
    Identify and express all the forces acting on $P$.
  • (e)
    Write down a set of second order differential equations for the evolution of the unknowns of the problem.
  • (f)
    Compute the initial conditions for the previous equations at $t = 0$.
  • (g)
    Is the mechanical energy of the particle conserved in time? Justify your answer.
  • (h)
    If/when the string separates from the bar, express the geometric condition as a relation between $\theta$ and and [sic] time.
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

A heavy particle $P$ of mass $m$ hangs at rest from the ceiling point $A$ by a string of length $L$. A bar turning at the constant rate $\omega$ about the vertical through its centre $O$, in a horizontal plane a distance $h$ below the ceiling, hits the string at the start and drags it; the string slides on the bar without friction, over the contact point $C$ (Problems.pdf, p. 24). The statement asks for the position and velocity of $A$ in the bar frame $S_1$, the position, velocity and acceleration of $P$ there, the length $AC$, $\ell$ and $\varphi$ in terms of $\xi$ and time, the forces on $P$, the equations of motion, their initial conditions, whether the energy is conserved, and the condition of separation. The bar is at rest in $S_1$, so the solution works there, with the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2 and the inertia forces of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$, $O$ the centre of the bar (fixed), $\mathbf k_0$ vertical, up, $\mathbf i_0$ horizontal from $O$ towards the point $A'$ of the plane of the bar directly below $A$
Moving frame$S_1 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_1\}$, attached to the bar: $\mathbf i_1$ along the bar, $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$, $\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1$; at $t = 0$ the bar lies along $\mathbf i_0$ (it hits the string at that instant), so $S_1$ coincides with $S_0$ then
Sense of rotationread from the left drawing: before the impact $A'$ lies at positive $x_1$ and positive $y_1$, so the bar turns from $\mathbf i_1$ towards $\mathbf j_1$: angular velocity $+\omega\,\mathbf k_1$ (the Coriolis force of the key implies the same sign)
String basis$\mathcal B_2 = \{\mathbf e_{CP}, \mathbf e_\theta, \mathbf e_\varphi\}$, with $\mathbf e_{CP}$ from $C$ to $P$ (deduced below)
Coordinates$\xi$ (distance $OC$ along the bar), $\ell$ (length $CP$), $\theta$ (angle between the vertical plane $Ox_1z_1$ and the plane bar–$P$, from the downward vertical; positive towards negative $y_1$, the sign of the key), $\varphi$ (angle between $\overrightarrow{CP}$ and the bar, in $(0, \pi)$)
Constraintsconstant string length, $AC + \ell = L$; frictionless contact (equal angles of the two segments with the bar, part (c)); string tense and in contact with the bar (the stage studied)
Degrees of freedomthe particle moves in space with one constraint (the string), so 3 minus 1: 2, taken as $\xi(t)$ and $\theta(t)$; $\ell$ and $\varphi$ are functions of $\xi$ and $t$ (part (c))
Data$m$ [kg], $L$ [m], $h$ [m], $R$ [m] (horizontal distance $OA$), $\omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$], $g$ [m s$^{-2}$]
Auxiliary symbol$D$, the length $AC$ [m]
Unknowns$\xi(t)$, $\theta(t)$ and the tension $T(t) \gt 0$
Applied forcesweight $-mg\,\mathbf k_1$; string pull $-T\,\mathbf e_{CP}$ (the bar touches the string, not $P$)
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)centrifugal and Coriolis; no origin or Euler terms ($O$ fixed, $\omega$ constant) (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial; uniform gravity; massless inextensible string; thin bar, long enough for $C$ to stay on it; no friction at $C$; $\omega$ imposed whatever the string does; $L \gt h$
Readings(1) "Separates" (part (h)) is read as the string straightening, so that the bar no longer bends it; the other way to lose contact, $C$ sliding off the end of the bar, is the condition that $\xi$ reaches the half-length of the bar, not a relation between $\theta$ and time. (2) No impulse at the impact: the string is perpendicular to the bar there, so its path length changes only to second order (part (f))

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. View from $+z_0$, with $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf k_1$ out of the paper ($\odot$), so $\mathbf j_0 = \mathbf k_0\times\mathbf i_0$ points up. $\mathbf i_1, \mathbf j_1$ are $\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0$ turned counter-clockwise by $\omega t$. $\mathbf i_1$ has legs $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$ and $\sin\omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$; $\mathbf j_1$ has legs $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$ and $\sin\omega t$ along $-\mathbf i_0$, hence its minus sign. The bar lies along $\mathbf i_1$.
Basis of the bar: rotation by omega t about k0 Law: elementary rotation about the third axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

View from above, along $\mathbf k_0$, which points out of the paper (⊙). With $\mathbf i_0$ to the right, $\mathbf j_0$, the cross product of $\mathbf k_0$ and $\mathbf i_0$, points up the page (thumb towards the reader, the fingers turn $\mathbf i_0$ counterclockwise by a quarter turn). The bar turns counterclockwise. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\omega t$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ along plus $\mathbf j_0$. $\mathbf j_1$ is $\mathbf j_0$ turned by the same angle; the counterclockwise turn carries its tip to the left, so its opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ lies along minus $\mathbf i_0$ (the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf j_1 = -\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles; axis)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\omega t\cos\omega t - \left(-\sin\omega t\right)\sin\omega t\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{3+3}$)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\omega t + \sin^2\omega t = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{12} = -\cos\omega t\sin\omega t + \sin\omega t\cos\omega t = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\omega t & -\sin\omega t & 0 \cr \sin\omega t & \cos\omega t & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: $[\omega t] = [1]$

Meaning: the matrix of Eq. 1.20 with the angle $\omega t$; the vertical is common to both frames.

Figure 2. Same view from $+z_0$. $A'$ is the point of the plane of the bar directly below the anchor $A$, at distance $R$ from $O$ along $\mathbf i_0$, that is $\omega t$ behind the bar. In the shaded right triangle $OFA'$ the hypotenuse is $R$, the leg along the bar is $R\cos\omega t$ and the leg $FA'$, parallel to $-\mathbf j_1$, is $R\sin\omega t$.
Position of the anchor A in S1 Law: right triangle in the plane of the bar; components through the transposed matrix Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.12; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Problems.pdf, p. 24

In the same view, $A'$ is at the distance $R$ from $O$ along $\mathbf i_0$, that is, the angle $\omega t$ behind the bar (clockwise from $\mathbf i_1$). Let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A'$ to the line of the bar: in the right triangle $OFA'$ (right angle at $F$) the hypotenuse is $OA'$, of length $R$; the leg adjacent to $\omega t$, $OF$, has length $R\cos\omega t$ along plus $\mathbf i_1$; the opposite leg $FA'$ has length $R\sin\omega t$ along minus $\mathbf j_1$, because $A'$ lies on the clockwise side of the bar. $A$ is a height $h$ above $A'$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_1^A &= \overrightarrow{OF} + \overrightarrow{FA'} + \overrightarrow{A'A} = R\cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_1 - R\sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_1 + h\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(the legs, with their directions)} \\ [{}_0R_1]^T\begin{pmatrix} R \cr 0 \cr h \end{pmatrix} &= \begin{pmatrix} \cos\omega t\cdot R + \sin\omega t\cdot 0 + 0\cdot h \cr -\sin\omega t\cdot R + \cos\omega t\cdot 0 + 0\cdot h \cr 0 + 0 + 1\cdot h \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} R\cos\omega t \cr -R\sin\omega t \cr h \end{pmatrix} \quad &\text{(check: Eq. 1.14, rows of the transpose times $\mathbf r_0^A$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^A = R\cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_1 - R\sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_1 + h\,\mathbf k_1}$$

Units: $[R\cos\omega t] = [h] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: seen from the bar, the anchor turns backwards on a circle of radius $R$ at the height $h$.

Figure 3. View along the bar, with $\mathbf i_1$ out of the paper ($\odot$) at $C$, so $\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1$ points right. The plane bar–$P$ is seen edge-on, at the angle $\theta$ from the downward vertical $-\mathbf k_1$. Its unit vector $\mathbf u$ is the hypotenuse of the shaded triangle: leg $\cos\theta$ along $-\mathbf k_1$ and leg $\sin\theta$ along $-\mathbf j_1$; $\mathbf e_\theta = d\mathbf u/d\theta$ is perpendicular to it.
Plane bar–P: rotation by theta about the bar Law: right triangle in the view along the bar; derivative of a unit vector with respect to its angle; relation with the standard azimuth Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.18; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.24; Problems.pdf, p. 24

View along the bar, with $\mathbf i_1$ out of the paper (⊙) at $C$ and $\mathbf k_1$ up; then $\mathbf j_1$, the cross product of $\mathbf k_1$ and $\mathbf i_1$, points to the right (fingers from $\mathbf k_1$, up, towards $\mathbf i_1$, towards the reader; the thumb points right). The plane bar–$P$ contains the line of sight, so it is seen as a line through $C$, at the angle $\theta$ from the downward vertical, towards the left (negative $y_1$) for positive $\theta$. Its unit vector $\mathbf u$, from $C$ towards the side of $P$, is the hypotenuse of the shaded right triangle: adjacent leg $\cos\theta$ along minus $\mathbf k_1$, opposite leg $\sin\theta$ along minus $\mathbf j_1$ (both minus signs: down and to the left). The standard azimuth $\chi$ about $\mathbf i_1$ is measured from $\mathbf j_1$ towards $\mathbf k_1$; $\theta$ is measured from minus $\mathbf k_1$ in the opposite sense, so $\chi$ is minus the sum of $\theta$ and a quarter turn.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf u &= -\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 - \cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(the two legs)} \\ \mathbf e_\theta &= \frac{d\mathbf u}{d\theta} = -\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = \sin\theta\cos\theta - \cos\theta\sin\theta = 0 \quad &\text{(derivative of each component; orthogonal, unit)} \\ \cos\chi &= \cos\left(\theta + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \cos\theta\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2} - \sin\theta\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} = -\sin\theta \quad &\text{($\chi = -\theta - \pi/2$; cosine even)} \\ \sin\chi &= -\sin\left(\theta + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\left(\sin\theta\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2} + \cos\theta\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\cos\theta \quad &\text{(sine odd)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf u = -\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 - \cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 = \cos\chi\,\mathbf j_1 + \sin\chi\,\mathbf k_1, \qquad \mathbf e_\theta = -\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1}$$

Units: dimensionless

Meaning: at zero $\theta$ the plane bar–$P$ is the vertical plane $Ox_1z_1$ and $\mathbf u$ points straight down: the hanging position.

Figure 4. True view of the plane bar–$P$, which contains $\mathbf i_1$ (along the bar) and $\mathbf u$ (down the page). In the shaded right triangle $CEP$ the hypotenuse is $\ell$, the leg along the bar is $\ell\cos\varphi$ and the leg along $\mathbf u$ is $\ell\sin\varphi$; $\overrightarrow{OP} = \xi\,\mathbf i_1 + \ell\,\mathbf e_{CP}$. $\mathbf e_{CP}$ and $\mathbf e_\varphi = \partial\mathbf e_{CP}/\partial\varphi$ in orange.
String basis and position of P Law: right triangle in the true view of the plane bar–$P$; partial derivatives of a unit vector; vector product; position through the contact point Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 24

True view of the plane bar–$P$: the bar to the right, $\mathbf u$ down the page. Let $E$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the bar: in the shaded right triangle $CEP$ (right angle at $E$) the hypotenuse is $CP$, of length $\ell$, the leg adjacent to $\varphi$ is $CE$, of length $\ell\cos\varphi$, along $\mathbf i_1$, and the opposite leg $EP$, of length $\ell\sin\varphi$, is along $\mathbf u$. The determinant is expanded along its first row, with the cofactor signs plus, minus, plus.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_{CP} &= \cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\varphi\,\mathbf u = \cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 - \sin\varphi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 - \sin\varphi\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(the two legs over $\ell$)} \\ \mathbf e_\varphi &= \frac{\partial\mathbf e_{CP}}{\partial\varphi} = -\sin\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf u = -\sin\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 - \cos\varphi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 - \cos\varphi\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(derivative in $\varphi$)} \\ \frac{\partial\mathbf e_{CP}}{\partial\theta} &= \sin\varphi\,\frac{d\mathbf u}{d\theta} = \sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(only $\mathbf u$ depends on $\theta$)} \\ \det[{}_1R_2] &= (+1)\cos\varphi\left(\cos\varphi\cos^2\theta + \cos\varphi\sin^2\theta\right) - 0 + (+1)\left(-\sin\varphi\right)\left(-\sin\varphi\sin^2\theta - \sin\varphi\cos^2\theta\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(columns $\mathbf e_{CP}, \mathbf e_\theta, \mathbf e_\varphi$; first row)} \\ \mathbf e_{CP}\cdot\mathbf e_\varphi &= -\cos\varphi\sin\varphi + \sin\varphi\cos\varphi\left(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta\right) = 0, \quad \mathbf e_{CP}\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = \sin\varphi\sin\theta\cos\theta - \sin\varphi\cos\theta\sin\theta = 0 \quad &\text{(orthogonal)} \\ \mathbf r_1^P &= \overrightarrow{OC} + \overrightarrow{CP} = \xi\,\mathbf i_1 + \ell\,\mathbf e_{CP} \quad &\text{(through the contact point)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} [{}_1R_2] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\varphi & 0 & -\sin\varphi \cr -\sin\varphi\sin\theta & -\cos\theta & -\cos\varphi\sin\theta \cr -\sin\varphi\cos\theta & \sin\theta & -\cos\varphi\cos\theta \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_1R_2] = 1, \quad \mathbf e_{CP}\times\mathbf e_\theta = \mathbf e_\varphi \cr \mathbf r_1^P = \left(\xi + \ell\cos\varphi\right)\mathbf i_1 - \ell\sin\varphi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 - \ell\sin\varphi\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[\xi] = [\ell] = [\mathrm{L}]$; the unit vectors are dimensionless

Meaning: $C$ plays the role of a moving centre of spherical coordinates: $\ell$ is the radius, $\varphi$ the angle from the bar and $\theta$ the azimuth about the bar.

Derivatives of the string basis in S1 Law: chain rule on unit vectors that depend on two angles; $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf k_1$ constant in $S_1$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.7
$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial\mathbf e_\varphi}{\partial\varphi} &= -\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 - \sin\varphi\,\mathbf u = -\mathbf e_{CP}, \quad \frac{\partial\mathbf e_\varphi}{\partial\theta} = \cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(component by component)} \\ \frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{d\theta} &= \sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 = -\mathbf u = -\left(\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_{CP} + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi\right) \quad &\text{($\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_{CP} + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi = \mathbf u$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_{CP}}{dt}\right|_1 &= \frac{\partial\mathbf e_{CP}}{\partial\varphi}\dot\varphi + \frac{\partial\mathbf e_{CP}}{\partial\theta}\dot\theta = \dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi + \dot\theta\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\varphi}{dt}\right|_1 &= -\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_{CP} + \dot\theta\cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{dt}\right|_1 = -\dot\theta\left(\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_{CP} + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi\right) \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\dot{\mathbf e}_{CP} = \dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi + \dot\theta\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta, \quad \dot{\mathbf e}_\varphi = -\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_{CP} + \dot\theta\cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta, \quad \dot{\mathbf e}_\theta = -\dot\theta\left(\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_{CP} + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi\right) \quad (\text{in } S_1)}$$

Units: $[\dot\varphi] = [\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: the string basis turns with the rates of the two angles, as a spherical basis does.

Kinematics

Motion of the bar frame and derivatives of its unit vectors Law: angular velocity of a simple rotation; derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf v_0^O = \mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(rotation about the fixed vertical through $O$; $\omega$ constant)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 to 3.5)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_0\right) &= -\omega\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \omega\cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(check: chain rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0}$$

Units: $[\omega] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: in $S_1$ the bar is a fixed line; in $S_0$ its basis turns at the constant rate.

(a) Position and velocity of A in S1

Velocity of the anchor seen from the bar Law: time derivative in $S_1$; check with the composition of velocities for a point fixed in $S_0$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.26; Problems.pdf, p. 24
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_1^A &= \left.\frac{d\mathbf r_1^A}{dt}\right|_1 = -R\omega\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_1 - R\omega\cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(chain rule on $\cos\omega t$ and $\sin\omega t$; $h$ constant)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^A &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(R\cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_1 - R\sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_1 + h\,\mathbf k_1\right) = R\omega\cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_1 + R\omega\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \mathbf v_0^A &= \mathbf v_0^O + \mathbf v_1^A + \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^A = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.26: $A$ is fixed in $S_0$, as it must be)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^A = R\cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_1 - R\sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_1 + h\,\mathbf k_1, \qquad \mathbf v_1^A = -R\omega\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_1 - R\omega\cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[R\omega] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: in $S_1$ the anchor goes round its circle with the angular velocity minus $\omega$ about the vertical: the end of the string moves in the frame of the bar.

(b) Position, velocity and acceleration of P in S1

Relative velocity and relative acceleration of P Law: time derivatives in $S_1$; product rule; derivatives of the string basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24; Problems.pdf, p. 24
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_1^P &= \dot\xi\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot\ell\,\mathbf e_{CP} + \ell\left(\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi + \dot\theta\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta\right) \quad &\text{(product rule on $\ell\,\mathbf e_{CP}$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\dot\ell\,\mathbf e_{CP}\right) &= \ddot\ell\,\mathbf e_{CP} + \dot\ell\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi + \dot\ell\dot\theta\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(product rule)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\ell\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi\right) &= \left(\dot\ell\dot\varphi + \ell\ddot\varphi\right)\mathbf e_\varphi - \ell\dot\varphi^2\,\mathbf e_{CP} + \ell\dot\varphi\dot\theta\cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(product rule)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\ell\dot\theta\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta\right) &= \left(\dot\ell\dot\theta\sin\varphi + \ell\ddot\theta\sin\varphi + \ell\dot\theta\dot\varphi\cos\varphi\right)\mathbf e_\theta - \ell\dot\theta^2\sin\varphi\left(\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_{CP} + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi\right) \quad &\text{(product rule on three factors)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P &= \ddot\xi\,\mathbf i_1 + \text{the three lines above, collected along } \mathbf e_{CP},\ \mathbf e_\varphi,\ \mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(sum)} \\ v_x &= \dot\xi + \dot\ell\cos\varphi - \ell\dot\varphi\sin\varphi \quad &\text{(derivative of the first component of $\mathbf r_1^P$; product and chain rules)} \\ v_y &= -\left(\dot\ell\sin\varphi\sin\theta + \ell\dot\varphi\cos\varphi\sin\theta + \ell\dot\theta\sin\varphi\cos\theta\right) \quad &\text{(second component)} \\ v_z &= -\left(\dot\ell\sin\varphi\cos\theta + \ell\dot\varphi\cos\varphi\cos\theta - \ell\dot\theta\sin\varphi\sin\theta\right) \quad &\text{(third component)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf r_1^P = \xi\,\mathbf i_1 + \ell\,\mathbf e_{CP}, \qquad \mathbf v_1^P = \dot\xi\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot\ell\,\mathbf e_{CP} + \ell\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi + \ell\dot\theta\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta, \cr \mathbf a_1^P = \ddot\xi\,\mathbf i_1 + \left(\ddot\ell - \ell\dot\varphi^2 - \ell\dot\theta^2\sin^2\varphi\right)\mathbf e_{CP} + \left(\ell\ddot\varphi + 2\dot\ell\dot\varphi - \ell\dot\theta^2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\right)\mathbf e_\varphi + \left(\ell\ddot\theta\sin\varphi + 2\dot\ell\dot\theta\sin\varphi + 2\ell\dot\theta\dot\varphi\cos\varphi\right)\mathbf e_\theta \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[\dot\xi] = [\ell\dot\varphi] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[\ddot\xi] = [\ell\dot\theta^2] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the acceleration along the bar of the moving centre $C$ plus the spherical acceleration about it; the components of the velocity in $\mathcal B_1$ are listed in the last three rows.

Absolute acceleration of P: centripetal and Coriolis terms Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of a vector written in the turning basis; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.8; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]

Write the position in $\mathcal B_1$ as $x\,\mathbf i_1 + y\,\mathbf j_1 + z\,\mathbf k_1$, with the components of the boxed position; their time derivatives are $v_x$, $v_y$, $v_z$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P &= \dot x\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y\,\mathbf j_1 + \dot z\,\mathbf k_1 + x\,\omega\,\mathbf j_1 - y\,\omega\,\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf v_1^P + \omega\left(x\,\mathbf j_1 - y\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; derivatives of $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1^P}{dt}\right|_0 &= \mathbf a_1^P + \omega\left(v_x\,\mathbf j_1 - v_y\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; the turning of $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$ inside $\mathbf v_1^P$)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left[\omega\left(x\,\mathbf j_1 - y\,\mathbf i_1\right)\right] &= \omega\left(v_x\,\mathbf j_1 - v_y\,\mathbf i_1\right) + \omega^2\left(-x\,\mathbf i_1 - y\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; derivatives of $\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf i_1$)} \\ 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P &= 2\omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(v_x\,\mathbf i_1 + v_y\,\mathbf j_1 + v_z\,\mathbf k_1\right) = 2\omega\left(v_x\,\mathbf j_1 - v_y\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(the two equal terms: Coriolis)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\omega\left(x\,\mathbf j_1 - y\,\mathbf i_1\right) = -\omega^2\left(x\,\mathbf i_1 + y\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(the last term: centripetal)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_0^P = \mathbf a_1^P - \omega^2\left(x\,\mathbf i_1 + y\,\mathbf j_1\right) + 2\omega\left(v_x\,\mathbf j_1 - v_y\,\mathbf i_1\right)}$$

Units: $[\omega^2x] = [\omega v_x] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the centripetal term points horizontally to the axis of the bar; the Coriolis term is horizontal and normal to the horizontal part of the relative velocity.

(c) AC, l and phi as functions of xi and time

Length AC and length l Law: distance between two points; constant length of the string Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.5; Problems.pdf, p. 24
$$\begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{AC} &= \mathbf r_1^C - \mathbf r_1^A = \left(\xi - R\cos\omega t\right)\mathbf i_1 + R\sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_1 - h\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf r_1^C = \xi\,\mathbf i_1$; part (a))} \\ D^2 &= \left(\xi - R\cos\omega t\right)^2 + R^2\sin^2\omega t + h^2 = \xi^2 - 2R\xi\cos\omega t + R^2\left(\cos^2\omega t + \sin^2\omega t\right) + h^2 \quad &\text{(square expanded)} \\ \ell &= L - D \quad &\text{(string of constant length)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{AC = D = \sqrt{\xi^2 - 2R\xi\cos\omega t + R^2 + h^2}, \qquad \ell = L - \sqrt{\xi^2 - 2R\xi\cos\omega t + R^2 + h^2}}$$

Units: $[D] = [\ell] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: the cosine law in the triangle $OA'C$ plus the height: as the anchor falls behind the bar, $AC$ grows and the hanging part shortens.

Figure 5. The piece of string at $C$ is massless, so the two equal pulls and the push $\mathbf N_b$ of the bar add up to zero. The smooth bar pushes only across itself, so the components of $\mathbf e_{CA}$ and $\mathbf e_{CP}$ along the bar are opposite: both segments make the same angle with the bar.
Angle phi from the frictionless contact Law: equilibrium of the massless piece of string at $C$; smooth contact: the bar pushes normal to itself Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.32; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.16; Problems.pdf, p. 24

Without friction the tension is the same on both sides of $C$. The piece of string at $C$ is massless, so the two pulls and the push $\mathbf N_b$ of the bar add up to zero, and $\mathbf N_b$ has no component along the bar.

$$\begin{aligned} T\,\mathbf e_{CA} + T\,\mathbf e_{CP} + \mathbf N_b &= \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf N_b\cdot\mathbf i_1 = 0 \quad &\text{(equilibrium; smooth bar)} \\ \mathbf e_{CP}\cdot\mathbf i_1 &= -\mathbf e_{CA}\cdot\mathbf i_1 = \frac{\overrightarrow{AC}\cdot\mathbf i_1}{D} \quad &\text{(projection on $\mathbf i_1$; $\mathbf e_{CA} = -\overrightarrow{AC}/D$)} \\ \cos\varphi &= \frac{\xi - R\cos\omega t}{D}, \quad \sin\varphi = \sqrt{1 - \cos^2\varphi} = \frac{\sqrt{R^2\sin^2\omega t + h^2}}{D} \quad &\text{($\varphi$ in $(0, \pi)$: positive sine; $D^2$ of the box above)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\varphi = \arccos\frac{\xi - R\cos\omega t}{\sqrt{\xi^2 - 2R\xi\cos\omega t + R^2 + h^2}}}$$

Units: $[\cos\varphi] = [\mathrm{L}]/[\mathrm{L}] = [1]$

Meaning: the two segments make equal angles with the bar, on opposite sides of the plane normal to it: the string passes over the bar like a light ray reflected by a mirror. The bar pushes the string only across itself.

Partial derivatives of l and phi with respect to xi and t Law: implicit differentiation of the two relations of part (c); chain rule Source: Problems.pdf, p. 24
