$$\begin{aligned} 2D\frac{\partial D}{\partial\xi} &= 2\xi - 2R\cos\omega t \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{\partial D}{\partial\xi} = \cos\varphi, \quad \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\xi} = -\cos\varphi \quad &\text{(derivative of $D^2$)} \\ 2D\frac{\partial D}{\partial t} &= 2R\xi\omega\sin\omega t \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial t} = -\frac{R\omega\xi\sin\omega t}{D} \quad &\text{(chain rule on $\cos\omega t$)} \\ \dot\ell &= \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\xi}\dot\xi + \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial t} = -\dot\xi\cos\varphi - \frac{R\omega\xi\sin\omega t}{D} \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ -\sin\varphi\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\xi} &= \frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\left(\frac{\xi - R\cos\omega t}{D}\right) = \frac{D - \left(\xi - R\cos\omega t\right)\cos\varphi}{D^2} = \frac{1 - \cos^2\varphi}{D} \quad &\text{(quotient rule)} \\ \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\xi} &= -\frac{\sin\varphi}{D}, \quad \ddot\varphi = \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\xi}\ddot\xi + \left(\text{terms in } \xi,\ \dot\xi,\ t\right) \quad &\text{(chain rule twice: $\ddot\xi$ appears only through the first factor)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\dot\ell + \dot\xi\cos\varphi = -\frac{R\omega\xi\sin\omega t}{D}, \qquad \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\xi} = -\cos\varphi, \qquad \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\xi} = -\frac{\sin\varphi}{D}}$$

Units: $[R\omega\xi/D] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[\partial\varphi/\partial\xi] = [\mathrm{L^{-1}}]$

Meaning: the string pays out along $CP$ (the left side is the rate of the projection of the relative velocity on $\mathbf e_{CP}$) only because the anchor moves; with the anchor fixed in $S_1$ the right side would vanish.

Forces and Equations of Motion

Figure 6. Forces on $P$ in $S_1$: the weight, the pull $-T\,\mathbf e_{CP}$ of the string towards $C$, the centrifugal force $m\omega^2(x\,\mathbf i_1 + y\,\mathbf j_1)$ away from the vertical axis through $O$ and the Coriolis force (dashed, both horizontal). The bar acts on the string at $C$, not on $P$.

(d) Forces acting on P

Actual and inertia forces on P Law: weight; string pull along the string; inertia forces of a non-inertial frame Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; Problems.pdf, p. 24
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf W &= -mg\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf T = -T\,\mathbf e_{CP} = -T\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + T\sin\varphi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + T\sin\varphi\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(weight; pull towards $C$, $T \gt 0$)} \\ \mathbf F_A &= -m\,\mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf F_E = -m\,\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{($O$ fixed; $\omega$ constant)} \\ \mathbf F_C &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) = m\omega^2\left(x\,\mathbf i_1 + y\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(composition box times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR} &= -2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P = 2m\omega v_y\,\mathbf i_1 - 2m\omega v_x\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(composition box times $-m$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf W = -mg\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf T = -T\,\mathbf e_{CP}, \quad \mathbf F_C = m\omega^2\left(\xi + \ell\cos\varphi\right)\mathbf i_1 - m\omega^2\ell\sin\varphi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1, \cr \mathbf F_{COR} = -2m\omega\left(\dot\ell\sin\varphi\sin\theta + \ell\dot\varphi\cos\varphi\sin\theta + \ell\dot\theta\sin\varphi\cos\theta\right)\mathbf i_1 - 2m\omega\left(\dot\xi + \dot\ell\cos\varphi - \ell\dot\varphi\sin\varphi\right)\mathbf j_1 \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[mg] = [m\omega^2\xi] = [m\omega\dot\xi] = [T] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: two actual forces (weight and string) and two inertia forces, both horizontal: the centrifugal force away from the axis, the Coriolis force normal to the horizontal relative velocity.

(e) Equations of motion

Projections of each force on the string basis Law: scalar products with the columns of $[{}_1R_2]$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63

From the columns of $[{}_1R_2]$: the projections of $\mathbf i_1$ on $\mathbf e_{CP}$, $\mathbf e_\varphi$, $\mathbf e_\theta$ are the cosine, minus the sine and 0; those of $\mathbf j_1$ are $-\sin\varphi\sin\theta$, $-\cos\varphi\sin\theta$ and $-\cos\theta$; those of $\mathbf k_1$ are $-\sin\varphi\cos\theta$, $-\cos\varphi\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$. In the Coriolis projections the terms in $\dot\varphi$ cancel along $\mathbf e_\varphi$ and the terms in $\dot\ell$ cancel along $\mathbf e_{CP}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf W\cdot\mathbf e_\theta &= -mg\sin\theta, \quad \mathbf W\cdot\mathbf e_\varphi = mg\cos\varphi\cos\theta, \quad \mathbf W\cdot\mathbf e_{CP} = mg\sin\varphi\cos\theta \quad &\text{(third row of $[{}_1R_2]$ times $-mg$)} \\ \mathbf F_C\cdot\mathbf e_\theta &= m\omega^2\left(-y\cos\theta\right) = m\omega^2\ell\sin\varphi\sin\theta\cos\theta \quad &\text{($\mathbf i_1\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = 0$)} \\ \mathbf F_C\cdot\mathbf e_\varphi &= m\omega^2\left(-x\sin\varphi - y\cos\varphi\sin\theta\right) = -m\omega^2\sin\varphi\left(\xi + \ell\cos\varphi - \ell\cos\varphi\sin^2\theta\right) = -m\omega^2\sin\varphi\left(\xi + \ell\cos\varphi\cos^2\theta\right) \quad &\text{($1 - \sin^2\theta = \cos^2\theta$)} \\ \mathbf F_C\cdot\mathbf e_{CP} &= m\omega^2\left(x\cos\varphi - y\sin\varphi\sin\theta\right) = m\omega^2\left[\left(\xi + \ell\cos\varphi\right)\cos\varphi + \ell\sin^2\varphi\sin^2\theta\right] \quad &\text{(first column)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR}\cdot\mathbf e_\theta &= -2m\omega v_x\left(-\cos\theta\right) = 2m\omega\cos\theta\left(\dot\xi + \dot\ell\cos\varphi - \ell\dot\varphi\sin\varphi\right) \quad &\text{(second column)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR}\cdot\mathbf e_\varphi &= 2m\omega\left(-v_y\sin\varphi + v_x\cos\varphi\sin\theta\right) = 2m\omega\left[\sin\theta\left(\dot\ell + \dot\xi\cos\varphi\right) + \ell\dot\theta\sin^2\varphi\cos\theta\right] \quad &\text{($\sin^2\varphi + \cos^2\varphi = 1$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR}\cdot\mathbf e_{CP} &= 2m\omega\left(v_y\cos\varphi + v_x\sin\varphi\sin\theta\right) = 2m\omega\left[\sin\theta\left(\dot\xi\sin\varphi - \ell\dot\varphi\right) - \ell\dot\theta\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\cos\theta\right] \quad &\text{(first column)} \\ \mathbf T\cdot\mathbf e_\theta &= \mathbf T\cdot\mathbf e_\varphi = 0, \quad \mathbf T\cdot\mathbf e_{CP} = -T \quad &\text{(string along $\mathbf e_{CP}$)} \\ m\,\mathbf a_1^P\cdot\mathbf e_\varphi &= m\left(\ell\ddot\varphi + 2\dot\ell\dot\varphi - \ell\dot\theta^2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi - \ddot\xi\sin\varphi\right), \quad m\,\mathbf a_1^P\cdot\mathbf e_{CP} = m\left(\ddot\ell - \ell\dot\varphi^2 - \ell\dot\theta^2\sin^2\varphi + \ddot\xi\cos\varphi\right) \quad &\text{($\ddot\xi\,\mathbf i_1$ projected)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{every projection of } \mathbf W,\ \mathbf T,\ \mathbf F_C,\ \mathbf F_{COR} \text{ and } m\,\mathbf a_1^P \text{ on } \mathbf e_\theta,\ \mathbf e_\varphi,\ \mathbf e_{CP} \text{ as listed}}$$

Units: every projection $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the tension appears only along $\mathbf e_{CP}$, so the two other projections are free of it.

Two equations of motion and the tension Law: Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame projected on $\mathcal B_2$; elimination of $\ell$ and $\varphi$ through part (c) Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; Problems.pdf, p. 24

Three scalar equations for the three unknowns $\xi$, $\theta$ and $T$. In the $\mathbf e_\varphi$ equation the second derivative of $\xi$ appears in $-\ddot\xi\sin\varphi$ and, through the chain rule of part (c), in $\ell\ddot\varphi$; their sum has a coefficient that does not vanish while the string is bent.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_\theta:\ \ell\sin\varphi\,\ddot\theta + 2\dot\ell\dot\theta\sin\varphi + 2\ell\dot\theta\dot\varphi\cos\varphi &= -g\sin\theta + \omega^2\ell\sin\varphi\sin\theta\cos\theta + 2\omega\cos\theta\left(\dot\xi + \dot\ell\cos\varphi - \ell\dot\varphi\sin\varphi\right) \quad &\text{(divided by $m$)} \\ \mathbf e_\varphi:\ \ell\ddot\varphi + 2\dot\ell\dot\varphi - \ddot\xi\sin\varphi - \ell\dot\theta^2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi &= g\cos\varphi\cos\theta - \omega^2\sin\varphi\left(\xi + \ell\cos\varphi\cos^2\theta\right) + 2\omega\left[\sin\theta\left(\dot\ell + \dot\xi\cos\varphi\right) + \ell\dot\theta\sin^2\varphi\cos\theta\right] \quad &\text{(divided by $m$)} \\ \mathbf e_{CP}:\ m\left(\ddot\xi\cos\varphi + \ddot\ell - \ell\dot\varphi^2 - \ell\dot\theta^2\sin^2\varphi\right) &= -T + mg\sin\varphi\cos\theta + \mathbf F_C\cdot\mathbf e_{CP} + \mathbf F_{COR}\cdot\mathbf e_{CP} \quad &\text{(gives $T$)} \\ \ell\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\xi}\ddot\xi - \sin\varphi\,\ddot\xi &= -\left(\frac{\ell}{D} + 1\right)\sin\varphi\,\ddot\xi = -\frac{L}{D}\sin\varphi\,\ddot\xi \quad &\text{(coefficient of $\ddot\xi$ in the $\mathbf e_\varphi$ equation; $\ell + D = L$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \ell\sin\varphi\,\ddot\theta + 2\dot\ell\dot\theta\sin\varphi + 2\ell\dot\theta\dot\varphi\cos\varphi = -g\sin\theta + \omega^2\ell\sin\varphi\sin\theta\cos\theta + 2\omega\cos\theta\left(\dot\xi + \dot\ell\cos\varphi - \ell\dot\varphi\sin\varphi\right) \cr \ell\ddot\varphi + 2\dot\ell\dot\varphi - \ddot\xi\sin\varphi - \ell\dot\theta^2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi = g\cos\varphi\cos\theta - \omega^2\sin\varphi\left(\xi + \ell\cos\varphi\cos^2\theta\right) + 2\omega\left[\sin\theta\left(\dot\ell + \dot\xi\cos\varphi\right) + \ell\dot\theta\sin^2\varphi\cos\theta\right] \cr T = -m\left(\ddot\xi\cos\varphi + \ddot\ell - \ell\dot\varphi^2 - \ell\dot\theta^2\sin^2\varphi\right) + mg\sin\varphi\cos\theta + m\omega^2\left[\left(\xi + \ell\cos\varphi\right)\cos\varphi + \ell\sin^2\varphi\sin^2\theta\right] + 2m\omega\left[\sin\theta\left(\dot\xi\sin\varphi - \ell\dot\varphi\right) - \ell\dot\theta\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\cos\theta\right] \end{gathered}}$$

Units: every term of the first two lines $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$; $[T] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: with $\ell$, $\varphi$ and their derivatives replaced by the functions of $\xi$, its rate and time of part (c), the first two lines are two second-order equations for $\xi$ and $\theta$ (the coefficients of their second derivatives, $\ell\sin\varphi$ and minus $L$ over $D$ times the sine, are not zero while the string is bent), with time present explicitly through the motion of the anchor. The third gives the tension; the solution holds while it stays positive.

Answers and Checks

(f) Initial conditions at t equal to zero

Initial position Law: geometry at the instant of the impact Source: Problems.pdf, p. 24

At the start the bar lies along $\mathbf i_0$ and meets the vertical string at $A'$, directly below $A$; the particle hangs in the vertical plane $Ox_1z_1$.

$$\begin{aligned} \xi(0) &= R, \quad D(0) = \sqrt{R^2 - 2R^2 + R^2 + h^2} = h, \quad \ell(0) = L - h \quad &\text{(part (c) at $t = 0$)} \\ \cos\varphi(0) &= \frac{R - R}{h} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \varphi(0) = \tfrac{\pi}{2}, \quad \theta(0) = 0 \quad &\text{(string normal to the bar, hanging)} \\ \mathbf e_{CP}(0) &= -\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf e_\varphi(0) = -\mathbf i_1, \quad \mathbf e_\theta(0) = -\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf r_1^P(0) = R\,\mathbf i_1 - \left(L - h\right)\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(columns of $[{}_1R_2]$ at these angles)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\xi(0) = R, \quad \theta(0) = 0 \qquad \left(\ell(0) = L - h,\ \varphi(0) = \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)}$$

Units: $[\xi] = [\ell] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: the particle is a depth $L - h$ below the bar, that is $L$ below the anchor.

Initial rates Law: continuity of the absolute velocity (no impulse); composition of velocities; the velocity of part (b) at the start Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.26; Problems.pdf, p. 24

The particle is at rest in $S_0$ just before the impact. The string meets the bar at a right angle, so its path length grows only to second order in time ($\dot\ell(0)$ is zero below) and no impulsive tension acts: the absolute velocity stays zero. The velocity of part (b) is written at the start before the components are matched.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_1^P(0) &= \mathbf v_0^P(0) - \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P(0) = \mathbf 0 - \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left[R\,\mathbf i_1 - \left(L - h\right)\mathbf k_1\right] = -\omega R\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.26 with $\mathbf v_0^O$ zero)} \\ \mathbf v_1^P(0) &= \dot\xi\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot\ell\left(-\mathbf k_1\right) + \left(L - h\right)\dot\varphi\left(-\mathbf i_1\right) + \left(L - h\right)\dot\theta\left(-\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(part (b) at $\varphi = \pi/2$, $\theta = 0$)} \\ \mathbf k_1:\ \dot\ell(0) &= 0, \quad \text{and part (c): } \dot\ell(0) = -\dot\xi(0)\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2} - \frac{R\omega R\sin 0}{h} = 0 \quad &\text{(consistent)} \\ \mathbf j_1:\ \left(L - h\right)\dot\theta(0) &= \omega R \;\Rightarrow\; \dot\theta(0) = \frac{\omega R}{L - h} \quad &\text{(sideways component)} \\ \dot\varphi(0) &= \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\xi}\dot\xi + \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial t} = -\frac{\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}}{h}\dot\xi(0) + 0 = -\frac{\dot\xi(0)}{h} \quad &\text{(chain rule; $\partial\varphi/\partial t$ is zero at $t = 0$, from $\cos\varphi\,D = \xi - R\cos\omega t$)} \\ \mathbf i_1:\ \dot\xi(0) - \left(L - h\right)\dot\varphi(0) &= \dot\xi(0)\left(1 + \frac{L - h}{h}\right) = \frac{L}{h}\dot\xi(0) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \dot\xi(0) = 0,\ \dot\varphi(0) = 0 \quad &\text{(component along the bar)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\xi(0) = R, \quad \dot\xi(0) = 0, \quad \theta(0) = 0, \quad \dot\theta(0) = \frac{\omega R}{L - h} \qquad \left(\dot\ell(0) = 0,\ \dot\varphi(0) = 0\right)}$$

Units: $[\dot\theta(0)] = [\omega R/(L - h)] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: seen from the bar, the particle starts moving backwards with the speed of the point of the bar that hits the string, swinging about $C$ as a pendulum of length $L - h$; $\theta$ grows from zero towards the side of the anchor. The time derivative of $\varphi$ at fixed $\xi$ vanishes at the start because the derivative of the cosine of $\omega t$ is zero there.

(g) Is the mechanical energy of the particle conserved?

Rate of the energy in S0 and in S1 Law: power of the forces on the absolute and on the relative velocity; potentials of the weight and of the centrifugal force Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.26; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.29; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]

In $S_0$ the weight has the potential $mgz$ and the only other force is the string pull. In $S_1$ the weight and the centrifugal force (constant rate, fixed axis) have potentials, the Coriolis force does no work, and again only the string pull is left. Let $E_0^P$ be one half of $m$ times the squared absolute speed plus $mgz$, and $E_1^P$ one half of $m$ times the squared relative speed plus $mgz$ minus one half of $m\omega^2(x^2 + y^2)$. The projection of the relative velocity on $\mathbf e_{CP}$ is $\dot\xi\cos\varphi + \dot\ell$.

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{dE_1^P}{dt} &= \mathbf T\cdot\mathbf v_1^P = -T\left(\dot\xi\cos\varphi + \dot\ell\right) = \frac{TR\omega\xi\sin\omega t}{D} \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.29 in $S_1$; part (c))} \\ \mathbf e_{CP}\cdot\omega\left(x\,\mathbf j_1 - y\,\mathbf i_1\right) &= \omega\left[-\left(\xi + \ell\cos\varphi\right)\sin\varphi\sin\theta + \ell\sin\varphi\sin\theta\cos\varphi\right] = -\omega\xi\sin\varphi\sin\theta \quad &\text{(the transport velocity of the composition box on $\mathbf e_{CP}$)} \\ \frac{dE_0^P}{dt} &= \mathbf T\cdot\mathbf v_0^P = \mathbf T\cdot\mathbf v_1^P - T\,\mathbf e_{CP}\cdot\omega\left(x\,\mathbf j_1 - y\,\mathbf i_1\right) = T\omega\xi\left(\frac{R\sin\omega t}{D} + \sin\varphi\sin\theta\right) \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.29 in $S_0$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\frac{dE_0^P}{dt} = T\omega\xi\left(\frac{R\sin\omega t}{D} + \sin\varphi\sin\theta\right) \ne 0, \qquad \frac{dE_1^P}{dt} = \frac{TR\omega\xi\sin\omega t}{D} \ne 0: \ \text{not conserved}}$$

Units: $[T\omega\xi] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-3}}]$, a power

Meaning: no. The string is a moving constraint: in $S_0$ the bar drags the bend of the string, in $S_1$ the anchor moves, and in both frames the tension works on the particle. While the anchor is behind the bar (the sine of $\omega t$ positive) and the string is tense, the energy in $S_1$ grows. The energy comes from the motor that keeps the rate of the bar constant (check box below).

(h) Separation of the string from the bar

Geometric condition of separation Law: the bar pushes the string only while the string is bent at $C$; straight string: $A$, $C$ and $P$ collinear Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.32; Problems.pdf, p. 24

The push of the bar is minus $T$ times the sum of $\mathbf e_{CA}$ and $\mathbf e_{CP}$ (contact box); it vanishes when the string is straight, and beyond that instant the bend would have to reverse, which a bar pushing from one side cannot impose. The components along $\mathbf i_1$ of $\mathbf e_{CP}$ and of minus $\mathbf e_{CA}$ are already equal (contact box); the other two components are equated, with the sine of $\varphi$ from part (c).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_{CP} &= -\mathbf e_{CA} = \frac{\overrightarrow{AC}}{D} \quad &\text{(straight string)} \\ \mathbf j_1:\ -\sin\varphi\sin\theta &= \frac{R\sin\omega t}{D} \;\Rightarrow\; \sin\theta = -\frac{R\sin\omega t}{\sqrt{R^2\sin^2\omega t + h^2}} \quad &\text{($\sin\varphi\,D = \sqrt{R^2\sin^2\omega t + h^2}$)} \\ \mathbf k_1:\ -\sin\varphi\cos\theta &= -\frac{h}{D} \;\Rightarrow\; \cos\theta = \frac{h}{\sqrt{R^2\sin^2\omega t + h^2}} \gt 0 \quad &\text{(vertical component)} \\ \tan\theta &= \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = -\frac{R\sin\omega t}{h} \quad &\text{(quotient)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\tan\theta = -\frac{R\sin\omega t}{h}, \qquad \theta_{sep}(t) = -\arctan\frac{R\sin\omega t}{h}}$$

Units: $[R\sin\omega t/h] = [1]$

Meaning: the string leaves the bar at the first instant at which the angle obtained from the equations of part (e) reaches this value. For the sine of $\omega t$ positive the value is negative: the particle must have swung forward, past the vertical plane of the bar, to the side opposite to the anchor, so that the straight line from $A$ through $C$ reaches it.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Anchor in $S_1$$\mathbf r_1^A = R\cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_1 - R\sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_1 + h\,\mathbf k_1$, $\mathbf v_1^A = -R\omega\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_1 - R\omega\cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_1$
(b) $P$ in $S_1$$\mathbf r_1^P = \xi\,\mathbf i_1 + \ell\,\mathbf e_{CP}$; $\mathbf v_1^P = \dot\xi\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot\ell\,\mathbf e_{CP} + \ell\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi + \ell\dot\theta\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\theta$; $\mathbf a_1^P$ as boxed in part (b), with $\mathbf e_{CP}, \mathbf e_\theta, \mathbf e_\varphi$ the columns of $[{}_1R_2]$
(c) $AC$, $\ell$, $\varphi$$AC = \sqrt{\xi^2 - 2R\xi\cos\omega t + R^2 + h^2}$, $\ell = L - AC$, $\cos\varphi = (\xi - R\cos\omega t)/AC$
(d) Forces$\mathbf W = -mg\,\mathbf k_1$, $\mathbf T = -T\,\mathbf e_{CP}$, $\mathbf F_C = m\omega^2(\xi + \ell\cos\varphi)\,\mathbf i_1 - m\omega^2\ell\sin\varphi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf F_{COR} = -2m\omega(\dot\ell\sin\varphi\sin\theta + \ell\dot\varphi\cos\varphi\sin\theta + \ell\dot\theta\sin\varphi\cos\theta)\,\mathbf i_1 - 2m\omega(\dot\xi + \dot\ell\cos\varphi - \ell\dot\varphi\sin\varphi)\,\mathbf j_1$; origin and Euler forces zero
(e) Equationsthe $\mathbf e_\theta$ and $\mathbf e_\varphi$ equations of part (e), closed with part (c): two second-order equations for $\xi(t)$, $\theta(t)$; the $\mathbf e_{CP}$ equation gives $T$
(f) Initial conditions$\xi(0) = R$, $\dot\xi(0) = 0$, $\theta(0) = 0$, $\dot\theta(0) = \omega R/(L - h)$ (and $\ell(0) = L - h$, $\varphi(0) = \pi/2$, $\dot\ell(0) = \dot\varphi(0) = 0$)
(g) Energynot conserved in $S_0$ nor in $S_1$: $dE_0^P/dt = T\omega\xi(R\sin\omega t/AC + \sin\varphi\sin\theta)$, $dE_1^P/dt = TR\omega\xi\sin\omega t/AC$
(h) Separation$\tan\theta = -R\sin\omega t/h$ (string straight); the other way to lose contact, $C$ reaching the end of the bar, is $\xi$ equal to the half-length of the bar

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 75 prints only the centrifugal and the Coriolis forces; both coincide term by term with part (d) (box below). The rest is checked independently with the power of the bar on the string and with limiting cases.

Comparison with the official key Law: term-by-term comparison Source: Problems.pdf, p. 75
$$\begin{aligned} \text{key: } \mathbf F_{cent} &= m\omega^2\left(\xi + \ell\cos\varphi\right)\mathbf i_1 - m\omega^2\ell\sin\varphi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf F_C \quad &\text{(part (d))} \\ \text{key: } \mathbf F_{Cori} &= -2m\omega\left(\dot\ell\sin\varphi\sin\theta + \ell\dot\varphi\cos\varphi\sin\theta + \ell\dot\theta\sin\varphi\cos\theta\right)\mathbf i_1 - 2m\omega\left(\dot\xi + \dot\ell\cos\varphi - \ell\dot\varphi\sin\varphi\right)\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf F_{COR} \quad &\text{(part (d))} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{both inertia forces coincide with the key}}$$

Units: $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the agreement also confirms the reading of the sense of rotation and of the sign of $\theta$.

Independent check: the energy comes from the bar Law: power of the push of the bar on the string at the moving contact point; the massless string transmits it to the particle Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.26; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.29

The contact point moves in $S_0$ with the velocity of part (b) for a point at $\xi$ on the bar, $\dot\xi\,\mathbf i_1 + \omega\xi\,\mathbf j_1$; the push of the bar has no component along $\mathbf i_1$. The anchor is fixed, so the string receives power only at $C$, and a massless string passes it on to the particle.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf N_b &= -T\left(\mathbf e_{CA} + \mathbf e_{CP}\right), \quad \mathbf e_{CA}\cdot\mathbf j_1 = -\frac{R\sin\omega t}{D}, \quad \mathbf e_{CP}\cdot\mathbf j_1 = -\sin\varphi\sin\theta \quad &\text{(contact box; part (c))} \\ \mathbf N_b\cdot\left(\dot\xi\,\mathbf i_1 + \omega\xi\,\mathbf j_1\right) &= 0 - T\omega\xi\left(-\frac{R\sin\omega t}{D} - \sin\varphi\sin\theta\right) = T\omega\xi\left(\frac{R\sin\omega t}{D} + \sin\varphi\sin\theta\right) \quad &\text{(power of the bar)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf N_b\cdot\mathbf v_0^C = \frac{dE_0^P}{dt}}$$

Units: $[\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-3}}]$

Meaning: the rate of the energy found in part (g) is exactly the power the bar puts into the string.

Limiting cases Law: the results at extreme values of the data Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]
$$\begin{aligned} R \to 0:\quad \frac{dE_1^P}{dt} &\to 0 \quad &\text{(anchor on the axis, fixed in $S_1$: the energy in $S_1$ becomes a first integral)} \\ h \to \infty:\quad \theta_{sep} &\to 0 \quad &\text{(very high ceiling: the string separates near the vertical plane of the bar)} \\ \omega t = \pi:\quad \theta_{sep} &= 0 \quad &\text{(anchor straight across the bar)} \\ \theta = 0,\ \varphi = \tfrac{\pi}{2}:\quad \mathbf e_{CP} &= \mathbf u = -\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(the hanging string)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{R \to 0: \ E_1^P \text{ conserved}; \qquad h \to \infty \text{ or } \omega t = \pi: \ \theta_{sep} = 0}$$

Units: dimensionless

Meaning: each limit matches the picture of an anchor that moves in the frame of the bar and feeds energy into the pendulum.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf (PDF page 24); key on PDF page 75
Problem 37

Particle on a Spinning Elliptic Cone

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 25
Rotating Constraint Surface

A heavy point particle $P$ with mass $m$ moves without friction on a cone of elliptic cross-section as shown in the figure. We define an auxiliary reference frame $S_1 : \{O; \mathcal{B}_1\}$ attached to the cone. The cone is defined in term [sic] of two parameters $\zeta$, $\beta$ as

$$ \text{Elliptic cone:} \quad \begin{cases} x_1 = \zeta\cos\beta \\ y_1 = 2\zeta\sin\beta \\ z_1 = \zeta \end{cases} \qquad (5) $$

The cone spins about its $Oz_1$ axis at a constant angular rate $\Omega$ with respect to the inertial reference frame $S_0 : \{O; \mathcal{B}_0\}$. At time $t = 0$, the reference frame $S_1$ coincides with $S_0$, the particle $P$ is located at $\mathbf{r}^P_{1,0} = 2\mathbf{j}_1 + \mathbf{k}_1$, and has a velocity $\mathbf{v}^P_{1,0} = \mathbf{i}_1$.

  • (a)
    How many degrees of freedom does the particle motion have?
  • (b)
    Obtain the general expression for the position, velocity, and acceleration of $P$ in reference frame $S_1$ as a function of $\zeta$, $\beta$ and their derivatives. Remember to define any unit vectors that you use in terms of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}_0$.
  • (c)
    Identify and express mathematically all the forces acting on $P$ as seen from $S_1$.
  • (d)
    Obtain two second-order differential equations for the evolution of $\zeta$, $\beta$ in time, which do not depend on any other unknowns in the problem.
  • (e)
    Find, justify, and write down one conservation law in this problem, including the value of any constants there might be.
  • (f)
    Find the equilibrium positions for $P$ in $S_1$ for $\zeta \gt 0$ as a function of the constants of the problem.
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

A heavy particle $P$ of mass $m$ moves without friction on a cone of elliptic cross-section, with vertex $O$ and vertical axis, described by the parameters $\zeta$ and $\beta$; the cone spins about its axis at the constant rate $\Omega$, and at the start the frames coincide, with the particle at $2\,\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf k_1$ and the velocity $\mathbf i_1$ (Problems.pdf, p. 25). The statement asks for the degrees of freedom, the position, velocity and acceleration in $S_1$, the forces seen from $S_1$, two equations of motion free of other unknowns, one conservation law with its constant, and the equilibria for positive $\zeta$. The cone is at rest in $S_1$, so the solution works there, with the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2 and the inertia forces of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$, $O$ the vertex (fixed), $\mathbf k_0$ vertical, up
Moving frame$S_1 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_1\}$, attached to the cone: $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$ along its axis, $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf j_1$ along the axes of its elliptic sections; it turns by $\Omega t$ about $\mathbf k_0$, from $x_0$ towards $y_0$ (figure), and coincides with $S_0$ at $t = 0$
Cone$x_1 = \zeta\cos\beta$, $y_1 = 2\zeta\sin\beta$, $z_1 = \zeta$ (Eq. (5) of the statement), fixed in $S_1$
Surface vectors at $P$$\mathbf e_\zeta$ and $\mathbf e_\beta$ (tangent, not unit; deduced below), unit normal $\mathbf n$
Coordinates$\zeta$ (height above the vertex), $\beta$ (angular parameter of the elliptic section, not the polar angle)
Data$m$ [kg], $g$ [m s$^{-2}$], $\Omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$]; initial position $2\,\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf k_1$ and velocity $\mathbf i_1$
Unknowns$\zeta(t)$, $\beta(t)$ and the reaction $N\,\mathbf n$
Applied forcesweight $-mg\,\mathbf k_1$
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)centrifugal and Coriolis; no origin or Euler terms (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial; uniform gravity; smooth contact; $\Omega$ constant
Readings(1) The initial data carry no units; they are read in SI units (metres and metres per second); with another unit of length the numbers of the constant of part (e) change accordingly. (2) The contact is taken as bilateral (the normal reaction may take either sign); the particle is on the inner surface of the cone, and the equilibria of part (f) need a positive reaction along the inward normal, which is checked there

(a) Degrees of freedom

Equation of the cone and number of degrees of freedom Law: elimination of the parameters; a holonomic constraint removes one coordinate Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.3; Problems.pdf, p. 25
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\beta &= \frac{x_1}{\zeta}, \quad \sin\beta = \frac{y_1}{2\zeta}, \quad \zeta = z_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. (5) solved for the parameters)} \\ \cos^2\beta + \sin^2\beta &= \frac{x_1^2}{z_1^2} + \frac{y_1^2}{4z_1^2} = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; x_1^2 + \frac{y_1^2}{4} - z_1^2 = 0 \quad &\text{(Pythagorean identity)} \\ \text{degrees of freedom} &= 3 - 1 = 2 \quad &\text{(one holonomic constraint, fixed in $S_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{x_1^2 + \frac{y_1^2}{4} - z_1^2 = 0, \qquad \text{2 degrees of freedom: } \zeta,\ \beta}$$

Units: $[x_1^2] = [y_1^2] = [z_1^2] = [\mathrm{L^2}]$

Meaning: each horizontal section at the height $\zeta$ is an ellipse of semi-axes $\zeta$ along $\mathbf i_1$ and $2\zeta$ along $\mathbf j_1$.

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. View from $+z_0$, with $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf k_1$ out of the paper ($\odot$), so $\mathbf j_0 = \mathbf k_0\times\mathbf i_0$ points up. $\mathbf i_1, \mathbf j_1$ are $\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0$ turned counter-clockwise by $\Omega t$: $\mathbf i_1$ has legs $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$ and $\sin\Omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$; $\mathbf j_1$ has legs $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$ and $\sin\Omega t$ along $-\mathbf i_0$, hence its minus sign.
Basis of the cone: rotation by Omega t about k0 Law: elementary rotation about the third axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

View from above, along $\mathbf k_0$, which points out of the paper (⊙). With $\mathbf i_0$ to the right, $\mathbf j_0$, the cross product of $\mathbf k_0$ and $\mathbf i_0$, points up the page. The figure measures $\Omega t$ from $x_0$ towards $y_0$, so the cone turns counterclockwise in this view. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\Omega t$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\Omega t$ along plus $\mathbf j_0$. $\mathbf j_1$ is $\mathbf j_0$ turned by the same angle; the counterclockwise turn carries its tip to the left, so its opposite leg $\sin\Omega t$ lies along minus $\mathbf i_0$ (the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf j_1 = -\sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles; axis)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\Omega t\cos\Omega t - \left(-\sin\Omega t\right)\sin\Omega t\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{3+3}$)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\Omega t + \sin^2\Omega t = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{12} = -\cos\Omega t\sin\Omega t + \sin\Omega t\cos\Omega t = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\Omega t & -\sin\Omega t & 0 \cr \sin\Omega t & \cos\Omega t & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: $[\Omega t] = [1]$

Meaning: these are the unit vectors of $\mathcal B_1$ in terms of $\mathcal B_0$, as the statement asks; at the start the matrix is the identity and the frames coincide.

Figure 2. Section $z_1 = \zeta$ seen from above ($\mathbf k_1$ out of the paper). $\beta$ is the polar angle of the point $B$ of the dashed auxiliary circle of radius $\zeta$; in the shaded triangle the legs are $\zeta\cos\beta$ and $\zeta\sin\beta$. The projection of $P$ has the same $x_1 = \zeta\cos\beta$ and twice the height, $y_1 = 2\zeta\sin\beta$; $\mathbf e_\beta$ (orange) is tangent to the ellipse.
Position vector of P: the elliptic section through P Law: position up the axis and across the horizontal section; auxiliary circle; stretch of the ellipse Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 25

The section at the height $\zeta$ is seen from above. Draw the auxiliary circle of radius $\zeta$ and its point $B$ at the polar angle $\beta$: in the shaded right triangle with hypotenuse $OB$, of length $\zeta$, the leg adjacent to $\beta$ is $\zeta\cos\beta$ along $\mathbf i_1$ and the opposite leg is $\zeta\sin\beta$ along $\mathbf j_1$. The point $P$ of the ellipse has the same abscissa and twice the ordinate: the ellipse is the circle stretched by 2 along $\mathbf j_1$. So $\beta$ is the polar angle of $B$, not of $P$; the polar angle $\alpha$ of the horizontal projection of $P$ is related to it below.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_0^O &= \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf r_0^P = \mathbf r_1^P = \zeta\,\mathbf k_1 + \zeta\cos\beta\,\mathbf i_1 + 2\zeta\sin\beta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(up the axis, then across the section; Eq. 3.16)} \\ \tan\alpha &= \frac{y_1}{x_1} = \frac{2\zeta\sin\beta}{\zeta\cos\beta} = 2\tan\beta \quad &\text{(polar angle of the projection)} \\ \zeta_0 &= 1, \quad \zeta_0\cos\beta_0 = 0, \quad 2\zeta_0\sin\beta_0 = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; \beta_0 = \tfrac{\pi}{2} \quad &\text{(initial position $2\,\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf k_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^P = \zeta\cos\beta\,\mathbf i_1 + 2\zeta\sin\beta\,\mathbf j_1 + \zeta\,\mathbf k_1, \qquad \zeta(0) = 1\ \mathrm{m}, \ \beta(0) = \tfrac{\pi}{2}}$$

Units: $[\zeta] = [\mathrm{L}]$; $[\beta] = [1]$

Meaning: the two angles coincide only on the axes of the ellipse; at the start the particle is at the end of the long axis of the section at height 1 m.

Figure 3. Principal vertical sections. Left, plane $x_1z_1$ ($\beta = 0$): legs $\zeta$ and $\zeta$, hypotenuse $\zeta\sqrt2$, $\mathbf e_\zeta = \mathbf i_1 + \mathbf k_1$. Right, plane $y_1z_1$ ($\beta = \pi/2$): legs $2\zeta$ and $\zeta$, hypotenuse $\zeta\sqrt5$, $\mathbf e_\zeta = 2\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf k_1$. The normal $\mathbf n$ is perpendicular to the generator in each plane.
Tangent vectors and unit normal of the cone Law: tangent vectors as partial derivatives of the position; normal as their vector product Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.9; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.10; Problems.pdf, p. 25

The determinant is expanded along its first row, with the cofactor signs plus, minus, plus.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_\zeta &= \frac{\partial\mathbf r_1^P}{\partial\zeta} = \cos\beta\,\mathbf i_1 + 2\sin\beta\,\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(along the generator through $P$)} \\ \frac{\partial\mathbf r_1^P}{\partial\beta} &= \zeta\,\mathbf e_\beta, \quad \mathbf e_\beta = -\sin\beta\,\mathbf i_1 + 2\cos\beta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(tangent to the ellipse; $\tfrac{d}{d\beta}\cos\beta = -\sin\beta$)} \\ \mathbf e_\zeta\times\mathbf e_\beta &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf i_1 & \mathbf j_1 & \mathbf k_1 \cr \cos\beta & 2\sin\beta & 1 \cr -\sin\beta & 2\cos\beta & 0 \end{vmatrix} = (+1)\left(0 - 2\cos\beta\right)\mathbf i_1 + (-1)\left(0 + \sin\beta\right)\mathbf j_1 + (+1)\left(2\cos^2\beta + 2\sin^2\beta\right)\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(first row; cofactor signs)} \\ \left|\mathbf e_\zeta\times\mathbf e_\beta\right|^2 &= 4\cos^2\beta + \sin^2\beta + 4 = 5 + 3\cos^2\beta \quad &\text{(squared length)} \\ \nabla\left(x_1^2 + \tfrac14 y_1^2 - z_1^2\right) &= \left(2x_1,\ \tfrac12 y_1,\ -2z_1\right) = -\zeta\left(-2\cos\beta,\ -\sin\beta,\ 2\right) \quad &\text{(check: parallel to the normal)} \\ \mathbf e_\zeta\cdot\mathbf e_\beta &= -\sin\beta\cos\beta + 4\sin\beta\cos\beta = 3\sin\beta\cos\beta \quad &\text{(the tangent vectors are not orthogonal in general)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf e_\zeta = \cos\beta\,\mathbf i_1 + 2\sin\beta\,\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf e_\beta = -\sin\beta\,\mathbf i_1 + 2\cos\beta\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf n = \frac{-2\cos\beta\,\mathbf i_1 - \sin\beta\,\mathbf j_1 + 2\,\mathbf k_1}{\sqrt{5 + 3\cos^2\beta}}}$$

Units: $[\mathbf e_\zeta] = [\mathbf e_\beta] = [\mathbf n] = [1]$

Meaning: the normal points into the cone and upwards. In the vertical plane $x_1z_1$ the generators make 45 degrees with the horizontal (legs $\zeta$ and $\zeta$, hypotenuse $\zeta\sqrt2$); in the plane $y_1z_1$ they rise one for two across (legs $2\zeta$ and $\zeta$, hypotenuse $\zeta\sqrt5$), as drawn.

Kinematics

Motion of the cone frame and derivatives of its unit vectors Law: angular velocity of a simple rotation; derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf v_0^O = \mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(rotation about the fixed vertical; $\Omega$ constant; vertex fixed)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\Omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 to 3.5)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0\right) &= -\Omega\sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \Omega\cos\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(check: chain rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\Omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0}$$

Units: $[\Omega] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: in $S_1$ the unit vectors are constant; in $S_0$ the horizontal ones turn with the cone.

(b) Position, velocity and acceleration in S1

Relative velocity and relative acceleration Law: time derivatives in $S_1$, where $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf k_1$ are constant; chain rule and product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24; Problems.pdf, p. 25
$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dt}\left(\zeta\cos\beta\right) &= \dot\zeta\cos\beta - \zeta\sin\beta\,\dot\beta, \quad \frac{d}{dt}\left(2\zeta\sin\beta\right) = 2\dot\zeta\sin\beta + 2\zeta\cos\beta\,\dot\beta \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule)} \\ \mathbf v_1^P &= \left(\dot\zeta\cos\beta - \zeta\dot\beta\sin\beta\right)\mathbf i_1 + 2\left(\dot\zeta\sin\beta + \zeta\dot\beta\cos\beta\right)\mathbf j_1 + \dot\zeta\,\mathbf k_1 = \dot\zeta\,\mathbf e_\zeta + \zeta\dot\beta\,\mathbf e_\beta \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.19; tangent to the cone)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\dot\zeta\cos\beta - \zeta\dot\beta\sin\beta\right) &= \ddot\zeta\cos\beta - \dot\zeta\dot\beta\sin\beta - \dot\zeta\dot\beta\sin\beta - \zeta\ddot\beta\sin\beta - \zeta\dot\beta^2\cos\beta \quad &\text{(product rule on each term)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\dot\zeta\sin\beta + \zeta\dot\beta\cos\beta\right) &= \ddot\zeta\sin\beta + \dot\zeta\dot\beta\cos\beta + \dot\zeta\dot\beta\cos\beta + \zeta\ddot\beta\cos\beta - \zeta\dot\beta^2\sin\beta \quad &\text{(product rule on each term)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf v_1^P = \left(\dot\zeta\cos\beta - \zeta\dot\beta\sin\beta\right)\mathbf i_1 + 2\left(\dot\zeta\sin\beta + \zeta\dot\beta\cos\beta\right)\mathbf j_1 + \dot\zeta\,\mathbf k_1, \cr \mathbf a_1^P = \left[\left(\ddot\zeta - \zeta\dot\beta^2\right)\cos\beta - \left(2\dot\zeta\dot\beta + \zeta\ddot\beta\right)\sin\beta\right]\mathbf i_1 + 2\left[\left(\ddot\zeta - \zeta\dot\beta^2\right)\sin\beta + \left(2\dot\zeta\dot\beta + \zeta\ddot\beta\right)\cos\beta\right]\mathbf j_1 + \ddot\zeta\,\mathbf k_1 \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[\dot\zeta] = [\zeta\dot\beta] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[\ddot\zeta] = [\zeta\dot\beta^2] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: with the unit vectors of $\mathcal B_1$ written in $\mathcal B_0$ in the rotation box, these are the vectors the statement asks for, as seen from $S_1$.

Initial rates Law: the velocity of part (b) written at the start, matched with the datum Source: Problems.pdf, p. 25
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_1^P(0) &= \left(\dot\zeta_0\cdot 0 - 1\cdot\dot\beta_0\cdot 1\right)\mathbf i_1 + 2\left(\dot\zeta_0\cdot 1 + 1\cdot\dot\beta_0\cdot 0\right)\mathbf j_1 + \dot\zeta_0\,\mathbf k_1 = -\dot\beta_0\,\mathbf i_1 + 2\dot\zeta_0\,\mathbf j_1 + \dot\zeta_0\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{($\zeta_0 = 1$, $\beta_0 = \pi/2$)} \\ -\dot\beta_0\,\mathbf i_1 + 2\dot\zeta_0\,\mathbf j_1 + \dot\zeta_0\,\mathbf k_1 &= \mathbf i_1 \;\Rightarrow\; \dot\beta_0 = -1\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}, \quad \dot\zeta_0 = 0 \quad &\text{(three components; the second agrees with the third)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\dot\zeta(0) = 0, \qquad \dot\beta(0) = -1\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}}$$

Units: $[\dot\beta] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: the initial velocity is horizontal and tangent to the section: the particle starts along the ellipse, towards decreasing $\beta$.

Absolute acceleration: centripetal and Coriolis terms Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the position written in the turning basis; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]

Write the position as $x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + z_1\,\mathbf k_1$ with the components of part (b); their time derivatives are the components of the relative velocity.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P &= \dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + \dot z_1\,\mathbf k_1 + x_1\Omega\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\Omega\,\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf v_1^P + \Omega\left(x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; derivatives of $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1^P}{dt}\right|_0 &= \mathbf a_1^P + \Omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; the turning of the basis inside $\mathbf v_1^P$)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left[\Omega\left(x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right)\right] &= \Omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) - \Omega^2\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; derivatives of $\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf i_1$)} \\ 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P &= 2\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + \dot z_1\,\mathbf k_1\right) = 2\Omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(the two equal terms: Coriolis)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) &= \Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\Omega\left(x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) = -\Omega^2\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(the last term: centripetal)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_0^P = \mathbf a_1^P - \Omega^2\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) + 2\Omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right)}$$

Units: $[\Omega^2x_1] = [\Omega\dot x_1] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: both rotation terms are horizontal; with the vertex fixed and the rate constant there are no origin or Euler terms.

Forces and Equations of Motion

Figure 4. Forces on $P$ in $S_1$ at the start ($\zeta = 1$, $\beta = \pi/2$). In the vertical plane $y_1z_1$: the weight, the reaction $N\,\mathbf n$ normal to the generator and the centrifugal force (dashed), away from the axis. Seen from above: the Coriolis force $-2m\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf v_1^P$ (dashed) for the initial velocity $\mathbf i_1$.

(c) Forces acting on P as seen from S1

Actual and inertia forces on the particle Law: weight; smooth reaction along the normal; inertia forces of a non-inertial frame Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.11; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf W &= -mg\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf N = N\,\mathbf n \quad &\text{(weight; smooth contact)} \\ \mathbf F_A &= -m\,\mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf F_E = -m\,\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(vertex fixed; $\Omega$ constant)} \\ \mathbf F_C &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) = m\Omega^2\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) = m\Omega^2\zeta\left(\cos\beta\,\mathbf i_1 + 2\sin\beta\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(composition box times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR} &= -2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P = 2m\Omega\left(\dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1 - \dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(composition box times $-m$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf W = -mg\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf N = N\,\frac{-2\cos\beta\,\mathbf i_1 - \sin\beta\,\mathbf j_1 + 2\,\mathbf k_1}{\sqrt{5 + 3\cos^2\beta}}, \quad \mathbf F_C = m\Omega^2\zeta\left(\cos\beta\,\mathbf i_1 + 2\sin\beta\,\mathbf j_1\right), \cr \mathbf F_{COR} = 4m\Omega\left(\dot\zeta\sin\beta + \zeta\dot\beta\cos\beta\right)\mathbf i_1 - 2m\Omega\left(\dot\zeta\cos\beta - \zeta\dot\beta\sin\beta\right)\mathbf j_1 \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[mg] = [m\Omega^2\zeta] = [m\Omega\dot\zeta] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: two actual forces and two inertia forces; the centrifugal force points horizontally away from the axis, the Coriolis force is horizontal and normal to the horizontal relative velocity. Newton's second law in $S_1$ is the sum of the four equal to the mass times the relative acceleration (Eq. 4.63).

(d) Two equations of motion free of the reaction

Projections on the two tangent vectors Law: Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame projected on $\mathbf e_\zeta$ and $\mathbf e_\beta$, which are normal to the reaction Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.11; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; Problems.pdf, p. 25

Write $a$ for $\ddot\zeta - \zeta\dot\beta^2$ and $b$ for $2\dot\zeta\dot\beta + \zeta\ddot\beta$, the two brackets of the relative acceleration.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf n\cdot\mathbf e_\zeta &\propto -2\cos^2\beta - 2\sin^2\beta + 2 = 0, \quad \mathbf n\cdot\mathbf e_\beta \propto 2\cos\beta\sin\beta - 2\sin\beta\cos\beta = 0 \quad &\text{(the reaction drops out)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P\cdot\mathbf e_\zeta &= a\left(\cos^2\beta + 4\sin^2\beta\right) + b\left(-\sin\beta\cos\beta + 4\sin\beta\cos\beta\right) + \ddot\zeta = \ddot\zeta + a\left(1 + 3\sin^2\beta\right) + 3b\sin\beta\cos\beta \quad &\text{(components of part (b))} \\ \mathbf W\cdot\mathbf e_\zeta &= -mg, \quad \mathbf F_C\cdot\mathbf e_\zeta = m\Omega^2\zeta\left(\cos^2\beta + 4\sin^2\beta\right) = m\Omega^2\zeta\left(1 + 3\sin^2\beta\right) \quad &\text{(weight; centrifugal)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR}\cdot\mathbf e_\zeta &= 4m\Omega\left(\dot\zeta\sin\beta + \zeta\dot\beta\cos\beta\right)\cos\beta - 4m\Omega\left(\dot\zeta\cos\beta - \zeta\dot\beta\sin\beta\right)\sin\beta = 4m\Omega\zeta\dot\beta \quad &\text{(the $\dot\zeta$ terms cancel)} \\ \mathbf a_1^P\cdot\mathbf e_\beta &= a\left(-\sin\beta\cos\beta + 4\sin\beta\cos\beta\right) + b\left(\sin^2\beta + 4\cos^2\beta\right) = 3a\sin\beta\cos\beta + b\left(1 + 3\cos^2\beta\right) \quad &\text{(components of part (b))} \\ \mathbf W\cdot\mathbf e_\beta &= 0, \quad \mathbf F_C\cdot\mathbf e_\beta = m\Omega^2\zeta\left(-\cos\beta\sin\beta + 4\sin\beta\cos\beta\right) = 3m\Omega^2\zeta\sin\beta\cos\beta \quad &\text{(weight; centrifugal)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR}\cdot\mathbf e_\beta &= -4m\Omega\left(\dot\zeta\sin\beta + \zeta\dot\beta\cos\beta\right)\sin\beta - 4m\Omega\left(\dot\zeta\cos\beta - \zeta\dot\beta\sin\beta\right)\cos\beta = -4m\Omega\dot\zeta \quad &\text{(the $\dot\beta$ terms cancel)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \ddot\zeta + \left(\ddot\zeta - \zeta\dot\beta^2\right)\left(1 + 3\sin^2\beta\right) + 3\left(2\dot\zeta\dot\beta + \zeta\ddot\beta\right)\cos\beta\sin\beta = -g + \Omega^2\zeta\left(1 + 3\sin^2\beta\right) + 4\Omega\zeta\dot\beta \cr 3\left(\ddot\zeta - \zeta\dot\beta^2\right)\cos\beta\sin\beta + \left(2\dot\zeta\dot\beta + \zeta\ddot\beta\right)\left(1 + 3\cos^2\beta\right) = 3\Omega^2\zeta\cos\beta\sin\beta - 4\Omega\dot\zeta \end{gathered}}$$

Units: every term $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: two second-order equations for $\zeta$ and $\beta$ alone, with the initial conditions $\zeta$ equal to 1 m, $\beta$ a quarter turn, zero rate of $\zeta$ and minus 1 rad/s for the rate of $\beta$. The Coriolis terms couple them antisymmetrically. The third projection, on $\mathbf n$, would give the reaction.

Answers and Checks

(e) A conservation law: the energy of the relative motion

Why the energy in S1 is conserved, and its value Law: power of each force on the relative velocity; potentials of the weight and of the centrifugal force; initial conditions Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]

Two reasons. First, the forces that do no work in $S_1$: the reaction (the cone is at rest in $S_1$ and the relative velocity is tangent to it), the Coriolis force (normal to the relative velocity), and the origin and Euler forces, which vanish. Second, the forces that work have potentials of the position in $S_1$: the weight, constant in $S_1$ because $\mathbf k_1$ is the fixed vertical, and the centrifugal force, because the rate is constant and the axis fixed. The squared distance to the axis is the sum of the squares of $x_1$ and $y_1$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf N\cdot\mathbf v_1^P &= N\,\mathbf n\cdot\left(\dot\zeta\,\mathbf e_\zeta + \zeta\dot\beta\,\mathbf e_\beta\right) = 0, \quad \mathbf F_{COR}\cdot\mathbf v_1^P = 2m\Omega\left(\dot y_1\dot x_1 - \dot x_1\dot y_1\right) = 0 \quad &\text{(no power)} \\ V_1 &= mgz_1 - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2\left(x_1^2 + y_1^2\right) = mg\zeta - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2\zeta^2\left(\cos^2\beta + 4\sin^2\beta\right) = mg\zeta - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2\zeta^2\left(1 + 3\sin^2\beta\right) \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.14; Slide 30)} \\ \left|\mathbf v_1^P\right|^2 &= \left(\dot\zeta\cos\beta - \zeta\dot\beta\sin\beta\right)^2 + 4\left(\dot\zeta\sin\beta + \zeta\dot\beta\cos\beta\right)^2 + \dot\zeta^2 \quad &\text{(components of part (b))} \\ &= \left(2 + 3\sin^2\beta\right)\dot\zeta^2 + \left(1 + 3\cos^2\beta\right)\zeta^2\dot\beta^2 + 6\zeta\dot\zeta\dot\beta\sin\beta\cos\beta \quad &\text{(squares expanded; cross terms $-2 + 8 = 6$)} \\ \frac{dE_1^P}{dt} &= \dot\zeta\left(m\,\mathbf a_1^P - \mathbf W - \mathbf F_C\right)\cdot\mathbf e_\zeta + \zeta\dot\beta\left(m\,\mathbf a_1^P - \mathbf W - \mathbf F_C\right)\cdot\mathbf e_\beta = \dot\zeta\left(4m\Omega\zeta\dot\beta\right) + \zeta\dot\beta\left(-4m\Omega\dot\zeta\right) = 0 \quad &\text{(check with the two equations of part (d))} \\ E_1^P(0) &= \tfrac12 m\left|\mathbf i_1\right|^2 + mg\cdot 1 - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2\cdot 1^2\left(1 + 3\cdot 1\right) = m\left(\tfrac12 + g - 2\Omega^2\right) \quad &\text{(initial data, SI units)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\frac{m}{2}\left[\left(2 + 3\sin^2\beta\right)\dot\zeta^2 + \left(1 + 3\cos^2\beta\right)\zeta^2\dot\beta^2 + 6\zeta\dot\zeta\dot\beta\sin\beta\cos\beta\right] + mg\zeta - \frac{m}{2}\Omega^2\zeta^2\left(1 + 3\sin^2\beta\right) = m\left(\tfrac12 + g - 2\Omega^2\right)}$$

Units: $[m\dot\zeta^2] = [mg\zeta] = [m\Omega^2\zeta^2] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$; the constant is $m(\tfrac12\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}} + g\cdot 1\ \mathrm{m} - 2\Omega^2\cdot 1\ \mathrm{m^2})$

Meaning: the energy of the motion relative to the cone is constant. The angular momentum about the axis is not: the section is not circular, so the normal reaction has a moment about the axis (next box).

Why the angular momentum about the axis is not conserved Law: moment of the reaction about the vertical axis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.48; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.53

The weight is parallel to the axis; the reaction is the only force with an axial moment. Its component along $\mathbf k_1$ is the first component of the position times the second of the force minus the second times the first.

$$\begin{aligned} \left(\mathbf r_1^P\times\mathbf N\right)\cdot\mathbf k_1 &= \frac{N}{\sqrt{5 + 3\cos^2\beta}}\left[\zeta\cos\beta\left(-\sin\beta\right) - 2\zeta\sin\beta\left(-2\cos\beta\right)\right] = \frac{3N\zeta\sin\beta\cos\beta}{\sqrt{5 + 3\cos^2\beta}} \quad &\text{(components of the position and of the normal)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{M_{O} \cdot\mathbf k_1 = \frac{3N\zeta\sin\beta\cos\beta}{\sqrt{5 + 3\cos^2\beta}} \ne 0 \text{ in general}}$$

Units: $[N\zeta] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: only on the principal planes of the cone, where the product of the sine and cosine vanishes, does the reaction pass through the axis; on a circular cone it always would.

(f) Equilibrium positions in S1 for positive zeta

Equilibria and the reaction there Law: relative equilibrium: constant coordinates, so the rates and accelerations vanish in the two equations of part (d) Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.32; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6; Problems.pdf, p. 25
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_\beta:\ 0 &= 3\Omega^2\zeta\cos\beta\sin\beta = \tfrac32\Omega^2\zeta\sin 2\beta \;\Rightarrow\; \beta = 0,\ \tfrac{\pi}{2},\ \pi,\ \tfrac{3\pi}{2} \quad &\text{($\zeta \gt 0$, $\Omega \ne 0$)} \\ \mathbf e_\zeta:\ 0 &= -g + \Omega^2\zeta\left(1 + 3\sin^2\beta\right) \;\Rightarrow\; \zeta_{eq} = \frac{g}{\Omega^2\left(1 + 3\sin^2\beta\right)} \quad &\text{(second equation)} \\ \beta = 0, \pi:\quad \zeta_{eq} &= \frac{g}{\Omega^2}; \quad \beta = \tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{3\pi}{2}:\quad \zeta_{eq} = \frac{g}{4\Omega^2} \quad &\text{($\sin^2\beta$ equal to 0 or 1)} \\ \beta = 0:\quad \mathbf 0 &= -mg\,\mathbf k_1 + m\Omega^2\zeta\,\mathbf i_1 + \frac{N}{\sqrt8}\left(-2\,\mathbf i_1 + 2\,\mathbf k_1\right) \;\Rightarrow\; N = \sqrt2\,mg \gt 0 \quad &\text{(check by the full balance, $\mathbf k_1$ component)} \\ \beta = \tfrac{\pi}{2}:\quad \mathbf 0 &= -mg\,\mathbf k_1 + 2m\Omega^2\zeta\,\mathbf j_1 + \frac{N}{\sqrt5}\left(-\mathbf j_1 + 2\,\mathbf k_1\right) \;\Rightarrow\; N = \tfrac{\sqrt5}{2}mg \gt 0, \ \zeta = \frac{g}{4\Omega^2} \quad &\text{(check by the full balance)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf r_1^P = \frac{g}{\Omega^2}\left(\pm\mathbf i_1 + \mathbf k_1\right) \ \ (\beta = 0, \pi), \qquad \mathbf r_1^P = \pm\frac{g}{2\Omega^2}\,\mathbf j_1 + \frac{g}{4\Omega^2}\,\mathbf k_1 \ \ \left(\beta = \tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[g/\Omega^2] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: the four equilibria lie on the generators of the two principal vertical planes, the only places where the normal lies in the vertical plane through the axis and can balance the weight and the horizontal centrifugal force with nothing left along the section. On the steeper generators (45 degrees) the particle sits four times higher than on the flatter ones. The reaction is positive along the inward normal at all four, so a particle on the inner surface stays in contact there.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Degrees of freedom2 ($\zeta$, $\beta$); the cone is $x_1^2 + y_1^2/4 - z_1^2 = 0$
(b) Kinematics in $S_1$$\mathbf r_1^P = \zeta\cos\beta\,\mathbf i_1 + 2\zeta\sin\beta\,\mathbf j_1 + \zeta\,\mathbf k_1$; $\mathbf v_1^P$, $\mathbf a_1^P$ as boxed in part (b); $\mathbf i_1 = \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0$, $\mathbf j_1 = -\sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0$, $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$
(c) Forces$-mg\,\mathbf k_1$; $N\,\mathbf n$, $\mathbf n = (-2\cos\beta, -\sin\beta, 2)/\sqrt{5 + 3\cos^2\beta}$; $\mathbf F_C = m\Omega^2\zeta(\cos\beta\,\mathbf i_1 + 2\sin\beta\,\mathbf j_1)$; $\mathbf F_{COR} = 4m\Omega(\dot\zeta\sin\beta + \zeta\dot\beta\cos\beta)\,\mathbf i_1 - 2m\Omega(\dot\zeta\cos\beta - \zeta\dot\beta\sin\beta)\,\mathbf j_1$; origin and Euler forces zero
(d) Equations of motionthe two boxed equations of part (d); initial conditions $\zeta(0) = 1$ m, $\beta(0) = \pi/2$, $\dot\zeta(0) = 0$, $\dot\beta(0) = -1$ rad/s
(e) Conservation lawenergy in $S_1$: $\frac m2[(2 + 3\sin^2\beta)\dot\zeta^2 + (1 + 3\cos^2\beta)\zeta^2\dot\beta^2 + 6\zeta\dot\zeta\dot\beta\sin\beta\cos\beta] + mg\zeta - \frac12 m\Omega^2\zeta^2(1 + 3\sin^2\beta) = m(\frac12 + g - 2\Omega^2)$ (SI units); in general units, with $z_0$ one unit of length and $v_0$ one unit of velocity, the constant is $m(\frac12 v_0^2 + gz_0 - 2\Omega^2z_0^2)$
(f) Equilibria$\beta = 0, \pi$: $\zeta = g/\Omega^2$; $\beta = \pi/2, 3\pi/2$: $\zeta = g/(4\Omega^2)$

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 75 prints the two equations of part (d); they coincide term by term (box below). The key prints nothing for the other parts; the energy is checked against the two equations, and the equilibria by the full force balance in part (f).

Comparison with the official key Law: term-by-term comparison Source: Problems.pdf, p. 75
$$\begin{aligned} \text{key, } \mathbf e_\zeta:\ \ddot\zeta + \left(\ddot\zeta - \zeta\dot\beta^2\right)\left(1 + 3\sin^2\beta\right) + 3\left(2\dot\zeta\dot\beta + \zeta\ddot\beta\right)\cos\beta\sin\beta &= -g + \Omega^2\zeta\left(1 + 3\sin^2\beta\right) + 4\Omega\zeta\dot\beta \quad &\text{(first equation of part (d))} \\ \text{key, } \mathbf e_\beta:\ 3\left(\ddot\zeta - \zeta\dot\beta^2\right)\cos\beta\sin\beta + \left(2\dot\zeta\dot\beta + \zeta\ddot\beta\right)\left(1 + 3\cos^2\beta\right) &= 3\Omega^2\zeta\cos\beta\sin\beta - 4\Omega\dot\zeta \quad &\text{(second equation of part (d))} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{both equations coincide with the key}}$$

Units: $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the signs of the Coriolis terms confirm the sense of rotation read from the figure.

Limiting cases Law: the results at extreme values of the data Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63
$$\begin{aligned} \Omega \to 0:\quad \zeta_{eq} &\to \infty \quad &\text{(a fixed smooth cone with its vertex down has no equilibrium above the vertex)} \\ \Omega \to 0:\quad E_1^P &\to \tfrac12 m\left|\mathbf v_1^P\right|^2 + mg\zeta \quad &\text{(ordinary energy of a fixed cone)} \\ \beta = \tfrac{\pi}{2}:\quad \mathbf e_\zeta &= 2\,\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf n = \frac{-\mathbf j_1 + 2\,\mathbf k_1}{\sqrt5}, \quad \mathbf e_\zeta\cdot\mathbf n = \frac{-2 + 2}{\sqrt5} = 0 \quad &\text{(generator of the plane $y_1z_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\Omega \to 0: \ \text{no equilibrium for positive } \zeta, \text{ and the energy becomes the ordinary one}}$$

Units: $[g/\Omega^2] = [\mathrm{L}]$

Meaning: the rotation is what holds the particle up the wall of the cone.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf (PDF page 25); key on PDF page 75
Problem 40

Spring-Coupled Particles on a Vertical Axis and a Revolving Ring

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 28
Two Particles in a Rotating Frame

Two heavy particles $P$ and $Q$, each of mass $m$, are connected with a spring of stiffness $k$ as shown in the figure. An inertial reference frame $S_0$ is defined with origin $O$ and vector basis $\mathcal{B}_0 = \{\mathbf{i}_0, \mathbf{j}_0, \mathbf{k}_0\}$. Particle $P$ slides without friction along the vertical axis, while particle $Q$ slides without friction on a ring of radius $R$ contained in the horizontal plane defined by $O$, $\mathbf{i}_0$ and $\mathbf{j}_0$. The center $D$ of this ring is located a distance $\ell$ from $O$ and rotates around the vertical axis of $S_0$ with a known constant angular rate $\Omega$. A rotating reference frame $S_1$ is defined so that the $\mathbf{j}_1$ vector follows the position of $D$. We define the generalized coordinates $\zeta$ (vertical position of $P$) and $\phi$ (angle of $Q$ on the circle from $\mathbf{j}_1$) as shown.

  • (a)
    How many degrees of freedom does the system have? Define the vectors $\mathbf{i}_1$, $\mathbf{j}_1$ and $\mathbf{k}_1$ in terms of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}_0$.
  • (b)
    Write down the general expression of the position, velocity, and acceleration of $P$ and $Q$ with respect to $S_1$ in terms of $\zeta$, $\phi$ and their derivatives.
  • (c)
    Identify and write down the general expression of all the forces acting on $P$ and $Q$.
  • (d)
    Using $S_1$ for your analysis, write down the scalar equations of motion of $P$ and $Q$.
  • (e)
    Starting from these equations, write down a system of two differential equations for $\zeta$ and $\phi$, that do not depend on any other unknowns of the problem.
  • (f)
    Find one conservation law of the problem (i.e., a first integral of motion) in reference frame $S_1$.
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

Two heavy particles $P$ and $Q$ of mass $m$ are joined by a spring of stiffness $k$. $P$ slides without friction on the vertical axis of $S_0$; $Q$ slides without friction on a horizontal ring of radius $R$, in the plane of $\mathbf i_0$ and $\mathbf j_0$, whose centre $D$ is at the distance $\ell$ from $O$ and revolves about the vertical at the constant rate $\Omega$ (Problems.pdf, p. 28). The statement asks for the degrees of freedom and the basis of $S_1$, the position, velocity and acceleration of both particles in $S_1$, the forces, the scalar equations of motion in $S_1$, two equations for $\zeta$ and $\phi$ alone, and one first integral. The ring is at rest in $S_1$, so the solution works there, with the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2 and the inertia forces of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$, $\mathbf k_0$ vertical, up; gravity $-g\,\mathbf k_0$
Moving frame$S_1 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_1\}$, same origin, $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$, $\mathbf j_1$ from $O$ towards $D$; it turns by $\Omega t$ about $\mathbf k_0$, from $\mathbf i_0$ towards $\mathbf j_0$ (figure), and coincides with $S_0$ at $t = 0$
Ring basis at $Q$$\{\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\phi, \mathbf k_1\}$: $\mathbf e_r$ from $D$ towards $Q$, $\mathbf e_\phi$ tangent to the ring in the sense of growing $\phi$ (deduced below)
Coordinates$\zeta$, height of $P$ on the axis; $\phi$, angle of $DQ$ measured from $\mathbf j_1$ about $\mathbf k_1$
Data$m$ [kg], $k$ [N m$^{-1}$], $R$ [m], $\ell$ [m], $\Omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$], $g$ [m s$^{-2}$]
Unknowns$\zeta(t)$, $\phi(t)$ and four reaction components $N_1, N_2$ (axis on $P$), $N_3, N_4$ (ring on $Q$)
Applied forcesweights $-mg\,\mathbf k_1$; spring between $P$ and $Q$
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)centrifugal and Coriolis; no origin or Euler terms (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial; uniform gravity; massless linear spring; smooth bilateral contacts; $\Omega$ constant; the ring is rigidly attached to $S_1$
Readings(1) The statement gives no natural length; the spring is read as one of zero natural length, force on $P$ equal to $k\,\overrightarrow{PQ}$. With a natural length $L_0$ the factor $k$ becomes $k(1 - L_0/\lvert PQ\rvert)$ in every spring term and the two equations of part (e) couple (box at the end of part (e)). (2) $\phi$ is read from the figure as positive from $\mathbf j_1$ towards $-\mathbf i_1$ (counterclockwise seen from above); this is also the sense in the official ring reaction, which contains $-\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\phi\,\mathbf j_1$. With the opposite sense $\phi$ changes sign everywhere and the equations of part (e) keep their form

(a) Degrees of freedom

Coordinates minus independent constraints Law: each holonomic constraint removes one coordinate; the motion of $D$ is prescribed and adds none Source: Notes.pdf, Ch. 6; Notes.pdf, Sec. 6.2; Problems.pdf, p. 28

In $S_1$ write $(x_1^P, y_1^P, z_1^P)$ and $(x_1^Q, y_1^Q, z_1^Q)$ for the Cartesian coordinates of the two particles.

$$\begin{aligned} P:&\quad x_1^P = 0, \quad y_1^P = 0 \quad &\text{(on the vertical axis: two constraints)} \\ Q:&\quad z_1^Q = 0, \quad \left(x_1^Q\right)^2 + \left(y_1^Q - \ell\right)^2 - R^2 = 0 \quad &\text{(horizontal plane and ring: two constraints)} \\ \text{degrees of freedom} &= 3 + 3 - 4 = 2 \quad &\text{(six coordinates, four constraints)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{2 degrees of freedom: } \zeta,\ \phi}$$

Units: $[\zeta] = [\mathrm L]$, $[\phi] = [1]$

Meaning: one coordinate per particle; the four constraints become the four reaction components.

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. View from $+z_0$, with $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf k_1$ out of the paper ($\odot$), so $\mathbf j_0 = \mathbf k_0\times\mathbf i_0$ points up. $\mathbf i_1, \mathbf j_1$ are $\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0$ turned counter-clockwise by $\Omega t$, and $\mathbf j_1$ points from $O$ to the centre $D$ of the ring. $\mathbf j_1$ has legs $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$ and $\sin\Omega t$ along $-\mathbf i_0$, hence its minus sign.
Basis of S1: rotation by Omega t about k0 Law: elementary rotation about the third axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

View from above, along $\mathbf k_0$, which points out of the paper (⊙). With $\mathbf i_0$ to the right, $\mathbf j_0$, the cross product of $\mathbf k_0$ and $\mathbf i_0$, points up the page. The figure measures $\Omega t$ from $\mathbf i_0$ towards $\mathbf j_0$, so $S_1$ turns counterclockwise in this view. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\Omega t$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\Omega t$ along plus $\mathbf j_0$. $\mathbf j_1$, the direction of $D$, is $\mathbf j_0$ turned by the same angle; the counterclockwise turn carries its tip to the left, so its opposite leg $\sin\Omega t$ lies along minus $\mathbf i_0$ (the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf j_1 = -\sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles; axis)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\Omega t\cos\Omega t - \left(-\sin\Omega t\right)\sin\Omega t\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{3+3}$)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\Omega t + \sin^2\Omega t = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{12} = -\cos\Omega t\sin\Omega t + \sin\Omega t\cos\Omega t = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\Omega t & -\sin\Omega t & 0 \cr \sin\Omega t & \cos\Omega t & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: $[\Omega t] = [1]$

Meaning: these are the vectors of $\mathcal B_1$ in terms of $\mathcal B_0$, as part (a) asks; the third row and column hold the fixed vertical.

Figure 2. Plane of the ring, fixed in $S_1$, seen from above ($\mathbf k_1$ out of the paper). $\overrightarrow{OQ} = \ell\,\mathbf j_1 + R\,\mathbf e_r$. In the shaded right triangle $DFQ$ the hypotenuse is $R$, the leg along $\mathbf j_1$ is $R\cos\phi$ and the leg along $-\mathbf i_1$ is $R\sin\phi$. $\mathbf i_1, \mathbf j_1$ in blue, $\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\phi$ in orange.
Position of Q: through the centre D of the ring Law: vector sum of positions; right triangle $DFQ$; standard polar angle Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 28

The plane of the ring is seen from above ($\mathbf k_1$ out of the paper, ⊙), with $\mathbf i_1$ to the right and $\mathbf j_1$ up, towards $D$. The distance that stays constant is $DQ$, so the path goes from $O$ to $D$ and then to $Q$. Let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $Q$ to the line through $D$ along $\mathbf j_1$. In the shaded right triangle $DFQ$ (right angle at $F$) the hypotenuse is $DQ$, of length $R$; the leg adjacent to $\phi$ is $DF$, of length $R\cos\phi$, along plus $\mathbf j_1$; the opposite leg is $FQ$, of length $R\sin\phi$, along minus $\mathbf i_1$, because a counterclockwise turn from $\mathbf j_1$ carries the point to the left.

$$\begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{OD} &= \ell\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \overrightarrow{DQ} = \overrightarrow{DF} + \overrightarrow{FQ} = R\cos\phi\,\mathbf j_1 - R\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(triangle $DFQ$)} \\ \mathbf e_r &= \frac{\overrightarrow{DQ}}{R} = -\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\phi\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(unit vector from $D$ to $Q$)} \\ \mathbf r_1^Q &= \overrightarrow{OD} + \overrightarrow{DQ} = -R\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \left(\ell + R\cos\phi\right)\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.16 with the common origin $O$)} \\ \cos\left(\phi + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) &= \cos\phi\cdot 0 - \sin\phi\cdot 1 = -\sin\phi, \quad \sin\left(\phi + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \sin\phi\cdot 0 + \cos\phi\cdot 1 = \cos\phi \quad &\text{(sum formulas)} \\ \mathbf e_r &= \cos\psi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\psi\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \psi = \phi + \tfrac{\pi}{2} \quad &\text{(standard polar angle about $D$, from $\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \mathbf r_1^P &= \zeta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{($P$ on the axis at the height $\zeta$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^P = \zeta\,\mathbf k_1, \qquad \mathbf r_1^Q = \ell\,\mathbf j_1 + R\,\mathbf e_r = -R\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \left(\ell + R\cos\phi\right)\mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[\ell] = [R] = [\zeta] = [\mathrm L]$

Meaning: $\phi$ is the polar angle about $D$ counted from the direction $OD$; at zero $Q$ is the point of the ring farthest from the axis, at a half turn the nearest.

Ring basis and its derivatives Law: tangent vector as the derivative of the radial unit vector; handedness by the vector product Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.5

The determinant is expanded along its first row, with the cofactor signs plus, minus, plus.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_\phi &= \frac{d\mathbf e_r}{d\phi} = -\cos\phi\,\mathbf i_1 - \sin\phi\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{($\tfrac{d}{d\phi}(-\sin\phi) = -\cos\phi$, $\tfrac{d}{d\phi}\cos\phi = -\sin\phi$)} \\ \mathbf e_r\cdot\mathbf e_\phi &= \sin\phi\cos\phi - \cos\phi\sin\phi = 0, \quad \left|\mathbf e_\phi\right|^2 = \cos^2\phi + \sin^2\phi = 1 \quad &\text{(orthonormal)} \\ \mathbf e_r\times\mathbf e_\phi &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf i_1 & \mathbf j_1 & \mathbf k_1 \cr -\sin\phi & \cos\phi & 0 \cr -\cos\phi & -\sin\phi & 0 \end{vmatrix} = (+1)(0)\,\mathbf i_1 + (-1)(0)\,\mathbf j_1 + (+1)\left(\sin^2\phi + \cos^2\phi\right)\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(first row; cofactor signs)} \\ \mathbf j_1 &= \left(\mathbf j_1\cdot\mathbf e_r\right)\mathbf e_r + \left(\mathbf j_1\cdot\mathbf e_\phi\right)\mathbf e_\phi = \cos\phi\,\mathbf e_r - \sin\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi \quad &\text{(projections)} \\ \mathbf i_1 &= \left(\mathbf i_1\cdot\mathbf e_r\right)\mathbf e_r + \left(\mathbf i_1\cdot\mathbf e_\phi\right)\mathbf e_\phi = -\sin\phi\,\mathbf e_r - \cos\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi \quad &\text{(projections)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_r}{dt}\right|_1 &= \frac{d\mathbf e_r}{d\phi}\,\frac{d\phi}{dt} = \dot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\phi}{dt}\right|_1 = \frac{d\mathbf e_\phi}{d\phi}\,\frac{d\phi}{dt} = \dot\phi\left(\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 - \cos\phi\,\mathbf j_1\right) = -\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(chain rule; $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$ constant in $S_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf e_\phi = -\cos\phi\,\mathbf i_1 - \sin\phi\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf e_r\times\mathbf e_\phi = \mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_r}{dt}\right|_1 = \dot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\phi}{dt}\right|_1 = -\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_r}$$

Units: $[\mathbf e_r] = [\mathbf e_\phi] = [1]$; $[\dot\phi] = [\mathrm T^{-1}]$

Meaning: $\{\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\phi, \mathbf k_1\}$ is a right-handed orthonormal basis attached to $Q$; $\mathbf e_\phi$ is the only direction in which the ring lets $Q$ move.

Kinematics

Motion of S1 and derivatives of its unit vectors Law: angular velocity of a simple rotation; derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf v_0^O = \mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(rotation about the fixed vertical; $\Omega$ constant; $O$ fixed)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\Omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 to 3.5)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(-\sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0\right) &= -\Omega\cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 - \Omega\sin\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0 = -\Omega\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(check: chain rule on $\mathbf j_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\Omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0}$$

Units: $[\Omega] = [\mathrm T^{-1}]$

Meaning: in $S_1$ the three unit vectors are constant; in $S_0$ the two horizontal ones turn with the ring.

(b) Position, velocity and acceleration of P and Q in S1

Relative kinematics of both particles Law: time derivatives in $S_1$; product rule and the derivatives of the ring basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24; Problems.pdf, p. 28

$\overrightarrow{OD}$ is constant in $S_1$, so only $R\,\mathbf e_r$ changes for $Q$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_1^P &= \left.\frac{d}{dt}\left(\zeta\,\mathbf k_1\right)\right|_1 = \dot\zeta\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf a_1^P = \ddot\zeta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1$ constant in $S_1$)} \\ \mathbf v_1^Q &= \left.\frac{d}{dt}\left(\ell\,\mathbf j_1 + R\,\mathbf e_r\right)\right|_1 = R\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi \quad &\text{(derivative of $\mathbf e_r$)} \\ &= -R\dot\phi\cos\phi\,\mathbf i_1 - R\dot\phi\sin\phi\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf e_\phi$ in $\mathcal B_1$)} \\ \mathbf a_1^Q &= R\ddot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi + R\dot\phi\left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\phi}{dt}\right|_1 = R\ddot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi - R\dot\phi^2\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(product rule; derivative of $\mathbf e_\phi$)} \\ &= \left(-R\ddot\phi\cos\phi + R\dot\phi^2\sin\phi\right)\mathbf i_1 - \left(R\ddot\phi\sin\phi + R\dot\phi^2\cos\phi\right)\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf e_r$, $\mathbf e_\phi$ in $\mathcal B_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf r_1^P = \zeta\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf v_1^P = \dot\zeta\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf a_1^P = \ddot\zeta\,\mathbf k_1, \cr \mathbf r_1^Q = \ell\,\mathbf j_1 + R\,\mathbf e_r, \quad \mathbf v_1^Q = R\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi, \quad \mathbf a_1^Q = R\ddot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi - R\dot\phi^2\,\mathbf e_r \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[\dot\zeta] = [R\dot\phi] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[\ddot\zeta] = [R\ddot\phi] = [R\dot\phi^2] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: $P$ moves on a straight line and $Q$ on a circle of radius $R$, with tangential and centripetal parts about $D$.

Absolute acceleration: transport and Coriolis terms as they arise Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of a position written in the turning basis; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]

Write the position of a point in the plane of the ring as $x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1$ (for $Q$, the components of $\mathbf r_1^Q$); the time derivatives of the components are the components of the relative velocity.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0 &= \dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + x_1\Omega\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\Omega\,\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf v_1 + \Omega\left(x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; derivatives of $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \ddot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \ddot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + \Omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) = \mathbf a_1 + \Omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; the basis turns inside $\mathbf v_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left[\Omega\left(x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right)\right] &= \Omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) - \Omega^2\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; $\Omega$ constant)} \\ \mathbf a_0 &= \mathbf a_1 + 2\Omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) - \Omega^2\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(the two equal terms add: Coriolis; the last: centripetal)} \\ 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^Q &= 2\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times R\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi = 2\Omega R\dot\phi\left(-\cos\phi\,\mathbf j_1 + \sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1\right) = -2\Omega R\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\mathbf i_1$)} \\ -\Omega^2\,\mathbf r_1^Q &= -\Omega^2\left(\ell\,\mathbf j_1 + R\,\mathbf e_r\right) = -\Omega^2\left(\ell\cos\phi + R\right)\mathbf e_r + \Omega^2\ell\sin\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi \quad &\text{($\mathbf j_1$ in the ring basis)} \\ \mathbf a_0^P &= \left.\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\left(\zeta\,\mathbf k_1\right)\right|_0 = \ddot\zeta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1$ does not turn)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_0^Q = \left(-R\dot\phi^2 - 2\Omega R\dot\phi - \Omega^2\left(\ell\cos\phi + R\right)\right)\mathbf e_r + \left(R\ddot\phi + \Omega^2\ell\sin\phi\right)\mathbf e_\phi, \qquad \mathbf a_0^P = \ddot\zeta\,\mathbf k_1}$$

Units: $[\Omega R\dot\phi] = [\Omega^2\ell] = [R\dot\phi^2] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the Coriolis term collects two equal halves, one from the turning of the basis inside the relative velocity and one from the change of the transport velocity; $P$, on the axis, has neither a transport nor a Coriolis term.

Forces and Equations of Motion

Figure 3. Forces seen from $S_1$. On $P$: weight, spring $k\,\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and the reaction of the axis, normal to it; no inertia force, since $P$ is on the axis. On $Q$: weight, spring $-k\,\overrightarrow{PQ}$, reaction $N_3\,\mathbf e_r + N_4\,\mathbf k_1$, and the centrifugal and Coriolis forces (dashed), both horizontal.

(c) Forces acting on P and Q

Actual and inertia forces on both particles Law: weight; smooth reactions normal to the allowed motion; linear spring; inertia forces of a non-inertial frame Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.13; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; Problems.pdf, p. 28

The axis lets $P$ move only along $\mathbf k_1$, so its smooth reaction has no $\mathbf k_1$ component; the ring lets $Q$ move only along $\mathbf e_\phi$, so its reaction has no $\mathbf e_\phi$ component. The spring vector is $\overrightarrow{PQ}$, the difference of the two positions.
