$$\begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{PQ} &= \mathbf r_1^Q - \mathbf r_1^P = -R\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \left(\ell + R\cos\phi\right)\mathbf j_1 - \zeta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(positions of part (b))} \\ \mathbf F_s^P &= k\,\overrightarrow{PQ}, \quad \mathbf F_s^Q = -k\,\overrightarrow{PQ} = -k\left(\ell\cos\phi\,\mathbf e_r - \ell\sin\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi + R\,\mathbf e_r\right) + k\zeta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(spring of zero natural length; $\mathbf j_1$ in the ring basis)} \\ \mathbf N_P &= N_1\,\mathbf i_1 + N_2\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf N_Q = N_3\,\mathbf e_r + N_4\,\mathbf k_1 = N_3\left(-\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\phi\,\mathbf j_1\right) + N_4\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(smooth axis; smooth ring)} \\ \mathbf F_A &= -m\,\mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf F_E = -m\,\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{($O$ fixed; $\Omega$ constant)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P &= \Omega\zeta\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf 0, \quad \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P = \Omega\dot\zeta\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{($P$ on the axis: no centrifugal, no Coriolis force)} \\ \mathbf F_C^Q &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^Q\right) = m\Omega^2\,\mathbf r_1^Q = m\Omega^2\left(\ell\cos\phi + R\right)\mathbf e_r - m\Omega^2\ell\sin\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi \quad &\text{(centripetal term of the composition box times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR}^Q &= -2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^Q = 2m\Omega R\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(Coriolis term of the composition box times $-m$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} P:\ -mg\,\mathbf k_1, \quad N_1\,\mathbf i_1 + N_2\,\mathbf j_1, \quad k\left[-R\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \left(\ell + R\cos\phi\right)\mathbf j_1 - \zeta\,\mathbf k_1\right], \quad \text{no inertia force} \cr Q:\ -mg\,\mathbf k_1, \quad N_3\,\mathbf e_r + N_4\,\mathbf k_1, \quad -k\left(\ell\cos\phi + R\right)\mathbf e_r + k\ell\sin\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi + k\zeta\,\mathbf k_1, \cr \mathbf F_C^Q = m\Omega^2\left(\ell\cos\phi + R\right)\mathbf e_r - m\Omega^2\ell\sin\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi, \quad \mathbf F_{COR}^Q = 2m\Omega R\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_r \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[mg] = [kR] = [m\Omega^2\ell] = [m\Omega R\dot\phi] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the spring pulls $Q$ towards $P$; the centrifugal force pushes $Q$ away from the axis, horizontally; the Coriolis force on $Q$ is radial in the ring and only loads the ring.

(d) Scalar equations of motion in S1

Newton's second law in S1 projected on the bases of the constraints Law: $m\,\mathbf a_1 = \mathbf F + \mathbf F_i$ for each particle, projected on $\mathcal B_1$ for $P$ and on the ring basis for $Q$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; Problems.pdf, p. 28
$$\begin{aligned} P,\ \mathbf i_1:&\quad 0 = N_1 - kR\sin\phi \quad &\text{($\mathbf a_1^P$ has no $\mathbf i_1$ part)} \\ P,\ \mathbf j_1:&\quad 0 = N_2 + k\left(\ell + R\cos\phi\right) \quad &\text{($\mathbf a_1^P$ has no $\mathbf j_1$ part)} \\ P,\ \mathbf k_1:&\quad m\ddot\zeta = -mg - k\zeta \quad &\text{(weight and spring)} \\ Q,\ \mathbf e_r:&\quad -mR\dot\phi^2 = N_3 - k\left(\ell\cos\phi + R\right) + m\Omega^2\left(\ell\cos\phi + R\right) + 2m\Omega R\dot\phi \quad &\text{(reaction, spring, centrifugal, Coriolis)} \\ Q,\ \mathbf e_\phi:&\quad mR\ddot\phi = k\ell\sin\phi - m\Omega^2\ell\sin\phi \quad &\text{(spring and centrifugal)} \\ Q,\ \mathbf k_1:&\quad 0 = -mg + N_4 + k\zeta \quad &\text{(weight, reaction, spring)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} N_1 = kR\sin\phi, \quad N_2 = -k\left(\ell + R\cos\phi\right), \quad m\ddot\zeta = -mg - k\zeta, \cr -mR\dot\phi^2 = N_3 + \left(m\Omega^2 - k\right)\left(\ell\cos\phi + R\right) + 2m\Omega R\dot\phi, \quad mR\ddot\phi = \left(k - m\Omega^2\right)\ell\sin\phi, \quad N_4 = mg - k\zeta \end{gathered}}$$

Units: every term $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: six scalar equations for six unknowns, the two coordinates and the four reaction components.

(e) Two equations free of the other unknowns

Projections along the allowed motions Law: the projections on $\mathbf k_1$ for $P$ and on $\mathbf e_\phi$ for $Q$ are normal to the reactions Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Problems.pdf, p. 28
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot\zeta &= -g - \frac{k}{m}\,\zeta \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1$ equation of $P$ divided by $m$)} \\ \ddot\phi &= \frac{\ell}{R}\left(\frac{k}{m} - \Omega^2\right)\sin\phi \quad &\text{($\mathbf e_\phi$ equation of $Q$ divided by $mR$)} \\ N_3 &= -mR\dot\phi^2 + \left(k - m\Omega^2\right)\left(\ell\cos\phi + R\right) - 2m\Omega R\dot\phi \quad &\text{($\mathbf e_r$ equation of $Q$ solved for $N_3$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\ddot\zeta + \frac{k}{m}\,\zeta = -g, \qquad \ddot\phi = \frac{\ell}{R}\left(\frac{k}{m} - \Omega^2\right)\sin\phi}$$

Units: $[k/m] = [\Omega^2] = [\mathrm T^{-2}]$; $[(k/m)\zeta] = [g] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the two equations are decoupled: the spring force is linear in $\overrightarrow{PQ}$, its vertical part acts only on the motion of $P$ along the axis and its horizontal part only on the motion of $Q$ in the horizontal plane. Once $\zeta$ and $\phi$ are known, the other four equations of part (d) give the reactions.

Reading with a natural length L0 (alternative) Law: spring force proportional to the stretch, along $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Problems.pdf, p. 28

With a natural length $L_0$ the force on $P$ is $k\left(|PQ| - L_0\right)$ times the unit vector of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$, so every spring term above gains the factor $1 - L_0/|PQ|$, with the squared length written out below.

$$\begin{aligned} |PQ|^2 &= R^2\sin^2\phi + \left(\ell + R\cos\phi\right)^2 + \zeta^2 = \ell^2 + R^2 + 2\ell R\cos\phi + \zeta^2 \quad &\text{(components of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$)} \\ \ddot\zeta &= -g - \frac{k}{m}\left(1 - \frac{L_0}{|PQ|}\right)\zeta, \quad \ddot\phi = \frac{\ell}{R}\left[\frac{k}{m}\left(1 - \frac{L_0}{|PQ|}\right) - \Omega^2\right]\sin\phi \quad &\text{(same projections)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{L_0 \ne 0: \ \text{the two equations couple through } |PQ| = \sqrt{\ell^2 + R^2 + 2\ell R\cos\phi + \zeta^2}}$$

Units: $[L_0/|PQ|] = [1]$

Meaning: only the zero natural length makes the problem separate; the forms of the reactions do not change.

Answers and Checks

(f) A conservation law in S1

Energy of the relative motion Law: power of each force on the relative velocity; potentials of the weight, the spring and the centrifugal force Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]

Two reasons. First, the forces that do no work in $S_1$: the reactions (the axis and the ring are at rest in $S_1$ and smooth, so each reaction is normal to the relative velocity of its particle), the Coriolis force on $Q$ (normal to its relative velocity; the one on $P$ is zero), and the origin and Euler forces, which vanish. Second, the forces that work have potentials of the positions in $S_1$: the weights, constant in $S_1$ because $\mathbf k_1$ is the fixed vertical; the spring, which depends only on $\overrightarrow{PQ}$; and the centrifugal force on $Q$, because the rate is constant and the axis fixed. $Q$ moves in the plane through $O$ normal to the axis, so its distance to the axis is the length of $\mathbf r_1^Q$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf N_P\cdot\mathbf v_1^P &= \left(N_1\,\mathbf i_1 + N_2\,\mathbf j_1\right)\cdot\dot\zeta\,\mathbf k_1 = 0, \quad \mathbf N_Q\cdot\mathbf v_1^Q = \left(N_3\,\mathbf e_r + N_4\,\mathbf k_1\right)\cdot R\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi = 0, \quad \mathbf F_{COR}^Q\cdot\mathbf v_1^Q = 2m\Omega R^2\dot\phi^2\,\mathbf e_r\cdot\mathbf e_\phi = 0 \quad &\text{(no power)} \\ V_1 &= mg\zeta + mg\cdot 0 + \tfrac12 k\,|PQ|^2 - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2\left|\mathbf r_1^Q\right|^2 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.14; Slide 30)} \\ \left|\mathbf r_1^Q\right|^2 &= R^2\sin^2\phi + \left(\ell + R\cos\phi\right)^2 = \ell^2 + R^2 + 2\ell R\cos\phi \quad &\text{(components of part (b))} \\ V_1 &= mg\zeta + \tfrac12 k\zeta^2 + \left(k - m\Omega^2\right)\ell R\cos\phi + \tfrac12\left(k - m\Omega^2\right)\left(\ell^2 + R^2\right) \quad &\text{(with $|PQ|^2$ of the previous box, $L_0$ zero)} \\ T_1 &= \tfrac12 m\left|\mathbf v_1^P\right|^2 + \tfrac12 m\left|\mathbf v_1^Q\right|^2 = \tfrac12 m\left(\dot\zeta^2 + R^2\dot\phi^2\right) \quad &\text{(velocities of part (b))} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(T_1 + V_1\right) &= m\dot\zeta\ddot\zeta + mR^2\dot\phi\ddot\phi + mg\dot\zeta + k\zeta\dot\zeta - \left(k - m\Omega^2\right)\ell R\sin\phi\,\dot\phi \quad &\text{(chain rule: $\tfrac{d}{dt}\cos\phi = -\sin\phi\,\dot\phi$, $\tfrac{d}{dt}\zeta^2 = 2\zeta\dot\zeta$)} \\ &= m\dot\zeta\left(\ddot\zeta + g + \frac{k}{m}\zeta\right) + mR\dot\phi\left(R\ddot\phi - \left(\frac{k}{m} - \Omega^2\right)\ell\sin\phi\right) = 0 \quad &\text{(check with the two equations of part (e))} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{E_1 = \frac12 m\left(\dot\zeta^2 + R^2\dot\phi^2\right) + mg\zeta + \frac12 k\zeta^2 + \left(k - m\Omega^2\right)\ell R\cos\phi = \text{const}}$$

Units: $[m\dot\zeta^2] = [mg\zeta] = [k\zeta^2] = [k\ell R] = [m\Omega^2\ell R] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the mechanical energy in $S_1$ is a first integral; the constant term of the potential is dropped and the constant is fixed by initial conditions, which the statement does not give. Since each bracket of the check vanishes on its own, the two parts, the one in $\zeta$ and the one in $\phi$, are also conserved separately.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Degrees of freedom; basis $\mathcal B_1$2 ($\zeta$, $\phi$); $\mathbf i_1 = \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0$, $\mathbf j_1 = -\sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0$, $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$
(b) Kinematics in $S_1$$\mathbf r_1^P = \zeta\,\mathbf k_1$, $\mathbf v_1^P = \dot\zeta\,\mathbf k_1$, $\mathbf a_1^P = \ddot\zeta\,\mathbf k_1$; $\mathbf r_1^Q = -R\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + (\ell + R\cos\phi)\,\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf v_1^Q = R\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi$, $\mathbf a_1^Q = R\ddot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi - R\dot\phi^2\,\mathbf e_r$, with $\mathbf e_r = -\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\phi\,\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf e_\phi = -\cos\phi\,\mathbf i_1 - \sin\phi\,\mathbf j_1$
(c) Forceson $P$: $-mg\,\mathbf k_1$, $N_1\mathbf i_1 + N_2\mathbf j_1$, $k\,\overrightarrow{PQ}$, no inertia force; on $Q$: $-mg\,\mathbf k_1$, $N_3\,\mathbf e_r + N_4\,\mathbf k_1$, $-k\,\overrightarrow{PQ}$, $\mathbf F_C^Q = m\Omega^2\mathbf r_1^Q$, $\mathbf F_{COR}^Q = 2m\Omega R\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_r$; origin and Euler forces zero
(d) Scalar equations$0 = N_1 - kR\sin\phi$; $0 = N_2 + k(\ell + R\cos\phi)$; $m\ddot\zeta = -mg - k\zeta$; $-mR\dot\phi^2 = N_3 + (m\Omega^2 - k)(\ell\cos\phi + R) + 2m\Omega R\dot\phi$; $mR\ddot\phi = (k - m\Omega^2)\ell\sin\phi$; $0 = N_4 - mg + k\zeta$
(e) Two equations$\ddot\zeta + (k/m)\zeta = -g$; $\ddot\phi = (\ell/R)(k/m - \Omega^2)\sin\phi$ (spring of zero natural length; with a natural length $L_0$ the factor $k$ becomes $k(1 - L_0/\lvert PQ\rvert)$ and they couple)
(f) First integral$\frac12 m(\dot\zeta^2 + R^2\dot\phi^2) + mg\zeta + \frac12 k\zeta^2 + (k - m\Omega^2)\ell R\cos\phi = \text{const}$ (energy in $S_1$)

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 76 prints only the reaction of the ring on $Q$, $N_3(-\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\phi\,\mathbf j_1) + N_4\,\mathbf k_1$; it coincides with the reaction of part (c), whose radial vector is the $\mathbf e_r$ of the position box. The other parts have no key; the energy is checked against the two equations in part (f), and the limiting cases follow.

Limiting cases and equilibria Law: the equations of part (e) at extreme values of the data; Taylor expansion about an equilibrium and the harmonic oscillator Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.6; Notes.pdf, Eq. 5.7; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63
$$\begin{aligned} \zeta_{eq} &= -\frac{mg}{k}, \quad \ddot\zeta + \frac{k}{m}\left(\zeta - \zeta_{eq}\right) = 0 \quad &\text{($P$: harmonic oscillator about $\zeta_{eq}$, frequency $\sqrt{k/m}$, Eq. 5.6)} \\ \phi &= \pi + \varepsilon:\quad \sin\left(\pi + \varepsilon\right) = -\sin\varepsilon \approx -\varepsilon \;\Rightarrow\; \ddot\varepsilon + \frac{\ell}{R}\left(\frac{k}{m} - \Omega^2\right)\varepsilon = 0 \quad &\text{(first-order Taylor expansion about the near point)} \\ \phi &= \varepsilon:\quad \sin\varepsilon \approx \varepsilon \;\Rightarrow\; \ddot\varepsilon - \frac{\ell}{R}\left(\frac{k}{m} - \Omega^2\right)\varepsilon = 0 \quad &\text{(first-order Taylor expansion about the far point)} \\ \ell &\to 0:\quad \ddot\phi = 0 \quad &\text{(ring centred on the axis: every point at the same distance)} \\ \Omega^2 &= \frac{k}{m}:\quad \ddot\phi = 0 \quad &\text{(spring and centrifugal forces cancel along the ring)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\Omega^2 \lt \frac{k}{m}: \ \phi = \pi \text{ oscillates with frequency } \sqrt{\frac{\ell}{R}\left(\frac{k}{m} - \Omega^2\right)}; \qquad \Omega^2 \gt \frac{k}{m}: \ \phi = 0 \text{ does}}$$

Units: $[(\ell/R)(k/m - \Omega^2)] = [\mathrm T^{-2}]$; $[mg/k] = [\mathrm L]$

Meaning: $P$ oscillates about the point below $O$ where the vertical pull of the spring balances its weight, unaffected by the rotation because it sits on the axis. For $Q$ the spring pulls towards the point of the ring nearest the axis and the centrifugal force pushes towards the farthest one: below the rate whose square is $k/m$ the near point is where small oscillations occur, above it the far one; the other point gives exponential departure.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf (PDF page 28); key on PDF page 76
Problem 41

Satellite Solar Panel: Composition of Rotations

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 29
Relative Kinematics

The angle $\theta$ describing the rotation of the solar panels of a reconnaissance satellite about the body-fixed axis $x$ is an arbitrary function of time. The satellite spins about the $z$ axis at the constant angular rate $\omega$. Derive expressions for the absolute velocity and acceleration of point $B$ in the figure relative to an inertial reference frame centered in $A$.

(Taken from Ginsberg, "Engineering Dynamics", Cambridge University Press, 2008.)

Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

A satellite spins about its $z$ axis at the constant rate $\omega$; its solar panel turns about the body-fixed $x$ axis through the angle $\theta$, an arbitrary function of time. The statement asks for the absolute velocity and acceleration of the corner $B$ of the panel with respect to an inertial frame centred at $A$ (Problems.pdf, p. 29). There are no forces: the problem is kinematics only, solved with the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2, and checked by a second route with the composition of angular velocities.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{A;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$, centred at the satellite centre $A$, $\mathbf k_0$ along the spin axis
Body frame$S_1 = \{A;\ \mathcal B_1\}$, the axes $x$, $y$, $z$ of the figure; $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$; turns by $\omega t$ about $\mathbf k_0$, from $\mathbf i_0$ towards $\mathbf j_0$; coincides with $S_0$ at $t = 0$
Panel frame$S_2 = \{C;\ \mathcal B_2\}$, attached to the panel; $C$ is the point of the hinge axis at the abscissa of $B$; $\mathbf i_2 = \mathbf i_1$ (hinge), $\mathbf j_2$ from $C$ towards $B$
Points$A$ centre of the satellite; $C$ on the $x$ axis at the distance $H$ from $A$; $B$ the corner of the panel; $B'$ the projection of $B$ on the plane $xy$
Data$H$ [m] (distance from $A$ to $C$ along $x$), $W$ [m] (distance from $B$ to the hinge axis), $\omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$], $\theta(t)$ [rad] with its derivatives
Unknowns$\mathbf v_0^B$, $\mathbf a_0^B$
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial with $A$ fixed in it; rigid body and panel; $\omega$ constant; $\theta(t)$ known
Readings(1) Read from the figure: $\theta$ is the angle of the panel about $+x$, measured from the body axis $y$, so for zero $\theta$ the segment $CB$ points along $+y$. If $\theta$ were measured from the body axis $z$ instead, the position of $B$ would be the one below with $\theta$ replaced by $\theta + \pi/2$, and so would every result. (2) $H$ is read as measured along $x$ from $A$ to the abscissa of $B$, and $W$ as the distance of $B$ from the $x$ axis

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. First rotation, seen from $+z$ with $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf k_1$ out of the paper ($\odot$): $\mathbf i_1, \mathbf j_1$ are $\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0$ turned counter-clockwise by $\omega t$. $\mathbf i_1$ has components $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$ and $\sin\omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$; the tip of $\mathbf j_1$ moves to the side of $-\mathbf i_0$, hence its component $-\sin\omega t$.
First rotation: the body frame turns by omega t about k0 Law: elementary rotation about the third axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

View from $+z$, along $\mathbf k_0$, which points out of the paper (⊙). With $\mathbf i_0$ to the right, $\mathbf j_0$, the cross product of $\mathbf k_0$ and $\mathbf i_0$, points up the page; a positive spin turns the body counterclockwise in this view. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\omega t$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ along plus $\mathbf j_0$. $\mathbf j_1$ is $\mathbf j_0$ turned by the same angle; the counterclockwise turn carries its tip to the left, so its opposite leg $\sin\omega t$ lies along minus $\mathbf i_0$ (the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf j_1 = -\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles; axis)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\omega t\cos\omega t - \left(-\sin\omega t\right)\sin\omega t\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{3+3}$)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\omega t + \sin^2\omega t = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{12} = -\cos\omega t\sin\omega t + \sin\omega t\cos\omega t = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\omega t & -\sin\omega t & 0 \cr \sin\omega t & \cos\omega t & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: $[\omega t] = [1]$

Meaning: the body axes in terms of the inertial ones; they coincide at the start.

Figure 2. Second rotation, seen along the hinge with $\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf i_2$ out of the paper ($\odot$), so $\mathbf j_1$ points right and $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf i_1\times\mathbf j_1$ up. The panel turns $\theta$ counter-clockwise: $\overrightarrow{CB} = W\,\mathbf j_2$ is the hypotenuse of the shaded triangle, with legs $W\cos\theta$ along $\mathbf j_1$ and $W\sin\theta$ along $\mathbf k_1$.
Second rotation: the panel turns by theta about the hinge i1 Law: elementary rotation about the first axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.16; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.18

View along the hinge, with $\mathbf i_1$ out of the paper (⊙). With $\mathbf j_1$ to the right, $\mathbf k_1$, the cross product of $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf j_1$, points up the page. $\theta$ is measured about $+\mathbf i_1$, counterclockwise in this view, from $\mathbf j_1$. $\mathbf j_2$ is $\mathbf j_1$ turned by $\theta$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\theta$ along $\mathbf j_1$, opposite leg $\sin\theta$ along plus $\mathbf k_1$. $\mathbf k_2$ is $\mathbf k_1$ turned by the same angle; the counterclockwise turn carries its tip to the left, so its opposite leg $\sin\theta$ lies along minus $\mathbf j_1$ (the minus sign). The determinant is expanded along the first row.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_2 &= \mathbf i_1, \quad \mathbf j_2 = \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf k_2 = -\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(axis; the two right triangles)} \\ \det[{}_1R_2] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\theta\cos\theta - \left(-\sin\theta\right)\sin\theta\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the first row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{1+1}$)} \\ \left([{}_1R_2][{}_1R_2]^T\right)_{22} &= \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1, \quad \left([{}_1R_2][{}_1R_2]^T\right)_{23} = \cos\theta\sin\theta - \sin\theta\cos\theta = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \\ \det[{}_0R_2] &= \det[{}_0R_1]\,\det[{}_1R_2] = 1\cdot 1 = 1 \quad &\text{(product of the two rotations, Eq. 1.16)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_1R_2] = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \cr 0 & \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \cr 0 & \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_1R_2] = 1, \quad [{}_1R_2][{}_1R_2]^T = I}$$

Units: $[\theta] = [1]$

Meaning: the panel axes in terms of the body axes; for zero $\theta$ the panel lies in the plane $xy$ of the body.

Figure 3. Body plane seen from $+z$ ($\mathbf k_1$ out of the paper): $C$ is at $H$ along $\mathbf i_1$ and the corner $B$ projects onto the point $B'$ at $W\cos\theta$ along $\mathbf j_1$ ($B$ itself is $W\sin\theta$ above the paper). $\mathbf r_\perp = H\,\mathbf i_1 + W\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1$ is the distance vector from the spin axis, the one that enters the centripetal term.
Position of B: through the hinge point C Law: vector sum of positions; the right triangle of the hinge view Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 29

The distance that stays constant is the one from the hinge, so the path goes from $A$ along the hinge to $C$ and then across the panel to $B$. In the shaded triangle of the hinge view the hypotenuse is $CB$, of length $W$; the leg adjacent to $\theta$ is $W\cos\theta$ along $\mathbf j_1$ and the opposite leg is $W\sin\theta$ along $\mathbf k_1$. The body-plane figure shows the projection $B'$ of $B$ on the plane $xy$.

$$\begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{AC} &= H\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \overrightarrow{CB} = W\,\mathbf j_2 = W\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + W\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(hinge; second column of $[{}_1R_2]$ times $W$)} \\ \mathbf r_1^B &= \overrightarrow{AC} + \overrightarrow{CB} = H\,\mathbf i_1 + W\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + W\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.16 with the common origin $A$)} \\ \overrightarrow{AB'} &= H\,\mathbf i_1 + W\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(part normal to the spin axis: drop the $\mathbf k_1$ component)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_0^B = \mathbf r_1^B = H\,\mathbf i_1 + W\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + W\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1}$$

Units: $[H] = [W] = [\mathrm L]$

Meaning: for zero $\theta$ the corner is at $H$ along $x$ and $W$ along $y$; a quarter turn lifts it to $W$ above the plane $xy$. The vector from the spin axis to $B$ is the one from $A$ to $B'$.

Kinematics

Motion of the body frame and derivatives of its unit vectors Law: angular velocity of a simple rotation; derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf v_0^A = \mathbf a_0^A = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(rotation about the fixed axis; $\omega$ constant; $A$ fixed)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 to 3.5)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_0\right) &= -\omega\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \omega\cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(check: chain rule on $\mathbf i_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0}$$

Units: $[\omega] = [\mathrm T^{-1}]$

Meaning: the body axes $x$ and $y$ turn with the spin; the spin axis does not.

Relative velocity and acceleration of B in the body frame Law: time derivatives in $S_1$, where $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf k_1$ are constant; chain rule and product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24
$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dt}\left(W\cos\theta\right) &= -W\sin\theta\,\dot\theta, \quad \frac{d}{dt}\left(W\sin\theta\right) = W\cos\theta\,\dot\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule; $H$ and $W$ constant)} \\ \mathbf v_1^B &= -W\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + W\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.19)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\dot\theta\sin\theta\right) &= \ddot\theta\sin\theta + \dot\theta^2\cos\theta, \quad \frac{d}{dt}\left(\dot\theta\cos\theta\right) = \ddot\theta\cos\theta - \dot\theta^2\sin\theta \quad &\text{(product rule, then chain rule)} \\ \mathbf a_1^B &= -W\left(\ddot\theta\sin\theta + \dot\theta^2\cos\theta\right)\mathbf j_1 + W\left(\ddot\theta\cos\theta - \dot\theta^2\sin\theta\right)\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.24)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf v_1^B = W\dot\theta\,\mathbf k_2, \qquad \mathbf a_1^B = W\ddot\theta\,\mathbf k_2 - W\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf j_2}$$

Units: $[W\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[W\ddot\theta] = [W\dot\theta^2] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: seen from the body, $B$ describes a circle of radius $W$ about the hinge, with a tangential part along $\mathbf k_2$ and a centripetal part towards the hinge.

Absolute velocity and acceleration: transport and Coriolis terms as they arise Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the position written in the turning basis; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.26; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]

Write $\mathbf r_1^B$ as $x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + z_1\,\mathbf k_1$ with $x_1$ equal to $H$, $y_1$ to $W\cos\theta$ and $z_1$ to $W\sin\theta$; the time derivatives of the components are the components of $\mathbf v_1^B$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^B &= \dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + \dot z_1\,\mathbf k_1 + x_1\omega\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\omega\,\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf v_1^B + \omega\left(x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; derivatives of $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ &= -W\omega\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \left(H\omega - W\dot\theta\sin\theta\right)\mathbf j_1 + W\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(components substituted)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1^B}{dt}\right|_0 &= \mathbf a_1^B + \omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; the basis turns inside $\mathbf v_1^B$)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left[\omega\left(x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right)\right] &= \omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) - \omega^2\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; $\omega$ constant)} \\ \mathbf a_0^B &= \mathbf a_1^B + 2\omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) - \omega^2\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(Coriolis: the two equal terms; centripetal: the last)} \\ 2\omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) &= 2\omega\left(0\cdot\mathbf j_1 + W\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1\right) = 2W\omega\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{($\dot x_1$ zero, $\dot y_1 = -W\dot\theta\sin\theta$)} \\ -\omega^2\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) &= -H\omega^2\,\mathbf i_1 - W\omega^2\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(minus $\omega^2$ times $\overrightarrow{AB'}$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf v_0^B = -W\omega\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \left(H\omega - W\dot\theta\sin\theta\right)\mathbf j_1 + W\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \cr \mathbf a_0^B = \left(2W\omega\dot\theta\sin\theta - H\omega^2\right)\mathbf i_1 - \left(W\ddot\theta\sin\theta + W\dot\theta^2\cos\theta + W\omega^2\cos\theta\right)\mathbf j_1 + \left(W\ddot\theta\cos\theta - W\dot\theta^2\sin\theta\right)\mathbf k_1 \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[W\omega] = [H\omega] = [W\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[W\omega\dot\theta] = [H\omega^2] = [W\ddot\theta] = [W\dot\theta^2] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the velocity adds to the relative one the transport velocity of the body point that coincides with $B$; the acceleration adds the centripetal term towards the spin axis and the Coriolis term, the two equal halves coming from the turning basis inside the relative velocity and from the change of the transport velocity. The components are in $\mathcal B_1$; multiplying by $[{}_0R_1]$ gives them in $\mathcal B_0$.

Second route: panel frame and composition of angular velocities Law: composition of angular velocities and accelerations; velocity and acceleration of a point fixed in a moving frame Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.26; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27

$B$ is fixed in $S_2$, so its velocity and acceleration relative to $S_2$ vanish; $C$ is fixed in $S_1$ at $H\,\mathbf i_1$. Vector products use $\mathbf i_1\times\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf k_1$, $\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf j_1$ and the reversed products with a minus sign.

$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{20} &= \boldsymbol\omega_{21} + \boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \dot\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \omega\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.14)} \\ \boldsymbol\alpha_{20} &= \boldsymbol\alpha_{21} + \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\boldsymbol\omega_{21} + \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \ddot\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \omega\dot\theta\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 + \mathbf 0 = \ddot\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \omega\dot\theta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.15)} \\ \mathbf v_0^C &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times H\,\mathbf i_1 = H\omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf a_0^C = \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times H\omega\,\mathbf j_1 = -H\omega^2\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{($C$ fixed in $S_1$, Eq. 3.26 and 3.27)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{20}\times\overrightarrow{CB} &= \left(\dot\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \omega\,\mathbf k_1\right)\times\left(W\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + W\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1\right) = -W\omega\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 - W\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + W\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(term by term)} \\ \mathbf v_0^B &= \mathbf v_0^C + \boldsymbol\omega_{20}\times\overrightarrow{CB} = -W\omega\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \left(H\omega - W\dot\theta\sin\theta\right)\mathbf j_1 + W\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.26 in $S_2$)} \\ \boldsymbol\alpha_{20}\times\overrightarrow{CB} &= \left(\ddot\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \omega\dot\theta\,\mathbf j_1\right)\times\left(W\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + W\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1\right) = W\omega\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 - W\ddot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + W\ddot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(term by term)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{20}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{20}\times\overrightarrow{CB}\right) &= \left(\dot\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \omega\,\mathbf k_1\right)\times\left(-W\omega\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 - W\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + W\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1\right) \quad &\text{(previous product)} \\ &= W\omega\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 - \left(W\dot\theta^2\cos\theta + W\omega^2\cos\theta\right)\mathbf j_1 - W\dot\theta^2\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(term by term)} \\ \mathbf a_0^B &= \mathbf a_0^C + \boldsymbol\alpha_{20}\times\overrightarrow{CB} + \boldsymbol\omega_{20}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{20}\times\overrightarrow{CB}\right) \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.27 in $S_2$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_0^B = \left(2W\omega\dot\theta\sin\theta - H\omega^2\right)\mathbf i_1 - \left(W\ddot\theta\sin\theta + W\dot\theta^2\cos\theta + W\omega^2\cos\theta\right)\mathbf j_1 + \left(W\ddot\theta\cos\theta - W\dot\theta^2\sin\theta\right)\mathbf k_1}$$

Units: $[\omega\dot\theta] = [\ddot\theta] = [\mathrm T^{-2}]$

Meaning: both routes give the same velocity and acceleration. Here the Coriolis term of the first route appears split in two equal halves: one inside the angular acceleration of the panel, from the turning of the hinge axis, and one in the double vector product.

Answers and Checks

Part of the statementAnswer
Absolute velocity of $B$$\mathbf v_0^B = -W\omega\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + (H\omega - W\dot\theta\sin\theta)\,\mathbf j_1 + W\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1$, in the body basis, with $\mathbf i_1 = \cos\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\omega t\,\mathbf j_0$, $\mathbf j_1 = -\sin\omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\omega t\,\mathbf j_0$, $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$ (with $\theta$ measured from $z$ instead, replace $\theta$ by $\theta + \pi/2$)
Absolute acceleration of $B$$\mathbf a_0^B = (2W\omega\dot\theta\sin\theta - H\omega^2)\,\mathbf i_1 - (W\ddot\theta\sin\theta + W\dot\theta^2\cos\theta + W\omega^2\cos\theta)\,\mathbf j_1 + (W\ddot\theta\cos\theta - W\dot\theta^2\sin\theta)\,\mathbf k_1$ (same remark on the reading of $\theta$)

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 76 prints both vectors in the body basis; they coincide term by term with the boxed results (box below). The two routes of the kinematics give the same result.

Comparison with the official key Law: term-by-term comparison Source: Problems.pdf, p. 76
$$\begin{aligned} \text{key: } \mathbf v_0^B &= -W\omega\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \left(H\omega - W\dot\theta\sin\theta\right)\mathbf j_1 + W\dot\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(same three components)} \\ \text{key: } \mathbf a_0^B &= \left(2W\omega\dot\theta\sin\theta - H\omega^2\right)\mathbf i_1 - \left(W\ddot\theta\sin\theta + W\dot\theta^2\cos\theta + W\omega^2\cos\theta\right)\mathbf j_1 + \left(W\ddot\theta\cos\theta - W\dot\theta^2\sin\theta\right)\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(same three components)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{velocity and acceleration coincide with the key}}$$

Units: $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$ and $[\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the key uses the same reading of $\theta$ and the same body basis.

Limiting cases Law: the results at extreme values of the data Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.26; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27
$$\begin{aligned} \dot\theta = \ddot\theta = 0:\quad \mathbf v_0^B &= \omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf r_1^B, \quad \mathbf a_0^B = -\omega^2\left(H\,\mathbf i_1 + W\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(panel locked: rigid rotation about the spin axis)} \\ \omega = 0:\quad \mathbf v_0^B &= W\dot\theta\,\mathbf k_2, \quad \mathbf a_0^B = W\ddot\theta\,\mathbf k_2 - W\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf j_2 \quad &\text{(no spin: circle of radius $W$ about the hinge)} \\ \theta = 0:\quad 2W\omega\dot\theta\sin\theta &= 0 \quad &\text{(panel in the plane $xy$: its relative velocity is parallel to the spin axis)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{each limit reduces to a single simple rotation}}$$

Units: $[\omega^2H] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the Coriolis term needs both rotations at once and a relative velocity with a part normal to the spin axis.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf (PDF page 29); key on PDF page 76
Problem 47

Two Repelling Particles on Concentric Wires in a Rotating Plane

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 32
Relative Equilibrium

We consider a system of two heavy particles of equal mass $m$. The first particle $P$ is constrained to move without friction along a circular wire of radius $a$. The second particle $Q$ is constrained to move without friction along a circular wire of radius $2a$. Both wires are contained in a plane $Ox_1y_1$ that rotates at a constant, known angular rate $\Omega$ about the axis $Oy_1 \equiv Oy_0$ with respect to a fixed reference frame $S_0$ with axes $Ox_0y_0z_0$ (not shown in the figure). We also define a moving reference frame $S_1$ with axes $Ox_1y_1z_1$. The two particles repel each other with a force that is proportional to their distance, with constant of proportionality, $k$.

  • (a)
    How many configuration degrees of freedom has this system?
  • (b)
    How many independent components of the reaction forces on the particles need to be considered? Write down the reaction force on each particle.
  • (c)
    Write down the relative accelerations of $P$ and $Q$ with respect to $S_1$ as a function of the coordinates of the problem and their derivatives.
  • (d)
    Express the applied forces on the particles as a function of the coordinates of the problem.
  • (e)
    Express the fictitious forces of inertia on the particles as seen from $S_1$, as a function of the coordinates of the problem and their derivatives.
  • (f)
    Write down a system of ordinary differential equations to determine the evolution of the coordinates of the problem as a function of time, free of any other unknowns. You do not need to solve this system (since no initial conditions have been provided) but we assume that we know how to solve it, so that from this point we know the coordinates as a function of time.
  • (g)
    Determine the values of the reaction forces from the wires as a function of time.
  • (h)
    Is the mechanical energy of this system conserved in $S_1$? If so, write down the corresponding equation.
  • (i)
    Determine the values of $\alpha = \dfrac{ka}{mg}$ and $\beta = \dfrac{a\Omega^2}{g}$ so that $\varphi = 30^\circ$, $\theta = -60^\circ$ is an equilibrium position of the system in the relative motion.
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

Two heavy particles of mass $m$ move without friction, $P$ on a circular wire of radius $a$ and $Q$ on a concentric circular wire of radius $2a$, both centred at $O$ in the plane $Ox_1y_1$. The plane turns at the constant rate $\Omega$ about the vertical axis $Oy_1$, which coincides with $Oy_0$; the particles repel each other with a force equal to $k$ times their distance (Problems.pdf, p. 32). The statement asks for the degrees of freedom, the reactions, the relative accelerations, the applied and the inertia forces, the equations of motion, the reactions as functions of time, the energy in $S_1$, and the values of two parameters that make one configuration an equilibrium. The wires are at rest in $S_1$, so the solution works there, with the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2 and the inertia forces of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$, $\mathbf j_0$ vertical, up; gravity $-g\,\mathbf j_0$
Moving frame$S_1 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_1\}$, attached to the plane of the wires; $\mathbf j_1 = \mathbf j_0$; it turns by $\Omega t$ about $\mathbf j_0$ and coincides with $S_0$ at $t = 0$
Polar basesat $P$: $\{\mathbf e_r^P, \mathbf e_\varphi, \mathbf k_1\}$; at $Q$: $\{\mathbf e_r^Q, \mathbf e_\theta, \mathbf k_1\}$ (deduced below)
Coordinates$\varphi$ and $\theta$, angles of $OP$ and $OQ$ measured from $Ox_1$, positive from $\mathbf i_1$ towards $\mathbf j_1$
Data$m$ [kg], $a$ [m], $k$ [N m$^{-1}$], $\Omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$], $g$ [m s$^{-2}$]; dimensionless $\alpha = ka/(mg)$, $\beta = a\Omega^2/g$
Unknowns$\varphi(t)$, $\theta(t)$ and the reaction components $N_1, N_2$ (on $P$), $N_3, N_4$ (on $Q$)
Applied forcesweights $-mg\,\mathbf j_1$; repulsion $k\,\overrightarrow{QP}$ on $P$ and $k\,\overrightarrow{PQ}$ on $Q$
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)centrifugal and Coriolis; no origin or Euler terms (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial; uniform gravity; smooth bilateral wires; $\Omega$ constant
Readings(1) The curved arrow of the figure is read as a turn in the positive sense about $+\mathbf j_0$ (counterclockwise seen from above), so the angular velocity is $\Omega\,\mathbf j_1$ with $\Omega$ positive. The opposite sense changes the sign of $\Omega$, hence the matrix $[{}_0R_1]$ and the derivatives of $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf k_1$ (their signs); among the dynamic results it changes only the Coriolis forces and the reactions $N_2$, $N_4$ (they change sign); the equations of motion, the energy and part (i) contain only the square of $\Omega$ and do not change. (2) $\mathbf k_1$, the cross product of $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf j_1$, points out of the paper in the figure

(a) Configuration degrees of freedom

Coordinates minus independent constraints Law: each holonomic constraint removes one coordinate; the motion of the plane is prescribed Source: Notes.pdf, Ch. 6; Notes.pdf, Sec. 6.2; Problems.pdf, p. 32
$$\begin{aligned} P:&\quad z_1^P = 0, \quad \left(x_1^P\right)^2 + \left(y_1^P\right)^2 - a^2 = 0 \quad &\text{(plane and circle of radius $a$)} \\ Q:&\quad z_1^Q = 0, \quad \left(x_1^Q\right)^2 + \left(y_1^Q\right)^2 - 4a^2 = 0 \quad &\text{(plane and circle of radius $2a$)} \\ \text{degrees of freedom} &= 3 + 3 - 4 = 2 \quad &\text{(six coordinates, four constraints)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{2 configuration degrees of freedom: } \varphi,\ \theta}$$

Units: $[\varphi] = [\theta] = [1]$

Meaning: one angle per particle; the four constraints become the four reaction components of part (b).

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. View from $+y_0$, with $\mathbf j_0 = \mathbf j_1$ out of the paper ($\odot$): $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf i_0\times\mathbf j_0$ points down the page. For $\Omega \gt 0$ the plane of the wires turns counter-clockwise by $\Omega t$; $\mathbf i_1$ has the components $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$ and $\sin\Omega t$ along $-\mathbf k_0$ (up the page), hence the minus sign.
Basis of S1: rotation by Omega t about the vertical j0 Law: elementary rotation about the second axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.19; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

View from above, along $\mathbf j_0$, which points out of the paper (⊙). With $\mathbf i_0$ to the right, $\mathbf k_0$, the cross product of $\mathbf i_0$ and $\mathbf j_0$, points down the page (fingers from $\mathbf i_0$ to the reader, thumb down). The plane turns counterclockwise in this view. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\Omega t$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\Omega t$ up the page, which is the direction of minus $\mathbf k_0$ (the minus sign). $\mathbf k_1$ is $\mathbf k_0$ turned by the same angle; the counterclockwise turn of a vector pointing down carries its tip to the right, so its opposite leg $\sin\Omega t$ lies along plus $\mathbf i_0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 - \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0, \quad \mathbf j_1 = \mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles; axis)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\Omega t\cos\Omega t - \sin\Omega t\left(-\sin\Omega t\right)\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the second row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{2+2}$)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\Omega t + \sin^2\Omega t = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{13} = -\cos\Omega t\sin\Omega t + \sin\Omega t\cos\Omega t = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \\ \mathbf i_1\times\mathbf j_1 &= \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0\times\mathbf j_0 - \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0\times\mathbf j_0 = \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0 + \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 = \mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(right-handed)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\Omega t & 0 & \sin\Omega t \cr 0 & 1 & 0 \cr -\sin\Omega t & 0 & \cos\Omega t \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: $[\Omega t] = [1]$

Meaning: the columns are the vectors of the plane frame in the fixed basis; the vertical is shared by both frames.

Figure 2. Plane $Ox_1y_1$, fixed in $S_1$, drawn at the configuration of part (i) ($\varphi = 30^\circ$, $\theta = -60^\circ$). For $P$ the hypotenuse of the shaded triangle is $a$, the leg adjacent to $\varphi$ is $a\cos\varphi$ (along $\mathbf i_1$) and the opposite one $a\sin\varphi$ (along $\mathbf j_1$); $Q$ works the same way with $2a$ and $\theta$ (here negative, below $Ox_1$). Polar bases $\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\varphi$ and $\mathbf e_r^Q, \mathbf e_\theta$ in orange.
Positions and polar bases in the plane of the wires Law: right triangles of the radii; tangent vector as the derivative of the radial unit vector Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 32

The plane $Ox_1y_1$ is drawn with $\mathbf i_1$ to the right, $\mathbf j_1$ up and $\mathbf k_1$ out of the paper (⊙). For $P$ the shaded right triangle has the hypotenuse $OP$, of length $a$; the leg adjacent to $\varphi$ is $a\cos\varphi$ along $\mathbf i_1$ and the opposite leg $a\sin\varphi$ along $\mathbf j_1$. For $Q$ the same triangle has the hypotenuse $2a$; with $\theta$ negative, as drawn, its leg $2a\sin\theta$ is negative and $Q$ lies below $Ox_1$. Both angles are the standard polar angles of the plane, so no conversion is needed.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_r^P &= \cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf e_\varphi = \frac{d\mathbf e_r^P}{d\varphi} = -\sin\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(triangle of $P$; $\tfrac{d}{d\varphi}\cos\varphi = -\sin\varphi$)} \\ \mathbf e_r^Q &= \cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf e_\theta = \frac{d\mathbf e_r^Q}{d\theta} = -\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(triangle of $Q$)} \\ \mathbf r_1^P &= a\,\mathbf e_r^P, \quad \mathbf r_1^Q = 2a\,\mathbf e_r^Q \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.16 with the common origin $O$)} \\ \mathbf e_r^P\times\mathbf e_\varphi &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf i_1 & \mathbf j_1 & \mathbf k_1 \cr \cos\varphi & \sin\varphi & 0 \cr -\sin\varphi & \cos\varphi & 0 \end{vmatrix} = (+1)(0)\,\mathbf i_1 + (-1)(0)\,\mathbf j_1 + (+1)\left(\cos^2\varphi + \sin^2\varphi\right)\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(first row; cofactor signs plus, minus, plus)} \\ \mathbf e_r^P\cdot\mathbf e_r^Q &= \cos\varphi\cos\theta + \sin\varphi\sin\theta = \cos\left(\varphi - \theta\right) \quad &\text{(difference formula)} \\ \mathbf e_r^Q\cdot\mathbf e_\varphi &= -\sin\varphi\cos\theta + \cos\varphi\sin\theta = -\sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right), \quad \mathbf e_r^P\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = -\sin\theta\cos\varphi + \cos\theta\sin\varphi = \sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right) \quad &\text{(difference formula)} \\ \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_r^P - \sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi, \quad \mathbf j_1 = \sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_r^P + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi \quad &\text{(projections; the same with $\theta$ at $Q$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf r_1^P = a\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + a\sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1, \qquad \mathbf r_1^Q = 2a\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + 2a\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[a] = [\mathrm L]$

Meaning: each polar triad is right-handed and orthonormal; the dot products between the two triads depend only on the difference of the angles.

Kinematics

Motion of S1 and derivatives of its unit vectors Law: angular velocity of a simple rotation; derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf v_0^O = \mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(rotation about the fixed vertical; $\Omega$ constant; $O$ fixed)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf i_1 = -\Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1\times\mathbf k_1 = \Omega\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 to 3.5)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 - \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0\right) &= -\Omega\sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 - \Omega\cos\Omega t\,\mathbf k_0 = -\Omega\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(check: chain rule on $\mathbf i_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf i_1}$$

Units: $[\Omega] = [\mathrm T^{-1}]$

Meaning: the horizontal axes of the plane frame turn; the vertical does not.

(c) Relative accelerations

Relative velocity and acceleration of P and Q Law: time derivatives in $S_1$; chain rule on the polar vectors; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24; Problems.pdf, p. 32
$$\begin{aligned} \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_r^P}{dt}\right|_1 &= \frac{d\mathbf e_r^P}{d\varphi}\,\frac{d\varphi}{dt} = \dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\varphi}{dt}\right|_1 = \frac{d\mathbf e_\varphi}{d\varphi}\,\frac{d\varphi}{dt} = \dot\varphi\left(-\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 - \sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1\right) = -\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_r^P \quad &\text{(chain rule; $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$ constant in $S_1$)} \\ \mathbf v_1^P &= a\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi, \quad \mathbf a_1^P = a\ddot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi + a\dot\varphi\left(-\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_r^P\right) = a\ddot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi - a\dot\varphi^2\,\mathbf e_r^P \quad &\text{(product rule)} \\ \mathbf v_1^Q &= 2a\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta, \quad \mathbf a_1^Q = 2a\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta - 2a\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf e_r^Q \quad &\text{(the same with $2a$ and $\theta$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_1^P = -a\dot\varphi^2\,\mathbf e_r^P + a\ddot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi, \qquad \mathbf a_1^Q = -2a\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf e_r^Q + 2a\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta}$$

Units: $[a\dot\varphi^2] = [a\ddot\varphi] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: circular motions about $O$ in the plane: a centripetal part towards $O$ and a tangential part along each wire.

Absolute acceleration: transport and Coriolis terms as they arise Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of a position written in the turning basis; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]

Both particles stay in the plane of the wires, so their positions are $x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1$; the time derivatives of the components are the components of the relative velocity.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0 &= \dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + x_1\left(-\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\right) = \mathbf v_1 - \Omega x_1\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; derivatives of $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \ddot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \ddot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + \dot x_1\left(-\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\right) = \mathbf a_1 - \Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; the basis turns inside $\mathbf v_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left(-\Omega x_1\,\mathbf k_1\right) &= -\Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1 - \Omega x_1\,\Omega\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; derivative of $\mathbf k_1$)} \\ \mathbf a_0 &= \mathbf a_1 - 2\Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1 - \Omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(Coriolis: the two equal terms; centripetal: the last)} \\ P:&\quad x_1 = a\cos\varphi, \ \dot x_1 = -a\dot\varphi\sin\varphi \;\Rightarrow\; -2\Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1 = 2\Omega a\dot\varphi\sin\varphi\,\mathbf k_1, \ -\Omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1 = -\Omega^2a\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ Q:&\quad x_1 = 2a\cos\theta, \ \dot x_1 = -2a\dot\theta\sin\theta \;\Rightarrow\; -2\Omega\dot x_1\,\mathbf k_1 = 4\Omega a\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1, \ -\Omega^2x_1\,\mathbf i_1 = -2\Omega^2a\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_0^P = \mathbf a_1^P - \Omega^2a\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + 2\Omega a\dot\varphi\sin\varphi\,\mathbf k_1, \qquad \mathbf a_0^Q = \mathbf a_1^Q - 2\Omega^2a\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + 4\Omega a\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1}$$

Units: $[\Omega^2a] = [\Omega a\dot\varphi] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the centripetal term points horizontally towards the axis, along minus $\mathbf i_1$ for a particle on the side of positive $x_1$; the Coriolis term is normal to the plane of the wires.

Forces and Equations of Motion

Figure 3. Forces seen from $S_1$ at the configuration of part (i). In the plane of the wires: weights, repulsion along $PQ$, radial reactions and the centrifugal forces (dashed), horizontal and away from the axis $Oy_1$. Seen from above: the Coriolis forces (dashed), normal to the plane, balanced by the reaction components $N_2$ and $N_4$.

(b) Reaction forces

Components of the reactions Law: a smooth wire exerts no force along its tangent; one reaction component per constraint Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.13; [Lecture 3, Slide 14]; Problems.pdf, p. 32

The tangent of the wire of $P$ is $\mathbf e_\varphi$ and that of $Q$ is $\mathbf e_\theta$; the plane normal to each tangent is spanned by the radial vector and $\mathbf k_1$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf N^P\cdot\mathbf e_\varphi &= 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \mathbf N^P = N_1\,\mathbf e_r^P + N_2\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(smooth wire of radius $a$)} \\ \mathbf N^Q\cdot\mathbf e_\theta &= 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \mathbf N^Q = N_3\,\mathbf e_r^Q + N_4\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(smooth wire of radius $2a$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{4 \text{ independent components: } \mathbf N^P = N_1\,\mathbf e_r^P + N_2\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf N^Q = N_3\,\mathbf e_r^Q + N_4\,\mathbf k_1}$$

Units: $[N_i] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: as many unknown components as constraints; each reaction lies in the plane normal to its wire.

(d) Applied forces

Weights and mutual repulsion in the polar bases Law: uniform weight; repulsion along the line of the particles, proportional to the distance, action and reaction Source: Problems.pdf, p. 32
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf W^P &= -mg\,\mathbf j_1 = -mg\sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_r^P - mg\cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi, \quad \mathbf W^Q = -mg\sin\theta\,\mathbf e_r^Q - mg\cos\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{($\mathbf j_1$ in each polar basis)} \\ \overrightarrow{QP} &= a\,\mathbf e_r^P - 2a\,\mathbf e_r^Q = a\left(\cos\varphi - 2\cos\theta\right)\mathbf i_1 + a\left(\sin\varphi - 2\sin\theta\right)\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(positions)} \\ \mathbf F_k^P &= k\,\overrightarrow{QP} = ka\left[1 - 2\cos\left(\varphi - \theta\right)\right]\mathbf e_r^P + 2ka\sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right)\mathbf e_\varphi \quad &\text{(dot products with $\mathbf e_r^P$, $\mathbf e_\varphi$)} \\ \mathbf F_k^Q &= k\,\overrightarrow{PQ} = ka\left[2 - \cos\left(\varphi - \theta\right)\right]\mathbf e_r^Q - ka\sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right)\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(dot products with $\mathbf e_r^Q$, $\mathbf e_\theta$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf F^P = -mg\,\mathbf j_1 + k\left(\mathbf r_1^P - \mathbf r_1^Q\right) = \left[-mg\sin\varphi + ka\left(1 - 2\cos\left(\varphi - \theta\right)\right)\right]\mathbf e_r^P + \left[-mg\cos\varphi + 2ka\sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right)\right]\mathbf e_\varphi \cr \mathbf F^Q = -mg\,\mathbf j_1 + k\left(\mathbf r_1^Q - \mathbf r_1^P\right) = \left[-mg\sin\theta + ka\left(2 - \cos\left(\varphi - \theta\right)\right)\right]\mathbf e_r^Q + \left[-mg\cos\theta - ka\sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right)\right]\mathbf e_\theta \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[mg] = [ka] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the applied forces lie in the plane of the wires; the tangential part of the repulsion on $P$ is largest when the two radii are perpendicular, and its radial part is then $ka$, outwards; the radial part vanishes and changes sign where the cosine of the angle between the radii is one half.

(e) Inertia forces seen from S1

Centrifugal and Coriolis forces Law: inertia forces of a non-inertial frame, the terms of the composition box times minus the mass Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf F_A &= -m\,\mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf F_E = -m\,\boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{($O$ fixed; $\Omega$ constant)} \\ \mathbf F_C^P &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) = m\Omega^2a\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 = m\Omega^2a\cos\varphi\left(\cos\varphi\,\mathbf e_r^P - \sin\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi\right) \quad &\text{(centripetal term times $-m$; $\mathbf i_1$ in the polar basis)} \\ \mathbf F_C^Q &= 2m\Omega^2a\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 = 2m\Omega^2a\cos\theta\left(\cos\theta\,\mathbf e_r^Q - \sin\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta\right) \quad &\text{(the same for $Q$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR}^P &= -2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P = -2m\Omega a\dot\varphi\sin\varphi\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf F_{COR}^Q = -4m\Omega a\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(Coriolis term times $-m$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf F_C^P = m\Omega^2a\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \mathbf F_C^Q = 2m\Omega^2a\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1, \cr \mathbf F_{COR}^P = -2m\Omega a\dot\varphi\sin\varphi\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf F_{COR}^Q = -4m\Omega a\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[m\Omega^2a] = [m\Omega a\dot\varphi] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the centrifugal force pushes each particle horizontally away from the vertical axis; the Coriolis force is normal to the plane of the wires, so only the reactions $N_2$ and $N_4$ can balance it.

(f) Equations of motion free of other unknowns

Newton's second law in S1 projected on the polar bases Law: $m\,\mathbf a_1 = \mathbf F + \mathbf N + \mathbf F_i$ for each particle; the tangential projections are free of the reactions and of the Coriolis forces Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; Problems.pdf, p. 32
$$\begin{aligned} P,\ \mathbf e_\varphi:&\quad ma\ddot\varphi = -mg\cos\varphi + 2ka\sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right) - m\Omega^2a\sin\varphi\cos\varphi \quad &\text{(weight, repulsion, centrifugal)} \\ Q,\ \mathbf e_\theta:&\quad 2ma\ddot\theta = -mg\cos\theta - ka\sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right) - 2m\Omega^2a\sin\theta\cos\theta \quad &\text{(weight, repulsion, centrifugal)} \\ P,\ \mathbf e_r^P:&\quad -ma\dot\varphi^2 = N_1 - mg\sin\varphi + ka\left[1 - 2\cos\left(\varphi - \theta\right)\right] + m\Omega^2a\cos^2\varphi \quad &\text{(with the reaction $N_1$)} \\ P,\ \mathbf k_1:&\quad 0 = N_2 - 2m\Omega a\dot\varphi\sin\varphi \quad &\text{(reaction and Coriolis)} \\ Q,\ \mathbf e_r^Q:&\quad -2ma\dot\theta^2 = N_3 - mg\sin\theta + ka\left[2 - \cos\left(\varphi - \theta\right)\right] + 2m\Omega^2a\cos^2\theta \quad &\text{(with the reaction $N_3$)} \\ Q,\ \mathbf k_1:&\quad 0 = N_4 - 4m\Omega a\dot\theta\sin\theta \quad &\text{(reaction and Coriolis)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\ddot\varphi = -\frac{g}{a}\cos\varphi + \frac{2k}{m}\sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right) - \Omega^2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi, \qquad \ddot\theta = -\frac{g}{2a}\cos\theta - \frac{k}{2m}\sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right) - \Omega^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}$$

Units: $[g/a] = [k/m] = [\Omega^2] = [\ddot\varphi] = [\mathrm T^{-2}]$

Meaning: six scalar equations for six unknowns; the two tangential ones are a closed system for the two angles, coupled through the repulsion.

(g) Reactions as functions of time

The four remaining projections solved for the reactions Law: the radial and normal projections of part (f), with the angles known Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Problems.pdf, p. 32
$$\begin{aligned} N_1 &= -ma\dot\varphi^2 + mg\sin\varphi - ka\left[1 - 2\cos\left(\varphi - \theta\right)\right] - m\Omega^2a\cos^2\varphi \quad &\text{($\mathbf e_r^P$ equation)} \\ N_2 &= 2m\Omega a\dot\varphi\sin\varphi \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1$ equation of $P$)} \\ N_3 &= -2ma\dot\theta^2 + mg\sin\theta - ka\left[2 - \cos\left(\varphi - \theta\right)\right] - 2m\Omega^2a\cos^2\theta \quad &\text{($\mathbf e_r^Q$ equation)} \\ N_4 &= 4m\Omega a\dot\theta\sin\theta \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1$ equation of $Q$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf N^P(t) = \left\{-ma\dot\varphi^2 + mg\sin\varphi - ka\left[1 - 2\cos\left(\varphi - \theta\right)\right] - m\Omega^2a\cos^2\varphi\right\}\mathbf e_r^P + 2m\Omega a\dot\varphi\sin\varphi\,\mathbf k_1 \cr \mathbf N^Q(t) = \left\{-2ma\dot\theta^2 + mg\sin\theta - ka\left[2 - \cos\left(\varphi - \theta\right)\right] - 2m\Omega^2a\cos^2\theta\right\}\mathbf e_r^Q + 4m\Omega a\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \end{gathered}}$$

Units: every term $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: with the solution of part (f) substituted, each reaction is an explicit function of time; the components normal to the plane come only from the Coriolis forces.

Answers and Checks

(h) Mechanical energy in S1

Why the energy in S1 is conserved, and its expression Law: power of each force on the relative velocity; potentials of the weights, the repulsion and the centrifugal forces Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]

Two reasons. First, the forces that do no work in $S_1$: the reactions (the wires are at rest in $S_1$ and smooth, so each reaction is normal to the relative velocity), the Coriolis forces (normal to the relative velocities), and the origin and Euler forces, which vanish. Second, the forces that work have potentials of the positions in $S_1$: the weights, constant in $S_1$ because $\mathbf j_1$ is the fixed vertical; the repulsion, which depends only on $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ (its potential has a minus sign because the force pushes the particles apart); and the centrifugal forces, because the rate is constant and the axis fixed. A point of the plane is at the distance of its $x_1$ coordinate from the axis $Oy_1$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf N^P\cdot\mathbf v_1^P &= \left(N_1\,\mathbf e_r^P + N_2\,\mathbf k_1\right)\cdot a\dot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi = 0, \quad \mathbf F_{COR}^P\cdot\mathbf v_1^P = -2m\Omega a^2\dot\varphi^2\sin\varphi\,\mathbf k_1\cdot\mathbf e_\varphi = 0 \quad &\text{(no power; the same for $Q$)} \\ \left|\overrightarrow{PQ}\right|^2 &= a^2 + 4a^2 - 4a^2\,\mathbf e_r^P\cdot\mathbf e_r^Q = 5a^2 - 4a^2\cos\left(\varphi - \theta\right) \quad &\text{(square of the difference)} \\ V_1 &= mga\sin\varphi + 2mga\sin\theta - \tfrac12 k\left|\overrightarrow{PQ}\right|^2 - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2a^2\cos^2\varphi - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2\left(2a\cos\theta\right)^2 \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.14; Slide 30)} \\ &= mga\left(\sin\varphi + 2\sin\theta\right) + 2ka^2\cos\left(\varphi - \theta\right) - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2a^2\left(\cos^2\varphi + 4\cos^2\theta\right) - \tfrac52 ka^2 \quad &\text{(expanded)} \\ T_1 &= \tfrac12 m\left(a\dot\varphi\right)^2 + \tfrac12 m\left(2a\dot\theta\right)^2 = \tfrac12 ma^2\left(\dot\varphi^2 + 4\dot\theta^2\right) \quad &\text{(relative velocities)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(T_1 + V_1\right) &= ma^2\dot\varphi\ddot\varphi + 4ma^2\dot\theta\ddot\theta + mga\left(\cos\varphi\,\dot\varphi + 2\cos\theta\,\dot\theta\right) - 2ka^2\sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right)\left(\dot\varphi - \dot\theta\right) + m\Omega^2a^2\left(\cos\varphi\sin\varphi\,\dot\varphi + 4\cos\theta\sin\theta\,\dot\theta\right) \quad &\text{(chain rule on each term)} \\ &= a\dot\varphi\left[ma\ddot\varphi + mg\cos\varphi - 2ka\sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right) + m\Omega^2a\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\right] + 2a\dot\theta\left[2ma\ddot\theta + mg\cos\theta + ka\sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right) + 2m\Omega^2a\sin\theta\cos\theta\right] = 0 \quad &\text{(grouped; both brackets vanish by part (f))} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{yes:}\quad \frac12 ma^2\left(\dot\varphi^2 + 4\dot\theta^2\right) + mga\left(\sin\varphi + 2\sin\theta\right) + 2ka^2\cos\left(\varphi - \theta\right) - \frac12 m\Omega^2a^2\left(\cos^2\varphi + 4\cos^2\theta\right) = E_1 = \text{const}}$$

Units: $[ma^2\dot\varphi^2] = [mga] = [ka^2] = [m\Omega^2a^2] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the energy of the relative motion is a first integral; the constant term of the repulsion potential is dropped, and the constant is fixed by initial conditions, which the statement does not give.

(i) Parameters for the equilibrium at 30 and minus 60 degrees

Relative equilibrium conditions Law: constant coordinates in $S_1$, so the rates and accelerations vanish in the two equations of part (f) Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.32; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6; Problems.pdf, p. 32

The first equation of part (f) is multiplied by $a/g$ and the second by $2a/g$, which brings in the two parameters.

$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -\cos\varphi + 2\alpha\sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right) - \beta\sin\varphi\cos\varphi, \quad 0 = -\cos\theta - \alpha\sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right) - 2\beta\sin\theta\cos\theta \quad &\text{(rates zero; $\alpha = ka/(mg)$, $\beta = a\Omega^2/g$)} \\ \varphi - \theta &= 30^\circ - \left(-60^\circ\right) = 90^\circ, \quad \sin 90^\circ = 1 \quad &\text{(the two radii are perpendicular)} \\ 0 &= -\frac{\sqrt3}{2} + 2\alpha - \frac{\sqrt3}{4}\,\beta \quad &\text{($\cos 30^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, $\sin 30^\circ = \tfrac12$)} \\ 0 &= -\frac12 - \alpha + \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\,\beta \quad &\text{($\cos(-60^\circ) = \tfrac12$, $\sin(-60^\circ) = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, so $-2\beta\sin\theta\cos\theta = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\beta$)} \\ \alpha &= \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\,\beta - \frac12 \quad &\text{(second equation)} \\ 0 &= -\frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \sqrt3\,\beta - 1 - \frac{\sqrt3}{4}\,\beta \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\,\beta = \frac{2 + \sqrt3}{2} \quad &\text{(substituted in the first)} \\ \beta &= \frac{2\left(2 + \sqrt3\right)}{3\sqrt3} = \frac{6 + 4\sqrt3}{9} = 1.43647 \quad &\text{(rationalised: times $\sqrt3/\sqrt3$)} \\ \alpha &= \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac{6 + 4\sqrt3}{9} - \frac12 = \frac{6\sqrt3 + 12 - 9}{18} = \frac{1 + 2\sqrt3}{6} = 0.74402 \quad &\text{(back-substituted)} \\ -\frac{\sqrt3}{2} + 2\left(0.74402\right) - \frac{\sqrt3}{4}\left(1.43647\right) &= -0.86603 + 1.48804 - 0.62201 = 0.00000 \quad &\text{(numerical check of the first equation)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\alpha = \frac{ka}{mg} = \frac{1 + 2\sqrt3}{6} \approx 0.744, \qquad \beta = \frac{a\Omega^2}{g} = \frac{6 + 4\sqrt3}{9} \approx 1.4365}$$

Units: $[ka/(mg)] = [a\Omega^2/g] = [1]$

Meaning: both values are positive, so the configuration can be an equilibrium. Along the wire of $P$ the repulsion pushes it towards larger angles, while its weight and the centrifugal force (towards the horizontal, away from the axis) push it back; along the wire of $Q$ the weight and the repulsion push it towards more negative angles and the centrifugal force pulls it back towards the horizontal.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Degrees of freedom2 ($\varphi$, $\theta$)
(b) Reactionsanswered under Forces and Equations of Motion, after part (c): 4 independent components: $\mathbf N^P = N_1\,\mathbf e_r^P + N_2\,\mathbf k_1$, $\mathbf N^Q = N_3\,\mathbf e_r^Q + N_4\,\mathbf k_1$
(c) Relative accelerationsanswered under Kinematics, before part (b): $\mathbf a_1^P = a\ddot\varphi\,\mathbf e_\varphi - a\dot\varphi^2\,\mathbf e_r^P$, $\mathbf a_1^Q = 2a\ddot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta - 2a\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf e_r^Q$, with $\mathbf e_r^P = \cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\varphi\,\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf e_\varphi = -\sin\varphi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\varphi\,\mathbf j_1$ (same with $\theta$)
(d) Applied forces$-mg\,\mathbf j_1 + k(\mathbf r_1^P - \mathbf r_1^Q)$ on $P$ and $-mg\,\mathbf j_1 + k(\mathbf r_1^Q - \mathbf r_1^P)$ on $Q$, in polar components as boxed in part (d)
(e) Inertia forces$\mathbf F_C^P = m\Omega^2a\cos\varphi\,\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf F_C^Q = 2m\Omega^2a\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf F_{COR}^P = -2m\Omega a\dot\varphi\sin\varphi\,\mathbf k_1$, $\mathbf F_{COR}^Q = -4m\Omega a\dot\theta\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1$; origin and Euler forces zero (opposite sense of rotation: Coriolis forces change sign)
(f) Equations of motion$\ddot\varphi = -(g/a)\cos\varphi + (2k/m)\sin(\varphi - \theta) - \Omega^2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi$; $\ddot\theta = -(g/2a)\cos\theta - (k/2m)\sin(\varphi - \theta) - \Omega^2\sin\theta\cos\theta$
(g) Reactions$N_1$, $N_3$ as boxed in part (g); $N_2 = 2m\Omega a\dot\varphi\sin\varphi$, $N_4 = 4m\Omega a\dot\theta\sin\theta$ (opposite sense of rotation: $N_2$, $N_4$ change sign)
(h) Energy in $S_1$conserved: $\frac12 ma^2(\dot\varphi^2 + 4\dot\theta^2) + mga(\sin\varphi + 2\sin\theta) + 2ka^2\cos(\varphi - \theta) - \frac12 m\Omega^2a^2(\cos^2\varphi + 4\cos^2\theta) = \text{const}$
(i) Parameters$\alpha = (1 + 2\sqrt3)/6 \approx 0.744$, $\beta = (6 + 4\sqrt3)/9 \approx 1.4365$

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 76 prints only the final quantities of part (i), 0.744 and 1.4365; the exact values of the box, 0.74402 and 1.43647, round to them. The other parts have no key; the energy is checked against the equations of motion in part (h), and the limiting cases follow.

Limiting cases Law: the equations of part (f) and the reactions of part (g) at extreme values of the data Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63
$$\begin{aligned} \Omega \to 0:\quad N_2 &= N_4 = 0, \quad \ddot\varphi = -\frac{g}{a}\cos\varphi + \frac{2k}{m}\sin\left(\varphi - \theta\right) \quad &\text{(fixed vertical wires)} \\ k \to 0:\quad \ddot\varphi &= -\frac{g}{a}\cos\varphi - \Omega^2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi \quad &\text{(two independent beads on spinning circles)} \\ k \to 0, \ \varphi = -\tfrac{\pi}{2}:\quad \ddot\varphi &= -\frac{g}{a}\cdot 0 - \Omega^2\left(-1\right)\cdot 0 = 0 \quad &\text{(the lowest point is an equilibrium)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\text{with no rotation the wires carry no load normal to the plane; with no repulsion the particles move independently}}$$

Units: $[\mathrm T^{-2}]$

Meaning: the Coriolis forces only load the wires; they never enter the equations of motion or the energy.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf (PDF page 32); key on PDF page 76
Problem 49

Particle on a Rotating Sphere Attracted to a Point

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 34
Relative Equilibria & BifurcationIn-Class Session 13

A point particle $P$ of mass $m$ slides without friction on a sphere of radius $a$ centered at the origin of the inertial reference frame $S_0$ as shown in the figure. The particle is attracted by a point $A$ in the equatorial plane, located a distance $a$ from the surface of the sphere as shown. The force of attraction is linearly proportional [sic] the distance between this point and $P$, with known constant of proportionality $k \gt 0$. The sphere and the point $A$ rotate rigidly about the vertical with a known angular velocity $\Omega\mathbf{k}_0$. We define the auxiliary reference frame $S_1$ that rotates with the sphere and point $A$, with $\mathbf{k}_1 = \mathbf{k}_0$ and $\mathbf{i}_1$ pointing in the direction of $A$. We introduce the angles $\phi$ and $\theta$ as shown to locate $P$ on the sphere. Note that there is no gravity in this problem.

  • (a)
    Express the position, velocity, and acceleration of $P$ with respect to $S_1$ in terms of $\phi$, $\theta$ and their derivatives. Remember to define any unit vectors that you want to use in terms of $\mathbf{i}_0, \mathbf{j}_0, \mathbf{k}_0$ first.
  • (b)
    Write down the (vector) equation of motion of $P$ in $S_1$, and derive from there a set of two scalar second-order differential equations for $\phi$, $\theta$ that do not depend on any other unknowns. To do so, first identify and write down all the forces needed in your analysis.
  • (c)
    Is the mechanical energy of $P$ conserved in $S_1$? Explain. If so, write down the corresponding conservation law.
  • (d)
    Identify all equilibrium configurations of the system, and discuss them as a function of the ratio $m\Omega^2/k$.
  • (e)
    Assuming the functions of time $\phi(t)$ and $\theta(t)$ are known, write down the expression of the reaction of the sphere on $P$.
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

A particle $P$ of mass $m$ slides without friction on a sphere of radius $a$ centred at the origin $O$ of the inertial frame $S_0$. A point $A$ of the equatorial plane, at the distance $a$ from the surface, attracts $P$ with a force equal to $k$ times their distance. The sphere and $A$ turn rigidly about the vertical with the angular velocity $\Omega\,\mathbf k_0$; there is no gravity (Problems.pdf, p. 34). The statement asks for the position, velocity and acceleration in $S_1$, the equation of motion and two scalar equations for the angles, the energy in $S_1$, the equilibria as functions of the ratio of $m\Omega^2$ to $k$, and the reaction. The sphere and $A$ are at rest in $S_1$, so the solution works there, with the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2 and the inertia forces of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$, $\mathbf k_0$ along the axis of rotation
Moving frame$S_1 = \{O;\ \mathcal B_1\}$, turning with the sphere and $A$: $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$, $\mathbf i_1$ towards $A$; it turns by $\Omega t$ from $\mathbf i_0$ towards $\mathbf j_0$ (figure) and coincides with $S_0$ at $t = 0$
Point $A$on the $\mathbf i_1$ axis, at the distance $a$ from the surface, so $OA$ is $2a$
Spherical basis at $P$$\{\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\phi, \mathbf e_\theta\}$ with the polar axis along $OA$ (deduced below); auxiliary unit vector $\mathbf u$ of the plane of $\mathbf j_1$ and $\mathbf k_1$; $P'$ the projection of $P$ on that plane
Coordinates$\phi$, angle at $O$ between $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\overrightarrow{OP}$; $\theta$, angle about the axis $OA$ from the equatorial plane (side of $\mathbf j_1$) towards $\mathbf k_1$
Data$m$ [kg], $a$ [m], $k$ [N m$^{-1}$], $\Omega$ [rad s$^{-1}$]; ratio $\Lambda = m\Omega^2/k$ [1]
Unknowns$\phi(t)$, $\theta(t)$ and the reaction $N\,\mathbf e_r$
Applied forceattraction $k\,\overrightarrow{PA}$; no gravity
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)centrifugal and Coriolis; no origin or Euler terms (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial; smooth sphere; $\Omega$ constant
Readings(1) Read from the figure: $\phi$ is the angle $AOP$ and $\theta$ the angle, seen at the point where $OA$ crosses the sphere, between the equator and the great circle through that point and $P$; so $\phi$ is a polar angle about $OA$ and $\theta$ its azimuth. If instead $\phi$ were the azimuth in the equatorial plane from $\mathbf i_1$ and $\theta$ the latitude, the position would be $a(\cos\theta\cos\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\theta\sin\phi\,\mathbf j_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1)$; the equilibria are the same points, with the coordinates given in the Answers table. (2) The contact is read as bilateral (the reaction may take either sign): the equilibrium $E_1$ always, and $E_2$ when $m\Omega^2$ exceeds $3k$, need the sphere to pull the particle in. With a one-sided contact on the outer face, the equilibria with a negative reaction are not admissible (Answers table)

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. View from $+z$, with $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf k_1$ out of the paper ($\odot$), so $\mathbf j_0$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned $90^\circ$ counter-clockwise. $S_1$ turns $\Omega t$ counter-clockwise: $\mathbf i_1$ has the legs $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$ and $\sin\Omega t$ along $\mathbf j_0$; the tip of $\mathbf j_1$ moves to the side of $-\mathbf i_0$, hence $-\sin\Omega t$. $A$ sits on the $\mathbf i_1$ axis at $OA = 2a$.
Basis of S1: rotation by Omega t about k0 Law: elementary rotation about the third axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

View from above, along $\mathbf k_0$, which points out of the paper (⊙). With $\mathbf i_0$ to the right, $\mathbf j_0$, the cross product of $\mathbf k_0$ and $\mathbf i_0$, points up the page. The figure measures $\Omega t$ from $\mathbf i_0$ towards $\mathbf j_0$, so $S_1$ turns counterclockwise in this view. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\Omega t$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\Omega t$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\Omega t$ along plus $\mathbf j_0$. $\mathbf j_1$ is $\mathbf j_0$ turned by the same angle; the counterclockwise turn carries its tip to the left, so its opposite leg $\sin\Omega t$ lies along minus $\mathbf i_0$ (the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf j_1 = -\sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles; axis)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\Omega t\cos\Omega t - \left(-\sin\Omega t\right)\sin\Omega t\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{3+3}$)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\Omega t + \sin^2\Omega t = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{12} = -\cos\Omega t\sin\Omega t + \sin\Omega t\cos\Omega t = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \\ \mathbf r_1^A &= 2a\,\mathbf i_1 \quad &\text{($A$ at the distance $a$ outside the surface)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\Omega t & -\sin\Omega t & 0 \cr \sin\Omega t & \cos\Omega t & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I, \quad \mathbf r_1^A = 2a\,\mathbf i_1}$$

Units: $[\Omega t] = [1]$; $[a] = [\mathrm L]$

Meaning: the vectors of $\mathcal B_1$ in terms of $\mathcal B_0$, which part (a) asks to define first; $A$ is at rest in $S_1$.

Figure 2. View along $OA$, with $\mathbf i_1$ out of the paper ($\odot$): then $\mathbf j_1$ points right and $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf i_1\times\mathbf j_1$ up. The azimuth $\theta$ turns counter-clockwise from $\mathbf j_1$: $\mathbf u = \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1$ (legs of the shaded triangle) and $\mathbf e_\theta = d\mathbf u/d\theta$. $P$ projects onto this plane at $P'$, at distance $a\sin\phi$ from the axis.
The azimuth theta: view along OA Law: elementary rotation about $\mathbf i_1$; right triangle of the unit vector $\mathbf u$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.18; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.5; Problems.pdf, p. 34

View along $OA$, with $\mathbf i_1$ out of the paper (⊙). With $\mathbf j_1$ to the right, $\mathbf k_1$, the cross product of $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf j_1$, points up the page. The azimuth starts at $\mathbf j_1$ (equatorial plane) and grows counterclockwise towards $\mathbf k_1$. The unit vector $\mathbf u$ of the plane of $\mathbf j_1$ and $\mathbf k_1$ in the direction $\theta$ is the hypotenuse of the shaded triangle: adjacent leg $\cos\theta$ along $\mathbf j_1$, opposite leg $\sin\theta$ along $\mathbf k_1$. $\mathbf e_\theta$ is $\mathbf u$ turned a further quarter turn counterclockwise; that carries its tip to the side of minus $\mathbf j_1$ (the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf u &= \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(shaded triangle)} \\ \mathbf e_\theta &= \frac{d\mathbf u}{d\theta} = -\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{($\tfrac{d}{d\theta}\cos\theta = -\sin\theta$, $\tfrac{d}{d\theta}\sin\theta = \cos\theta$)} \\ \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf e_\theta &= -\cos\theta\sin\theta + \sin\theta\cos\theta = 0, \quad \frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{d\theta} = -\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 - \sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1 = -\mathbf u \quad &\text{(orthogonal; second derivative)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf u = \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1, \qquad \mathbf e_\theta = -\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1}$$

Units: $[\theta] = [1]$
