Meaning: $\mathbf u$ points from the axis $OA$ towards the projection $P'$ of the particle; $\mathbf e_\theta$ is the direction in which the particle moves when only $\theta$ grows.

Figure 3. Meridian plane of $P$ (it contains $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf u$; $\mathbf e_\theta = \mathbf i_1\times\mathbf u$ is out of the paper). $\phi$ is measured at $O$ from $OA$: in the shaded triangle the hypotenuse is $a$, the leg adjacent to $\phi$ is $a\cos\phi$ along $\mathbf i_1$ and the opposite one $a\sin\phi$ along $\mathbf u$. $\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\phi$ in orange; the attraction acts along $PA$.
The polar angle phi: meridian plane, position and spherical basis Law: right triangle of the radius; tangent vectors as derivatives of the radial unit vector; determinant by cofactors Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 34

The meridian plane of $P$ contains the axis $OA$ and $\mathbf u$; it is drawn with $\mathbf i_1$ to the right and $\mathbf u$ up, so $\mathbf e_\theta$ points out of the paper. In the shaded right triangle the hypotenuse is $OP$, of length $a$; the leg adjacent to $\phi$ is $a\cos\phi$ along $\mathbf i_1$ and the opposite leg is $a\sin\phi$ along $\mathbf u$, the distance $OP'$ of the axis view. This is the usual spherical system with its polar axis along $OA$: the usual roles of $\mathbf k$, $\mathbf i$, $\mathbf j$ are taken by $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf k_1$, a cyclic permutation, which keeps the triad right-handed. The determinant of the matrix whose columns are $\mathbf e_r$, $\mathbf e_\phi$, $\mathbf e_\theta$ is expanded along its first row, with the cofactor signs plus, minus, plus.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_r &= \cos\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\phi\,\mathbf u = \cos\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\phi\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \sin\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf r_1^P = a\,\mathbf e_r \quad &\text{(meridian triangle; Eq. 3.16)} \\ \mathbf e_\phi &= \frac{\partial\mathbf e_r}{\partial\phi} = -\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\phi\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \cos\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(derivative in $\phi$; unit length)} \\ \frac{\partial\mathbf e_r}{\partial\theta} &= \sin\phi\,\frac{d\mathbf u}{d\theta} = \sin\phi\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(derivative in $\theta$; length $\sin\phi$)} \\ \det\left[\mathbf e_r\ \mathbf e_\phi\ \mathbf e_\theta\right] &= (+1)\cos\phi\left(\cos\phi\cos^2\theta + \cos\phi\sin^2\theta\right) + (-1)\left(-\sin\phi\right)\left(\sin\phi\cos^2\theta + \sin\phi\sin^2\theta\right) + (+1)\cdot 0 = 1 \quad &\text{(first row; cofactor signs)} \\ \mathbf e_r\cdot\mathbf e_\phi &= -\cos\phi\sin\phi + \sin\phi\cos\phi\left(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta\right) = 0, \quad \mathbf e_r\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = \mathbf e_\phi\cdot\mathbf e_\theta = 0 \quad &\text{(orthogonality)} \\ \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\phi\,\mathbf e_r - \sin\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \sin\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf e_r + \cos\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf e_\phi + \cos\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(projections: third components of the three vectors)} \\ \mathbf e_r &= \left(\cos\Omega t\cos\phi - \sin\Omega t\sin\phi\cos\theta\right)\mathbf i_0 + \left(\sin\Omega t\cos\phi + \cos\Omega t\sin\phi\cos\theta\right)\mathbf j_0 + \sin\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{($[{}_0R_1]$ times the components)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf r_1^P = a\,\mathbf e_r, \quad \mathbf e_r = \cos\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\phi\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \sin\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1, \cr \mathbf e_\phi = -\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\phi\cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \cos\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf e_\theta = -\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf k_1 \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[\mathbf e_r] = [\mathbf e_\phi] = [\mathbf e_\theta] = [1]$

Meaning: a right-handed orthonormal basis at $P$, written in $\mathcal B_1$ and, through $[{}_0R_1]$, in $\mathcal B_0$; with the polar axis along $OA$ the distance to $A$ depends on $\phi$ only.

Kinematics

Motion of S1 and derivatives of its unit vectors Law: angular velocity of a simple rotation; derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf v_0^O = \mathbf a_0^O = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(rotation about the fixed vertical; $\Omega$ constant; $O$ fixed)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\Omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 to 3.5)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0\right) &= -\Omega\sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \Omega\cos\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(check: chain rule on $\mathbf i_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\Omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0}$$

Units: $[\Omega] = [\mathrm T^{-1}]$

Meaning: in $S_1$ the three unit vectors are constant; in $S_0$ the two horizontal ones turn with the sphere.

(a) Position, velocity and acceleration of P in S1

Derivatives of the spherical basis and relative kinematics Law: time derivatives in $S_1$; chain rule through $\phi(t)$ and $\theta(t)$; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24; Problems.pdf, p. 34

$\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf k_1$ are constant in $S_1$, so the spherical vectors change only through the two angles.

$$\begin{aligned} \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_r}{dt}\right|_1 &= \frac{\partial\mathbf e_r}{\partial\phi}\dot\phi + \frac{\partial\mathbf e_r}{\partial\theta}\dot\theta = \dot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi + \sin\phi\,\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\phi}{dt}\right|_1 &= \left(-\cos\phi\,\mathbf i_1 - \sin\phi\,\mathbf u\right)\dot\phi + \cos\phi\,\frac{d\mathbf u}{d\theta}\,\dot\theta = -\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_r + \cos\phi\,\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(chain rule; $\mathbf e_\phi = -\sin\phi\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\phi\,\mathbf u$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{dt}\right|_1 &= \frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{d\theta}\,\dot\theta = -\dot\theta\,\mathbf u = -\sin\phi\,\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_r - \cos\phi\,\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\phi \quad &\text{(chain rule; $\mathbf u = \sin\phi\,\mathbf e_r + \cos\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi$)} \\ \mathbf v_1^P &= a\left.\frac{d\mathbf e_r}{dt}\right|_1 = a\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi + a\sin\phi\,\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{($a$ constant)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(a\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi\right) &= a\ddot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi - a\dot\phi^2\,\mathbf e_r + a\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(product rule)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(a\sin\phi\,\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta\right) &= a\left(\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\dot\theta + \sin\phi\,\ddot\theta\right)\mathbf e_\theta - a\sin^2\phi\,\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf e_r - a\sin\phi\cos\phi\,\dot\theta^2\,\mathbf e_\phi \quad &\text{(product rule, chain rule on $\sin\phi$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf r_1^P = a\,\mathbf e_r, \qquad \mathbf v_1^P = a\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi + a\sin\phi\,\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta, \cr \mathbf a_1^P = -a\left(\dot\phi^2 + \sin^2\phi\,\dot\theta^2\right)\mathbf e_r + a\left(\ddot\phi - \sin\phi\cos\phi\,\dot\theta^2\right)\mathbf e_\phi + a\left(\sin\phi\,\ddot\theta + 2\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\dot\theta\right)\mathbf e_\theta \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[a\dot\phi] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[a\dot\phi^2] = [a\ddot\phi] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the relative velocity is tangent to the sphere; the radial part of the relative acceleration is the centripetal one of the motion on the sphere.

Absolute acceleration: transport and Coriolis terms as they arise Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the position written in the turning basis; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]

Write the position as $x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + z_1\,\mathbf k_1$, the components of $a\,\mathbf e_r$; their time derivatives are the components of the relative velocity.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P &= \dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + \dot z_1\,\mathbf k_1 + x_1\Omega\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\Omega\,\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf v_1^P + \Omega\left(x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; derivatives of $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1^P}{dt}\right|_0 &= \mathbf a_1^P + \Omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; the basis turns inside $\mathbf v_1^P$)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left[\Omega\left(x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right)\right] &= \Omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) - \Omega^2\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; $\Omega$ constant)} \\ 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P &= 2\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + \dot z_1\,\mathbf k_1\right) = 2\Omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(the two equal terms: Coriolis)} \\ \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) &= \Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\Omega\left(x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) = -\Omega^2\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) = -\Omega^2\left(\mathbf r_1^P - z_1\,\mathbf k_1\right) \quad &\text{(the last term: centripetal)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_0^P = \mathbf a_1^P - \Omega^2\left(\mathbf r_1^P - z_1\,\mathbf k_1\right) + 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P, \qquad z_1 = a\sin\phi\sin\theta}$$

Units: $[\Omega^2 a] = [\Omega a\dot\phi] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the centripetal term points horizontally to the vertical axis; with $O$ fixed and the rate constant there are no origin or Euler terms.

Forces and Equations of Motion

Figure 4. Forces seen from $S_1$. Top: at the equilibrium $E_3$ ($m\Omega^2/k = 4$) in the meridian plane through $A$, the attraction $k\,\overrightarrow{PA}$, the centrifugal force (dashed), horizontal and away from the axis, and the reaction $N\,\mathbf e_r$ with $N = ka$; the other equilibria are marked. Bottom: the Coriolis force (dashed) of a moving particle, normal to $\mathbf k_1$ and to the relative velocity.

(b) Forces, vector equation and two scalar equations

Actual and inertia forces in the spherical basis Law: linear attraction towards $A$; smooth reaction along the normal; inertia forces of a non-inertial frame Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.11; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; Problems.pdf, p. 34

The vector products with $\mathbf k_1$ are determinants in the right-handed basis $\{\mathbf e_r, \mathbf e_\phi, \mathbf e_\theta\}$, with the components of $\mathbf k_1$ in the second row, expanded along the first row with the cofactor signs plus, minus, plus.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf F_k &= k\left(\mathbf r_1^A - \mathbf r_1^P\right) = k\left(2a\,\mathbf i_1 - a\,\mathbf e_r\right) = ka\left(2\cos\phi - 1\right)\mathbf e_r - 2ka\sin\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi \quad &\text{($\mathbf i_1$ in the spherical basis)} \\ \mathbf N &= N\,\mathbf e_r, \quad \mathbf F_A = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf F_E = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(smooth sphere; $O$ fixed; $\Omega$ constant)} \\ \mathbf F_C &= -m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) = m\Omega^2\left(a\,\mathbf e_r - a\sin\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf k_1\right) \quad &\text{(centripetal term times $-m$)} \\ &= m\Omega^2a\left[\left(1 - \sin^2\phi\sin^2\theta\right)\mathbf e_r - \sin\phi\cos\phi\sin^2\theta\,\mathbf e_\phi - \sin\phi\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta\right] \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1$ in the spherical basis)} \\ \mathbf k_1\times\mathbf e_\phi &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf e_r & \mathbf e_\phi & \mathbf e_\theta \cr \sin\phi\sin\theta & \cos\phi\sin\theta & \cos\theta \cr 0 & 1 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = (+1)\left(-\cos\theta\right)\mathbf e_r + (-1)(0)\,\mathbf e_\phi + (+1)\sin\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(first row; cofactor signs)} \\ \mathbf k_1\times\mathbf e_\theta &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf e_r & \mathbf e_\phi & \mathbf e_\theta \cr \sin\phi\sin\theta & \cos\phi\sin\theta & \cos\theta \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = (+1)\cos\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf e_r + (-1)\sin\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf e_\phi + (+1)(0)\,\mathbf e_\theta \quad &\text{(first row; cofactor signs)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR} &= -2m\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(a\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi + a\sin\phi\,\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta\right) \quad &\text{(Coriolis term times $-m$)} \\ &= 2m\Omega a\left[\left(\cos\theta\,\dot\phi - \sin\phi\cos\phi\sin\theta\,\dot\theta\right)\mathbf e_r + \sin^2\phi\sin\theta\,\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\phi - \sin\phi\sin\theta\,\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_\theta\right] \quad &\text{(the two products above)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{m\,\mathbf a_1^P = k\left(2a\,\mathbf i_1 - a\,\mathbf e_r\right) + N\,\mathbf e_r - m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) - 2m\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P}$$

Units: $[ka] = [m\Omega^2a] = [m\Omega a\dot\phi] = [N] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: one actual applied force, the reaction and two inertia forces; the attraction lies in the meridian plane, the centrifugal force is horizontal and away from the axis, the Coriolis force is normal to the relative velocity.

Projections on the two tangent vectors Law: Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame projected on $\mathbf e_\phi$ and $\mathbf e_\theta$, which are normal to the reaction Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; [Lecture 3, Slide 14]; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_\phi:\quad ma\left(\ddot\phi - \sin\phi\cos\phi\,\dot\theta^2\right) &= -2ka\sin\phi - m\Omega^2a\sin\phi\cos\phi\sin^2\theta + 2m\Omega a\sin^2\phi\sin\theta\,\dot\theta \quad &\text{(attraction, centrifugal, Coriolis)} \\ \mathbf e_\theta:\quad ma\left(\sin\phi\,\ddot\theta + 2\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\dot\theta\right) &= -m\Omega^2a\sin\phi\sin\theta\cos\theta - 2m\Omega a\sin\phi\sin\theta\,\dot\phi \quad &\text{(centrifugal, Coriolis)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \ddot\phi - \sin\phi\cos\phi\,\dot\theta^2 = -\frac{2k}{m}\sin\phi - \Omega^2\sin\phi\cos\phi\sin^2\theta + 2\Omega\sin^2\phi\sin\theta\,\dot\theta \cr \sin\phi\,\ddot\theta + 2\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\dot\theta = -\Omega^2\sin\phi\sin\theta\cos\theta - 2\Omega\sin\phi\sin\theta\,\dot\phi \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[k/m] = [\Omega^2] = [\Omega\dot\theta] = [\ddot\phi] = [\mathrm T^{-2}]$

Meaning: two second-order equations for the two angles, free of the reaction; the projection on $\mathbf e_r$ gives the reaction in part (e). Away from the poles of the coordinates, where the sine of $\phi$ vanishes, the second equation may be divided by that sine.

Answers and Checks

(c) Mechanical energy in S1

Why the energy in S1 is conserved, and its expression Law: power of each force on the relative velocity; potentials of the attraction and of the centrifugal force Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; [Lecture 5, Slide 29]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]

Yes, for two reasons. First, the forces that do no work in $S_1$: the reaction (the sphere is at rest in $S_1$ and smooth, so the reaction is normal to the relative velocity), the Coriolis force (normal to the relative velocity), and the origin and Euler forces, which vanish. Second, the forces that work have potentials of the position in $S_1$: the attraction, because $A$ is at rest in $S_1$, and the centrifugal force, because the rate is constant and the axis fixed. The squared distance to the vertical axis is the squared radius minus the square of $z_1$.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf N\cdot\mathbf v_1^P &= N\,\mathbf e_r\cdot\left(a\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi + a\sin\phi\,\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta\right) = 0 \quad &\text{(no power)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR}\cdot\mathbf v_1^P &= 2m\Omega a^2\left(\sin^2\phi\sin\theta\,\dot\theta\,\dot\phi - \sin\phi\sin\theta\,\dot\phi\,\sin\phi\,\dot\theta\right) = 0 \quad &\text{(components of the two boxes)} \\ \left|\mathbf r_1^P - \mathbf r_1^A\right|^2 &= a^2 - 4a^2\,\mathbf e_r\cdot\mathbf i_1 + 4a^2 = 5a^2 - 4a^2\cos\phi \quad &\text{(square of the difference)} \\ V_1 &= \tfrac12 k\left(5a^2 - 4a^2\cos\phi\right) - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2\left(a^2 - a^2\sin^2\phi\sin^2\theta\right) \quad &\text{(Eq. 4.14; Slide 30)} \\ T_1 &= \tfrac12 m\left|\mathbf v_1^P\right|^2 = \tfrac12 ma^2\left(\dot\phi^2 + \sin^2\phi\,\dot\theta^2\right) \quad &\text{(orthonormal components)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(T_1 + V_1\right) &= ma^2\dot\phi\left(\ddot\phi - \sin\phi\cos\phi\,\dot\theta^2\right) + ma^2\sin\phi\,\dot\theta\left(\sin\phi\,\ddot\theta + 2\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\dot\theta\right) + 2ka^2\sin\phi\,\dot\phi + m\Omega^2a^2\left(\sin\phi\cos\phi\sin^2\theta\,\dot\phi + \sin^2\phi\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\theta\right) \quad &\text{(chain rule; terms regrouped)} \\ &= a\dot\phi\left(2m\Omega a\sin^2\phi\sin\theta\,\dot\theta\right) + a\sin\phi\,\dot\theta\left(-2m\Omega a\sin\phi\sin\theta\,\dot\phi\right) = 0 \quad &\text{(the two equations of part (b))} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathcal E_1 = \frac12 ma^2\left(\dot\phi^2 + \sin^2\phi\,\dot\theta^2\right) - 2ka^2\cos\phi + \frac12 m\Omega^2a^2\sin^2\phi\sin^2\theta = \text{const}}$$

Units: $[ma^2\dot\phi^2] = [ka^2] = [m\Omega^2a^2] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the constant terms of the potential are dropped; the constant is fixed by initial conditions, which the statement does not give. What is left of the check is exactly the power of the Coriolis force, which vanishes.

(d) Equilibrium configurations

Relative equilibria away from the poles of the coordinates Law: constant coordinates, so the rates and accelerations vanish in the two equations of part (b) Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.32; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6; Problems.pdf, p. 34

With $\Lambda$ the ratio of $m\Omega^2$ to $k$, and the sine of $\phi$ not zero:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_\theta:\quad 0 &= -\Omega^2\sin\phi\sin\theta\cos\theta \;\Rightarrow\; \sin\theta = 0 \ \text{ or } \ \cos\theta = 0 \quad &\text{($\Omega \ne 0$, $\sin\phi \ne 0$)} \\ \mathbf e_\phi:\quad 0 &= -\sin\phi\left(2k + m\Omega^2\cos\phi\sin^2\theta\right) \;\Rightarrow\; 2 + \Lambda\cos\phi\sin^2\theta = 0 \quad &\text{(divided by $-k\sin\phi$)} \\ \sin\theta = 0:\quad 2 &= 0 \quad &\text{(impossible: no equilibrium off the axis in the equatorial plane)} \\ \cos\theta = 0,\ \sin^2\theta = 1:\quad \cos\phi^* &= -\frac{2}{\Lambda} = -\frac{2k}{m\Omega^2} \quad &\text{(needs $\Lambda \gt 2$ for $\sin\phi^* \ne 0$)} \\ \mathbf r_1^P &= a\cos\phi^*\,\mathbf i_1 \pm a\sin\phi^*\,\mathbf k_1 = -\frac{2a}{\Lambda}\,\mathbf i_1 \pm a\sqrt{1 - \frac{4}{\Lambda^2}}\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{($\theta = \pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\sin\phi^* \gt 0$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{E_3, E_4:\ \theta = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}, \ \cos\phi^* = -\frac{2k}{m\Omega^2}, \ \text{only for } \frac{m\Omega^2}{k} \gt 2}$$

Units: $[2k/(m\Omega^2)] = [1]$

Meaning: these two equilibria lie in the meridian plane through $A$ and the axis, on the half of the sphere away from $A$, one above and one below the equator.

The poles of the coordinates and the reaction at each equilibrium Law: full vector balance of the forces at rest (the angle $\theta$ is undefined at the poles of the coordinates) Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6

At rest the Coriolis force vanishes; the applied force and the centrifugal force must be balanced by the radial reaction alone. At the equilibria of the previous box the centrifugal force is the product of $m\Omega^2$, which is $\Lambda k$, and the horizontal part $x_1\,\mathbf i_1$ of the position, with $x_1$ equal to $-2a/\Lambda$.

$$\begin{aligned} E_1,\ \mathbf r_1^P = a\,\mathbf i_1:\quad \mathbf F_k + \mathbf F_C &= k\left(2a - a\right)\mathbf i_1 + m\Omega^2a\,\mathbf i_1 = \left(k + m\Omega^2\right)a\,\mathbf e_r \;\Rightarrow\; N = -\left(k + m\Omega^2\right)a \quad &\text{(both forces radial, along $\mathbf e_r = \mathbf i_1$)} \\ E_2,\ \mathbf r_1^P = -a\,\mathbf i_1:\quad \mathbf F_k + \mathbf F_C &= k\left(2a + a\right)\mathbf i_1 - m\Omega^2a\,\mathbf i_1 = -\left(3k - m\Omega^2\right)a\,\mathbf e_r \;\Rightarrow\; N = \left(3k - m\Omega^2\right)a \quad &\text{(radial, along $\mathbf e_r = -\mathbf i_1$)} \\ E_3, E_4:\quad \mathbf F_k + \mathbf F_C &= k\left(2a\,\mathbf i_1 - \mathbf r_1^P\right) + \Lambda k\left(-\frac{2a}{\Lambda}\right)\mathbf i_1 = -k\,\mathbf r_1^P = -ka\,\mathbf e_r \;\Rightarrow\; N = ka \quad &\text{(the horizontal pulls cancel)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{E_1:\ N = -\left(k + m\Omega^2\right)a, \qquad E_2:\ N = \left(3k - m\Omega^2\right)a, \qquad E_3, E_4:\ N = ka}$$

Units: $[ka] = [m\Omega^2a] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: $E_1$ (the point nearest $A$) and $E_2$ (the farthest) exist for every rate, because there both forces are radial. At $E_1$ the reaction points inwards: the sphere must pull the particle in, which needs the bilateral contact of the readings. At $E_2$ it points outwards while $m\Omega^2$ is below $3k$, vanishes when they are equal and points inwards beyond. At $E_3$ and $E_4$ the reaction points outwards.

(e) Reaction of the sphere

Projection on the normal Law: Newton's second law in $S_1$ projected on $\mathbf e_r$, the only projection that contains $N$ Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; [Lecture 3, Slide 14]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_r:\quad -ma\left(\dot\phi^2 + \sin^2\phi\,\dot\theta^2\right) &= N + ka\left(2\cos\phi - 1\right) + m\Omega^2a\left(1 - \sin^2\phi\sin^2\theta\right) + 2m\Omega a\left(\cos\theta\,\dot\phi - \sin\phi\cos\phi\sin\theta\,\dot\theta\right) \quad &\text{(radial components of part (b))} \\ \phi = 0, \ \dot\phi = \dot\theta = 0:\quad N &= -ka - m\Omega^2a \quad &\text{(check: equals the value at $E_1$)} \\ \phi = \pi, \ \dot\phi = \dot\theta = 0:\quad N &= -\left[ka\left(-2 - 1\right) + m\Omega^2a\right] = \left(3k - m\Omega^2\right)a \quad &\text{(check: equals the value at $E_2$)} \\ E_3, E_4:\quad N &= -\left[ka\left(-\frac{4}{\Lambda} - 1\right) + m\Omega^2a\,\frac{4}{\Lambda^2}\right] = ka + \frac{4ka}{\Lambda} - \frac{4ka}{\Lambda} = ka \quad &\text{(check: $\sin^2\theta = 1$, $1 - \sin^2\phi^* = \cos^2\phi^*$, $m\Omega^2 = \Lambda k$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf N = -\left[ma\left(\dot\phi^2 + \sin^2\phi\,\dot\theta^2\right) + ka\left(2\cos\phi - 1\right) + m\Omega^2a\left(1 - \sin^2\phi\sin^2\theta\right) + 2m\Omega a\left(\cos\theta\,\dot\phi - \sin\phi\cos\phi\sin\theta\,\dot\theta\right)\right]\mathbf e_r}$$

Units: every term $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: once the two angles are known as functions of time, the reaction follows; $\mathbf e_r$ in terms of $\mathbf i_0$, $\mathbf j_0$, $\mathbf k_0$ is in the meridian box.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Kinematics in $S_1$$\mathbf r_1^P = a\,\mathbf e_r$, $\mathbf v_1^P = a\dot\phi\,\mathbf e_\phi + a\sin\phi\,\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta$, $\mathbf a_1^P = -a(\dot\phi^2 + \sin^2\phi\,\dot\theta^2)\,\mathbf e_r + a(\ddot\phi - \sin\phi\cos\phi\,\dot\theta^2)\,\mathbf e_\phi + a(\sin\phi\,\ddot\theta + 2\cos\phi\,\dot\phi\dot\theta)\,\mathbf e_\theta$; $\mathbf i_1 = \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0$, $\mathbf j_1 = -\sin\Omega t\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\Omega t\,\mathbf j_0$, $\mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0$, spherical vectors as boxed
(b) Forces and equations$\mathbf F_k = k(2a\,\mathbf i_1 - a\,\mathbf e_r)$, $\mathbf N = N\,\mathbf e_r$, $\mathbf F_C = m\Omega^2(\mathbf r_1^P - z_1\mathbf k_1)$, $\mathbf F_{COR} = -2m\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf v_1^P$; the two boxed scalar equations of part (b)
(c) Energy in $S_1$conserved: $\frac12 ma^2(\dot\phi^2 + \sin^2\phi\,\dot\theta^2) - 2ka^2\cos\phi + \frac12 m\Omega^2a^2\sin^2\phi\sin^2\theta = \text{const}$
(d) Equilibria$E_1$: $\phi = 0$ (point nearest $A$), $E_2$: $\phi = \pi$ (farthest point), for every $m\Omega^2/k$; $E_3$, $E_4$: $\theta = \pm\pi/2$, $\cos\phi = -2k/(m\Omega^2)$, only when $m\Omega^2/k \gt 2$; they branch off $E_2$ at the value 2 and tend to the top and bottom of the sphere as the ratio grows. In the other reading of the angles (azimuth $\phi$ in the equator, latitude $\theta$): $E_1$ at $(0, 0)$, $E_2$ at $(\pi, 0)$, $E_3$, $E_4$ at $\phi = \pi$, $\theta = \pm\arccos(2k/(m\Omega^2))$. With a one-sided contact on the outer face (reaction outwards only), $E_1$ is not admissible, and $E_2$ only when $m\Omega^2 \le 3k$
(e) Reaction$\mathbf N = -[ma(\dot\phi^2 + \sin^2\phi\,\dot\theta^2) + ka(2\cos\phi - 1) + m\Omega^2a(1 - \sin^2\phi\sin^2\theta) + 2m\Omega a(\cos\theta\,\dot\phi - \sin\phi\cos\phi\sin\theta\,\dot\theta)]\,\mathbf e_r$

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 76 prints no answer for problem 49. Independent checks: the energy of part (c) is constant along the equations of part (b), the reaction of part (e) gives at rest the values of the vector balance at the equilibria, and the limiting cases follow.

Limiting cases Law: the results at extreme values of the data Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.31; Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63
$$\begin{aligned} \Omega \to 0:\quad \mathcal E_1 &= \tfrac12 ma^2\left(\dot\phi^2 + \sin^2\phi\,\dot\theta^2\right) - 2ka^2\cos\phi \quad &\text{(fixed sphere: only the attraction works)} \\ \Lambda \to 2^+:\quad \cos\phi^* &= -\frac{2}{\Lambda} \to -1 \quad &\text{($E_3$ and $E_4$ merge with $E_2$)} \\ \Lambda \to \infty:\quad \cos\phi^* &\to 0, \quad \mathbf r_1^P \to \pm a\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{($E_3$, $E_4$ tend to the top and bottom of the sphere)} \\ E_3:\quad \left|\mathbf r_1^P\right|^2 &= \frac{4a^2}{\Lambda^2} + a^2\left(1 - \frac{4}{\Lambda^2}\right) = a^2 \quad &\text{(check: on the sphere)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\frac{m\Omega^2}{k} \le 2: \ E_1, E_2 \text{ only}; \qquad \frac{m\Omega^2}{k} \gt 2: \ E_1, E_2, E_3, E_4}$$

Units: $[\Lambda] = [1]$

Meaning: the rotation must be fast enough, compared with the stiffness of the attraction, for the centrifugal push away from the axis to balance the attraction off the line $OA$. The statement does not ask for stability, which is not discussed here.

Worked Solution Source: Problems.pdf (PDF page 34); no official key
Problem 51

Particle inside a Hollow Sphere in a Rotating Frame

Original statement · Problems.pdf, p. 36
Non-Inertial Frame + Surface Constraint

A heavy point particle $P$ of mass $m$ is constrained to move inside the surface of a hollow sphere of radius $R$ and center $C$ located at $\mathbf{r}_1^C = R(\mathbf{j}_1 + \mathbf{k}_1)$. The surface of the sphere is smooth. The reference frame $S_1$ shown in the figure is a non-inertial reference frame, because it rotates with a known angular velocity $\boldsymbol{\omega}_{10} = \Omega(t)\,\mathbf{k}_1$ with respect to inertial space. We introduce the two coordiantes [sic] $\theta$ and $\phi$ as shown in the figure, in order to characterize the configuration of $P$.

  • (a)
    Give the expressions for the position, velocity, and acceleration vectors of $P$ with respect to $S_1$, as functions of $\theta$, $\phi$ and their derivatives. Remember that you may use any unit vectors in your solution, provided that you define them first.
  • (b)
    Identify and write down all forces (actual and fictitious) on $P$ as seen from $S_1$.
  • (c)
    Write down two differential equations for $\theta$ and $\phi$, free of any other unknowns.
  • (d)
    Write down an expression for the reaction unknown. This expression may depend on $\theta, \dot{\theta}, \phi, \dot{\phi}$ and the known parameters of the problem. What is the mathematical condition for the particle to separate from the surface?
  • (e)
    In the case that $\Omega = \text{const}$, determine and discuss the value of $\theta$, $\phi$ and the reaction unknown for the equilibrium configurations of $P$.
Worked Solution [ Click to Expand ]

Reference Frames, Bases and Coordinates

A heavy particle $P$ of mass $m$ moves on the smooth inner surface of a hollow sphere of radius $R$ whose centre $C$ is at $R(\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf k_1)$ in the frame $S_1$. $S_1$ is not inertial: it turns with the known angular velocity $\Omega(t)\,\mathbf k_1$ (Problems.pdf, p. 36). The statement asks for the position, velocity and acceleration in $S_1$, all the forces seen from $S_1$, two equations for $\theta$ and $\phi$, the reaction and the condition for the particle to leave the surface, and the equilibria when the rate is constant. The sphere is at rest in $S_1$, so the solution works there, with the composition of motions of Notes.pdf, Sec. 3.2 and the inertia forces of Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.9; since the rate may change, the Euler force appears.

ItemDefinition
Fixed (inertial) frame$S_0 = \{A;\ \mathcal B_0\}$, $\mathcal B_0 = \{\mathbf i_0, \mathbf j_0, \mathbf k_0\}$, with $A$ the origin of $S_1$ (on the axis of rotation) and $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf k_1$
Moving frame$S_1 = \{A;\ \mathcal B_1\}$ of the figure, $\mathbf k_1$ vertical, up; it has turned the angle $\Psi(t)$ about $\mathbf k_0$, from $\mathbf i_0$ towards $\mathbf j_0$, whose rate of change is $\Omega$; $S_1$ and $S_0$ coincide when $\Psi$ is zero
Spherecentre $C$, $\mathbf r_1^C = R(\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf k_1)$, radius $R$, fixed in $S_1$; it touches the axis of rotation at $R\,\mathbf k_1$ and the plane $z_1 = 0$ at $R\,\mathbf j_1$
Bases at $P$horizontal unit vector $\mathbf e_h$ from $C$ towards the projection $P'$ of $P$ on the horizontal plane through $C$; spherical basis $\{\mathbf u_r, \mathbf u_\theta, \mathbf u_\phi\}$ (deduced below)
Coordinates$\theta$, azimuth of $CP'$ measured at $C$ from the direction of $\mathbf i_1$ towards $\mathbf j_1$; $\phi$, elevation of $CP$ above the horizontal plane through $C$
Data$m$ [kg], $R$ [m], $g$ [m s$^{-2}$], $\Omega(t)$ [rad s$^{-1}$] and its derivative $\dot\Omega(t)$ [rad s$^{-2}$]
Unknowns$\theta(t)$, $\phi(t)$ and the reaction $-N\,\mathbf u_r$
Applied forceweight $-mg\,\mathbf k_1$
Inertia forces (in $S_1$)Euler, centrifugal and Coriolis; no origin term (Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62)
Hypotheses$S_0$ inertial; uniform gravity; $A$ fixed; smooth surface; $\Omega(t)$ known
Readings(1) Read from the figure: $\theta$ is drawn in the horizontal plane through $C$ from the direction of $\mathbf i_1$ towards the side of $\mathbf j_1$, and $\phi$ from that plane upwards. If $\phi$ were the colatitude $\phi_c$ (measured from $\mathbf k_1$ downwards, the complement of $\phi$), the cosine and the sine of the angle would swap in every result, and every term linear in the rate or in the second derivative of the angle would change sign, because those of $\phi_c$ are minus those of $\phi$ and $\mathbf u_\phi$ reverses; the converted equations are in the Answers table. (2) The particle is inside the sphere and the statement asks when it separates, so the contact is read as one-sided: the reaction points towards $C$, written $-N\,\mathbf u_r$ with $N$ non-negative while in contact. For a contact that holds on both sides, every solution of part (e) would be admissible

Change of Basis and Position Vector

Figure 1. View from $+z$, with $\mathbf k_0 = \mathbf k_1$ out of the paper ($\odot$). $S_1$ has turned the angle $\Psi(t)$, $\dot\Psi = \Omega(t)$, counter-clockwise: $\mathbf i_1$ has the legs $\cos\Psi$ along $\mathbf i_0$ and $\sin\Psi$ along $\mathbf j_0$; the tip of $\mathbf j_1$ moves to the side of $-\mathbf i_0$, hence $-\sin\Psi$.
Basis of S1: rotation by Psi about k0 Law: elementary rotation about the third axis; change of basis matrix and its checks Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.14; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.15; Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; [Lecture 5, Slide 16]

View from above, along $\mathbf k_0$, which points out of the paper (⊙). With $\mathbf i_0$ to the right, $\mathbf j_0$, the cross product of $\mathbf k_0$ and $\mathbf i_0$, points up the page; a positive rate turns $S_1$ counterclockwise in this view. $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf i_0$ turned by $\Psi$: hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg $\cos\Psi$ along $\mathbf i_0$, opposite leg $\sin\Psi$ along plus $\mathbf j_0$. $\mathbf j_1$ is $\mathbf j_0$ turned by the same angle; the counterclockwise turn carries its tip to the left, so its opposite leg $\sin\Psi$ lies along minus $\mathbf i_0$ (the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \dot\Psi &= \Omega(t) \quad &\text{(definition of the angle turned: $\Psi$ is an antiderivative of the known rate)} \\ \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\Psi\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\Psi\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf j_1 = -\sin\Psi\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\Psi\,\mathbf j_0, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \mathbf k_0 \quad &\text{(the two right triangles; axis)} \\ \det[{}_0R_1] &= (+1)\cdot 1\cdot\left(\cos\Psi\cos\Psi - \left(-\sin\Psi\right)\sin\Psi\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(expansion along the third row, cofactor sign $(-1)^{3+3}$)} \\ \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{11} &= \cos^2\Psi + \sin^2\Psi = 1, \quad \left([{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T\right)_{12} = -\cos\Psi\sin\Psi + \sin\Psi\cos\Psi = 0 \quad &\text{(rows times rows)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{[{}_0R_1] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\Psi & -\sin\Psi & 0 \cr \sin\Psi & \cos\Psi & 0 \cr 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det[{}_0R_1] = 1, \quad [{}_0R_1][{}_0R_1]^T = I}$$

Units: $[\Psi] = [1]$; $[\Omega] = [\mathrm{T^{-1}}]$

Meaning: the orientation of $S_1$ is known at every instant because the rate is known; the rate of change of the angle is the given rate.

Figure 2. Horizontal plane through $C$ seen from above ($\mathbf k_1$ out of the paper, $\odot$). The azimuth $\theta$ is measured at $C$ from $\mathbf i_1$ towards $\mathbf j_1$: $\mathbf e_h = \cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1$ (legs of the shaded triangle) and $\mathbf u_\theta = d\mathbf e_h/d\theta$. $P$ projects to $P'$ at distance $R\cos\phi$ from $C$; the axis of rotation is at distance $R$ from $C$, on the side of $-\mathbf j_1$.
The azimuth theta: horizontal plane through C Law: right triangle of the horizontal unit vector; tangent vector as its derivative Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.20; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.5; Problems.pdf, p. 36

Seen from above ($\mathbf k_1$ out of the paper, ⊙), with $\mathbf i_1$ to the right and $\mathbf j_1$ up, the centre $C$ is at the distance $R$ from the axis of rotation, on the side of $\mathbf j_1$. The horizontal unit vector $\mathbf e_h$ at the azimuth $\theta$ is the hypotenuse of the shaded triangle: adjacent leg $\cos\theta$ along $\mathbf i_1$, opposite leg $\sin\theta$ along $\mathbf j_1$. $\mathbf u_\theta$ is $\mathbf e_h$ turned a further quarter turn counterclockwise, which carries its tip to the side of minus $\mathbf i_1$ (the minus sign).

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf e_h &= \cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(shaded triangle)} \\ \mathbf u_\theta &= \frac{d\mathbf e_h}{d\theta} = -\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{($\tfrac{d}{d\theta}\cos\theta = -\sin\theta$, $\tfrac{d}{d\theta}\sin\theta = \cos\theta$)} \\ \mathbf k_1\times\mathbf e_h &= \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1 - \sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf u_\theta, \quad \mathbf k_1\times\mathbf u_\theta = -\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 - \cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 = -\mathbf e_h \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf j_1$, $\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\mathbf i_1$)} \\ \mathbf i_1 &= \cos\theta\,\mathbf e_h - \sin\theta\,\mathbf u_\theta, \quad \mathbf j_1 = \sin\theta\,\mathbf e_h + \cos\theta\,\mathbf u_\theta \quad &\text{(projections)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf e_h = \cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1, \qquad \mathbf u_\theta = -\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1}$$

Units: $[\theta] = [1]$

Meaning: $\mathbf e_h$ points from $C$ towards the projection $P'$; $\mathbf u_\theta$ is the horizontal direction in which $P$ moves when only $\theta$ grows.

Figure 3. Vertical plane through $C$ that contains $\mathbf e_h$ ($\mathbf u_\theta$ points into the paper, $\otimes$). The elevation $\phi$ is measured at $C$ from the horizontal: in the shaded triangle the hypotenuse is $R$, the leg adjacent to $\phi$ is $R\cos\phi$ along $\mathbf e_h$ and the opposite one $R\sin\phi$ along $\mathbf k_1$. $\mathbf u_r, \mathbf u_\phi$ in orange; the reaction $\mathbf N = -N\,\mathbf u_r$ (pink) pushes towards $C$.
The elevation phi: vertical plane through C and P, position and spherical basis Law: right triangle of the radius $CP$; vector sum of positions; determinant by cofactors Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.13; Notes.pdf, Eq. 2.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Problems.pdf, p. 36

The vertical plane through $C$ that contains $\mathbf e_h$ is drawn with $\mathbf e_h$ to the right and $\mathbf k_1$ up; the cross product of $\mathbf e_h$ and $\mathbf k_1$ is minus $\mathbf u_\theta$, so $\mathbf u_\theta$ points into the paper (⊗). In the shaded right triangle the hypotenuse is $CP$, of length $R$; the leg adjacent to $\phi$ is $R\cos\phi$ along $\mathbf e_h$ (the distance $CP'$ of the horizontal view) and the opposite leg is $R\sin\phi$ along $\mathbf k_1$. $\mathbf u_\phi$ is $\mathbf u_r$ turned a quarter turn counterclockwise in this view, which carries its tip to the side of minus $\mathbf e_h$ (the minus sign). The usual spherical polar angle is measured from $\mathbf k_1$ downwards and equals a quarter turn minus $\phi$, so its sine is $\cos\phi$ and its cosine $\sin\phi$ (difference formulas). The distance that stays constant is $CP$, so the path goes from $A$ to $C$ and then to $P$. The determinant of the matrix whose columns are $\mathbf u_r$, $\mathbf u_\theta$, $\mathbf u_\phi$ is expanded along the third row, with the cofactor signs plus, minus, plus.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf u_r &= \cos\phi\,\mathbf e_h + \sin\phi\,\mathbf k_1 = \cos\phi\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \sin\phi\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(shaded triangle; $\mathbf e_h$ in $\mathcal B_1$)} \\ \mathbf u_\phi &= \frac{\partial\mathbf u_r}{\partial\phi} = -\sin\phi\,\mathbf e_h + \cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1 = -\sin\phi\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 - \sin\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(derivative in $\phi$)} \\ \frac{\partial\mathbf u_r}{\partial\theta} &= \cos\phi\,\frac{d\mathbf e_h}{d\theta} = \cos\phi\,\mathbf u_\theta \quad &\text{(derivative in $\theta$; length $\cos\phi$)} \\ \det\left[\mathbf u_r\ \mathbf u_\theta\ \mathbf u_\phi\right] &= (+1)\sin\phi\left(\sin\phi\sin^2\theta + \sin\phi\cos^2\theta\right) + (-1)\cdot 0 + (+1)\cos\phi\left(\cos\phi\cos^2\theta + \cos\phi\sin^2\theta\right) = 1 \quad &\text{(third row; cofactor signs)} \\ \mathbf u_r\cdot\mathbf u_\phi &= -\cos\phi\sin\phi + \sin\phi\cos\phi = 0, \quad \mathbf u_r\cdot\mathbf u_\theta = \mathbf u_\phi\cdot\mathbf u_\theta = 0 \quad &\text{(orthogonality)} \\ \mathbf e_h &= \cos\phi\,\mathbf u_r - \sin\phi\,\mathbf u_\phi, \quad \mathbf k_1 = \sin\phi\,\mathbf u_r + \cos\phi\,\mathbf u_\phi \quad &\text{(projections)} \\ \mathbf r_1^P &= \overrightarrow{AC} + \overrightarrow{CP} = R\left(\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf k_1\right) + R\,\mathbf u_r \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.16 with the origin $A$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf r_1^P = R\cos\phi\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + R\left(1 + \cos\phi\sin\theta\right)\mathbf j_1 + R\left(1 + \sin\phi\right)\mathbf k_1, \cr \mathbf u_r = \cos\phi\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \sin\phi\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf u_\theta = -\sin\theta\,\mathbf i_1 + \cos\theta\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \mathbf u_\phi = -\sin\phi\cos\theta\,\mathbf i_1 - \sin\phi\sin\theta\,\mathbf j_1 + \cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1 \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[R] = [\mathrm L]$; the unit vectors $[1]$

Meaning: a right-handed orthonormal basis at $P$; $\mathbf u_r$ points from $C$ to $P$, the outward normal of the sphere. The poles of the coordinates, where the cosine of $\phi$ vanishes, are the top and bottom points of the sphere.

Kinematics

Motion of S1 and derivatives of its unit vectors Law: angular velocity of a simple rotation; angular acceleration; derivative of a unit vector of a turning basis Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 1.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.3; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.4; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.5; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.9
$$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\omega_{10} &= \Omega(t)\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf v_0^A = \mathbf a_0^A = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(rotation about the fixed vertical; $A$ fixed)} \\ \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} &= \left.\frac{d\boldsymbol\omega_{10}}{dt}\right|_0 = \dot\Omega\,\mathbf k_1 + \Omega\left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \dot\Omega\,\mathbf k_1 \quad &\text{(product rule; $\mathbf k_1$ does not turn)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 &= \Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf i_1 = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf j_1 = -\Omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{(Eq. 3.3 to 3.5)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\cos\Psi\,\mathbf i_0 + \sin\Psi\,\mathbf j_0\right) &= \frac{d\Psi}{dt}\left(-\sin\Psi\,\mathbf i_0 + \cos\Psi\,\mathbf j_0\right) = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1 \quad &\text{(check: chain rule on $\mathbf i_1$)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\boldsymbol\omega_{10} = \Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \boldsymbol\alpha_{10} = \dot\Omega\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf i_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \Omega\,\mathbf j_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf j_1}{dt}\right|_0 = -\Omega\,\mathbf i_1, \quad \left.\frac{d\mathbf k_1}{dt}\right|_0 = \mathbf 0}$$

Units: $[\Omega] = [\mathrm T^{-1}]$; $[\dot\Omega] = [\mathrm T^{-2}]$

Meaning: the angular acceleration is along the fixed axis and vanishes only when the rate is constant.

(a) Position, velocity and acceleration of P in S1

Derivatives of the spherical basis and relative kinematics Law: time derivatives in $S_1$; chain rule through $\theta(t)$ and $\phi(t)$; product rule Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.16; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.19; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.24; Problems.pdf, p. 36

$\mathbf r_1^C$ and $\mathbf k_1$ are constant in $S_1$; $\mathbf e_h$ and the spherical vectors change only through the two angles.

$$\begin{aligned} \left.\frac{d\mathbf u_r}{dt}\right|_1 &= \frac{\partial\mathbf u_r}{\partial\theta}\dot\theta + \frac{\partial\mathbf u_r}{\partial\phi}\dot\phi = \dot\theta\cos\phi\,\mathbf u_\theta + \dot\phi\,\mathbf u_\phi \quad &\text{(chain rule)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf u_\theta}{dt}\right|_1 &= \frac{d\mathbf u_\theta}{d\theta}\dot\theta = -\dot\theta\,\mathbf e_h = -\dot\theta\cos\phi\,\mathbf u_r + \dot\theta\sin\phi\,\mathbf u_\phi \quad &\text{(chain rule; $\mathbf e_h$ in the spherical basis)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf u_\phi}{dt}\right|_1 &= -\dot\phi\cos\phi\,\mathbf e_h - \sin\phi\,\dot\theta\,\mathbf u_\theta - \dot\phi\sin\phi\,\mathbf k_1 = -\dot\phi\,\mathbf u_r - \dot\theta\sin\phi\,\mathbf u_\theta \quad &\text{(product and chain rules on $-\sin\phi\,\mathbf e_h + \cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1$)} \\ \mathbf v_1^P &= R\left.\frac{d\mathbf u_r}{dt}\right|_1 = R\dot\theta\cos\phi\,\mathbf u_\theta + R\dot\phi\,\mathbf u_\phi \quad &\text{($\mathbf r_1^C$ constant)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(R\dot\theta\cos\phi\,\mathbf u_\theta\right) &= R\left(\ddot\theta\cos\phi - \dot\theta\dot\phi\sin\phi\right)\mathbf u_\theta - R\dot\theta^2\cos^2\phi\,\mathbf u_r + R\dot\theta^2\sin\phi\cos\phi\,\mathbf u_\phi \quad &\text{(product rule; chain rule on $\cos\phi$)} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\left(R\dot\phi\,\mathbf u_\phi\right) &= R\ddot\phi\,\mathbf u_\phi - R\dot\phi^2\,\mathbf u_r - R\dot\phi\dot\theta\sin\phi\,\mathbf u_\theta \quad &\text{(product rule)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf r_1^P = R\left(\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf k_1\right) + R\,\mathbf u_r, \qquad \mathbf v_1^P = R\dot\theta\cos\phi\,\mathbf u_\theta + R\dot\phi\,\mathbf u_\phi, \cr \mathbf a_1^P = -R\left(\dot\phi^2 + \dot\theta^2\cos^2\phi\right)\mathbf u_r + R\left(\ddot\theta\cos\phi - 2\dot\theta\dot\phi\sin\phi\right)\mathbf u_\theta + R\left(\ddot\phi + \dot\theta^2\sin\phi\cos\phi\right)\mathbf u_\phi \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[R\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}]$; $[R\dot\phi^2] = [R\ddot\theta] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the relative velocity is tangent to the sphere; the radial part of the relative acceleration points to the centre $C$.

Absolute acceleration: Euler, transport and Coriolis terms as they arise Law: time derivative in $S_0$ of the position written in the turning basis; product rule with a variable rate Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.17; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.21; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.22; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.23; Notes.pdf, Eq. 3.27; [Lecture 5, Slide 24]; [Lecture 5, Slide 25]

Write the position as $x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + z_1\,\mathbf k_1$, with the components of the position box; their time derivatives are the components of the relative velocity.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf v_0^P &= \dot x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + \dot y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + \dot z_1\,\mathbf k_1 + x_1\Omega\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\Omega\,\mathbf i_1 = \mathbf v_1^P + \Omega\left(x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; derivatives of $\mathbf i_1$, $\mathbf j_1$)} \\ \left.\frac{d\mathbf v_1^P}{dt}\right|_0 &= \mathbf a_1^P + \Omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; the basis turns inside $\mathbf v_1^P$)} \\ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\left[\Omega\left(x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right)\right] &= \dot\Omega\left(x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) + \Omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) - \Omega^2\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) \quad &\text{(product rule; the rate changes)} \\ \boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P &= \dot\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1 + z_1\,\mathbf k_1\right) = \dot\Omega\left(x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(the new term: Euler)} \\ \mathbf a_0^P &= \mathbf a_1^P + \dot\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf r_1^P - \Omega^2\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right) + 2\Omega\left(\dot x_1\,\mathbf j_1 - \dot y_1\,\mathbf i_1\right) \quad &\text{(Euler; centripetal; Coriolis, the two equal terms)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf a_0^P = \mathbf a_1^P + \boldsymbol\alpha_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P + \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) + 2\,\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf v_1^P, \qquad \boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\left(\boldsymbol\omega_{10}\times\mathbf r_1^P\right) = -\Omega^2\left(x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1\right)}$$

Units: $[\dot\Omega R] = [\Omega^2R] = [\Omega R\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: a changing rate adds the Euler term, horizontal and normal to the horizontal part of the position; the origin $A$ is fixed, so there is no origin term.

Forces and Equations of Motion

Figure 4. Forces seen from $S_1$. Top: at the admissible equilibrium ($\theta = \pi/2$, $\phi_1 = -30.3^\circ$ for $\Omega = 3$ rad/s, $R = 1$ m) the weight, the reaction $-N\,\mathbf u_r$ towards $C$ and the centrifugal force (dashed), away from the axis. Bottom: seen from above, the Euler force (dashed, only while the rate changes), the Coriolis force (dashed, normal to the relative velocity) and the centrifugal force.

(b) Forces on P seen from S1

Actual and inertia forces in the spherical basis Law: weight; one-sided smooth reaction towards the centre; inertia forces of a non-inertial frame Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.62; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.11; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]; [Lecture 5, Slide 30]; [Lecture 5, Slide 31]

Only the horizontal part of the position, $x_1\,\mathbf i_1 + y_1\,\mathbf j_1$, enters the products with $\mathbf k_1$; call it $\mathbf r_\perp$. It is written in $\{\mathbf e_h, \mathbf u_\theta\}$ with the projections of the azimuth box, and then $\mathbf e_h$ in the spherical basis.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf r_\perp &= R\cos\phi\cos\theta\left(\cos\theta\,\mathbf e_h - \sin\theta\,\mathbf u_\theta\right) + R\left(1 + \cos\phi\sin\theta\right)\left(\sin\theta\,\mathbf e_h + \cos\theta\,\mathbf u_\theta\right) = R\left(\cos\phi + \sin\theta\right)\mathbf e_h + R\cos\theta\,\mathbf u_\theta \quad &\text{(components collected)} \\ \mathbf W &= -mg\,\mathbf k_1 = -mg\sin\phi\,\mathbf u_r - mg\cos\phi\,\mathbf u_\phi, \quad \mathbf N = -N\,\mathbf u_r \quad &\text{(weight; reaction towards $C$)} \\ \mathbf F_A &= -m\,\mathbf a_0^A = \mathbf 0 \quad &\text{($A$ fixed)} \\ \mathbf F_E &= -m\dot\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf r_\perp = -m\dot\Omega R\left[\left(\cos\phi + \sin\theta\right)\mathbf u_\theta - \cos\theta\,\mathbf e_h\right] \quad &\text{($\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf e_h = \mathbf u_\theta$, $\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf u_\theta = -\mathbf e_h$)} \\ &= m\dot\Omega R\left[\cos\theta\cos\phi\,\mathbf u_r - \left(\cos\phi + \sin\theta\right)\mathbf u_\theta - \cos\theta\sin\phi\,\mathbf u_\phi\right] \quad &\text{($\mathbf e_h$ in the spherical basis)} \\ \mathbf F_C &= m\Omega^2\,\mathbf r_\perp = m\Omega^2R\left[\left(\cos\phi + \sin\theta\right)\cos\phi\,\mathbf u_r + \cos\theta\,\mathbf u_\theta - \left(\cos\phi + \sin\theta\right)\sin\phi\,\mathbf u_\phi\right] \quad &\text{(centripetal term times $-m$)} \\ \mathbf k_1\times\mathbf u_\phi &= -\sin\phi\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf e_h + \cos\phi\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf k_1 = -\sin\phi\,\mathbf u_\theta \quad &\text{($\mathbf u_\phi$ through $\mathbf e_h$ and $\mathbf k_1$)} \\ \mathbf F_{COR} &= -2m\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\left(R\dot\theta\cos\phi\,\mathbf u_\theta + R\dot\phi\,\mathbf u_\phi\right) = 2m\Omega R\left(\dot\theta\cos\phi\,\mathbf e_h + \dot\phi\sin\phi\,\mathbf u_\theta\right) \quad &\text{(Coriolis term times $-m$)} \\ &= 2m\Omega R\left[\dot\theta\cos^2\phi\,\mathbf u_r + \dot\phi\sin\phi\,\mathbf u_\theta - \dot\theta\sin\phi\cos\phi\,\mathbf u_\phi\right] \quad &\text{($\mathbf e_h$ in the spherical basis)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \mathbf W = -mg\,\mathbf k_1, \quad \mathbf N = -N\,\mathbf u_r, \quad \mathbf F_A = \mathbf 0, \quad \mathbf F_E = -m\dot\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf r_1^P, \quad \mathbf F_C = m\Omega^2\,\mathbf r_\perp, \quad \mathbf F_{COR} = -2m\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf v_1^P \cr \text{with the spherical components written above} \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[mg] = [m\dot\Omega R] = [m\Omega^2R] = [m\Omega R\dot\theta] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: two actual forces and three inertia forces. The centrifugal force pushes $P$ horizontally away from the axis; the Euler force acts only while the rate changes, horizontally and against the sense of the angular acceleration; the Coriolis force is normal to the relative velocity.

(c) Two differential equations for theta and phi

Projections on the two tangent vectors Law: Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame projected on $\mathbf u_\theta$ and $\mathbf u_\phi$, which are normal to the reaction Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; [Lecture 3, Slide 14]; [Lecture 5, Slide 28]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf u_\theta:\quad mR\left(\ddot\theta\cos\phi - 2\dot\theta\dot\phi\sin\phi\right) &= m\Omega^2R\cos\theta - m\dot\Omega R\left(\cos\phi + \sin\theta\right) + 2m\Omega R\dot\phi\sin\phi \quad &\text{(centrifugal, Euler, Coriolis; no weight, no reaction)} \\ \mathbf u_\phi:\quad mR\left(\ddot\phi + \dot\theta^2\sin\phi\cos\phi\right) &= -mg\cos\phi - m\Omega^2R\left(\cos\phi + \sin\theta\right)\sin\phi - m\dot\Omega R\cos\theta\sin\phi - 2m\Omega R\dot\theta\sin\phi\cos\phi \quad &\text{(weight, centrifugal, Euler, Coriolis)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\begin{gathered} \ddot\theta\cos\phi - 2\dot\phi\sin\phi\left(\dot\theta + \Omega\right) = \Omega^2\cos\theta - \dot\Omega\left(\cos\phi + \sin\theta\right) \cr \ddot\phi + \dot\theta\left(\dot\theta + 2\Omega\right)\sin\phi\cos\phi + \frac{g}{R}\cos\phi + \Omega^2\sin\phi\left(\cos\phi + \sin\theta\right) + \dot\Omega\cos\theta\sin\phi = 0 \end{gathered}}$$

Units: $[\ddot\theta] = [\Omega^2] = [\dot\Omega] = [\Omega\dot\phi] = [g/R] = [\mathrm T^{-2}]$

Meaning: two coupled non-linear equations, forced through the known functions $\Omega(t)$ and its derivative; with initial conditions they give the two angles. Each was divided by $mR$, and the Coriolis terms were grouped with the relative ones.

(d) Reaction and separation condition

Projection on the normal Law: Newton's second law in $S_1$ projected on $\mathbf u_r$, the only projection that contains $N$; one-sided contact Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; Notes.pdf, Eq. 6.11; [Lecture 3, Slide 14]; [Lecture 3, Slide 21]
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf u_r:\quad -mR\left(\dot\phi^2 + \dot\theta^2\cos^2\phi\right) &= -N - mg\sin\phi + m\Omega^2R\cos\phi\left(\cos\phi + \sin\theta\right) + m\dot\Omega R\cos\theta\cos\phi + 2m\Omega R\dot\theta\cos^2\phi \quad &\text{(radial components of part (b))} \\ N &= mR\dot\phi^2 + mR\cos^2\phi\left(\dot\theta^2 + 2\Omega\dot\theta + \Omega^2\right) + m\Omega^2R\cos\phi\sin\theta + m\dot\Omega R\cos\phi\cos\theta - mg\sin\phi \quad &\text{(solved for $N$; the $\cos^2\phi$ terms grouped)} \\ \dot\theta^2 + 2\Omega\dot\theta + \Omega^2 &= \left(\dot\theta + \Omega\right)^2 \quad &\text{(perfect square)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{N = mR\dot\phi^2 + mR\cos^2\phi\left(\dot\theta + \Omega\right)^2 + m\Omega^2R\cos\phi\sin\theta + m\dot\Omega R\cos\phi\cos\theta - mg\sin\phi; \qquad \text{separation when } N = 0 \text{ and it would become negative}}$$

Units: every term $[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: the reaction depends only on the two angles, their rates and the known data. The inner surface can only push towards $C$, so the solution of part (c) holds while $N$ stays non-negative; the particle leaves the surface at the first instant at which $N$ reaches zero with a negative rate of change.

Answers and Checks

(e) Equilibria for a constant rate

Relative equilibria: theta first Law: constant coordinates and constant rate, so the rates, accelerations, Euler and Coriolis terms vanish in the equations of part (c) Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.32; Notes.pdf, Sec. 4.6; Problems.pdf, p. 36

Take a non-zero rate (the case of zero rate is in the limiting cases) and write $\lambda$ for the ratio of $\Omega^2R$ to $g$. At the poles of the coordinates (top and bottom of the sphere) the tangent plane is horizontal and the centrifugal force there, $m\Omega^2R\,\mathbf j_1$, is horizontal and not zero, so no pole is an equilibrium; away from the poles the cosine of $\phi$ is positive.

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf u_\theta:\quad 0 &= \Omega^2\cos\theta \;\Rightarrow\; \theta = \frac{\pi}{2} \ \text{ or } \ \theta = -\frac{\pi}{2} \quad &\text{($\Omega \ne 0$)} \\ \mathbf u_\phi:\quad 0 &= \frac{g}{R}\cos\phi + \Omega^2\sin\phi\left(\cos\phi + \sin\theta\right) \quad &\text{(rates and $\dot\Omega$ zero)} \\ \theta = \frac{\pi}{2}:\quad 0 &= 1 + \lambda\,\frac{\sin\phi\left(\cos\phi + 1\right)}{\cos\phi} = 1 + \lambda\left(\tan\phi + \sin\phi\right) \quad &\text{(divided by $g\cos\phi/R$)} \\ \theta = -\frac{\pi}{2}:\quad 0 &= 1 + \lambda\,\frac{\sin\phi\left(\cos\phi - 1\right)}{\cos\phi} = 1 - \lambda\left(\tan\phi - \sin\phi\right) \quad &\text{(divided by $g\cos\phi/R$)} \\ f(\phi) &= \tan\phi + \sin\phi, \quad f'(\phi) = \frac{1}{\cos^2\phi} + \cos\phi \gt 0 \quad &\text{(on $(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2})$: increasing, from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$, zero at $0$)} \\ h(\phi) &= \tan\phi - \sin\phi, \quad h'(\phi) = \frac{1}{\cos^2\phi} - \cos\phi \ge 0 \quad &\text{(zero only at $\phi = 0$; $h(0) = 0$, $h \to +\infty$ at the top)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\theta_1 = \frac{\pi}{2}: \ \tan\phi_1 + \sin\phi_1 = -\frac{g}{\Omega^2R}, \ \phi_1 \in \left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right); \qquad \theta_2 = -\frac{\pi}{2}: \ \tan\phi_2 - \sin\phi_2 = \frac{g}{\Omega^2R}, \ \phi_2 \in \left(0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)}$$

Units: $[g/(\Omega^2R)] = [1]$

Meaning: exactly one root on each branch, both in the vertical plane through the axis and $C$; the first lies below the horizontal plane of $C$ on the side away from the axis, the second above it on the side of the axis.

Reaction at the equilibria and admissibility Law: the reaction of part (d) at rest, with the equilibrium relation substituted; vertical balance Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63; [Lecture 3, Slide 21]

At both roots the sine of $\phi$ is not zero, so the $\mathbf u_\phi$ condition gives the product of $\Omega^2R$ and the sum of $\cos\phi$ and $\sin\theta$ as minus $g\cos\phi/\sin\phi$.

$$\begin{aligned} N &= m\Omega^2R\cos\phi\left(\cos\phi + \sin\theta\right) - mg\sin\phi \quad &\text{(part (d) at rest, $\dot\Omega$ zero)} \\ &= -\frac{mg\cos^2\phi}{\sin\phi} - mg\sin\phi = -\frac{mg\left(\cos^2\phi + \sin^2\phi\right)}{\sin\phi} = -\frac{mg}{\sin\phi} \quad &\text{(equilibrium relation substituted)} \\ \mathbf k_1\cdot\left(\mathbf W - N\,\mathbf u_r\right) &= -mg - N\sin\phi = 0 \quad &\text{(check: the centrifugal force is horizontal, so the vertical balance gives the same)} \\ \Omega = 3\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}},\ R = 1\ \mathrm m:\quad \tan\phi_1 + \sin\phi_1 &= -0.5850 - 0.5050 = -1.0900 = -\frac{9.81}{9}, \quad \phi_1 = -30.33^\circ, \quad N_1 = \frac{mg}{0.5050} = 1.98\,mg \quad &\text{(numerical example)} \\ \tan\phi_2 - \sin\phi_2 &= 1.9829 - 0.8929 = 1.0900, \quad \phi_2 = 63.24^\circ, \quad N_2 = -\frac{mg}{0.8929} = -1.12\,mg \quad &\text{(numerical example)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{N = -\frac{mg}{\sin\phi}: \quad \text{branch 1 } (\phi_1 \lt 0): \ N_1 \gt 0, \ \text{admissible}; \qquad \text{branch 2 } (\phi_2 \gt 0): \ N_2 \lt 0, \ \text{not admissible}}$$

Units: $[mg] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: on branch 1 the particle sits in the lower half, on the side away from the axis, where the inward normal points up and towards the axis and balances the weight and the centrifugal force. On branch 2 the surface would have to pull the particle away from $C$, which the inner face cannot do; it would be an equilibrium only for a contact that holds on both sides.

Part of the statementAnswer
(a) Kinematics in $S_1$$\mathbf r_1^P = R(\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf k_1) + R\,\mathbf u_r$, $\mathbf v_1^P = R\dot\theta\cos\phi\,\mathbf u_\theta + R\dot\phi\,\mathbf u_\phi$, $\mathbf a_1^P = -R(\dot\phi^2 + \dot\theta^2\cos^2\phi)\,\mathbf u_r + R(\ddot\theta\cos\phi - 2\dot\theta\dot\phi\sin\phi)\,\mathbf u_\theta + R(\ddot\phi + \dot\theta^2\sin\phi\cos\phi)\,\mathbf u_\phi$; unit vectors as boxed
(b) Forces in $S_1$$-mg\,\mathbf k_1$; $-N\,\mathbf u_r$; origin force zero; Euler $-m\dot\Omega\,\mathbf k_1\times\mathbf r_1^P$; centrifugal $m\Omega^2\mathbf r_\perp$ with $\mathbf r_\perp = R(\cos\phi + \sin\theta)\,\mathbf e_h + R\cos\theta\,\mathbf u_\theta$; Coriolis $2m\Omega R(\dot\theta\cos\phi\,\mathbf e_h + \dot\phi\sin\phi\,\mathbf u_\theta)$
(c) Equations$\ddot\theta\cos\phi - 2\dot\phi\sin\phi(\dot\theta + \Omega) = \Omega^2\cos\theta - \dot\Omega(\cos\phi + \sin\theta)$; $\ddot\phi + \dot\theta(\dot\theta + 2\Omega)\sin\phi\cos\phi + (g/R)\cos\phi + \Omega^2\sin\phi(\cos\phi + \sin\theta) + \dot\Omega\cos\theta\sin\phi = 0$
(d) Reaction and separation$N = mR\dot\phi^2 + mR\cos^2\phi(\dot\theta + \Omega)^2 + m\Omega^2R\cos\phi\sin\theta + m\dot\Omega R\cos\phi\cos\theta - mg\sin\phi$; separation when $N$ reaches zero and would become negative
(c), (d) with the colatitude $\phi_c = \pi/2 - \phi$$\ddot\theta\sin\phi_c + 2\dot\phi_c\cos\phi_c(\dot\theta + \Omega) = \Omega^2\cos\theta - \dot\Omega(\sin\phi_c + \sin\theta)$; $-\ddot\phi_c + \dot\theta(\dot\theta + 2\Omega)\sin\phi_c\cos\phi_c + (g/R)\sin\phi_c + \Omega^2\cos\phi_c(\sin\phi_c + \sin\theta) + \dot\Omega\cos\theta\cos\phi_c = 0$; $N = mR\dot\phi_c^2 + mR\sin^2\phi_c(\dot\theta + \Omega)^2 + m\Omega^2R\sin\phi_c\sin\theta + m\dot\Omega R\sin\phi_c\cos\theta - mg\cos\phi_c$
(e) Equilibria, constant $\Omega$$\theta = \pi/2$ with $\tan\phi_1 + \sin\phi_1 = -g/(\Omega^2R)$, $\phi_1 \in (-\pi/2, 0)$, $N = mg/\lvert\sin\phi_1\rvert \gt 0$: the only admissible equilibrium; $\theta = -\pi/2$ with $\tan\phi_2 - \sin\phi_2 = g/(\Omega^2R)$, $\phi_2 \in (0, \pi/2)$, $N = -mg/\sin\phi_2 \lt 0$: not admissible for the one-sided contact (admissible for a two-sided one); with zero rate: the bottom point, $N = mg$

Check against the official key: Problems.pdf, p. 76 prints no answer for problem 51. Independent checks: the reaction at the equilibria agrees with the vertical balance (box above), and the limiting cases follow.

Limiting cases Law: the results at extreme values of the data; first-order Taylor expansion Source: Notes.pdf, Eq. 4.63
$$\begin{aligned} \Omega = 0:\quad \ddot\theta\cos\phi - 2\dot\theta\dot\phi\sin\phi &= 0, \quad \ddot\phi + \dot\theta^2\sin\phi\cos\phi + \frac{g}{R}\cos\phi = 0 \quad &\text{(spherical pendulum in a fixed sphere)} \\ \Omega = 0,\ \text{rest}:\quad \cos\phi &= 0, \quad \phi = -\frac{\pi}{2}: \ N = -mg\sin\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = mg \quad &\text{(bottom point; the top would need $N = -mg$)} \\ \lambda \gg 1:\quad \tan\phi + \sin\phi &\approx \phi + \phi = 2\phi \;\Rightarrow\; \phi_1 \approx -\frac{g}{2\Omega^2R}, \quad N_1 \approx \frac{mg}{\left|\phi_1\right|} = 2m\Omega^2R \quad &\text{(first-order Taylor expansion about zero)} \\ \lambda \to 0:\quad \tan\phi_1 + \sin\phi_1 &\to -\infty \;\Rightarrow\; \phi_1 \to -\frac{\pi}{2}, \quad N_1 \to mg \quad &\text{(slow rotation: back to the bottom)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\boxed{\Omega \to 0: \ \phi_1 \to -\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \ N_1 \to mg; \qquad \Omega \to \infty: \ \phi_1 \to 0^-, \ N_1 \approx 2m\Omega^2R}$$

Units: $[m\Omega^2R] = [mg] = [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}]$

Meaning: as the rate grows the particle climbs towards the horizontal plane of $C$, at the distance $2R$ from the axis, and the reaction becomes the centripetal force of a circle of radius $2R$. The statement does not ask for stability, which is not discussed here.
